Chapter Text
Part 1 | The Arrival

She was running.

The air was thick with smoke that caught in her lungs, pressing heavy against the pain in her legs. The sky cracked open, and the rain came sideways, cold enough to sting against the rips in her sleeves. But the downpour couldn't drown out the mechanical shriek closing in behind her— a grinding, rhythmic churn that rose and fell with each pounding step.

Somewhere to her left, a laser split the gray sky and scorched the ground a foot from her heel.

Everything was burning.

The rain did little to slow it. Lasers whizzed closer; she couldn’t run anymore. She braced herself for the pain that would surely follow from the horrid machines.

In her last fleeting moments, she wished for one more day, even just one more moment, to be with him as they were. One more moment to scent the pine in his hair, anything to erase the smell of burning carnage all around. Just one more touch before the world ended—

She awoke. Sunbeams and glittering dust replaced the choking smoke and squeezing pain upon her limbs. She scrubbed her face, wiping away that too vivid nightmare upon her dewy skin. It was the same startling abruptness pulling her out of the repeated nightmare for the third time this week. Increasingly more frequently since they started months ago.

She had to stop watching animal documentaries before bed; it was starting to blur and twist reality into the abomination she dreamt up.

She slipped out of her navy cotton sheets, feeling the tight pull against her gray shorts and white T-shirt. Her feet hit the floor with a surge against the cool tile; it was abnormally colder for an August morning, yet she had woken up in a sweat.

A few languid strides carried her through her entire apartment: bedroom, bathroom, kitchen. The space was small, but it was hers.

Everything had its place, a welcome order after the upheaval of her last breakup. By the time the coffee began to brew, its rich scent had filled the living room and crept back to her bedroom door, a comforting start to the day. The only clutter was the stacks of books, ancient empires and fae courts, piled by the sofa, a testament to the worlds she’d rather live in.

She opened her stained-glass door, decorated in blooming flowers and bows, to enjoy her morning coffee on the deck as she did every nice summer day. She felt the warmth of the sun’s rays on her bare legs, and heard Marin stir at the top of the steps.

Her apartment was designed as an on-suite from the main house where her landlord, Marin, lived. Landlord was probably too proper a term for what Marin was to her. An old family friend that nice enough to offer the on-suite after building it for her own son, who moved out years prior.

Marin waved from atop the second-story deck, “Good morning, dear!” Her face was wrinkled with years of cherished warmth, her amber eyes captivating and pulling in for more.

Sunlight caught the stubborn red tints fighting the gray in Marin’s hair. She was too nice, too eccentric— a woman born in the wrong decade. That friendliness, however, was a double-edged sword. She loved Marin, had known her most of her life, but the woman’s loneliness in her big house often translated into a complete disregard for boundaries, like the uninvited entries into her apartment.

She smiled, cupping her mug to warm her fingers. “Good morning, Marin, it’s chilly today. Why is that?” She braced herself for the inevitable folklore that would follow.

“It is honey, this happens when a debt needs to be settled in nature. The goddess has a balance that needs adjusting.” Her voice wise and kind as she spoke of the old witch folklore. Marin lowered her chin, knowing and pushing that worship of the Mother into her, “The goddess will always balance itself, no matter the cost or the price.”

She bristled, coincidentally, as a colder breeze flittered by.

Marin shifted her tone, “You have your friend’s engagement party today? The goddess will warm the earth by this afternoon; she is blessing them with a beautiful day.”

She rolled her eyes, “I’m sure that’s exactly what the goddess has intended.” Sarcasm practically dripped from her tongue. Marin laughed, waved her away, and went back to watering her jungle of potted exotic plants above her.

She sauntered over to the knitted porch swing and slipped her headphones on, lifted her legs, and hugged her knees, her eyes drifting across the property while the music filled in the space.

A sad, calming melody filled her ears. She watched two squirrels spiral up an oak tree as a lyric about loss snagged on a memory she kept trying to bury. Her throat tightened, but she focused on the chase, letting the music hold the feeling for her.

She let out a long breath, shaking the memory away. Her gaze fell on the familiar shapes of the bushes of drooping flowers and the leaves starting to yellow in the dense covering of the woods. The steady, quiet life of it all settled something inside her. She was thankful to live here, this refuge.

After losing herself in nature for the better part of an hour, it was time to shower. She flicked the light on in her bathroom, staring in the mirror as she tried to rub the shadows away, deep green and specks of gold staring back— her mother’s eyes, and she pulled away unable to further that thought. Water hit the tiles, steam lifting to the fan, as she stepped in, and the scent of lavender soap filled her nostrils.

She savored the daily cleansing, the one place where nightmares of death and fire could melt from her imagination and swirl down the drain with the warm water’s embrace.

Toweling herself off, she combed through her long, wet hair, annoyed by a particularly stubborn knot near her neck. She brushed through it painfully, preparing to style her hair in an effortless look, despite it being anything but effortless, when her gaze snagged on the creamy compostable invitation with mint sprigs.

Linda and Anton were inevitable since grade school. She smiled, picturing them running through the woods, Linda teasing a shy Anton. It had taken him years to finally ask her out, but once he did, that was it. Honestly, the only surprise was that he’d waited so long after secondary school to propose.

She thought about her romances, a word so plural it felt like a joke. One serious attempt had ended with her hauling boxes into this very apartment. Linda could have her soulmate; she’d rather not have the drama. What was the point, anyway?

She started to apply beige eyeshadow, a neutral color meant to be unnoticed, but the mindless blending pulled her thoughts to the place she kept buried in that cave within herself. To her parents.

In the photographs she kept buried in her mind, their hair was untouched by time, branded in her memories forever young. Her heart squeezed; they were meant to be.

She pressed her lips together and shook her head, turning back to methodically blending the eyeshadow. But the vivid images were too much, the architect set for her of a perfect match. Blinking back watery eyes, she smudged all the fine work she had made on applying her eyeshadow, “Great.“ She whispered to no one.

Finally happy with her hair and makeup, the invitation requested a black-and-white dress code. She rolled her eyes. Wearing black in the middle of the summer’s hottest month sounded so delightful.

But she had the perfect white dress, a strapless high-low number she’d bought in the spring for just such an occasion. The bodice fit perfectly, shaping her curves before the skirt flowed to her ankles in the back while stopping just above her knees in front. A timeless classic she was glad she had purchased.

Critiquing her final appearance in her floor-length mirror, she had her blonde hair effortlessly blown out with large waves cascading down her back. Blended eyeshadow— correctly applied the second time around— mascara to lift her lashes, and clear lip gloss to enhance the natural pink in her lips. Her tan from the summer sun helped pop the white in the dress even more.

She tied her beige sandals around her ankles and swapped out one of the studs in her three lobe piercings for a tight hoop that went with the diamonds and gold studs. For the final touch, she zeroed in on the faded, well-worn jean jacket on her rocking chair.

And not a moment later, Marin’s knock on her main door startled her. “Come in.”

Marin opened the door quickly, as if she had been waiting an eternity for an invitation. She turned to face her and froze. “Oh honey, you look like the goddess.” Her eyes were shining as sincerely as can be. High praise from someone who self-proclaims to be a goddess worshiper.

“Thank you, Marin.” She fussed with the small gold band adorned with a dainty triangle on her right ring finger, one piece of jewelry she always wore. “It’s not too much?”

“You're perfect. If you looked any better, I’d be sure it was your wedding we’d be attending.”

The smile that came was anything but forced.

“What time does the party start?” Marin asked while turning her back to check on the health of her indoor plants.

“It starts at three. I’m going to head over now. Linda asked if I could help her set up.”

As if remembering a vital task, Marin spotted the watering can under the hallway table. She picked it up and began tending to a nearby plant. “It’s at that lovely winery near the city, right?”

She nodded before realizing Marin wasn’t actually facing her. “Yes.”

”It’s so beautiful there. What a perfect day you’ll have.” Her eyes focused on the next plant she deemed necessary to be saved from her neglect. “Don’t worry, dear. I’ll be here when you get back. Enjoy.”

”Thank you, Marin. I shouldn’t be back too late.” She turned, glanced back at her colorful apartment and Marin still inside, and left out the stained-glass door.

A gentle breeze cut through the hot sun as she walked toward the winery’s castle-like façade. Inside, the main tasting room was enormous and buzzing with guests. She spotted the patio through two large doorways, a sea of white tables and mint-colored glass glittering in the afternoon light.

It was stunning.

Linda’s voice cut across the patio. “Hey, babe!”

Before she could even register the loud exclamation, Linda was making her way through the beautifully decorated tables, taking the most direct path to her. Her dark hair was elegantly styled, pieces tied back in a low top knot and the rest cascading down her shoulders as she wore a thin silk mint-colored dress.

She smiled and wrapped her friend in a long hug, smiling into her friend’s shoulder. “You look incredible.”

“I know, right?” Linda laughed, pulling apart from the embrace. “I had to get these extensions redone, but I think it was worth it.” She ran her fingers through the half-artificial hair.

“Definitely worth it,” she confirmed with a smirk. Linda’s confidence always amplified her beauty, the raven-black hair, the warm coffee eyes, the carefree energy that had captivated Anton his whole life. “Shouldn’t you be somewhere drinking champagne, not setting up your party?”

“I am.” She smiled and pointed to the far table with an open bottle and a full champagne flute. She grabbed her hand to drag her over to the table she just referred to.

“So, where is the luckiest man alive?” She raised one brow.

“Oh, he’s over there. His family is being unbearable.” She picked up the half-empty bottle and started to pour a glass for her, before tilting her head towards the grassy area below the balcony patio. “They were driving me nuts.” She drained the glass in one large gulp. “They are so particular with their questions. Where we’re going to live, if he’s going to finish uni, when we’re having kids… on and on.”

“Oh yeah, just those small things.” She rolled her eyes.

“I know, but we have years to figure that out.” Linda poured more of the bubbly drink into her empty glass. “You know how they are. They are always so serious. Our parents had to bring them back down to reality.”

She swallowed a large gulp, the bubbles burning down her throat as she inhaled sharply. Linda noticed and grabbed her hand. “Hey. I’m sorry. I know it’s hard hearing about all the parents together.” The unspoken history hung between them, the shared holidays, the barbecues where they’d first met as toddlers.

“It’s okay.” She shook her head. “So what do you need help setting up?” Squeezing her friend’s hands back in reassurance.

“Oh, nothing.” She narrowed her red lips at her, “I just wanted someone to complain to while drinking.”

They laughed, and somehow the glasses emptied just as quickly as they were filled.

The champagne bubbles had worked their magic. Laughter came easily as she chatted with friends at her table, the remnants of an incredible dinner before them. As the sun set, a welcome chill brushed against her flushed cheeks, and she gratefully draped her jacket over her shoulders.

She leaned back, watching the horizon soften into twilight. A long breath of wild summer air seemed to loosen a knot in her chest she hadn't realized was there. For a moment, the weight of the past few years lifted, and she fixed her gaze on Linda, determined to hold onto the feeling with her friend’s easygoing exuberance.

But, Linda must have been trying to get her attention for a while now because the scowl on her face deepened, and her eyes widened. As if telepathically trying to tell her something, her chin tilted slightly to the left of her shoulder. As she turned to follow Linda’s gaze, she finally realized what Linda was trying to tell her and her mood dissolved.

Cole. He stood taller than she remembered, that handsome smirk fixed on his face as he talked to a stranger. As he turned, his hazel eyes, the ones that had once made her swoon, caught hers, and she saw the same dark twinkle in their depths.

Glancing back at Linda, who looked absolutely murderous, staring at him from her designated high table, she knew why.

They dated for almost a year while attending university.  He came across as charming and kind when she was at a low point in her life. Almost, as if he was lying in wait, ready to pounce when she was at her weakest. Linda had hated him from the start.

The stranger he was talking to entered her line of sight, which allowed her to visibly see why Linda was looking deadly. A cute girl, about her age, perhaps no more than 20, was standing next to him, arm in arm. In a black dress that almost concealed a large, swollen belly. It would have, if not for the angle she was currently slack-jawed staring at her from.

Cole caught her line of sight and smirked. His smile hadn’t changed, charming, sharp, and empty. He started to make his way over to her with the girl still linked to his arm. She stood up; she wasn’t going to take this sitting down. She braced against the table, as her head was full of bubbles. Hoping this sudden wave of unsteadiness was from the champagne she was drinking all night, not the fact she hadn’t seen him in six months, and he was heading straight towards her like a shark about to breach its meal. Just as he reached her table, Linda appeared at her side, a protective hand on her arm.

“Hi, Cole,” she said, her voice tight.

“Hey, long time.” He said smoothly as his eyes raked over her body, like he knew every inch from memory. The girl with him didn’t notice before he turned his attention to Linda, “Congratulations. About time for you and Anton, huh?”

“Not long enough,” Linda said. “We didn’t think you would make it since you couldn’t bother to respond to the invite.” Her knuckles were white where she gripped her champagne flute, her whole body tensed as if fighting against an invisible urge.

“I told Anton we’d probably make it, but weren’t sure how she’d be feeling.” Gesturing to the girl on his arm and her very large belly. She smiled faintly. “This is Beth, my fiancée.”

Before she could retort, Linda did first. “You move fast.”

She tried her best to be neutral to Beth. It wasn’t her fault Cole was an asshole disguised with the face of a charming man. “Congratulations. How far along are you?”

It was obvious that the girl was fairly far along. Her belly was round on her petite frame. “About 34 weeks,” she said, her voice small.

Seven and a half months. A cold knot formed in her stomach. They had only been broken up for nine. It didn’t surprise her that he’d moved on so quickly, but the timeline was a slap in the face.

Linda looked inquisitive. “What about this proposal? That’s big of you, Cole. I mean, big for you.” She smiled venomously at the most likely intentional slip of the tongue. Cole noticed. Before he could respond, a small voice did.

“Well, we’ve been together for about a year and a half. So not that surprising.” Beth beamed at him. A slow, careful smile forming.

They had only broken up less than a year ago. Her breath hitched. It wasn’t the memory of their breakup that hurt, that had been a relief. It was the casual cruelty of his lie. The champagne turned to acid in her stomach, and for a second, she couldn’t hear anything over the sudden, roaring rush in her ears.

Linda spoke first. “Really, how interesting? 18 months ago, Cole, weren’t you otherwise… entangled at that time?” Cole received a look that could have flattened a building.

He met Linda’s jab with a slow blink, his expression unchanged. “Well, ladies, we don’t want to monopolize the bride-to-be’s time. Glad we could catch up.” He placed a hand on the small of Beth’s back, guiding her away as if they’d just been discussing the weather.

Linda was glaring daggers at the back of his head. “He’s a grade A-Asshole,” she said, her tone immediately softening. “You’re way better off cutting him out of your life. Poor Beth, though. I almost feel sorry for her.”

“It’s okay. I’m fine, really.” The wine she’d been enjoying churned in her stomach. “I’m going to get some air.”

“Let me come with you,” Linda said, gently holding the back of her arms as if to steady herself.

“No, really, I could use the solitude. Plus, Anton is looking like a lost puppy over there.” She pointed to the poor man looking for his lost love. “I’ll catch up with you later.”

Linda huffed. “Yes, what will he do without me?” Smiling and gripping her wrist almost painfully, “I’ll come check on you in a bit.”

She turned the corner on the balcony, and the cool air hit her, thick with the smell of sour grapes and damp earth. Tears burned at the back of her eyes, hot with humiliation. She remembered the person she’d become with him, a light that had dimmed. Small and forgotten.

She pressed her palms against the cool, rough stone of the balcony wall, anchoring herself. The sting of the stone was real, solid.

Screw him.

He didn’t get to make her feel small anymore. Her jaw ached from clenching it, but as she pushed off the wall, the tension shifted into resolve. He would not ruin this night. Blinking back the moisture, she stiffened her shoulders and walked back to the party.

The rest of the night passed quickly, filled with happy toasts to the beautiful couple, laughing at jokes with inappropriate undertones, and recalling fond memories of the two. As the room started to empty, she made her way over to Linda to say goodbye. She pulled her friend into a long, warm embrace. “I’m so happy for you. You both deserve the world.” 

“Thanks, but don’t get sappy on me.” Linda’s tone was tough, but she saw tears welling in her eyes. “I love you. Call me when you get home?”

“Of course.” She smiled brightly at her best friend. Releasing the embrace made her feel that familiar emptiness as she headed towards the dark parking lot.

Driving through the quiet backcountry roads, windows down, the cool wind blowing her hair, darkness pressed in the deeper she drove into the tangled woods. Images from the party flashed in her mind— how each and every time she looked to Anton, his eyes were on Linda, near or far, that gaze transcended the space. Images of parents, grandparents, uncles and aunts, laughing, reminiscing of catching the two to-be-wed’s in a compromising position, or arguing about where the couple would spend holidays.

She tried to keep her mind on the double yellow line, until the image of Beth’s fingers curled around Cole’s arm, the platinum band that held a large diamond, cut and shining now clear as a sunlit day. Her rounded belly, the family they would create. How Linda and Anton were merging their own.

She swallowed that cocktail of emotions, choking it down to stir inside of her. How small and insignificant she felt, an interloper in her best friend’s life. With no family to merge. How she wished she had said anything else to Cole, something clever. Something braver.

A sudden movement in the rearview mirror caught her attention. She hadn’t seen another car for miles, but something crept along behind her. She pressed the gas a little harder, not because she was afraid, since there was nothing out here except deer and silhouettes of trees, but because the idea of being alone on the road suddenly seemed worse.

The road narrowed, and the trees pressed in tighter, branches reaching overhead like the fingers of a giant. She was coming around a rather sharp bend on the road, and then something moved in the shadows ahead. She barely registered it, a flicker of darkness crossing the beams of her headlights. There it was, directly in her path.

It wasn’t any animal that should exist in this part of the world. It was colossal, a brute silhouette that reared up on two legs, its outline jagged with fur and something like horns. Its eyes shone, no— glowed, bright red, two orbs that caught her in their gaze. There was a flash of muscle, a glimmer of teeth, and then she was barreling toward it with no time to think. Her gut lurched; this was no wildlife, no hallucination brought on by drinks. It was real, and it was utterly, terribly wrong.

Instinct took over, and she jerked the wheel hard, tires squealing against pavement, the leather burning in her palms as she twisted.

There was a hopeless stillness, a heartbeat where time stretched, and she knew, with an icy certainty, that this was going to hurt. The world outside her windshield blurred into streaks of black and green. The headlights caught the gnarled trunk of an ancient oak, and for a moment, she saw every line and groove of the bark.

A single, sharp thought cut through the chaos: Linda’s face at the party, radiant and happy. The image shattered, replaced by the certainty that her friend would soon be planning a funeral.

Her car slammed, hard, into the large tree. Her windshield had shattered, and now she was barreling headfirst towards the trunk. She braced for the—

She slowly opened her eyes. The air was cool and drafty and smelled of dust, earth, and clay. A dull pain flared in her back and throbbed behind her eyes, a deep, insistent pounding. She was on a soft mattress, atop heavy quilts. This wasn't the peaceful oblivion she'd expected. This wasn't death at all.

But how would she know the shadowed claw of death?

Her vision sharpened. She was still in her dress and jacket, lying on a bed in a cold, stone room. A desk sat across the space, a matching table beside her. Banners bearing an unfamiliar crest hung from the ceiling, and ancient-looking weapons adorned the walls. A strange and cold decorating decision. Nothing about this made sense. A wave of panic began to rise.

What was this? The spirit realm? It looked suspiciously like something from a forgotten age long since passed. She didn’t feel dead, but she remembered the tree, the splintering crack of the windshield. There was no way she survived that. Her heart began to pound against her ribs as she slowly sat up, the room tilting around her. That’s when she saw him, and the air froze in her lungs.

A man sat on the opposite side of the room. 

He looked serious as he was angled towards the banner, lost in some thought, his mouth in a straight line, his brows drawn down. He was unable to see her staring.

She was alone. In a strange room, with a strange man. She took a breath, expecting her heart to hammer against her ribs, but it was steady. The goosebumps on her arms were from the cold air, not fear. She was entranced, her focus narrowing on him.

She had thought Cole was out of her league, handsome, but this guy was in a conference of his own, even with a small scowl pulling on his full lips. He was devastatingly beautiful. His sandy-colored hair was pulled into a short ponytail in the back of his head, with two pieces not long enough to make the pull hanging loose on either side of his face. He had pointed ears; oddly enough, they fit his face. They weren’t obnoxious, just slightly pointed compared to her rounded ones, and they were decorated with two small blue hoops.

She raked over his body, as she finally remembered to exhale.

He was lean but broad-shouldered, his frame hinting at a wiry strength beneath the layers of his strange clothing. A long red tunic over a high-necked green shirt, beige pants, and brown boots. Her stomach flipped. Was this an angel, sent to guide her to the afterlife? She gulped, certain she hadn’t lived a life holy enough to warrant a welcome like this.

Then the motion of his head whipping towards her stopped her from exhaling.

Despite his clenched jaw, his soft, young face had strong, defined features. Similar to her age, yet a hardness nestled underneath. His eyes were so blue, captivatingly so. Large enough to dive into them and drown. She couldn’t look away; they were locked into this stare until his narrowed, deepening the shadows underneath.

Shaking her head to clear it, she found her voice. “Where am I?”

He stood, and she tried not to flinch as his tall frame unfolded. He crossed his arms, his voice low and steady when he finally spoke. “Hyrule Castle.”

He spoke her language, perhaps with a hint of an unidentifiable accent. She understood him enough to know he hadn’t minced words. The name meant nothing to her, a strange, storybook word. Her own voice was a whisper. “Where? Am I dead?”

He slightly tilted his head as a reaction to her inane question, “No, you’re not dead.” His voice dripped flat.

Ignoring the sting of his tone, she ran a hand through her hair, a nervous tic from childhood. Her own long, blond waves fell over her face, a brief curtain to hide behind. Clearing her throat, she found her voice again. “Who are you?”

He paused, the muscle in his throat working before his expression softened just slightly. “My name is Link,” he said, his voice low. “What’s your name?”

When he said his name, something shifted in her chest, a strange recognition, as if she had been mispronouncing a word her whole life and had only now heard it spoken correctly. She wanted to know what her own name would sound like in his mouth.

She took a long, shaky breath, forcing it out in a slow, measured stream. The single word that followed was surprisingly steady. “Zelda.”

Chapter 2: Fate p. II
Notes:
(See the end of the chapter for notes.)

Chapter Text
The air smelled like sulfur. Despite the heavy rain pouring down, craters in the ground were pits of ever-burning fire, exploded from some unknown chaos.

He was in Hyrule Field, or perhaps not. The density of the trees and haze of rain had obstructed his vision; it was hard enough to see a few feet in front of him.

He ran strategically through the silhouette of trees, ducking low-hanging branches and thorny shrubs as he headed toward an unknown destination, an unfamiliar sword in his hand. Though he didn’t recognize it, his body did; his fingers had already found the grip before he’d thought to look at it, settling into the contours of the handle as if he’d spent years wearing it down to that shape. Indigo-colored wings adorned either side of the hilt, and above them an etching of the Triforce. He could tell that it was sharper than anything made by a mere mortal as it glowed an ethereal blue. The blade wasn’t heavy; actually, it was perfectly balanced, like it was meant for him.

Where did he get it?

The weight in his non-sword hand vanished. He had been pulling something, or rather someone.

A beautiful woman with golden hair lay in the earth behind him. Gold, not blond, strands fell in weeping strands in front of her face. She was bruised and bloody; her clothing covered in ichor and filth. She was so familiar. He scooped her in his arms and held her close. A pained whimper escaped her lips, her brow furrowed in a deep crease. A fierce, protective urge rose in his chest, a need to erase her pain as she sobbed in his arms.

Every snap of a twig in the fiery woods sent a jolt through him. He glanced over his shoulder, then at her tear-streaked face. They had to keep going. He held her broken spirit close and they continued. Cold rain hit his face, like sharp pricks digging into his skin.

“Link, wait…” her voice faded. The weight in his hands vanished.

Where was she?

“Link—!”

He needed to help her. Where was—

He jolted awake, the phantom sting of rain still sharp on his skin. His shirt clung to him, damp and cold, not with dream-water, but with sweat. He brought his calloused fingers to rub his temples, to check for blood.

The same nightmare. Again. The woman, the foreign sword, the frantic escape from a threat he could never see. It had been coming more often this past month, each time leaving him with a residue of unease.

He should ask Impa what it meant. He made a mental note, knowing he would probably forget by breakfast.

Warm morning light cast long, bright beams from the cold stone floor to the ceiling on the opposite wall. Dust sparkled, flying lazily in each beam. He lifted his hand to feel the warmth, letting the August sun seep into his skin. It was a welcome defense against the castle's constant, deep-set chill. Made less warm by hard stone floors and even harder knights.

He gave himself a few more moments to soak up the first rays of light blaring through the neat row of windows on the opposite wall. Each day, the sun shone through later than the day before. Soon enough, Nayru’s harvest would be here, followed by colder months and fighting over spare quilts and pelts. The more senior knights had their pick of the available locations of beds, opting for beds opposite the windows, while young squires and newly appointed knights got the drafty window beds. 

His feet hit the floor, and he crossed to the chest at the foot of his bed that held all his possessions. He tied his messy hair to the back of his head with his favorite blue tie and picked through the messy pile to find a clean tunic to wear, ignoring the leather guards and cuirass, scowling at the thought of the wasted opportunity to don them.

Breakfast first, always, then the yard. He ran his drills alone until the dew burned off the grass, then joined formations with the others. Afternoons varied, the usual rotation of chores and sessions; most days were siege tactics, a senior knight pointing at maps and raising hypothetical scenarios to attack, to defend.

And frankly, sitting in a dark, musty room with a bunch of sweat-soaked males was preferable to the bit of courtly lessons they required of him. Today being the latter.

A knight was expected to navigate a ballroom as skillfully as a battlefield, but the thought of it made his muscles ache more than any sparring session. Unlike squires, knights often escorted the young ladies of court that were from titled families. Thus, they had to learn proper procedures, as not to embarrass the brotherhood of the guard.

Enjoying it, however, was not part of the code.

After the suffering of small feet stepping on him and slight dizziness from twirling in circles, he’d have some downtime to tend to his horse, train again, or visit the armory. Followed by supper and, on some occasions, entertainment. Today he’d spend all his extra time training, as he did most days, but he did make sure to tend to his horse at least twice in a week.

As he tied the belt fastening his sword and dagger around his chest, he inadvertently picked up the conversation behind his shoulder. “No way they consider him.” Pipit shook his head violently, his voice assured. “He’s absolute rubbish with his long swords.” 

“Maybe, but his archery and short sword play is better than most.” Cawlin considered back, still lying lazily in bed, his elderberry hair sticking every which way.

“A knight in service of her royal majesty can’t be subpar with long swords. Can’t be deficient in anything! One mistake out there, and we no longer have a princess.” Pipit fired back, awaiting the challenge in his conviction, his copper eyes to match his hair blazing at him. “Groose will need to vastly improve at all aspects of weaponry and defenses if he has a shot in hell of even being considered.”

“You’re right,” Cawlin said quietly before sliding out of bed.

Pipit opened his mouth but shut it tightly; he clearly wanted to continue arguing.

“Link is the only real contender for the position. Let’s face it, he’s good at everything.” Strich said, shooting a glare over to him, trying to hold back his contempt. “It’s in his blood, I suppose. All the talent of his father, with none left for the rest of us.” Link knew it was meant as an insult, though the sarcasm was soured with a grudging respect from the abnormally tall knight to his back.

Link ignored the flattery and the growing pit in his stomach. Humility was engrained in him at a young age. ‘Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit; in humility, consider others better than yourself.’ His father used to tell him, and he was objectively considered one of the best knights based on his skills alone, not because of flattery or noble blood. The passing thought about his father made the unease in his stomach seize, but he stamped it down quickly.

The castle had been in a frenzy of excitement as of late. Knights were personally selected by senior members of the brotherhood to be considered for the open position to enter the royal guard, more specifically to be Princess’ appointed knight.

Since she had come of age, the King determined that she would travel around Hyrule and make her offerings to the goddesses in return for protection over the kingdom.

Link didn’t care for any of that, but being her appointed knight came with the benefits of being in the royal guard, a most prestigious title someone of his birth could hope to achieve.

But what he really vied for was the freedom in the wilds, rather than the drafty, frigid, hard castle he had grown uncomfortably used to in his adolescence. The princess often enjoyed trips to the Royal Tech Lab and Mabe Village, even annual expeditions to far-off regions such as Gerudo Town and Rito Village.

He much preferred slack in his leash than one pulled too short, even if it was gripped tight in the princess’s hands.

His father had taken him all over Hyrule as a child. He knew Zora’s Domain just as well as his hometown of Hateno. He longed for the thrill of an unmarked trail and the sharp, clean air of the highlands. Out there, away from stone walls, every sense came alive; it was the only time he felt truly whole. As a knight of his standing, he was allowed the freedom to travel to Castle Town or to local villages nearby, but he wasn’t allowed to leave for days on end without requesting permission. And even then, it had to be for a good reason. The longest he’d been out since becoming a squire was on a patrol that lasted only a moon phase.

“Link, are you ready for the final tournament tomorrow?” Fledge, his shy squire, asked. His question shattered his daydream as all the other knights had dressed and left for breakfast, and he was still standing at his chest like an imbecile. 

Grateful, as missing breakfast would certainly ruin his day. “Yes, I feel good about it.” He had thrown more training rotations into his routine to better elevate himself for this prized position. 

A crinkle formed in Fledge’s leather-colored eyes, as he gave a weak smile and left Link alone to finish his routine.

The light beat heavily upon the cobblestone from the west above as he slunk out of the library, the phantom rhythm of a waltz still pulsing in his head. What a waste of an afternoon learning steps he’d take any excuse to avoid. A fleeting thought crept into his head: did he even want to be in the royal guard if this is what they expect of him? He hated all the pomp and circumstance that came with being associated with the royal family.

Since he was young enough to remember, he wanted to be in the royal guard, to make his father proud. But now that he was facing down that very real possibility, something in him resisted. No more solo adventures or the freedom he had now. He would be a statue, always silently guarding the king and princess and any future generations to come. His hand moved to reach for the hilt at his back without thinking, gripping it the way he always did when he needed to feel certain of something.

Training would clear his head, and he needed all the extra practice he could get, since the tournament was tomorrow.

Grabbing his sword, he headed towards the knight’s courtyard to train. Not the typical location for knights to train since they had the castle ward to train or if he wanted more advanced practice, the military training camp. Where the young pages, squires, and freshly appointed knights would spend weeks sore, bruised, and nearly broken. He had spent many nights throwing up from exhaustion at repeated drills.

However, the latter was a half-a-morning’s ride by horseback and the ward was always overcrowded, risking serious injury if he wanted to use his actual sword rather than a practice one.

While he wouldn’t gain the full access to all the available equipment of the ward, especially the straw-stuffed dummies, scarred and battered from countless beatings, he would revel in the feeling of his steel slicing the thick summer air. Additionally, he enjoyed his drills in solitude.

He spent the better part of an hour hacking, slashing, thrusting, and slicing at a faceless enemy. He lost his heavy tunic midway through his fictionalized battle; the sun’s midday rays at their hottest, adding more tanned layers to his torso.

He grabbed his undershirt to wipe the beads of sweat dripping from his forehead. As he moved, he caught the eyes of two maids staring at him from the walls above, both of whom promptly turned red, giggled at each other, and left.

He wasn’t unaware of the effect his presence had on women, but none held his interest. He was young for a knight. He would be the youngest in the royal guard, if he made it. And with that title would come the expectation of a wife. It was a great honor for a young woman to marry a knight, even more so to be married to a knight in the royal guard.

And rather than marry for love, most knights married for financial or political gain. Fathers from well-to-do houses would offer their noble daughter’s hand to a respected knight; and the better the knight, the better daughters offered or the larger the dowry. He had a sour taste in his mouth at the thought.

He never gave much thought about settling down for himself. He could marry now if he so chose; he already had a few proposals from noblemen who knew his father, but he rejected them. Always polite in his rejections to the eager papas to avoid slighting them or their daughters, he explained his refusals with reasonings such as focusing his dedication to his military career or that he didn’t have a permanent assignment, so having a wife at this time would be a nuisance for stability. They were weak excuses, but enough that proud noblemen came to accept, leaving the denial open-ended with a ‘maybe in a few years you’ll change your mind’ or ‘let’s talk when you’re posted permanently.’

Marriage for knights did bring added wages and status. But he made more than enough to support himself, and his status was already higher than most knights of his age, at 20. He stared out over the eastern moat as the western setting sun hit the rolling hills of Crenel and thought deeply about that potential reality. Those reasons he gave when denying those eager fathers were true, but really, he didn’t know those women.

At least he was able to have a say in his future wife, rather than Hylian noble women not having a choice in who would provide for them and their children. Then he thought of his mother; she was lucky to have chosen his father, and for his father to have chosen her.

He snapped back to reality when his stomach growled. How long had he been staring into the distance contemplating marriage? If his captain had been there and caught him like that, he’d be assigned night duty until the next new moon. He turned west and saw the sun well past midday. It was almost his favorite time of the day: supper. He picked up his discarded tunic and belts, sheathed his blade, and headed to the barracks.

The sun’s warm rays were a welcome feeling on his bare skin. Typically, knights did not walk around the castle shirtless; it was frowned upon in practices of politeness, but his wet tunic lay upon his forearm, and the thought of pulling it on was torture. And it was rare others walked this path to the barracks.

And as he wiped sweat from his forehead, his dream from earlier came into focus.

But rather than focusing on the sword or the carnage, he tried to recall the lines of the woman’s face. Without ever meeting her, she was as familiar as his own hand to a hilt. He recalled the impossible treasured hue of her hair against the smoke, the desperate grip of her hand in his. It wasn't just a duty he'd felt; it was a deep, aching need to keep her safe, a feeling that resonated in his bones.

The Sheikah believe dreams and nightmares are powerful omens. Fates and destinies that are set to come to pass, in some form or another. Thus, he should really remember to speak to Impa about her theories.

But as he rounded the corner near the gatehouse, he almost barreled into a familiar figure.

“Link!” the sweet, soft voice of Ilya. His elbow had pierced against hers, and he had instinctively reached out to her.

“Ilya?” His hand still firmly grasped her shoulder. “Fancy running into you here.”

She giggled at his flat and sarcastic tone before her eyes left his to trail down his arm to his bare chest. Her face ignited with a red flush that climbed to the tips of her ears. “Ah— sorry, I was taking a shortcut to the kitchens,” she stammered. 

He realized he may have embarrassed her; it wasn’t proper for a young lady to be caught with a half-naked man in the castle, even one she’d grown up with and seen bare-chested hundreds of times. He dropped his hand from her shoulder, and she shook loose at the loss of contact. “Sorry, Ilya. I didn’t think anyone would be on this path.” He pulled his sweaty tunic on, grimacing at the scrape of the damp fabric against his skin.

The light in her eyes flickered, and the corners of her smile fell—slightly. “That’s alright. What are you up to?”

“I finished training. I’m heading back to change and then to the dining hall,” he said.

Ilya seemed to bounce back to herself. “Of course, I know how important supper is for you.” She snickered. “I’ll be in the dining hall later, but that bard— I don’t remember his name, but he’s renowned for his talent with a lute— is in town at the tavern tonight. I’m heading there with some of the kitchen girls. It would be great if you can join us.” Her tone was sweet and sincere.

“Perhaps. Tomorrow is the tournament. I want to be well-rested for it.”

“Of course! I’m very excited for you. You are going to do amazing.” Ilya smiled like she meant every word of it. “Well, you should try to make it, I’ll even buy you a drink.” She winked.

A grin touched his lips as he nodded. “I’ll hold you to it. See you later, Ilya.” She bounced away opposite him. 

He made it back to the empty barracks, not surprising as the warm weather had everyone outside longer. He changed into his spare red tunic and quickly smoothed his hair back.

“Sir Link!” Fledge called from across the barracks. He looked frantic, his short, fawn-colored hair askew as he ran at full speed directly for him. By the time he reached Link, he was wheezing.

“What is it, Fledge?” His tone was sharper than he intended; his stomach was already protesting the delay. But the squire was clearly desperate.

“You need to see for yourself. A girl has appeared in the west gardens.” Fledge was able to get out the full sentence amidst catching breaths.

“A girl? Link’s brow lifted curiously. Why would he care about a girl? Fledge was testing his patience.

And his stomach.

“It looks like it could be a young Hylian woman, but different.” Fledge looked stupefied. “She’s not moving either.”

Link’s frown eased. A woman, unconscious and appearing from nowhere? His annoyance gave way to a flicker of curiosity. “Take me there.”

They briskly wound their way through the barracks, the west passage, the guards’ chamber, and finally taking the shortcut to the courtyard, where the center pavilion stood. An area of the castle where soldiers mostly gathered with handmaids they were courting or where younger women gossiped about castle comings and goings. 

As they approached the aged oak tree that shaded the whole pavilion with its lush foliage, she looked as if she had landed from the sky and hadn’t moved since, her body half curled upon herself, yet her arms askew.

He nimbly crept to the pile of foreign fabric and long golden hair. The girl looked like a young woman. Her eyes were closed; most likely unconscious but seemingly uninjured; no blood or bruises visible.

Link brushed her silken hair from her neck to feel for a pulse. An odd surge ran up his fingers as he skimmed against her skin. The shape of her ears startled him. Small and rounded. Not a Hylian.

A Gerudo? Perhaps with her piercings, with enough gold to put those women to envy, as dainty gold hoops and gemmed studs glittered, climbing up her lobes. He also caught a glimpse of another small piercing in the deep center of her ear. He wasn’t sure if he should be impressed or intimidated; that had to hurt.

He gently brought his two fingers to the soft skin under her round ears. The warmth and soft cadence of her heart elevated his own.

“She has a pulse.” Link whispered to himself in mystifying relief.

“I didn’t think to check.” He could hear the chagrin in Fledge’s voice. “I was walking by, then my ears pulled the air out of my head before the sound of a door slamming popped it. It was similar to when we leave a window open in the barracks on a breezy day and the door slams shut behind you. I thought I was delusional before I turned to the sound, and there she was.”

Link couldn’t tear his eyes from her, tilting his head expecting her to suddenly reveal those secrets to him. “Then what?”

“I ran to get you.” 

“No one else knows she’s here?” Link studied Fledge’s face.

“No, only you, sir.”

“Alright, I’m going to bring her to the East Barracks. Let her have some privacy to come to.” Link bent down to roll her on her back, to easily lift her, but as he did, he was stunned as a gentle lavender scent grazed his nostrils and the sight unfolded almost made him lose his balance. 

When she was on her side, it looked as though her dress went to her ankles, but now front-facing, long bare legs were displayed in the front of her. The dress barely covered her and by modesty standards, as she was, she seemed better suited in the buildings at the far end of Castle Town where soldiers spent their wages for female company.

He could practically feel Fledge nervously fidgeting behind him. Link quickly gathered her into his arms, the scent of lavender heavy as he adjusted her, trying carefully to avoid touching bare skin, whisking her down the pavilion steps as her head and long hair cascaded limply over his arm.

He headed for the East Barracks. With most of its knights dispatched on patrol, the wing was temporarily abandoned… and empty. He knew it would be at least a few days until they returned, which made it the perfect place to place the mystery guest. He carried her past the armory and through the East passage, careful not to be noticed.

Entering the shades of gray and darkened barracks, he tried two spare bedroom doors until the third, with a quick scan of the room, confirmed it was clean enough. He gently laid her on the mattress, carefully preserving her modesty. His hand instinctively brushed a rogue blond lock from her face and tucked it behind her ear. Her face was soft, lashes long above closed lids, lips full and colored like the bloom of a dusty orchard.

“Who do you think she is?” Fledge had stepped closer, his voice louder than Link had ever heard it. The boy’s usual shyness seemed to have vanished. 

“I don’t know,” Link contemplated. He stared at her unconscious body, her chest faintly rising. “I’ll stay with her until she wakes to ask.” The words were out before he’d thought to question them.

“I can stay too.” Fledge’s growing confidence surprised him.

“No, that’s alright, go back to the dorms. If anyone asks where I am, tell them I’m at the armory.” He was surprised at his quickly formulated lie.

Fledge hesitated, something he rarely did when given a direct command. Link felt a prick of unease at asking the boy to lie for him. But then his squire nodded, his expression firming. “I’ll check on you if you don’t make it to supper.” The heavy door closed behind him.

He wasn’t sure why he felt protective over this woman. Things had been increasingly tumultuous as of late, with more monsters appearing and more disappearances. A lone woman could be dismissed as a trespasser, but materializing within the castle’s inner sanctum would send the entire garrison into a state of high alarm. 

So, he settled himself, positioning himself near the door while still maintaining direct sight of her. The move was strategic, allowing him to swiftly grab her if she attempted to escape—if she was here under nefarious intentions.

The white of her gown was a shock to his system. He’d seen women in the lower part of town wear less, but always in dark, forgiving colors that spoke of their trade. White was for brides and prayer. However, he thought of the Gerudo and their common dress; exposed skin and light fabric to accommodate the heat. Perhaps this was common dress where she was from.

He stroked his chin as he analyzed her. Truly noticing her small-shaped face and the features decorating it. The sharpness of her cheekbones, a dainty nose, eyebrows slightly darker than her light-kissed hair. His eyes raked down from head to neck to arms, catching the polished gold band on her ring finger. It was the only ring she had on, on her right side, with a small gold triangle adorning the top.

Two hours passed. And while Link had patience, more than most men, but it was supper time, and he was hungry. Shifting in his seat uncomfortably, he realized that he had asked his squire to lie for him, while he was alone with a woman in an off-limits ward of a castle.

And he was hungry.

He started to grow angry at himself for being so brash. A scowl growing on his face, he turned to the woman and was staggered by the lustrous emerald eyes staring at him.

When did she wake? How long had she been staring at him as he was scowling at the large banner with the royal family’s crest hanging as a looming shadow to torment him for his brash actions?

“Where am I?” Her voice was confident, calmer than he had imagined.

He stood from the chair to be closer to her, for whatever reason. “We’re in Hyrule Castle.”

Her expression was blank, as if the words meant nothing to her. His brows furrowed. How could she not know the ruling kingdom of the land?

She repeated “Where?” followed by “Am I dead?”

Was she addled from her fall? She had no obvious injuries that would explain the blatant confusion. His stomach grumbled loudly, a sharp reminder of the supper he was missing. “No, you are not dead,” he said, his hunger making his tone more cutting than he intended.

A faint blush rose on her cheeks, and her eyes glistened. Her hand instinctively went to the top of her head, fingers speared through the silky fibers as she combed it behind her head. A few loose waves fell across her face. 

“Who are you?” Her tone sharpened, each word enunciated and accusatory.

He debated telling her his name. Did he want this stranger to know his name— making it easier for her to report him?

He stared at her for a long moment, then decided. “My name is Link. What’s your name?”

An invisible string seemed to pull her spine straight. Her gemmed green eyes widened, cutting and piercing him with an expression of stark recognition that sent a chill through him. Her hands gripped the quilts at her sides.

With a shaky exhalation, she replied, “Zelda.”

He stood there. The name moved through him like a current, and for a moment the room, the hunger, the scowl fell away. He had the sudden, unverifiable certainty that his life had just divided itself into before and after.
