Chapter 3: Hyrule
Chapter Text
The man named Link looked like he was staring at a particularly difficult puzzle after her name slipped by her lips. “Your name is Zelda?” he asked.

“Yes.” 

“Where exactly are you from?” He was calm as he spoke, but she noted how his jaw clenched back tight.

She started with her state, then her country, yet his stare remained blank. She listed neighboring countries, continents, anything she could think of. The silence stretched. In a last, desperate attempt, she asked, “Earth? The planet?”

Still nothing.

She fisted her hand to stop the tremor. Maybe he’d start laughing at her in the prank that this surely was.

But no laughter came. Actually, nothing came. No reaction. The silence pressed in, and her breath hitched. She forced a painful swallow, remembering that she needed to still breathe. Her heart was going to launch out of her chest.

She dared ask, “Are you an elf? A faerie?”

It was not lost on her how insane she had become to ask such a question. He seemed to agree as his lip curled and said, “I’m a Hylian.”

She blinked back the growing darkness, forcing the light to stay with each rapid open. It was an effort to suck in breath, more so to expel it as she tried to center herself. She was a logical, rational person. Something or someone had to explain this. “So you don’t recognize those places… but I might recognize yours. You said Hyrule? Is that a town? A country? What’s near it?” She wondered if he could hear the growing shrillness in her tone after the endless string of questions.

His blank expression was growing to a hint of concern, his eyes softening. “We are in Hyrule Castle. The kingdom is Hyrule, ruled by His Majesty King Rhoam. It’s a vast country, home to many races. Hylians like myself—” he made the point to emphasize that last bit. “And also the Sheikah, Zora, Gerudo, Gorons, and Rito.”

“What year is it?” Ignoring the odd-sounding names and saying a silent appeal for his next response.

“It’s the 22nd year of His Majesty King Rhoam’s reign.” His impossible blue eyes still on her own.

She quickly thought to her history lessons: back in the single- and double-digit centuries, some countries used the monarchy’s reigns to document years. But that hasn’t been used in hundreds or almost a thousand years, forever ago.

Had the champagne at the vineyard been stronger than she thought? Laced with something devious? Maybe she was in a coma or hit her head so hard she was confused.

She needed to stand. To ground herself to a hard surface. She swung her legs out and grazed the stone floor with her sandals. She braced herself with her palms on the quilted bed and pushed herself up. But immediately upon standing, the light started to escape, stars and flickering spots filled her head as her legs turned soft, and she started to crumble beneath herself.

Strong hands darted swiftly to grab her arms just before her knees hit the painfully hard floor. His touch was a shock to her system and the world snapped back into focus as that beat in her chest reminded her of being alive.

Link held her steady and effortlessly raised her straight as her eyes lined with his chin, his hands still clutching her ribs. Could he hear her heart beating abnormally? The scents of pine hit her nose, but not just pine— a fir with a sweet and earthy scent. She looked up and caught his eye before she could think to look away.

A blue greeted her, she forgot what she’d been about to say— they were not just cerulean, but something layered— a lagoon at midday, rippling, but closer to the center the deeper the water. A particular blue that was his and perhaps now, her favorite shade of blue.

She pulled her eyes down to his chest. Not a much better sight to gain clarity, but better than getting lost in his eyes. “Thank you for catching me.” A deep breath, and she steadied her footing.

“Of course,” he murmured. He released his grip, the warmth leaving with them.

The solid ground beneath her feet felt real again. “Okay,” she sighed, more to herself than to him. “One thing at a time.” She finally took in the room, noticing a small window streaked with orange, pink, and purple. “Is that the sunset?”

He turned to the window, thought briefly, and nodded.

“What do you usually do in the evenings?” she asked.

“I should be in the dining hall eating supper right now,” he said.

It was a feat not to shrink at the remark, an interruption in his neat, orderly life. A flush of heat crept up her neck. “Okay, well, what if we went to the dining hall together?”

“No,” he said at once. “I can’t take you there.” 

She tried not to let the stinging feeling of rejection show on her face. She glanced from his tunic to her own dress and jacket, suddenly acutely aware of how out of place she must look. Perhaps, wherever she was, her appearance would cause more than just stares.

She tried not to balk at that thought.

“What if you brought me a change of clothes? So I fit in better?” She gestured to her body with her hand.

“That could help somewhat, but…” he raised his hand to gently tuck her hair behind her ear, his fingers ghosting the top of her ear, burning at his touch. “Your ears are different. Someone will notice eventually.”

“You all have pointed ears?” 

“Yes.”

How was he so calm?

She straightened herself, trying to smooth the frustration growing in her joints at the fishing she was doing. “Then what do you propose to do with me?”

“You can stay here until I can get you a change of clothes and get you out of the castle without raising alarms. That would be best.” He paused, his gaze serious. “It would be bad if the guards were to catch you.”

She didn’t want to panic. “When will you be back?”

“My captain will notice my absence soon. I will gather clothing for you. If I can manage to slip away unnoticed, I will come when the moon is high. Otherwise, when the sun rises.”

“Alright.” Zelda had a thousand more questions, but the set of his jaw told her they wouldn’t be answered now. She had no choice but to trust this stranger. He hadn’t offered empty comforts, but it was that directness, the same steady focus she’d seen when he caught her, that made her nod. “But, what about water or food?”

“I’ll send food up soon. Stay in your room,” he said. 

She crossed her arms. He wasn’t her rescuer; he was her warden. He hadn’t asked how she got here, hadn’t shown an ounce of curiosity past the initial shock. Not that she could explain the car, the creature, the tree... but he could have asked.

“Thank you so much,” she said, dragging out the words.

“You are very welcome,” he said, his voice void of warmth. He turned and left without another word.

She was alone.

Her head was swimming. One moment his curtness annoyed her, the next she was replaying the secure grip of his hands on her arms, the startling gentleness of his fingers against her ear. She remembered the look in his eyes as they held hers. An intensity that was something wild just beneath the unflappable surface.

She had to get it together. She brought her hands to the back of her neck, pressing her fingers into the tense muscles as she forced herself to breathe.

With nothing to do and nowhere to go, she spotted a mirror in the corner of the room and decided to take a glance. She expected to see the worst, but instead she found no bruises, no stains, no blood. It was impossible. Aside from the knots in her hair and a few creases in her dress, she looked exactly as she had before leaving her apartment. Even her makeup hadn’t smudged.

It was all so bizarre. She still didn’t know what happened to her, how she ended up here. She was so frantic that she didn’t even ask Link where he found her. Her back hurt slightly, so she probably wasn’t on the soft mattress she had woken up from. He probably carried her here.

Despite Link’s warning, she couldn’t stay put. She eased the heavy door open into a windowless, shadowed hallway. She propped her door to allow the escaping light to show her path. Groping her way along the cold stone wall, her fingers found the handle of the first door. Locked, as was the second. She paused at the third, pressing her ear to the wood, but heard only silence, only the faint, masculine scent, like old leather and sweat, lingered in the air. She opened the final door and was pleasantly surprised to find a bathroom with familiar amenities.

It was a small relief.

At the end of the hallway, a spiral staircase led down. She descended to the first floor, where a spacious room greeted her with more windows. Multiple beds lined the walls, and a large wooden chest stood at the foot of each one. It looked like some kind of barracks, now empty. The simple, uniform layout stood in contrast to the private room she had woken up in. Admiring the craftsmanship of each chest, her curiosity piqued, she chose the one closest to her. Inside, she discovered a collection of knightly uniform attire: pairs of tunics, pants, padding, leather belts, guards, and boots.

Her fingers paused over a folded tunic. This was someone’s life, their private space. She glanced over her shoulder at the empty doorway, her stomach twisting. But the need to understand where she was, to find any clue, gnawed at her. With a sigh, she reluctantly closed the chest.

Heading back to the room— not wanting to go so far as to call it her bedroom— she shut the heavy door behind her. She hadn’t been alone since she arrived. She walked over to the small window; the oranges, pinks, and purples had faded to twilight blue against a silhouetted, unknown mountain range.

She let herself be engrossed by the sight until everything was dark. Turning from the window, she took in her cage in better detail.

A sconce lit the space with a surprisingly steady glow, enabling her to see the banner in detail. The crest featured three golden triangles supported by what appeared to be spread wings on either side, resembling a bird without a head. Her gaze circled the room to the overlapping weaponry that she had missed before, next to a complete set of armor in the corner, reminiscent of what she had seen at a museum when she was a child. The pristine shine upon the metal had shown no marks, with the exception of a layer of dust that covered it.

As she daydreamed about how inconvenient it would be to walk, let alone fight, in such heavy armor, the door creaked open. An unfamiliar face poked a head through the door.

“Who are you?” She was coiled tight in an instant, but clocked the hung weapons upon the walls within her reach. “I’m sorry, miss. I didn’t mean to startle you,” a stammering voice said. His body was halfway in the doorway, awaiting an invitation to enter fully. “My name is Fledge, Link sent me.”

Relief washed over her at the familiar name. “Alright, come in.” 

He entered the room slowly, as if she were a caged animal he had to be cautious of. He was young, shorter than Link and slighter of build, with shoulders hunched forward. He held the bundle out, his gaze fixed on the floorboards. “I brought you some food and water,” he murmured, his voice barely a whisper.

He was the definition of trepidation.

“Thank you.” She gave him a grateful smile, trying to catch his eye-line as she reached to grab the cloth. She noted a red flush crawling up his cheeks. 

She glanced down her front — nothing accidentally exposed, nothing she’d consider immodest. But Link had warned her. The man in front of her was red as an apple, eyes fixed on the floor. She smiled to herself. He’d probably never been alone in a room with a strange woman before, let alone one dressed like this.

She pieced together the clues: a monarchy, a calendar based on a king’s reign, the medieval feel of the room. It was all pointing to a time period so far removed from her own that it felt impossible. If her history lessons were right, a man and woman being alone like this would be a serious transgression.

But Link didn’t fumble at the sight of her. The thought pulling her elsewhere—

“Here is water for you too.” He held out a small leather bag. Snapping her out of a slight pang growing in her chest.

She took the bag handed to her, his eyes still angled at the floor. “Fledge, was it?” A faint smile, hoping to calm his nerves.

Big round chocolate eyes finally lifted to meet hers. So adorably round, like a puppy. “Yes.”

“While I very much appreciate you bringing me food, where is Link?”

Fledge swallowed, his gaze dropping to the floor again. “The captain pulled him aside after he barely made it to supper; he would not have been able to make it up to you without raising suspicions. He asked if I could run up food and drink to you, as you may have been hungry.”

Zelda’s smile grew slightly. “I’m surprised he told you I was here. He made it sound dangerous if anyone knew about me.”

Fledge looked slightly surprised. “I was the one that found you.”

Zelda couldn’t stop her eyebrows shooting up. “Really? Link didn’t mention that, or where I was found. Can you tell me what happened?” 

“Erm, yes.” Fledge fidgeted. “I was walking past the center pavilion. There was this sound and sudden shift in the air. Like when the window is open and it slams the door shut. It was a pressurized rip. I turned to where the sound had been, and you were just... there. Lying on the grass next to the tree.”

“In what state did you find me?”

“Uhh… you were unconscious. Lying on your side, next to the oak tree in the pavilion.” Fledge said. “I ran to the barracks to find Link. He always knows how to handle unexpected situations.”

Zelda reached to the top of her head. The oak tree. She remembered flying towards it and then… nothing. Could this tree be some portal back to her world? She rolled her eyes at the implication— how insane it was she was even entertaining this idea, but she wasn’t about to discuss it with a stranger. “Did Link say when he’d be back with the clothes he mentioned?”

His shoulders slumped, and his big, round eyes seemed to dim. “He didn’t say. I’m sorry.” 

“No worries, I can stay in these clothes until then.” She sucked her lip. “Actually, what— month… is it?” Wondering if ‘month’ was the proper calendar term to measure here.

“It’s August.”

Well, look at that, one thing in common.

She sat down at the sturdy desk to unwrap the cloth he brought. There was a slice of thick bread, some hard cheese, and an apple. Not exactly the meal she would serve a guest, but she’d eaten less— and worse, after a night out. 

Fledge seemed to read her hesitation. “I apologize there isn’t more. Link grabbed what he could.”

“Please don’t apologize. This is very considerate. Bread and cheese are my staples.” A genuine smile touched her lips as she briefly wondered if they had a version of pizza here. “And thank you for taking care of me after you found me.”

“It was all Link. He knew exactly what to do.” He smiled, able to look her in the eyes now. “He’s quick-thinking.”

Fledge had started to leave, but she had hundreds of questions— and frankly, she didn’t want to be alone. “Do you both live in the castle?”

“Yes.”

Link had a sword strapped behind him, but Fledge did not. “Are you a—” she tried to think of the appropriate word, “A scullion? A tradesman?”

Fledge twisted his face slightly, “I am Link’s squire.”

Link was a knight then.

“He seems a little young to be a knight?” She wanted to know more about him. She couldn’t help but continue to prod. At the mention of his friend, Fledge’s whole posture changed, his back straightening and a proud light entering his eyes.

“He became a knight at sixteen— years before most,” Fledge said, his posture straightening. “You should have seen him fight the lynel on Ploymus Mountain.” He spoke the name in a hushed, reverent whisper. “That’s how he got the scar on his collarbone.”

“A lynel?”

Fledge shuddered. “A terrifying beast. But then, he also saved a noble from a whole pack of bokoblins once. Nothing seems to faze him.”

So Link wasn’t just a knight; in this man’s eyes, he was a legend.

“And where does he live?”

“The barracks.”

Zelda’s eyes fell to the floor. “That must be trying for your families… your significant others.”

“I miss my family, yes. But the barracks doesn’t leave much room for a wife.”

Interesting to know.

Fledge also let slip that a tournament was being held tomorrow, one that would place a knight into the prestigious royal guard, with the honor of guarding the Princess herself.

“So there is a Princess?” Fledge nodded. “And Link wants to be her guard?” Another nod.

Something stung in her chest. “I see. Is that why he’s so standoffish?”

Fledge paused for what seemed like a long time. “He’s always been stoic, never says much.”

She was about to ask why when a yawn cracked its way out of her mouth. Fledge backed up at the motion, then quickly bowed his head. “Goodnight, malady.”

She smiled wholeheartedly at the sentiment. “Good night, Fledge.”

He gave a very slight bow and left.

She sat on the bed, bringing the food with her before shoving the massive piece of bread into her mouth.

Her eyes fluttered back. The bread was the best she’d ever had— a fresh sourdough with a perfect crust. The cheese was sharp and crumbly, and the apple was so crisp it snapped when she bit into it. Everything tasted real and vibrant, a stark contrast to the sterile, packaged food from her place. She ate quickly, the simple meal a small comfort in the overwhelming strangeness of it all.

She pulled her sandals off her feet, and delicately matched one next to the other on the floor next to the bed before sliding her feet onto the bed, shifting them under the quilt covers. She was still in her white dress; it wasn’t the most comfortable piece of fabric to sleep in, but better than nothing. The jean jacket, on the other hand, was scratchy and had to go. She pulled her arms out of the sleeves, folded it, and laid it gently at the foot of the bed. Laying back under the covers, she yanked the quilt up to warm her chest.

The quilt smelled of cobwebs and pollen, simultaneously. She imagined it must have been laundered and hung out on the castle walls to dry, catching and storing the fresh summer air. The faint smells of dust showed how recently abandoned the room had been. She guessed maybe a few weeks. Staring at the ceiling, she breathed deeply, and the day’s events washed over her. She wasn’t sure how long it had been since she’d left home, but a bone-deep weariness settled in her limbs, weighing them down against the mattress.

Would she ever make it home again?

A boot seemed to press harder on her chest. She breathed in counts, slow and deliberate, until it loosened. 

After the last well-timed breath, her eyes suddenly felt too heavy. Tomorrow was a new day to answer all the questions that lingered. She turned to her side, and promptly fell asleep to the sound of nothing.

The smell of wood burning and metal smoldering was stinging her nose. It was day, but the sky was dark with clouds. She was running, cold rain pelting her naked arms with invisible welts. Her clothing was ripped, bloody knees and shins beneath her. She didn’t dare look back at what was chasing her, but she knew she had to run. The sick sounds of metal clanking and clashing around her. Her vision sharpened through the dark rain to a hand gripping her wrist, pulling her faster than she could go. The hand was gloved with worn brown leather, and the fingerless holes showed calloused fingers that burned into her wrist. Trailing her shaky vision forward, hung a scabbard on the man’s back, shiny gold buried under soot and hazy darkness. An indigo hilt stuck out above his shoulder, almost glowing in contrast.

She could barely breathe, he was pulling her so hard. Her legs had given up. Knees hit the punishing ground, dirt mixing in with bloody shins as the agony vibrated through her. Her vision was clouded by salt and water as she blinked through it, the man turned, walked over to her, and crouched to meet her. His hand cradled her cheek. 

Link.

“Zelda,” Link’s voice was a soft breath in the shell of her ear.

She stared at him with such intensity that she thought she might splinter had he looked away. Everything was broken. But why?

“Zelda, wake up.” His lips weren’t moving, but his voice came from somewhere near. His hand came to her face, and she leaned into his touch. She felt every sensation, every nerve.

“Zelda!”

Chapter 4: Cordial
Chapter Text
 

He knocked. Nothing.

He knocked again, harder this time.

Silence.

A barb of unease rose, what if she’d vanished as strangely as she’d appeared? With a last glance down the empty hall, he pushed the door open.

The room was cast in the warm light of morning, a sharp contrast to the previous night. His eyes went straight to the bed, to the twisting lump under the quilt— Zelda.

Her small frame was taut, the quilt clutched to her neck. Her head thrashed against the pillow, tangling the blonde strands. A low moan escaped her lips, a sound of pure distress. All thoughts of propriety vanished; he had to wake her.

He cautiously put his hand where he was sure her arm resided under the quilt, silently saying a prayer that she didn’t scream at the sight of him when she woke, and gently shook her. Nothing. 

He’d never woken a sleeping woman before.

He jostled her a little harder, saying her name, “Zelda.” Still nothing. He brought his mouth to her ear so she could hear him better, “Zelda, wake up.”

Leaning close, he saw goosebumps rise on the smooth, unblemished skin of her neck. Her pulse beat a frantic rhythm against her vein, a silent alarm. Then she whimpered— a sound so soft he almost missed it, a sound that twisted in the air until it sounded like his own name.

The air caught in his lungs. A familiar, electric hum ignited under his skin, the soldier's instinct to find the threat. But there was no enemy here, only her.

He had to compose himself. He took a slow inhale, calling on his Sheikah training. He pictured himself a great tree, roots latched deep in the earth, and focused on the stillness, the quiet strength to just be. Grounding, solid, strong.

He felt his pulse slow from its frantic rhythm, the electric hum under his skin fading to a manageable thrum. Grounded. He was the steady, unwavering man he needed to be.

Once his heart rate slowed to a steady rhythm, he turned back to the woman on the bed. Not giving himself a reason for it to rise again, this time he stayed his distance and loudly said her name. 

She shot awake, eyes wide. 

“Are you alright?” He clenched his hand at his side, fighting the impulse to reach out to her. “I was trying to wake you for a while; you were tossing around.”

“Uhm, yeah, I’m good,” she said, her voice raspy. The sharp fear in her eyes faded, replaced by dark smudges beneath them and a weariness that pulled at the corners of her mouth. A part of him was grateful he woke her. “I’m sorry; how long have you been here?” Her hand went to her temples, before threading through her hair.

“Not long; a few minutes.” He tried to shake the tension still lingering in his shoulders at the thought of watching her toss and turn. “I brought you breakfast and some essentials.” He gestured towards the desk where he placed clothing, oil for her teeth, and a wash towel. Bare essentials, really. “I’ll give you a moment.”

He resolved to wait outside the door to allow her to collect herself, but she shot her legs out from beneath the quilts; she was still in the white dress, the hem high on her long, toned legs. He looked, unhurried, taking her in from the ground up.

As her bare feet hit the porous stoned floor, she arched into a long stretch. All her muscles flexed on her legs. His eyes were as lazy as she was, slowly skimming from her feet to her shoulders, which had also been bare and kissed by the sun as she rolled everything casually. Baring her neck, the same pulse point he had brushed against just a few seconds ago, he ended his survey at her lips, which were pulled into a smirk; he moved to her gemmed eyes, which had been watching him like fond entertainment.

 “Did you bring me clothes?” Her question formed back into the smirk.

Heat crept up his neck, but he kept his voice even. “Yes, I left them there. I guessed your size.” He tilted his chin toward the desk where a neat pile of plain clothes sat. 

She narrowed her eyes at him before striding to the neatly folded clothes. Organized from head to toe.

He watched as her hands lifted each one: the dark, hooded cloak with embroidered trim, a simple sleeved cotton shirt, a worn leather corset, and black riding pants with brown boots— all typical attire for a non-noble woman, practical enough to be inconspicuous.

After carefully inspecting the set, her fingers tracing the embroidery on the hood, she said, “Thank you, it’s quite lovely.” She smiled down at the clothes before turning to him. “I suppose I should get changed.”

He nodded and left the room.

The latch clicked shut. He tilted his head back to rest against the door, his breath shuddering out in a long sigh. One look from her had him sputtering. He was a soldier, trained for control, yet the memory of her smirk sent a tremor through his hands. The scent of lavender still clung to him, a faint, intoxicating aroma that made the pressure in his head build.

As daylight poured in, the image of her smirk returned, and with it, the unsettling comparison. He realized that she truly resembled the princess, albeit with subtle distinctions. They were not identical— at least what he’d seen from his very limited view of the crowned princess. Apart from this, Zelda’s round ears, her sun-kissed skin suggested a life of labor, a stark contrast to the fair-skinned princess. But when he looked closer, her hands were smooth, with no calluses. Still, the toned muscle in her arms and legs spoke of training, of a strength that didn’t quite fit the picture.

Her voice, too, was different. He recalled the princess’s bell-like tones from public addresses; this Zelda’s was lower, with a smoky quality, enticing someone in.

And her hair—

Her hair wasn’t just blond; it was gold. Yet, not polished or brassy gold that made up crowns and fine jewelry. But a wild gold that miners plucked from the streams. Her golden locks had a slight silken wave that cascaded well down her back compared to the princess’s pin-straight locks. And the indistinct glow that seemed to radiate from her, almost shining. And her body… 

He brought his hands up, fingers scrubbing his face. He had to get a grip.

The last twelve hours had been nothing short of strange.

He thought of his captain’s suspicious glare over supper, the careful deflection he fed him, instead sending Fledge with food for Zelda before slipping out to the Castle Town tavern. 

As he pressed in between packed bodies, the bard’s lute coaxing him further into the small, charming space, until he found the bright smile he’d been looking for.

He pulled Ilya outside, away from her friends, and the memory of her curious look at his request for clothes still pricked at him. He’d promised to explain, promised to make up for his recent distance after the tournament. But how could he, when his thoughts were consumed by the woman now changing on the other side of the door?

He’d barely slept, her image in that strange, foreign fabric curled in the grass superimposed over his exhaustion. The pre-dawn trip to retrieve the clothes from Ilya, the quick stop at the kitchens... it all felt like a dream leading back to this moment.

And now... What did he plan to do with her after today? Planning was never his strongest skill.

Bringing her clothes would help disguise her temporarily, the more she lingered around the castle, the more everyone would talk. He couldn’t possibly leave her in the barracks alone; the space was not guaranteed to be vacant after this very moment, and he couldn’t treat her like a prisoner when she had done nothing wrong.

It was risky, harboring an unknown within castle walls. He would probably be locked up, certainly stripped of all rank and titles. She would probably be sent to the lockup, to be questioned for information. Once they were satisfied, she would be sent away— or worse, simply disappear.

He had to swallow against the sudden, unknown taste in his mouth.

That would be the worst-case scenario. Instead, he would try to get her out of the castle into Castle Town. She would be secure there until he could figure out what to do next.

He’d find out today if he’d be assigned to the royal guard. That assignment would give him more flexibility to handle this from a political standpoint. Royal guards were sworn to the service of the royal family, but they did have some pull.

Impa was the perfect example of a dual-edged blade, their own military and political mastermind. She knew things no one else knew about the royal family and the castle. King Rhoam heeded her advice with little to no resistance. Link could ask her to help with this… other Zelda.

The other Zelda? The not-princess Zelda?

A less than delicate voice pulled him from thought, “You can come in now.”

He hadn’t expected the practical clothes Ilya had given him to look quite like this on her.

The black riding pants fit her snugly, accentuating the curve of her hips. A simple shirt clung to her torso, and the leather corset pulled tight over it, lifting her chest and clenching her waist. She was admiring the embroidery on the hood as she swung it over her shoulders, delicately tying it around her neck.

He tore his gaze away, fixing it on the far wall. “You should eat, we’ll be leaving soon.”

She gave herself one more glance in the mirror, smoothing her still wavy blond locks over her left shoulder, and made her way to the bedside table, where he placed the small bag with food and water. She popped a berry in her mouth, a small satisfied hum escaping.

“The food is incredible, thank you for everything from last night and today.” She smiled, picking up the goat cheese to identify it by smell. 

“Of course, it’s no trouble.” He ran a hand over the back of his head, a nervous tick he’d tried to suppress over the years. “The kitchens are fairly stocked with fresh fruits and breads for anyone to help themselves to.” 

She nodded and thoughtfully asked, “How does the castle feed everyone in it?” Sitting on the bed, crossing her legs so casually.

She could have asked about her strange surroundings, about Hyrule, about what he planned for her. Instead, she asked about the food. The simplicity of it, the uncomplicated curiosity, caught him off guard. He was more than happy to oblige her curiosity. He instinctively relaxed his shoulders, leaned against the nearest wall, and explained.

“And the Hearty Truffles,” he found himself explaining, “if you cook them, they’ll restore you completely.”

Her eyes widened as she leaned in. “Just one? The truffles from my world are just… brown.”

He watched, delighted, as her eyebrows shot up. A laugh escaped him, small and rusty. Her smile was brighter than the food she’d just finished, and as she urged him to tell her more, he found he couldn’t suppress his own.

“So what are you planning to do with me today?” she asked, finishing every crumb left.

“I have a tournament.” He said. “I can bring you to Castle Town before, and we can regroup after.”

She narrowed her knowing eyes at him, “A tournament?”

“It’s a tournament for the chosen knights, five of us. They test our skills with bows, spears, two-handed weapons, shields, and long swords.” He studied her face to gauge her reaction, but nothing. “They score us in each category, and the highest score will be assigned to the royal guard—“ He stopped himself, unsure if he wanted to tell her the last part, but she tilted her head, waiting for him to continue, “To be assigned to the Princess— Princess Zelda.”

Her jaw dropped. “Princess Zelda? You have a princess named Zelda and didn’t think to mention it to me until now?” She shot to her feet, her hands flying upwards.

“Yes. And—“ He let an exasperated breath loose, “You look very similar to her.”

Her mouth opened, but no words came out. She tried again, “How do we look alike?” Her brows pulled so close together that the wrinkles formed deep between them.

“Besides the name… you both have yellow hair, a similar build. Your face… it’s close. Except—” He wasn’t planning on elaborating, but her eyes were pleading at him to continue. He pulled his hand to the back of his neck to itch an invisible scratch, nervous under the intensity of her green eyes. “Your eyes are different. The shape is maybe the same, but the green is more… I don’t know the word for it. You look like you could be cousins. Or maybe even sisters.” 

Her eyebrows still drew close, but now her mouth twisted into a scowl. “You didn’t think to mention this to me when you first spoke to me?” Before letting him answer, she kept going, “This cannot be a coincidence that I landed in a place where the princess and I share a name and look alike. It’s not a common name where I come from. Is it common here?” Her voice grew shrill.

“No, only women in the royal family are named Zelda.” Heat crept up his neck. Of course, he should have told her immediately; the omission now felt like a deception. He could see the confusion and panic in her eyes, very different from the smiling, happy woman talking about food a few moments ago.

“Don’t you think all this is unsettlingly unusual? Aren't you a knight, trained to capture people like me?” The words escaped her before the expression shifted, and for a moment he saw a flicker of fear in her eyes, as if she’d just realized she’d backed herself into a corner.

“It is, and I am.”

She crossed her arms, “Why are you helping me?”

He shifted his stance. Wondering how much of the truth he could reveal. Frankly, he hadn't known what that truth was.

“I would help anyone in need.”

“Even a stranger? Who isn’t from here? Who could be a threat?”

“You’re no threat.”

Her shoulders fell, the words echoed between them.

His hand twitched again at his side; it was almost overwhelming. “I didn’t know what to do with you when I first found you. I still don’t. I was hoping to have more answers first.” He steeled himself. “I knew that had anyone else found you as you were, they may have treated you differently, more aggressively.” He met her eyes. “I just did what I thought was right and brought you here until we could resolve this.”

She was quiet for a moment, her eyes searching his. Finally, she offered a muted smile. “I’m still not convinced that where I am is real. And that being dead is a more likely conclusion over this reality… but I’m willing to go with it. To go with you.”

“I’ll protect you.”

The words left his mouth before he realized the gravity of them. She gave a small, almost imperceptible shake of her head, her gaze flicking away from his as if to dismiss the weight of his words.

He chose his next words carefully. “These clothes will let you walk through the castle and town without suspicion for the day, if you keep the hood up and your head down. Most of the castle will be watching the tournament.” He almost forgot about that. He glanced out the window. They had been talking for at least an hour. He should get going; otherwise, his captain would be suspicious yet again. “And with that, I have to go.” 

Her eyebrows no longer pulled but slightly relaxed. The fight drained from her posture, and the sharp defensiveness in her eyes softened to a distant, troubled look. She nodded.

“I promise, I’ll get you answers—“ He paused. He wanted to reassure her, but he had nothing to show for it. He should be focusing on the Princess Zelda, not this Zelda. But he couldn’t stop himself from continuing. “And I’ll do everything to keep you safe.” He held out his hand for her to follow.

When she extended her hand, her fingers faintly grazed the calloused tips of his, just beyond the edge of his leather gloves. He tried not to flinch as he held the door for her and ushered her through it.

He heaved open another heavy wooden door. Bright morning light flooded the hallway, forcing him to squint as they stepped outside. They were standing on cobblestones that led out to the fenced area where knights and soldiers ran drills, piled carts and crates stacked against it, notably from lack of use in the past few weeks. 

“This building is the barracks, where the soldiers stay?” she asked. He looked back at the masonry-crafted three-story building, with wooden support beams outlining the frame of it. 

“Yes, the soldiers that typically board here are out on patrol or were moved to the West Barracks.” He said, walking her towards the gate opening.

“Is that where you stay?” she asked, her voice quiet. 

“Yes, it’s on the other side of these buildings.” He pointed west, past the structures that held dorms for the kitchen staff, the chapel, and their collective dining hall. “A short walk.”

“That far?” She arched her neck to try to see the impossible. “How large is this castle?”

He hid a grin. Her head swiveled, trying to take in everything at once, her expression one of pure awe at the stone and walls he had long since found unremarkable. “It’s large, but I don’t have another castle to compare it to. Do you have castles where you come from?” 

“We have them, but they’re mostly ruins. No one’s lived in one for centuries.” She glanced at him, her tone softening. “Our royalty… it’s not the same. They’re more like symbols, I guess. We elect the people who actually pass the laws.” He felt her eyes on him, as if trying to gauge his reaction to this strange new world.

“What about knights?” He asked, deciding to stare at the cobblestones in front of them.

“We have a military, but they are not named as knights, just soldiers. Our warfare is very different from swords and shields.” Her words trailed off.

He didn’t think what her world would do to him. This world was all he knew; he couldn’t imagine a world where knights and royalty were no longer needed or missed. Luckily, before he could put more thought into that reality, they were fast approaching a busier intersection of castle pathways. Link was scanning the area. “We’re heading this way. Can you put your hood up?”

She obliged, damping the sun’s radiating glow upon her crown, and Link led her out of the barracks plaza into the high walls that snaked the river on their left. They rounded a corner and started going through a tunnel, built into the stone. Sunlight peeked through unglazed stone windows as they passed. Exiting the tunnel, castle town now in sight, but the rooftops looked trivial from their vantage. They still had a ways to go.

They had been walking for a quarter-hour, rounding the high stone walls as they weaved downhill. The few people they passed were too focused on their destinations to take notice of them, except for a pack of young girls who stopped to whisper and giggle as Link passed. He ignored them, but caught Zelda watching the exchange with highbrows. Leaning closer, she whispered, “Are they part of your fan club?” He felt the sarcasm lacing every word.

He shook his head, rolling his eyes where she couldn’t see.

After rounding another bend on the path and the town below looking much larger, they almost barreled over someone as they blindly rounded the corner. Zelda’s arm instinctively reached out to the stranger to catch her before she lost her balance. The young woman’s face broke into her classic bright smile, the corners of her eyes crinkling as she looked at Zelda; she then turned to Link.

“Link! What are you doing here?”

Chapter 5: Tournament
Chapter Text
“Ilya, what are you doing here?” Link’s voice dropped incredibly low, his face close to hers.

His eyes widened as he registered the woman, before he grabbed Zelda’s arm, his grip tight, and pulled them both behind a half-crumbling wall. He scanned the surroundings, his shoulders tense, before turning his attention back to the woman.

Ilya. Link knew her well enough to question her presence so casually. Zelda instinctively pulled her hood lower, trying to disappear behind the fabric.

“I promised Agatha last night that I would bring her a basket of fresh breads and fruit for the bard’s breakfast. He’s staying at the tavern a few nights, and I think she’s trying to impress him to stay longer.” Ilya replied, her voice soft and melodic.

She continued, smiling but not meeting Link’s eyes. “You know that Moza bakes the best bread— so good it makes you want to—” she cut off before meeting his stare, a flush climbing her cheeks before she could stop it.

They knew each other well enough indeed. Zelda glanced sidelong to Link, his face still on edge, lines deep from tension.

This Ilya wasn’t entirely wrong; the bread she had eaten last night would certainly make her contemplate proposing to the baker.

She used the distraction to trail the young woman, who was about the same age as herself. She was pretty—a plain beauty, in the best way, with small, delicate features. Petite and mousy, her pointed ears stuck out from short, wheat-colored hair that suited her bone structure perfectly. Her bright, kelp-colored eyes were gazing longingly at Link.

Zelda turned her gaze to Link for a reaction to Ilya’s obvious flirting. Wondering if he felt the same about the pretty girl. He only nodded.

He told her the truth… or most of it. Zelda watched the exchange, a new understanding dawning. He must trust Ilya… completely.

Zelda adjusted her hood position, pulling her hair over her ears, as Link adjusted his stance ever so slightly to lean in front of her.

Maroon banners adorned the towers on either side, their gold embroidered symbols now recognizable as Hyrule’s crest.

The weather had been the perfect mix of sun, breeze, and seasonality. A gentle lick of air blew beneath her hood, and with it, the delightful scents of flowers and earth. She yearned to pull down her hood and soak in the sun, feel the air, and inhale the scents more deeply.

They arrived at the drawbridge minutes later. The crowd had grown significantly, far larger than the original group that had witnessed the alter ceremony. It seemed that the entire castle had planned to be present. Turning left from the bridge, they joined the rest of the crowd.

After the Princess settled in her seat, Zelda’s hood still raised to cover her, she felt an intense stare at the back of her covered head. Her jaw tightened instinctively, and her fingers went stiff against her lap, as though her body had registered something her mind had not yet caught up to. She turned knowingly to the direction of the gaze to see what or who was making her so unsettled, landing on the royal box, where the woman advisor with the gray hair from the alter ceremony was staring at her. She had a purple tattooed eye on her forehead with a line drawn down to the bridge of her nose, the symbol placed precisely where her third eye would be. Her facial features were unreadable, trained, no doubt, to be emotionless and flat when zeroing in on potential threats near the princess.

The energy reminded Zelda of the sporting stadiums back home—the same hum of anticipation, the same boisterous cheers. Zelda spotted Fledge beside Link, his chest puffed with a pride so fierce it was almost comical, polishing an already gleaming helmet as if his own honor depended on it.
