The spear competition followed the same pattern. Where others struck the training dummies, and Groose managed solid hits, Link’s five spears each found the painted heart with pinpoint precision. A quiet murmur of awe began to build in the crowd.

Next was strength. Each knight had to swing an extraordinarily large two-handed weapon at wooden targets. They had to hit all 10 targets within 60 seconds. Zelda watched as each knight carried their large claymore out one by one. This time each knight struggled to make it to the last target. Even more surprising was Groose; despite being the largest knight, he barely made it to the last target in time. She realized then that strength and stamina didn’t necessarily play hand in hand.

Link was up next. He had been smaller than the knights she had seen, so she thought he might falter, but he never broke his pace. He was perfect as he swung the large two-handed sword each time and smashed each wooden target, leaving a few seconds to spare. Zelda involuntarily went slack-jawed at the display. Ilya noticed and laughed. 

“I know…” Ilya said, pressing her lips together as if trying to contain something, “he’s spectacular to watch.”

“Yeah—.” Zelda’s jaw was still hanging open. “But how? That sword is nearly as big as he is. Groose could barely manage it.”

“Link has always been unnaturally strong for his size. He trains hard, of course, but he’s also just blessed with good stock.”

Sure, Zelda thought. Genetics. That explained the archery, the spears, the sword, all of it—genetics. A warm thread pulled throughout her, her heart pounding with an uncharted beat.

For the shield trial, the knights emerged in full silver-plated armor. From a high platform, squires began launching arrows and spears. Pipit and Karane deflected most, but staggered under the onslaught. Groose held his ground like a stone wall, batting projectiles away with brute force. Grante held longest, but eventually yielded. When Link took his place, he was fluid as a raging river, his shield a blur that met every single spear and arrow until the launchers were empty.

Swords, a melee style, were the last event. Each knight continued in full armor and was positioned in the center of the arena. They would fight each other until a blow was landed. One blow, and they were out, until only one was left standing. A low murmur rolled through the stands, a current of anticipation. People leaned forward on their benches, clutching programs as the final combatants entered the arena.

The familiar trumpet sounded, and each knight circled and feinted, testing reach and footing. Zelda couldn’t take her eyes off Link; he moved with such finesse and grace, playing the perfect balance of offense and defense. While her eyes watched him, Groose landed a blow onto Pipit’s shoulder, followed by the herald indicating that he was out. Shortly after, Grante landed a blow on Karane’s shin, and she was now out. All three remaining men formed a triangle; Groose and Grante seemed to strategize telepathically as they both laid their sights on Link. Planned or not, it was easier to take out the best man two-on-one.

Grante circled behind Link while Groose charged from the front. Zelda squirmed in her seat, praying the knight who rescued her wouldn’t be so traitorously eliminated. Just as Groose committed to his attack, Link sidestepped, planting a foot on the charging knight’s shield and vaulting over him. Unable to stop his momentum, Groose barreled directly into Grante. Before they could recover, Link landed behind them and brought his sword down flat on Groose’s armored back. The large man fell to his stomach with a crash. The crowd erupted.

Now there were two. Grante’s plan had backfired. He faced Link directly, and remembering what Ilya had said, Zelda knew this was a contest of stealth against skill. They circled each other, a long, tense standoff that silenced the crowd. Then, in a blur of motion, they met. Steel rang on steel as Grante unleashed a flurry of rapid, deceptive strikes. Link parried each one, not giving an inch. He forced Grante back toward the arena wall, waiting for an opening. Grante lunged, a desperate gamble, and Link twisted aside. After minutes of quiet tension, Link’s sword clanged loudly against Grante’s chest. The crowd exploded into applause. Link extended a hand to his opponent in good spirit as the herald’s trumpet signaled the end of the melee.

It was the most thrilling scene she’d ever witnessed. She buzzed with the high that a winner would feel.

But as the knights exited, that heady feeling shifted to something else. Her curiosity compelled her to peek at the royal box. She expected to see the three in hushed tones, choosing Link as the obvious winner. Instead, Impa’s were fixed on her again. Impa looked at her fiercely, a flicker of something knowing—and dismissive—in her gaze before her eyes narrowed. Zelda turned quickly from the advisor’s sharp stare.

She just had to make it a few more moments, then she could leave and disappear into the crowd.

The knights came back, all lined up perfectly in front of the royal box. When her eyes found Link, the tension in her chest unwound, Impa’s burning stare dissolving like smoke.

Watching him stand there, bruised but victorious, a strange ache bloomed in her chest— a fierce, protective hope for him. And as if she had just shouted that thought into the world, Link’s eyes met hers. He stood tall, incredibly humble, with strands of hair stuck to his forehead with sweat. Faced with his steady gaze, Zelda couldn’t help but soften and smile fondly at him.

She now understood the reason behind Ilya’s and everyone’s infatuation with him. However, she managed to tear her gaze away from the handsome and deserving knight, fearing the look might give her away. The crowd buzzed with excitement as the collective volume decreased against the blaring trumpet, and Impa rose from her seat. 

“Good people of Hyrule,” Impa’s voice was loud and commanding as she stood tall from her seat, “We have seen exceptional displays from the knights before us. Each one has competed honorably and scrupulously with you all as a witness. We do not take the choosing of the Princess’ knight lightly. The knight we choose today shall owe his life to our Princess forever more; “their very life is hers to command until his or her death.”

Zelda gulped, her eyes fixed on Link’s profile. Forever. The word landed tight in her stomach. His entire future, marriage, children, a quiet life in the country with someone like Ilya, would be forfeit. The image of Ilya by his side sent a hot, sharp sting through her, an ugly feeling she didn’t want to name. No wonder Ilya had gone so quiet. This vow wasn’t an honor; it was a cage.

As Zelda tried to shake off the twitchy new feeling, she focused on Impa’s speech. “Captain Auru and I have made our choice. The skills displayed today were exceptional. But skill alone does not make a royal guard. We looked for unwavering loyalty, a history of steadfast service, and a temperament suited to the unique demands of protecting the Princess.” Impa’s eyes scanned the knights, pausing for a fraction of a second on Link. “We have considered all these factors. The winner is… Sir Groose of Kolomo.”

Chapter 6: Field
Chapter Text
What?

Gasps and hushed whispers rippled through the packed arena. Jaws went slack as hundreds of heads turned to Impa, seeking confirmation of what their ears had just heard. Instead, she stood tall, unwavering. Sensing the crowd’s confusion, she continued, “Let us celebrate Sir Groose, now Princess Zelda’s appointed knight.” “Congratulations to him, and to the other knights before us as honorable mentions.”

Well, there were no muddy waters there. Impa was clear as summer air.

Zelda glanced at Ilya, whose jaw hung open, her eyes wide and unblinking as if she’d forgotten how to breathe. A low, disappointed murmur rippled through the stands— the sound of a hundred bets suddenly lost.

Turning to Link, he stood tall with his shoulders pulled back, chin held high. The perfect picture of composure. But when Zelda looked upon him, she saw the shame he held back, within the slight clench of his jaw, or how his blue eyes pulled down.

Impa’s followed silence had finally registered, and half the arena erupted in cheers and applause. The large, broad-shouldered, red-coiffed Sir Groose flinched, finally registering the declaration. He scanned the faces of his fellow knights for some sign this was a joke, his gaze landing on Link. Link gave him a slight, confirming nod. Sir Groose nervously made his way towards the royal box, slow and careful. Impa, despite proclaiming the chosen winner, had her eyes fixed on Link’s, as if telepathically trying to tell him something. Link didn’t register any acknowledgment.

Groose made it to Princess Zelda and the two advisers. Princess Zelda stood from her seat, and the crowd fell so quiet that she could hear the fabric of her gown settle against the floor.

Groose picked up on the gravity of the situation, kneeling and bowing as gracefully as the large man could muster. Princess Zelda opened her mouth; a light soprano voice followed. “I am honored that Sir Groose has been selected as my new appointed knight. He will surely honor the traditions of Hyrule, in service of the royal family while proudly upholding his family’s name.” A ghost of a smile settled on her face for all to witness.

The crowd clapped and cheered again. “The royal family and I thank all the knights that participated before us for proudly and honorably displaying their skills and fortitude. They will continue to serve the royal military and be given assigned appointments hereafter.”

She scanned over all four knights, her eyes lingering longer on Link. He had to be crestfallen. Surely Sir Groose was capable, but everyone saw Link’s spectacular performance. Why would anyone settle for second best? 

Why? The royal advisers had to have seen it. Link was more talented than all four other knights combined—Zelda had witnessed it herself. What could have possibly been the reason?

Princess Zelda descended from the seclusion of the royal box, exiting through the opposite tunnel. Her new, imposing bodyguard and the two royal advisers who had chosen him followed her. Once all four had disappeared, the knights were dismissed, exiting through the tunnel to the left of Ilya and her seats. Zelda attempted to catch Link’s gaze and convey her sympathy— sympathy she suspected he wouldn’t want, least of all from her. But he held his face high and straight ahead as he vanished into the tunnel. Finally, it was the crowd’s turn to make their way to the exits.

Zelda and Ilya stood. Zelda glanced over, but Ilya’s gaze was fixed on the ground, her mouth a thin line. It was the longest silence Zelda had experienced with the girl all day. They reached the narrow exit, and as they squeezed past the strangers, the dam of silence broke. “I cannot believe Sir Groose was chosen!” Ilya burst out. A few heads turned in surprise at the petite girl’s sudden outburst.

“Why was he chosen? I’m not familiar with your customs, but Link was undoubtedly…incredibly, impressive.” Zelda paused to whisper the last part, mindful of potential listeners and their opinions. They were shoulder to shoulder within the crowd, floating mindlessly through the colorful wooden archway before splitting off on their own.

“I’m not sure,” Ilya said, her teeth pulling on her lip. “Whenever previous tournaments or appointments took place, the best performer has been chosen. Something must have happened between when we last saw Link and now.” Ilya’s mouth fell into a pout, and she ran a hand through her hair. “I’m going to find him,” she said. “—uh, we should go find him.” She corrected herself.

Zelda hesitated. She barely knew these people; inserting herself into their medieval politics felt sketchy. Besides, Link had been adamant she stay away from the royal court. She was in the town now, just as he’d wanted.

“Maybe just you should go. I’m sure he’ll be happy to see you right now,” Zelda’s tongue felt heavy. “I can stay in here in town. Link had been trying to get me here before the tournament happened anyway.”

“Oh, sure, that’s— good.” Ilya’s eyes kept darting past Zelda, scanning the path back toward the castle. She seemed desperate to rush to Link’s side. “The central square is south, just over there.” She pointed opposite of the castle. “There is a market, shops, and a tavern. You can walk around, but the sun will set soon.” With a gesture to the west, she indicated the sun, which looked to be a few hours from slipping under the mountains. “It’s not dangerous in town, but— just don’t wander outside the town walls after sunset.” Ilya grabbed her hand and squeezed, “I’ll come back later and find you. Let’s meet in the tavern.”

Zelda offered a sympathetic smile to Ilya, “Thanks, Ilya. I’ll be alright.” Ilya shot a quick smile back and pulled her hand away. A sudden cold spread across Zelda’s skin where their hands had touched. She watched as Ilya turned and walked briskly towards the domineering castle walls. 

The moment Ilya was out of sight, Zelda froze. South? North? The directions meant nothing. She didn’t know these people. A frantic check of her pockets had her realizing she had no money. Her hands went to her neck, caressing the strands and rubbing in a familiar, nervous rhythm.

Why had she insisted on staying? It wasn’t about Link’s wishes. The truth coiled in her stomach: she couldn’t face his disappointment. This strange pull she felt toward him was just misplaced gratitude. He was a knight, and she was the person in need. It wasn’t her place to comfort him; she was a complication he didn’t deserve. She had to remember that.

Get answers, go home, never see him again.

The thought steadied her. She took a deep breath and started walking in the direction Ilya had pointed.

Her boots hit a puddle on the cobblestone pathway, water splashing. Her head whipped around, checking if she had splashed any passersby. 

She was instead surrounded by stone buildings with blue rooftops that lined her path, leading her to the heart of the unassuming town. Recognized maroon banners with Hyrule’s crest proudly on display along the way, leading up to the castle.

Each humble home was no more than two or three stories high, all uniform in shape and exterior, except for the small personal touches by their owners. A flower basket or two, a chest of children’s toys, clothes hanging in the backyard lines, each home telling the story of the owners’ unique tastes and lifestyle. The panic she felt moments earlier started to melt away as she marveled around her. She breathed deeply and smelled the fresh scents around her; the warm summer blooms of flowers and fresh-baked breads were intoxicating, stronger than the streets of home, smelling of exhaust and hot pavement and the faint rot of uncollected rubbish.

As the cobblestones led her toward growing sounds of laughter and conversation, she emerged into a central square. A stunning fountain ran with clear water, surrounded by vibrant market stalls and open shop windows. Most vendors were packing up, some giving away leftover baked goods. Her eyes could barely stay on one scene; adults in hushed conversations, children playing tag, and wives calling husbands home for supper. Yet despite the busy surroundings, something settled over Zelda, easing the frantic tightness in her chest.

She languidly walked around, eyeing the stalls that were still open. Selling crafts and home wares: wooden bowls and cutlery, small steel knives, toys, flowers, and hand-blown glass cups. As she picked up and admired a delicately crafted purple glass, she was astounded by the talent that went into creating it.

Stands were littered with food, from ripe fruits and vegetables, smoked meats and cheeses, and freshly baked breads. She hadn’t realized how hungry she was. She was lingering by the stall with meat kabobs and had to stop herself from drooling at the delicious sight. A middle-aged woman who had a no-nonsense look about her stood behind the makeshift wooden stand, staring at Zelda. “That will be 15 rupees.”

Zelda had no idea what a rupee was, but if she had to deduce it, it was their form of currency. “It looks very good and smells even better, but I forgot my purse. I have no rupees.” Better to lie about her nonexistent money rather than say she was shopping without it.

The owner eyed her, her gaze catching on the fine stitching of Zelda’s hood. She grunted. “Tournament day. Everyone’s distracted.” She shoved the meat stick into Zelda’s hand. “Don’t make it a habit.”

Zelda stammered her thanks, took a large, unsophisticated bite, and almost melted on the spot. She gave the owner a wide-eyed, grateful nod and walked away.

She found an empty bench by the fountain to eat. As she savored the kabob, she watched the people around her. They looked so normal, their clothes were simple and practical, not costumes from a history book. They had the same human faces, the same gestures. Only the slight point of their ears marked them as different, a detail so subtle she felt she could almost belong.

And within that divulge to belong, she lowered her hood; no one was paying attention to her anyway. She wanted to bask in the setting sun’s rays, to feel their warmth on her blonde locks.

An hour or so had passed; Twilight rolled over the land, merging with the orange and pink sky in the west. Zelda watched the Hylians from her seat, a small, unconscious smile touching her lips as she took in the simple rhythm of their lives.

She stood from the bench, remembering Ilya had mentioned meeting at the tavern soon. She investigated the buildings in the center for a familiar mug sign or smell of spirits, but nothing had jumped out at her in recognition.

She headed south, away from the fading buzz of the central plaza. The path forked between two dimly lit alleyways. Down one, she spotted a festive crowd spilling from a doorway, their boisterous laughter echoing off the stone. That had to be the place.

As she suspected, she was standing in front of the tavern. Smells of hoppy ales and heady lagers now filled her nostrils, as she stepped in unnoticed. It was as she had expected, poorly lit and wood-paneled with a long bar on her right, tended by a bartender whose mouth was set in a firm, unwelcoming line. On the left, wooden tables and chairs filled the large space, well-placed partitions dividing sections of large groups from smaller private areas meant for more intimate conversations. Servers buzzed around serving food and drinks. She didn’t have any money, or rather, rupees, but she eyed an unoccupied table near the back and made her way to it.

She passed festive groups, catching snippets of slurred stories— bragging about monster patrols, arguments over unfamiliar armies called the Gerudo and Rito. Then one conversation cut through the noise, its topic sharp and painfully familiar: the shocking turn of events at the tournament. 

She made it to the secluded table and sat. The soldiers in conversation about the day’s tournament were speaking loudly enough that she would have had to actively try not to eavesdrop.

“What were the royal advisors thinking, deciding on the giant oaf over one of the best knights to ever grace Hyrule’s barracks?” The middle-aged soldier with a salt and pepper beard said to his slightly younger friend with chestnut hair.

“Choosing that giant over Link lost me 100 rupees!” An older gray-haired soldier, mostly hidden from her view, exclaimed angrily and pounded his fist on the table.

“Either they have other delegation plans for Link or he disgraced himself and the knighthood right before the ceremony.” The chestnut-haired man said. Zelda’s tongue felt heavy in her mouth as she listened. “If they had planned to assign Link before the tournament, they wouldn’t have let him compete. Why go through the trouble?” He leaned down to whisper to his comrades, but his volume didn’t actually lower. “He must have done something dishonorable. It’s the only thing that makes sense. A blind man could see he was the best choice to protect the Princess after that display alone!”

A dagger twisted in Zelda’s stomach. It was her fault.

The soldier’s word echoed in her mind. Dishonorable. Link had protected her, hidden her, lied for her. They must have found out. They wouldn’t see it as chivalry; they would see it as treason, aiding an unknown intruder, a spy sent to infiltrate their sanctuary.

She bristled against the cold chill straightening her spine, her hands came together in the familiar fidgeting motion to the back of her neck. A heavy weight suddenly settled on the seat beside her, the air filling with the sour reek of ale. She flinched as a voice slurred in her ear.

“Hey there. What’s a— pretty thing like you doing by yourself?” A toothy smile flashed in the gloom. The smell alone was enough to make her drunk.

“I, um— was just leaving.” The intrusion sobered her, and she pushed her chair back to stand.

“Pretty girls shouldn’t be— walkin’ alone.” He hiccuped, squinting at her. “Say... you look familiar. A lot like... like the Princess!” The man swayed, but his words, though slurred, were loud enough to carry.

Zelda’s hand shot to her ear; it had been exposed during her nervous fidgeting. She quickly pulled up her hood and turned her head. The three soldiers that had been discussing Link’s fate turned to her when the drunk man said ‘Princess’. Before she could let them approach, she darted out of the tavern and down the alleyway.

The sun had set, and the darkness was on her side. She made her way down the opposite way she’d come. Unsure of where she’d end up, as long as it was far away from suspecting soldiers and drunk men that said she looked like their famed princess. 

She kept going, running through the dark alleys. Of course, the alleys were unlit, she thought bitterly. Because there is no electricity.

Sure, darkness was on her side to hide, but it didn’t do her any good if she didn’t know where she was.

The cobblestones had turned more uneven, and dirt filled the larger cracks. She came upon a large, thick, stoned wall; there were torches lit in a uniform row. She assumed she was on the edge of the town, facing the large stonework of the battlement. She followed along the wall at a brisk pace; maybe no one had been following her, and she could slow down.

Or maybe they were right behind her and knew everything. She picked up her pace again. 

The wall and lanterns she had been following finally gave way to a small archway. Large enough for a person to slip through, she looked around and, seeing no one, ducked inside. The room was small and cold. There was a ladder leading up to the second story and another archway on the opposite side.

This must have been constructed as a quick shortcut to town, suitable for single tradespeople or travelers who didn’t want to use the main entrance. Slowly, she fitted her head around the archway and noticed the field was pitch black. She could hide in this den to be sure, but the warm summer breeze hit her face from the slotted window. The smells of earth were… enticing.

The silence from the field was absolute, raising a fresh wave of chills. It was an unknown darkness. But behind her was the town, with its soldiers and questions. The open land, however frightening, felt like the only escape. A thread around her middle, pulling her to choose the darkness.

And she walked out into the pitch-black field.

Chapter 7: Field, p. II
Chapter Text
—“Sir Groose of Kolomo,” Impa’s commanding voice rang out.

What?

Groose? Link’s spine went rigid, a guard against the sudden, ringing silence from the crowd. He wasn’t the only one; he could feel their confusion as his own. He lifted his eyes past the bewildered faces to Impa, who was staring directly at him. Her gaze was a physical force, tightening the already painful clench in his jaw.

Impa's expressions were a language he'd learned to read, a necessary skill for any knight. The slight, almost imperceptible narrowing of her eyes, the tightening at the corner of her mouth—it wasn't anger, but a summons. An urgent one.

He knew Impa. Her words carried the weight of law, and her loyalty to the crown was as old and unyielding as the Sheikah themselves. Every choice she made was deliberate, every glance a calculation. Which made this one so impossible to understand.

So why didn’t she choose him?

Her stare pressed on him like a punch to an already bruised rib. His father had always said that a knight's worth was measured in silence and service, not glory— words that had never felt so hollow as they did now, with hundreds of eyes watching his every emotion.

He had spent years on this. Every drill, every callus, every missed beat of something more— all of it pointed here, and she had looked past him as though he were no better than a knave. His jaw tightened as Princess Zelda turned to Groose beside him, her voice warm, and Link fixed his gaze on some middle distance and made himself stay seated.

Groose had even looked to Link, his eyes wide, brows reaching for his hairline in a silent, desperate question. He took a staggering step forward, then another, his movements stiff and clumsy as he approached the Princess, a man walking toward a destiny he never asked for.

Impa still glared at him. He fixed his gaze on the far wall, counting the stones in the archway, anything to avoid the weight of her stare. A few more moments. Then he could escape this tunnel, find his horse, and just run. Let the wind tear the questions from his mind.

Then he remembered Zelda, not the Princess, but the woman he'd carried to the barracks just yesterday. The thought of her made the knot in his jaw loosen, a slow warmth spreading across his face. Ilya was with her. Capable Ilya, who could find answers and a way home for her. He pictured them together, a problem he didn't have to solve, a life he couldn't fix.

The Princess finished her speech. Link scanned the crowd, his gaze shifting until he landed on Impa in the royal box. He expected the same impassive stare, but she wasn’t looking at him. Following her gaze, he saw a hooded woman sitting next to Ilya. And on Impa’s face, a face he’d only ever seen as a mask of calm duty, was something new and unsettling.

But as she stared at the hooded woman, her composure seemed to shift. Her brow furrowed, just slightly, her focus absolute— the way a hunter might stare down unexpected prey. Link felt a strange, protective urge to rush to the woman’s side and pull her from Impa’s imposing gaze.

Impa turned her glare forward, and Link was grateful that he hadn’t made any impulsive decisions at that moment as the royal box group began their descent to exit. He and the other knights bowed low as the Princess swept past him, then Groose, the Captain, and bringing up the rear, Impa. They slowly rose from their practiced positions and Link led the way for the knights and their appointed squires to exit through the opposite tunnel. He knew Ilya and Zelda were there, but he couldn’t manage to look them in the eye.

He felt something inside him collapse, a hollow space where his certainty used to be. Farore’s Courage had left him.

Once he, the three other knights, and the five squires made it to the changing tent outside the arena, the room erupted.

“What the hell just happened?” Grante asked, his brows shooting toward his hairline.

“How in the depths was Groose chosen?” Karane rubbed her temples.

“Link, what the fuck did you do to piss off Impa?!” Pipit said, ever so eloquent.

All eyes were on him, a fresh weight of expectation he couldn’t bear. The questions swirled into a hot, buzzing pressure behind his eyes. “I didn’t do anything,” he spat, the anger a welcome shield.

“You had to have done something,” Grante eyed Link knowingly. “Impa doesn’t make mistakes. She saw something. You were the obvious winner; they’ve never chosen a winner not based on merit before.”

He would know best, being the only Sheikah among them.

Fledge stood by the far wall, his usual quiet post. But when Link caught his eye, Fledge looked away so quickly it was like a flinch. His shoulders were slumped, his mouth a tight, unhappy line, and the skin around his eyes was pinched with a tension Link had never seen on his friend’s face before.

Their questions were nothing new, but still unanswerable, echoing in his skull. He turned from the noise, the pressure building until he had to move. He threw himself onto a bench at the edge of the room, letting his rigid posture serve as a wall. He motioned to Fledge to help him with the armor; it weighed him down, in every sense of the word. Fledge promptly came over to carry out his duty.

As Fledge worked tediously to pull laces and straps, he remained quiet. Deafeningly so against the scrape of leather and metal.

“What is it, Fledge?”

Fledge’s apprehension in his response set Link on edge. “Do you think not being chosen has anything to do with Zelda?” A pregnant pause. “Not the Princess.”

Link only stared straight ahead.

The thought had already surfaced in his own mind, a cold possibility he’d shoved back down. He refused to give it voice. Why would she have anything to do with his destined appointment to the princess? Only Fledge and himself knew about her, and Ilya, as of this morning, only people in his life he trusted. If anyone had seen him with her, they would have reported it. The captain, despite their earlier confrontation, would never have let him compete for such an honor if there were any suspicion against him.

“I don’t think so, Fledge. It’s just a coincidence.”

Fledge stayed quiet, making Link’s skin itch. 

A few minutes later, Link was free of his polished silver armor, though the phantom weight lingered. He promptly exited the space, leaving the squabbling knights and squires to debate his own shortcomings for him. Fledge didn’t follow. 

Link didn’t have a plan. He hadn’t been humble. He was supposed to be in the sanctum now, discussing his new duties with the royal advisors. He should have been hearing how proud his father would be, learning the details of his new life— the lodgings next to the princess’s rooms, the fitting for royal armor. The entire shape of his future, gone.

But it wasn’t him, it was Groose in the sanctum talking about new armor, new apartments, and what his daily routine now looked like.

He made it back to the barracks; it was unsurprisingly empty. He grabbed his saddlebags from the chest at the end of his bed. He checked the stock inside: a bedroll, blanket, and flint. The leather water skin was empty.

Next, he dug out his rupee pouch. The weight of it was surprising; years of a knight’s salary, with little to spend it on, had left him with more than enough to disappear for a while.

He tucked everything in his saddlebag, grabbed his sword, and headed for the exit before anyone could question him further. Though he felt like he was missing something—

He stepped out into the late afternoon sun. The sky was a vibrant smear of pink and orange, a beautiful sight that only seemed to mock the bitterness in his throat. Then a small, delicate voice called out for him.

“Link,” it was Ilya’s voice, but it lacked the familiar, bright tone he was so accustomed to.

“Ilya, what are you doing here?” he demanded, but immediately felt terrible for his testy retort. “I’m sorry, I meant— how did you find me?”

Ilya gave him a small smile; he knew she wouldn’t take his tone personally. “I was worried; I saw everything that happened. I’m sure everyone is asking you, and it’s frustrating, but do you know why you weren’t chosen?”

“I don’t know why.” He said, the words feeling worn from overuse. “Everyone seems to be speculating with their own thoughts on the matter.”

“I’m so sorry, Link. I’m sure Auru or Impa will explain when you see them. Maybe they are giving you a more important appointment.” Her voice almost sounded optimistic, but he knew better as he adjusted the bag slung over his shoulder.

“You’re leaving.” Her eyes were drawn to the strap. “I did figure you might want to leave the castle for a few days. So I brought you some apples, jerky, and cheese.” She handed him a neatly wrapped cloth.

“Thank you, Ilya.” He looked his friend in the eye as he grabbed the cloth; her eyes sparkled.

A pink flush crept up her cheeks, and he pretended not to notice. Her kindness sparked a sudden, cold thought. Something was wrong. Something— someone— was missing.

“Ilya, where’s Zelda?” The question burst out of him, a sudden cold shock that cut through the fog of his own failure. He’d forgotten his ward.

“She and I were at the tournament. She stayed in town as I came to find you. She thought, given the circumstances, that it might be best to stay out of the way, especially since you wanted her out of the castle. I told her that I would come get her in the evening at the tavern in town and regroup.” Her tone wavered as she finished.

That was true; he did want her out of the castle, but not alone or at least not without a plan. “Which tavern was she going to?”

“Uh, I didn’t specify…” Ilya’s familiar smile became tight-lipped.

Link’s tongue felt like lead; a cold prickle, sharp as a needle, traced its way up his spine. “I have to go.”

“I’ll go with you,” Ilya said.

“Can you stay here, in case she comes back? Either nearby the east barracks or perhaps the gatehouse?” Barracks, gatehouse, Fledge— the possibilities fractured in his mind, too many places to check, too little time. “Maybe have Fledge help; have him wait at the opposite of you?”

“Yes,” Ilya pulled on her lips. “She’ll be alright; she has wits about her.” Her tone was steady, but it did little to reassure him.

Link left the saddlebags at Ilya’s feet, leaving all but his sword behind.

By the time he made it to the center square, twilight had arrived. The sky was a deep royal blue, with faint bits of orange and purple bleeding into it from his right. Fortunately, the main path from the castle to the town was well-lit with lanterns. 

He was walking at a brisk pace, and at this rate, it would take him a quarter-hour to reach the first tavern. He was disgruntled with Ilya for not specifying a particular tavern for Zelda to meet at. Did she already forget that she was a foreigner here?

But it wasn’t Ilya’s responsibility. It was his. The thought hit him with the force of a physical blow, knocking the anger right out of him. First the tourney, now this. Twice in one day. The cold weight in his gut didn’t just double; it threatened to drag him under.

Why would Zelda want to stay in town? Alone? He did tell her that’s where he wanted her, but— did she have no fear? Castle Town was fairly safe, not as safe as a castle full of knights and soldiers, but it was rare that any real trouble occurred; the occasional bar fight, petty theft, or general vandalism on properties.

She’d be alright. The thought was thin, against the rising unease.

He made it to the first tavern, which happened to be the popular spot for castle workers and where Ilya’s bard was performing a series of shows. It was the nicer of the two taverns, just west of the entrance to the castle. With a quick pass of the space, there was no sight of her, so he made his way east. 

The next tavern was a sour-smelling den wedged into a narrow alleyway. Inside, the air was thick with smoke and cheap ale, drawing the kind of men who kept their hoods up and their voices low. He scanned the shadowed corners, no sign of her. He was turning to leave when he heard his name slurred from a nearby table.

“LINK!” A vaguely familiar voice. He recognized the soldier’s face but didn’t know his name. He rolled his eyes at the sloppy display and made his way over to the boisterous man. “Link, my boy—” the soldier said. “—I’m very sorry about the tourney today, you were robbed.” He sounded earnestly sincere through the heavy smell of spirits wafting off of him.

“I lost 100 rupees over it!” The older gray-haired soldier slammed his heavy mug down, spilling what little remained all over the table. 

Link feathered his jaw, quietly nodded to the men, “I appreciate that.” 

“Did that Sheikah tell you why?”

They knew Impa’s name, everyone knew Impa, but contempt for the Sheikah still ran deep in the older generations.

Link shook his head. That’s enough. He wasn’t going to get sucked into their contempt over his losing. “I have to go. I’m meeting a friend of mine.” He nodded to each of the men. Technically, he outranked them, and they should be calling him Sir, but Link was not one to stand on principle. And, he always felt uncomfortable that he already outranked the majority of the men older than him. He turned on his heel until another conversation stopped him cold.

“—the girl with those ears, she looked like— the princess! I’m tellin’ ya! Maybe even— prettier! I wouldn’t lie.” Hiccups interrupted the flow of words.  Link knew instantly. He turned to see a drunk man talking to an uninterested group next to him.

Link slammed both hands on the table, grabbing the drunk’s full attention. “Where did this girl you speak of go?”

The drunk looked at him suspiciously, then slowly registered his question. “The pretty girl, the one who looked like Princess— Zelda?”

“Right. Tell me where she went.” His patience frayed. He leaned forward, his knuckles white as he pressed his palms into the sticky wood of the tabletop.

“She left— got all spooked like a wild horse. Darted out of here to the left.”

Link was gone before the drunk could say more. A knot of tension burned beneath the weight of the sword at his back.

He went down the alleyway, trying to gauge where she’d end up. The alley split into two paths, instinctively, he took the left path.

As he walked parallel to the high walls, he scanned the ground near a small postern gate, one used for quick passage. In the soft earth, he saw a fresh track, a small boot print, not a soldier's. He followed the faint trail leading away from the wall.

She was here.

She went out into the field. His stomach coiled into a cold knot. These fields weren’t empty pastures; they were hunting grounds for things that lurked in shrouds. The thought spurred him into a run, his boots slipping on the dark, wet grass.

He got deep into the plain, that he could barely see the town walls anymore, just faint glowing orbs where torches hung. He grabbed the hilt of his sword over his shoulder and unsheathed it. Something was pulling his sense of direction; logic told him to go to the right where the light was still faintly visible, but his instincts told him to go left, deeper into the darkness. His ears were buzzing. He calmed himself in a brief meditation, then he heard it.

A scream to his left. He took off running, adrenaline already coursing through his blood.

He made it to a single tree where the scream originated; Zelda was hiding behind it. Her hood was down, her pupils so dark the green wasn’t visible. She tried to use the tree to hide, but two Bokoblins surrounded her on either side. They had an excellent sense of smell for how stupid they were, so hiding wasn’t going to work.

Oddly, they weren’t attacking, just circling her, as if awaiting some signal. He didn’t wait to find out what it was.

He snuck behind the one closest to him and angled his sword and stabbed straight and true. Taken by surprise, the unarmed Bokoblin fell forward to the ground, dead. He couldn’t remember the last time he had raised his voice like that. The fear he knew from battle was a clean, sharp thing that honed his senses. This was different. A jagged, hot poison clawing its way up his throat, making him reckless.

He had failed to earn his knighthood, failed to honor his father, and failed to protect the person who needed him most. He didn’t deserve to guard anyone.

“I’m sorry,” he said. The words sounded hollow and small in the vast quiet. Even his apology was a failure. “Let me take you back.” Her head hung low. Even she couldn’t look at him anymore. She pulled her hood over her head to shield herself from his gaze.

They made the long walk back, passing through the familiar cobblestone streets, leading to the abandoned barracks. Both were silent the whole walk, and thankfully they passed no one.

It must have been close to midnight. With every step toward the castle, his limbs grew heavier. The high walls loomed over them, silent stone witnesses to the day’s humiliation. Each battlement was a fresh reminder of the honor he’d lost. 

As they neared the barracks, he ushered her through the fenced garden and held the door for her. The small act of chivalry felt hollow.

They made their way up to the second floor and down the dark hallway. He was careful to keep his distance as she walked in front of him, as if even breathing on her would violate the wall she’d built against him.

As they neared her makeshift bedroom, the hair on the back of his neck prickled. A floorboard creaked from within the room, a sound that wasn’t the wind. His hand went to his sword’s hilt as he moved in front of her.

“Stay behind me,” he murmured. She quietly acknowledged, and he sensed her tensing against his back.

He steeled himself in front of the slightly ajar door and pushed it open. By the time his eyes registered what was in front of him, his body went perfectly still.

A woman sat opposite the door. She had moved the chair to a better position to face the guests she’d been patiently waiting for.

Slack-jawed, he managed to muster, “Impa?”

You will journey to the four regions and speak with their leaders.” She pointed to four white envelopes on a far table. “These letters will grant you an audience. Present them, answer all questions with honesty, and listen. Listen to everything they tell you, and then report back to me.” 

Zelda shot her gaze from the letters to Link to see if any of this sounded as insane to him as it did to her. His brows were drawn in his sharp features, but he stayed quiet.

She would have to be the one to ask. “Why do we need to visit regions?” Impa glared at her, eyebrow raised. “I don’t mean to be presumptuous, but can’t you send letters directly and wait for a response?”

“Because their people have legends not known to Hylians. You must go in person. With my encouragement—” she gestured to the envelopes “—and you there to tell your story, they will be more willing to share. I suspect one of them has the insight you need. Also, we can’t risk letters about your… foreign background… getting intercepted.”

Zelda paused, contemplating the heavy burden of information dropped in her lap. “And what does that have to do with getting home?”

She had a sinking feeling that seemed to be secondary to the mission at hand.

“I am not a scholar, versed in all our realm’s secrets. I rely on my dreams, your sudden appearance, and my interpretation of fate. I theorize that the answers you—and I—seek will be found in the outer regions. However, you are the only one you can test my theory.”

Zelda rolled her shoulders, the weight of Impa’s words pressing down. A guaranteed way home? It sounded like a fantasy. This quest, this reliance on dreams and legends, felt like a fool’s errand. But to refuse the only hand offered in this exotic world was to surrender completely.

“Okay. I’ll do it,” Zelda said. “But I don’t want to force him.” She looked at Link while emphasizing.

“Link is a knight of Hyrule. He does what he is told.” Impa spoke for him.

“I don’t want someone who is resentful to protect me. That’s not going to end well.” Zelda shot her a disillusioned look.

“Regardless of his feelings, he will do his duty. Isn’t that correct, Sir Link?” Impa deliberately enunciated his title.

“Yes. It will be my honor to guard her—” He caught her eye, she narrowed at him, daring him silently to choose his words wisely, “—ladyship.”

That single hesitation was enough. It confirmed everything she feared. He wasn’t honored; he was obligated. Just as he’d yelled at her last night, he would resent every moment of this forced duty. She was nothing more than a consolation prize for the princess he’d actually wanted to serve. When he looked at her, she was certain all he saw was the pathetic girl he’d found by a tree.

“Great,” Zelda said through clenched teeth.

Impa continued, “You will both leave tomorrow morning to go to Rito Village. Spend the rest of the day preparing for your journey. Link, you will be anointed before you leave in a private ceremony at first light tomorrow. Zelda, you can ride, I hope?”

Her frustration quickly shifted, disarming her. “A horse?”

Impa nodded, the tightness in her jaw awaiting an answer.

A faint memory of a frustrated mare not following the grip on her reins surfaced. The few lessons she had as a child quickly made clear she lacked the patience to keep up with it, but she guessed Impa didn’t really care for that excuse.

“Somewhat.”

“Link, have Ilya provide Zelda with her own horse and run through the basics while you prepare for the journey.” Impa stood, making Zelda feel like a child as her short frame seemed to loom over both of them. “I wish I had more information for you. I believe in time, you’ll receive the answers you’re looking for. Know that while I could be mistaken, I am rarely wrong.” She gave them both a look that pinned them in place. And just like that, she was gone. The grand door snapped shut, the sound echoing in the sudden emptiness. Zelda’s breath hitched. Link simply stared at the spot where Impa had stood, his jaw a hard line. 

The silence sat between them like a forbidden door, and she refused to be the one to open it. She would not let another man make her feel small. It wasn’t her fault he was bound by orders, and she refused to carry the burden of his resentment.

He stood. “We should find Ilya and get you a horse,” he said quietly. He then went to the door and held it open, waiting patiently for her.

Zelda scoffed. The nerve of him not to deny, comment, or remark on anything Impa said. She unhurriedly got up and walked to the door. While perhaps childish, if he was going to treat her like duty, she wasn’t going to make it easy on him.

Only when she stopped inches from his face, she shot him her most withering glare and said, “Of course, my honorable knight, lead the way.” She didn’t wait to see his reaction as she breezed past him, and she wasn’t about to give him the satisfaction of turning around.

Chapter 9: Vow
Chapter Text
“Am I still your squire or…” Fledge trailed off.

Link stopped brushing his chestnut mare. “I’m not sure. I am to be Zelda’s sword, her personal knight, and similar to the royal guard, they do not have squires.” Link’s own words echoed back to him in taunting pulses in the large, open stable he and Fledge currently occupied.

Zelda and Ilya were preoccupied, checking her compatibility with the available steeds in the stable next door. The only ears listening to their conversation were those of the horses next to them.

Fledge scrunched his nose. “I’ll be disappointed, of course. But maybe it’s my chance to train to become a knight on my own.” 

Link offered Fledge a half smile, but his gaze drifted past him, unfocused, toward the stable door.

He opened his mouth to offer some words of support, but nothing came. Impa’s pronouncements from the morning echoed in his head, a leaden weight settling in his gut. He remembered the walk to the stables, each of Zelda’s footsteps ahead of him a sharp, angry thud on the cobblestones. He’d trailed her like a shadow, the silence between them heavier than his shield.

He knew Zelda was upset. Sure, he could be oblivious at times, but she made her disdain very clear with the last words she spoke to him. Her sarcasm was a shield, and her tongue the weapon, sharp enough to find his deepest insecurities and make them bleed. “ “My knight” sounded filthy coming out of her mouth.

And then the morning…

His routine to train every morning would not change because he had an assignment. That much he could hold on to. Now that his new residence was further from his usual spot, he found the small plaza just below his new apartment perfect. He could practice and still be close if the unlikely possibility arose that Zelda needed him.

He didn’t know she would be watching him, and he had not intended to size her up inappropriately, but it was hard to miss. Her white nightdress hugged her curves like a second skin, her long hair messy and tangled from sleep, and the cold breeze ruffled it. She was stunning—

He looked away quickly to provide her with decorum, even though it was hard to. It was his job to look away. It was also his job to notice everything, and he had noticed, and part of him wanted to look back, and that part of him disgusted the rest of him, because she was not a thing to be noticed. She was his charge. She was a woman from another world who had no one, and he was the one person sworn to put her above himself, and here he was cataloguing the shape of her in a nightdress at dawn.

“What else did Impa say this morning?” Fledge asked, and the question pulled him back to the stable, to the smell of hay and horse sweat made him agonizingly sober. He had stopped brushing Epona and she nickered for him to continue.

He trusted Fledge completely, but he himself hadn’t had time to comprehend it all yet. “Like I said, I am Zelda’s appointed knight, we are to travel to each region to gather information on how to send her home.” He left out all the heavy foreshadowing.

Fledge eyed him curiously, but he wouldn’t push the issue. “How are the new apartments?”

Link huffed a small laugh, the tension leaving his face, “It’s very nice. Much better than listening to Cawlin snoring every night.”

He didn’t mention the conjoining door or how he stared at it the night before for far too long.

“I bet. Those apartments are used to impress the dignitaries when they stay. I suppose they’ve been left vacant for some time; it makes sense Impa put you both there.”

Most likely, they would have the whole wing to themselves for however long he served her. It was rare that the King hosted guests since the Queen’s untimely passing.

But something else was bugging Link. Impa barely spoke to him over the years, yet now, he’s to be some hero?

While she was unyielding to emotion, her ability to convince one to like peanuts when they were allergic was a demonstration of cunning grace. Yet there was something uncertain in her eyes as she spoke. She even squeezed Zelda’s shoulder. He never saw her engage with anyone that way.

He was just a knight, a sword and shield for others to wield. His job wasn’t to question prophecies or grand plans, but to follow orders. To do as he was told until he died or was dismissed. There was no room for this knot of conflict in his gut. 

“I like Zelda.” Fledge’s voice knocked into his skull. “I hope you find a way to get her home.”

“Yeah— me too.” Unsure which he was agreeing to.

Ilya and Zelda appeared in the doorway. Zelda’s posture had loosened as she smiled at something Ilya said. But as the two approached them, Zelda’s eyes found his, her smile fading on the approach.

“We found Zelda the perfect horse, a young stud by the name of Storm.” Ilya said, her mossy eyes like sunlight beaming upon him, “She did a few loops with him, a little rough at first, but they seem to get along swimmingly.”

“A stud, huh? Seems you’d be better suited to a mare.” The snide comment left his lips before he could stop it. And just as quickly, her piercing gaze landed on him.

“I get along with studs just fine when they are nice to me.” Zelda said.

Fledge found something interesting about the far wall as Zelda’s stare latched to him. 

“I’m going to take Zelda to the storage room for saddlebags and supplies. We’ll meet you both for dinner later.” The half smile she offered still wasn’t warm enough to fill the icy chill between them.

“Thanks, Ilya.” 

Ilya warmly squeezed his arm. Zelda’s eyes narrowed at the exchange before silently trailing Ilya as they exited the stables.

Fledge pursed his lips before dragging his eyes to his own horse. Link audibly huffed before handing Epona an apple.

They finished at the stables, making the long uphill walk back to the castle. Fledge offered to go to the armory for him; he needed more sinew and fibers to restring his bow. He lifted his chin to his friend as they parted; one less task he had to do himself was a relief.

One day of preparation was not enough for the six weeks they’d be gone.

Before anything, he mapped the route in his head: a week to Rito Village, assuming she could ride— and that was a big assumption— then double back to make the ascent to Goron City. He could hunt as they went, but they needed more than meat. Two tents? Did she even know they would be sleeping outside? His own survival was second nature; he could live off the land for months. But keeping her alive... he remembered her in Hyrule Field, moments from death. He was responsible for this stranger, and he had his work cut out for him.

He should ask her what her expectations were, but he imagined her face twisting with displeasure as he did.

He’d have Ilya do it.

But, he shouldn’t be a knight if he couldn’t ask her a few simple questions?

He reached for the hilt of his blade behind him— that reassurance like another limb to steady him. He changed course, his boots slipping against the worn stone. He would find her now, before supper. The journey would be long enough without this muzzle stretching between them.

He opened the door to his new room; the grandness of it had him unmeasured.

He never had a room with a bed to himself; it was always the barracks or outdoors, the latter being preferable. Being as free as a winged creature and as fearsome as a beast, all while serving?

Impossible. But he could dream.

His worn chest had been moved to the edge of this new bed. Inside were his saddlebags, a hammock, a bedroll, some elixirs he’d have to decipher, and his thick purse with rupees. He pulled the thread open, and the unknown amount of colorful gems in the bag shone back.

Bringing money would be wise, mainly for Zelda’s small comforts. While he didn’t mind sleeping outdoors, Zelda might. There were two stables on the way that they could stay at to split the distance. A warm, comfortable bed as a reprieve from his bedroll he planned to give her might ease her disdain.

At the mere thought of her, he heard her muffled voice.

He opened his door to see Ilya hugging Zelda goodbye. As Zelda’s door shut, he caught Ilya’s eye and gestured for her to come in. Her smile was lopsided.

“Wow, Link, this room is incredible.” Her chin lifted as she spun in the grand room. “It’s a… whirlwind, to say for certain.” Link hadn’t spoken with his old friend since everything happened, but from the lack of questions, he gathered Zelda had already told her plenty.

“Yeah, this new reality hasn’t fully set in yet.”

“I imagine.” She was scanning the large room. Her eyes stopped at the bed.

He trailed her gaze, leaning on the barrier wall that gave a false illusion of privacy. “First time I’ve had a bed that nice since I was a boy.”

“I bet it is.” She jerked her head towards his balcony and the desk next to it as she made herself comfortable.

“Thank you for helping Zelda today. I wanted to ask if she needed anything else that you weren’t able to provide for her? I have some extras and I can go to the stores to get anything else.”

She cleared her throat, “Oh. Yes, I provided her with her own saddlebags. She has her personal essentials covered. Impa provided her warm clothes. The only thing not covered is your sleeping arrangements.”

“Alright, I’ll make sure she’s provided for. Thanks, Ilya.”

“Anything you need, Link.” Ilya smiled brightly. She glanced at the glaring door on the shared wall. “How do you feel about this situation?”

“I’m honored to be a personal knight—”

He started his structured reply, but she swiftly cut him off. “No, Link, genuinely, how do you feel? I’m not your captain or Impa, so you can drop the formal act.” Ilya rarely took a serious tone, her face uncharacteristically firm, it was hard to look at.

“I—” he shook his head. “I’m apprehensive. I have no idea why Impa chose me, other than that I was directly involved in the beginning, but I have this sinking feeling that it’s wrong. What if Fledge never found her or dragged me into it? Would I still be here? Is this where I’m meant to be?”

“Is it a mistake because it’s not what you expected or because you feel you are not good enough?”

Link thoroughly contemplated Ilya’s question. Would he have been out of sorts if he was chosen as Princess Zelda’s protector, or because this wasn’t the Zelda he expected to watch over?

“Both.” He admitted. “Regardless, she hates me, she doesn’t want me to protect her.”

“That’s not true.” Ilya’s hands folded on the edge of the chair to rest on her chin. “She’s afraid. I’m sure you’ve tried your best to help her, but did you put yourself in her position?” Ilya glanced again at the adjoining door that seemed to grow larger every time he looked at it. “Everything is different for her. Everything.” She drawled. “And she knows not a soul. You were the first person who greeted her in her new reality, she bonded with you, you made her feel safe, but yelling at her...” Ilya gave him a knowing glare. “She must have felt so small, as if saving her life was just some big inconvenience. You put all that together... I’m surprised she’s holding up at all.”

Now the foolishness sat with him instead. “I’ll apologize.”

“That’s a start. Give her a chance. And give yourself a chance.” Ilya smiled sympathetically at him, her warmth easing him. “Anyway, I’m sure you’ll find answers to get her back home soon. Then things can go back to the way they were.”

“Thanks, Ilya, for everything.” He made the conscious effort to walk towards her to squeeze her forearm. “I’m going to finish packing, and there are a few other things I need to take care of. We can meet for supper later?”

“Absolutely, I would love that.” She rose from her seat to exit. “Zelda is in her room, packing. Would you like me to tell her?”

“No, I’ll do it. I’ll see you in a bit.” Ilya gave him a final, comforting look and left Link alone with this new perspective.

He stared at the adjoining door long enough that his feet had become numb. He had stood his ground against things that could kill him without breaking a sweat, but the thought of apologizing to her and having her look at him the way she had in the hallway kept him rooted.

He exited into the hallway and knocked on her main door. The shared door was too… intimate. 

She cracked the door open cautiously, golden waves falling over her face before she ran them back behind her ear. And when her eye landed on his, she opened the door wider. “Yes, Link?”

He froze at the sight of her moving lips. The flash of memory of her snug nightgown. Why was he here again?

She narrowed her eyes.

Stumbling to get the words out, “I—uh, just wanted to let you know… I spoke with Ilya about the trip. I have the food and sleeping gear covered, if you can pack your clothes and other needs.”

“What are the sleeping arrangements?” She opened the door wider before crossing her arms.

“I have a tent, a bedroll, and a hammock. You can use the tent and bedroll, and I’ll sleep outside in the hammock, to keep watch.”

Her expression soured with a curl of her lip. “Great, looking forward to it. I’m going to finish packing.”

She pushed the door shut, but his hand instinctively went out to stop it before the thought had formed. He expected fire and brimstone to rip out of her, but instead she tilted her head, slow and with a practiced steadiness. 

“Zelda, I’m sorry. I’m sorry for yelling at you. I was—” He closed his eyes, the image of her surrounded by monsters flashing in his mind— the way she’d looked right before he intervened. With fear and gratefulness. He took a steady breath. He could only get the rest out if he didn’t look her in the eye, so he stared at her lips, “That was my fear talking, not me. I’m sorry.”

Her hands fell to her sides, the sharp edges of her expression smoothed out. Her gaze met his, and for the first time, he saw no defensiveness in it. She looked at him for a moment, then said quietly, “Thank you for saying that.” 

“Of course.” He tried not to smile. “I’m going to finish packing. Fledge and Ilya would like to have supper with us before we leave tomorrow. Would you like to join us?”

“Sure, I’d like that.” She smiled. He hadn’t seen it since the previous morning; he forgot how stunning it was.

“Great, we’ll meet up in a few hours.” He gave her an awkward head bow and turned before he could say something stupid. As he walked back to his room, he realized the knot in his shoulders had loosened. For the first time all day, he was actually hungry.

After he lost himself in the familiar ritual of organizing his saddlebags, hours had passed. To save room, he only brought one piece of cold weather gear for himself and a few elixirs. He could source ingredients or buy more as they traveled. Instead, he used the space for an extra blanket for Zelda.

A faint knock sounded at his door, but his eyes went to the window. The sun hung low just above the horizon; he had lost track of time.

He pulled open the door with vigor, expecting Fledge returning with his arrows and string. Instead, the foreign woman stood in his doorway.

“Zelda—”

“Hey.” She said. “I’m packed for tomorrow, and I wasn’t sure how we left things, so I thought I’d come to you.”

“I’m sorry, I lost track of time. I’m sure Fledge and Ilya are waiting outside. Let me just take this off,” he indicated to his bracer.

Zelda eyed the leather bracer. “Do you want help?”

Before he could say no, she made her way into his room and shut the door.

She analyzed every corner of the room, turning from her position at the entrance, eyeing his desk, balcony, bed, and bath. “Your room is the mirror image of mine. Except, maybe more masculine,” as she fixed on the decayed, empty weapon rack near the bed.

“These rooms are for visiting dignitaries. They’d usually put the husband in here and the wife in the other room, with that door between them if they chose to... spend time together.” An inappropriate thought crossed his mind, but he quickly stomped it down.

“Married couples don’t sleep together?” she asked.

“I haven’t taken a survey, but most marriages are business arrangements. Separate rooms, leading separate lives.”

Her gaze drifted to their adjoining door, and the light in her eyes seemed to dim. A small sound escaped her closed lips, before she quickly schooled her expression back to neutral to fix upon his arm.

She closed the space between them, before lifting her brows in silent question to his bracer. He only nodded and rotated his forearm, the silence thundering in the shared space.

He watched her beneath lowered lashes as her fingers were long and nimble, as she methodically untied and then pulled on the delicate leather string. Every scrape of the cord against the leather was a small, sharp sound in the quiet room. With each pull, the lacing grew longer, the bracer looser, and the skin of his forearm more exposed.

The final thread remained, loose enough for him to slip out of. His instinct to jerk his arm away to finish the rest dissolved as she turned his arm to grab the outer shell, to pull it off herself.

But she stopped, her brows twitched as her fingers went to the thick shell in the center, to a small carved dent.

“A lynel’s axe.”

“What?” Her question was a breathless sound.

“That mark, it was from a lynel’s axe, a few years back.”

Not even before he finished his sentence, her eyes found his own. The tinseled emerald had turned into almost a forest shroud in this light, but the gold still held a preternatural light and streaked in a few uneven bursts from her pupil.

He couldn’t look away— even if a horde of monsters blew the horn to alert him to their presence.

Her eyes drifted down towards his mouth, as she calmly opened to say something, and he waited for the words to slip past, but they never did.

But she lowered her chin and dropped her hands, his forearm held foolishly in the air as she backed away.

“Thank you.” He grunted, putting the bracer on the desk behind him. “Let’s go.” The words died in the air between them. She was already a step into the corridor, the door frame a solid boundary where that moment ended.

As suspected, Fledge and Ilya were waiting patiently outside the building for them. Greeted by smiles and comments on being late. But they didn’t mention the way he avoided meeting their eyes.

As they entered the communal dining hall, a wave of cheerful chatter washed over them. They took seats at the end of a long table, where food was laid out banquet-style, more than the four of them could finish, and then some. Roasted chicken, dusted with spices, sat beside scalloped potatoes and a sautéed medley of vegetables in every color. His stomach growled before he could stop it. He snatched up a spare plate and fork and piled it high, stabbing at each dish in turn until his plate looked like a harvest festival. Ilya snorted a laugh.

“Just a warning, Zelda— if you don’t eat fast, Link will clear the table before you get a bite.” Ilya shot a wink to Link. “The upside is that it forced him to learn how to cook. You’ll never go hungry on your journey.”

Link rolled his eyes as he inhaled a chicken leg. Ilya and Fledge laughed, and yet Zelda’s small smile lingered as she politely grabbed a piece of chicken for herself.

They chatted about nothing of significance as they ate. Fledge filled in Zelda on the lore of the Tabantha region. Ilya told Zelda the origin of Storm—Zelda’s horse. Zelda asked Fledge what his plans were now that Link would be gone—all while Link ate in silence, happy to savor a good meal before they departed in the morning.

Plates empty, delightfully satisfied. Link snagged the attention of Pipit— who was rapidly heading in their direction. And before Link could rise, or excuse himself or do anything to avoid the sinking sand in his full gut, Pipit’s hands were slamming upon the edge of the table, a shit grin slowly forming.

“Fledge, Ilya, Link, nice to see you all.” The words were pleasant, but his tone was not as his direction went to Link, “I heard you’re on a special assignment. Perhaps the same reason two Sheikahs were seen hauling your stuff out of the barracks last night.”

The smug smile on Pipit’s face was one Link had seen a hundred times on the training grounds, usually when he thought he had the upper hand, but magically removed right before Link disarmed him. Link set his jaw, the warmth of the meal curdling in his stomach. He just wanted the man to go away.

“At least I have an assignment.” Link replied.

A flex of his arms, he leaned down towards Link’s face. His breath stunk of ale. “It’s all very hush-hush, but the barracks chatter is that Impa tasked you in particular with something, not anything to do with the Princess, of course. Feel like sharing with the rest of us?”

Link did not. He matched the glare leveled at him. The rest of them didn’t exist in this dual between them.

And he knew, Fledge and Ilya hadn’t spoken a word, but castle gossip was traded better than the best merchant. And perhaps Link could have held out, until Pipit’s gaze locked behind Link to the new face.

“My apologies, my lady. I have not had the pleasure of meeting you yet. What is your name?” He performed an exaggerated bow that meant anything but sincere.

“My name is Zelda, very nice to meet you, Sir...?”

“Pipit.” He flashed a toothy white smile, one brow drawn up. “Interesting name. Where are you from, Zelda?”

No one spoke as Pipit stared at her intently. Zelda opened her mouth, but before she could speak, Ilya cut in, “She’s my cousin. She was visiting for a few days to enjoy the tournament and festivities, but she’s set to leave tomorrow. Link is escorting her back home before his assignment.”

Pipit eyed her suspiciously, still not buying enough of what Ilya put down. “Too bad you’re leaving. It would have been nice to get to know you better.”

Link was white-knuckling under the table, jaw tense, ready to lunge at Pipit and wipe the shit-eating grin off his face with a swift punch in the mouth. Link leveled a stare that could rival an eruption on Death Mountain, and Pipit’s smile widened for a moment before he finally turned away.

“It was a pleasure to meet you, my lady,” he threw back over his shoulder, turning to cap his fingers in mock salute. “I hope you visit again soon.”

The table stayed silent. Pipit’s retreating footsteps were a small echo as the clatter in the room came back into focus.

“It was bound to happen, coming out in public. Now the castle will buzz with this gossip. Luckily, you both leave tomorrow.” Ilya’s gaze drifted for a moment. “By the time you’re back, things will be blown over.”

Link finally let the blood flow back into his extremities. He stole a glance at Zelda. The hardness had left her eyes, replaced by a quiet look of understanding.

Fledge and Ilya walked them both back to their apartments. Well wishes and goodbyes exchanged, and Ilya left both with a long embrace. And as they descended the castle steps in the fresh air of twilight, Link and Zelda were alone again.

The quiet shuffling of their feet against each step was all his focus could bear before stopping at Link’s door. “We should leave at sunrise. Impa will meet us outside the castle before we depart.” Link told her but quickly posed it as a question. “If that’s alright?”

“Sure.” And without hesitation, she headed for her room.

The next morning, the glow of the sun illuminated the sky before showing itself as they reached the stables. Where Epona and the midnight-dark stud, Storm, greeted them, their resulting huffs turning into steam against the cooler summer morning.

Saddlebags secure, feet in stirrups, hands in reins, and they were off to the ceremonial grounds just outside the town.

As they led their steeds through the castle town gates, with only the single guard to witness their departure, the clop of hooves on stone was the only sound between them. Link focused on the weight of the sword on his back, how heavy it would press upon him as he would kneel before her and bind that blade, and his life, to her service.

He hadn’t dwelled on those thoughts long as the intimate clearing opened ahead. The circular space, with perfect, pristine marble and columns all aligned with trimmed bushes and shrubs, was kept in good order. The mystery of why it was maintained so methodically so far from the castle proper was even less odd than wondering who had commissioned it in the first place.

Impa sat in the exact middle, cross-legged on the refined stone, her back perfectly straight, her hands resting on her knees. Her silver hair was unruffled by the breeze, just as the columns that stood next to her.

They tied off their horses and made their way to the center. Standing side by side, they waited for her to acknowledge them. Impa, eyes still closed, commanded, “Let’s get started.”

She stood in one smooth motion before her red eyes landed on him. “Link, please kneel.”

He did as he was told, sinking to one knee. He placed his sword arm across it and bowed his head, the motions ingrained from years of training. He could hear the soft shuffle of Zelda’s boots on the stone as she moved to stand beside Impa.

“Sir Link of Hateno Village, do you solemnly and truly declare to be faithful and bear true allegiance to His Majesty King Rhoam, His Heirs, and Successors?”

“I do.”

“You are duty-bound to honestly and faithfully defend the royal line against those who wish to harm them. Do you swear to protect them, even if your life becomes forfeit?”

“I do.”

“Do you swear to the goddess Hylia to honor the harmony of power, wisdom, and courage and protect the sacred realm from those who wish ill will upon the land?”

“I do.”

The weight of those two words repeated in perfect practice hadn’t felt as heavy as he imagined. He kept his head bowed, now seeing only the flocked texture of her mahogany boots. He fixed on that texture, still as a statue.

“Link, go ahead.” Impa moved out of the way, leaving only them upon the altar of promises to hold too.

“I vow before thee to give my sword when blood is called for and my silence when it is not. I will stand between you and those who would see you diminished—by rumor, by blade, or by the slow cruelty of indifference. Whatever name they give the years ahead, I will be found at your side, bound not by compulsion but by the choosing of it, again and again, for as long as I draw breath.” He spoke without wavering. His voice was firm and unfaltering to give to this stranger he’d known for three sunrises.

“Please, repeat after me, Zelda,” Impa whispered. “I vow to accept your sword, heed your counsel, and never ask you for service to dishonor. I swear by the goddess Hylia.”

The silence stretched. He kept his head bowed, his knee beginning to ache against the stone. The blood pounded in his ears. Still, she said nothing. A cold dread began to seep into his bones. Did she refuse?

His head lifted unceremoniously to catch her gaze. To see her snarling, scoffing, looking at him with contempt— anything he probably deserved from her.

But her nose flared, the pressure threatening to break the glazed look in her eyes. She wasn’t breathing.

He didn’t think. He instinctively reached out to her hand.

A surge shot through his fingers and up his arm, a warmth that made the stone floor seem to tilt. He locked his knees, an instinct to steady himself against the unseen force, and only then met her gaze. Her breath hitched, but as he traced circles over the frantic pulse in her wrist, the panic in her green eyes softened to a fragile calm.

Impa did not exist. It was only them as the pressure dissolved.

Once her heartbeat steadied, Link retracted his hand and resumed his position, head bowed.

The impulse was instinctual, absolute— a need to reach for her, to anchor her before the weight of the moment swept her away.

She held her arm out towards him, palm facing, “I vow to accept your sword, heed your counsel, and never ask of you a service that would bring dishonor. I swear this by the goddess Hylia.” Her voice cracked.

“Link, please rise,” Impa said.

He rose, his posture straightening until he was almost eye level with Zelda. Her eyes were wide, wild, and his hand itched to reach for her again, to soothe the unfamiliar tightness in his own throat.

“Congratulations, Sir Link.” Impa’s voice sliced through the charged silence. “You are now a knight in service of the royal family.” Link’s eyes remained on Zelda. “Remember my words.” Her voice sharpened. “And remember your duty.” The command finally pulled his gaze to meet hers. “Keep her alive. I’ll see you in a few weeks.”

Link took a step back, the formal distance a stark contrast to the moment before. With a slight dip of his chin, he acknowledged her command. Impa was already gone, melting into the dawn without a sound and leaving them to take the opposite path.

Just the two of them as the sun breached the horizon behind them.

Chapter 10: Wind
Chapter Text
Part 2: The Journey

A wooden structure shaped like a giant horse head appeared in the distance as they rounded a bend in the road. People— Hylians— bustled in and around it, surrounded by common farm animals fenced in their respective breeds. A perfect destination for weary travelers to find respite.

But the horse head, for all its fantastical whimsy, failed to sow harmony within her. Each time she shut her eyes, she half-expected to open them to the hum of a refrigerator, to Marin leaning into her doorway with some pointless, rambling inquiry about leftover takeout.

Yet each time she opened them, the rough bark of the trees, the damp soil, the wind against her cheek—all of it told her otherwise.

The landscape had started as a sea of pale grass, flat and unfaltering with only arbitrary pockets of trees with rust-colored leaves in various stages of decay. Beyond the never-ending plain, steep ridges and burnt mountains against sturdier forest clearings started to form. Yet their routine remained the same. Waking to Link’s labored breaths as he trained or the smells of heavenly spices as he cooked for them, whichever sound or smell greeted her depended on how long she could withstand the heat as the sun baked her tent.

They rode for hours, their progress marked by the rhythm of hooves and the need for occasional stops. They would pause to share pieces of dried fruit, to let the horses drink from a stream, or to slip behind a thicket for privacy. The latter necessity had been a source of looming dread at first, but the awkwardness had faded swiftly.

At night, the routine held, Link would listen for running water, then stop at the first pocket of trees nearby. He would unpack their bags, set up her tent, his hammock, and cook. Then either rotate between sharpening his sword, stringing his bow, or washing small linens.

She wouldn’t stray far, she didn’t test the invisible leash between them, but she imagined if she wanted to, he would soon loom as a shadow behind her.

Even weirder still, when the sky chased all the color away and the crickets came out to sing, how the unseeing landscape felt so vast in the dark, and immenser still, the feeling of loneliness she felt. She crawled into her tent, to find and feel some relief, but the space would suddenly feel so small, it pressed into her, swift and disorienting.

Yet— 

The sounds of the relative stranger’s breathing nearby caused her own breath to finally fill her lungs. How this stranger just days before swore his life for hers. Until death do them part. And while that notion should frighten her. It didn’t.

A stranger who had sworn his life to her twice over.

Since then, the tension from the ceremonial grounds had eased, in its place, a heavy shyness had settled between them. Barely more than polite questions about sleep, rest, and breaks in between. But that hadn’t stopped the memory of the ceremony rearing its head every now and again. His vow, and hers in return, overwhelmed her with an intensity she hadn’t anticipated.

When it did, she would catch herself staring at him. Sitting pin-straight upon his chestnut mare, he was an image of discipline: hair pulled back, a crisp red tunic, that did little for his eyes, and the weapons he carried with unnerving ease. A large, crafted bow hung behind him along with the familiar sword sheathed at his back, the brushed metal hilt wrapped with leather, worn from use.

And when she exhausted those thoughts, she thought of him swinging that blade. How many lives had he cut down with that gleaming polished steel? 

She tried not to look too long.

Then they made it to the stable, situated across from a massive canyon, and they crossed on the swaying bridge.

She marveled at the change of scenery. The incredible depth of the canyon beneath her feet that separated the warmer Hyrule field from the now colder breeze hitting her cheeks. They made it far into the valley and decided to camp above a lake.

As Link set up their camp, she sat upon a discarded log, and a doe and fawn darted into the brush. They looked just like the deer from home, as did the squirrels and birds chattering in the maple and pine trees. The familiarity was jarring.

This world had the same bones as hers, just stripped of the asphalt and rebar.
