And she’d catch herself staring into the clouds, expecting to see chem trails and hear a deep pressurized roar to follow, but those sounds were replaced with clear air, so fresh it made her head high as she pulled it in her lungs, and the endless green expanse felt less like a wilderness and more like a liberation.

After another uncomfortable evening and awkward morning, they made their descent into the outskirts of Rito Village. The view as they descended was that of a pristine boreal forest. Unstained snow lay upon the various pines in the far distance, as if the gods had painted it themselves.

The weather in Hyrule was something of a scientific marvel. Less than two days ago, she was cooking upon Storm’s black coat.

They dismounted at the stable, and as her boots hit the ground her eyes went wide as she scrambled to find purchase upon Storm’s reins.

A creature taller than she stood before them—a bird, but standing on two hind legs, gripping a spear in a feathered hand. Before she could process the sight, she found herself stepping behind Link, using his back as a shield.

He turned his brows lowered. “What’s the matter?”

“Is that— another monster, like the ones from the field?” she asked, her voice low. 

A hesitant smile pulled on his face. “No, that’s a Rito. Natives to this area,” he said.

“You didn’t think to warn me?” she hissed at him, eyes still glued to the apparent Rito.

“I honestly hadn’t realized you didn’t know,” his satisfaction at her expense faded to seriousness. “Do you have Gorons and Zora where you’re from?”

She curled her lip. “I don’t know what those are, but we just have humans, or ‘Hylians’ as you’d call them,” she said, making air quotes.

“Interesting. We have a lot of sentient species. Wait until you meet them all.” He walked towards the large bird person. “Come on, I promise you’re not in danger.”

Her movements were slow and precise behind Link as he approached the bird person. She watched as he extended a hand in familiarity. “Gesane, nice to see you.”

Gesane, the Rito, was beautifully poised, in both his elegant movements and look. His coat of feathers was a pale sand and faded to shades rich as autumn leaves that held to trees before falling. His face flashed between the stoic guard’s tightness to an animated delight all within a steady motion with a surprising baritone voice replying, “Link! What are you doing here?”

“I’m here to request a meeting with your chief. I have a letter from Master Impa,” Link held out the parchment with an unbroken seal. Zelda had slid behind Link as quietly as a mouse, the Rito’s rich pine bark-colored eyes met hers behind Link’s shoulder. 

Gesane’s posture stiffened, his velvet wings ruffled. “The chief has taken ill health the past few weeks. He’s put a temporary chief in charge. I’m sure you know—”

“Don’t say it.” Link cut him off with a scowl.

Gesane shot him a sympathetic look. “Revali is temporarily chieftain.”

She swore she heard a beastly noise escape from Link.

They traded in their routine for feather beds and already prepared food, sleeping in the stable for the night. Gesane had flown to the village to announce their arrival for the next morning, as was customary for those on royal business. They would stable their horses for the next few days, trekking to the village on foot.

Gesane greeted them in the early morning light with the all-clear. He pulled Link aside, whispering something in his ear. Zelda saw Link’s jaw clench, a muscle feathering along the bone.

Each chain bridge swayed under her boots, and she kept her eyes on the planks instead of the gaps between them. Through those gaps, she could see the water, a long way down but still an enticing glacier blue, and when the sun cut through the clouds, it threw light across the surface in broken white lines. The village sat on an island of sheer rock that rose out of the lake like a spire, and at its top, a long perch stretched over the drop. Wooden huts climbed the slope in a spiral, colored linens snapping on their railings in the wind. Rito children dove off ledges without looking first, caught themselves with a flap, and landed laughing. She gripped the railing with both hands and crossed one bridge at a time.

And when they made it to solid ground, another Rito delegate with a darker coat ushered them the rest of the way. Climbing an endless number of stairs left her legs in a watery state, she couldn’t help hunching over, her palm finding the stitch in her side to hold as her lungs sought for sustenance in the high altitude.

A glance at Link made her scowl. His breathing was even, his posture relaxed, not a single hair out of place. Gods, she really hated how perfect he was.

They were ushered into a larger hut covered with vibrant patterned pillows and benches. The young Rito delegate motioned for them to sit and wait.

She had taken the delegate up on his invitation, still huffing and puffing minutes later, until a slender, proud Rito entered the door frame. Link stood opposite the room, arms tightly crossed, feet apart—a stark contrast to how he had greeted anyone else, particularly a chief.

The Rito was at least a foot and a half taller than she was, similar in height to all other Ritos she passed by. Her first thought, gazing upon him, was that he was a majestic eagle in another life, his lean frame adorned with cloud-gray feathers, fading to white lining the edges of his wings. His feathers were silken and smooth— perfect, not one out of place against the rough wind blowing through her own mane. Four raven-dark braids hung in the back of his head, adorned with moss-colored beads that matched his eyes. He didn’t have traditional clothes on but rather lightweight armor on his chest and hips, with a brown belt holding a large, colorfully threaded bow on his back. He carried himself with an arrogant grace she found both infuriating and, to her surprise, compelling.

His hands lifted to clasp dramatically in front of him. “The Hylians have arrived. How honored we are.” His voice was a flat, nasally drawl that robbed the words of any warmth. “Sorry, no ceremonial pomp for your arrival.” Zelda realized with a jolt that she might have met her match in biting commentary.

Link turned to face him. “You couldn’t be bothered to greet us before, as is customary for royal emissaries?”

“Maybe we can pull out some dusty trumpets if you’d like to go back down and try again.” Revali brushed away invisible dirt on his shoulder, turning to smirk at Link.

A long moment passed as they stared at each other, neither willing to be the first to break eye contact.

They both forgot, or perhaps didn’t care, that she was even in the room. They clearly had a history, and it was ugly. She had no time to watch their childish standoff. She loudly cleared her throat.

Revali broke his glare with Link, and his gaze fell on her. The harsh lines of his face softened into something like curiosity, his head tilting. “Princess Zelda?” He paused, assessing her. “No. Who are you?”

“I’m not the Princess, but my name is Zelda.” She lowered her hood that had been covering her ears from the biting cold. Her round ear was on full display as she swept her hair to the side. “Pleasure to meet you. Revali, I’m assuming?” She hung out her arm to shake.

He stared at her, long enough that it made her skin prickle. He motioned himself between them, placing his back to Link. A large smile spread across his mouth, “Zelda, the pleasure is mine.” He took his wing and grabbed her hand to kiss it in an exaggerated bow. His feathers were soft and silky as he delicately clasped her hand and his beak poked her cold skin in what resembled a kiss.

He straightened himself, “What can I do for you?”

She wasn’t entirely sure if his tone had been sincere.

“Chieftain Revali? Is that the proper title to address you?” He nodded, a flicker of smug pride crossing his beak as he heard the title spoken aloud. “Great. Chieftain Revali, we’ve been sent here by Master Impa to give you this and ask that you lend us your aid with knowledge or information you can provide on the subject.” She held out her hand towards Link, indicating the parchment be handed over. He stiffly pulled the parchment from his tunic and pressed it into her outstretched palm without meeting her eyes.

Gods, this was annoying. She resolved to ask him what his problem was later.

She handed Revali the letter. He opened it and read, leaving her to decipher his facial expressions as he read. After finishing, he paused, bringing a wing to his mouth in thought.

“We’ve provided beds for you at the inn. You can stay for a few days. I will address this tomorrow with you.” He gestured with the parchment held in his wing. “Now I must be going. Feel free to explore the town. Link knows his way around.” He shot Link a lowered glare before strolling out and onto an open ledge, and in one smooth motion, pushed his feet off, wings extended before catching in an exquisite arc— flying towards the white-tipped mountains opposite of them.

And that familiar quiet settled in the space. That was the most she had spoken in days.

Link rolled all the tension out of his shoulders before scrubbing at his face to do the same. “I’ll show you around. We might as well get comfortable. Revali is going to drag this out,” Link said, offering her the lead out of the room.

“What’s with you two? I’d assume you were friends based on that interaction.” Zelda said.

“It’s complicated.” Link either missed her sarcastic joke or chose to ignore it. Either way, she glowered at him to elaborate. “I’ll explain later. Too many ears.”

They made their way down to the inn, another quaint room with a handful of hammocks in the open. The innkeeper ushered them over to a corner where the delegate had placed their belongings, and as swiftly as the delegate left, Zelda resolved to get answers, nudging her head to Link to elaborate.

First, he detoured to the community kitchen. He moved with quiet efficiency, crafting a meal while she watched, her fingers drumming against her leg. He was going to drag this out, just like Revali. The silence stretched, and she had to resist the urge to tap her foot.

After an hour, a meal of flaky salmon cooked with mountain herbs was eaten between the two of them, and the sun was getting lower. Zelda rested her hands on her hips in a sign of impatient waiting. He let out a huffed sigh, indicating for her to follow. 

He led her back down the way they had come earlier, settling far enough away from town on one of the islands between the village and the stable.

It was quiet, peaceful, and serene. A small, made pond nestled under a tree. He took off his scabbard to allow his rigid posture some respite. He leaned against a boulder across from her on the grass and began working a small crack out of the scabbard’s leather with his thumbnail.

“It was at my knighting tournament,” he began, his gaze fixed on the scabbard. “I was sixteen. Revali was there representing his people. He was… the best of them. By far.” He paused, working at the leather. “I won most of the events, and was crowned the day’s victor. He wanted the recognition. It didn’t sit well with him that I got it instead.”

“But you said you won most, not all,” Zelda prompted.

“Not archery. No one beats him at archery.” He finally looked up, his eyes distant. “He kept pushing for a private rematch. On everything. I finally gave in.” He unsheathed his sword, the memory seeming to harden his grip on the hilt. “It ended with both of us coming to blows. They had to pull us apart.”

“So he’s jealous of you? That’s why he has so much contempt for you?” Zelda asked before crossing her arms.

Link dropped his sword in hand, his eyesight not meeting Zelda’s. “I don’t think it’s jealousy necessarily. I think he saw I had it easy, where he had to work hard and still came up short.”

“You had it easy?” Zelda dropped her arms.

“No, he just thought I did.”

Zelda considered his explanation, but it felt too simple, a story smoothed over at the edges. The venom she’d seen between them seemed too potent for a simple grudge over a tournament. Still, she sensed that pushing him further now would only make him retreat completely, so she held her tongue.

They sat in silence for a time before making their way back to the inn. That had been the most Link, and she had spoken for a week. He did open up, even if she didn’t quite buy what he was selling.

As they arrived back at their lodgings, the townsfolk invited them to their community dinner. Zelda accepted, eager to learn more about the Rito and exercise her vocal cords again. Link grunted.

The next morning, she awoke to find Link’s hammock empty. She stretched in the swaying, soft fabric, a satisfying crack running down her spine. The conversations from the night before, the stories of the Rito, echoed in her mind with a clarity that felt new. It was fascinating, more real than any dream. She recalled Link's quiet presence at the edge of the gathering, his posture rigid, and wondered if Revali's absence was the cause.

Zelda changed into a warm coat. The dawn’s exiting air was chilly but rejuvenating. She decided to relish her rare solitude, and walked to the same spot she and Link had shared the previous afternoon. She sat, breathing in the scent of mountain forests she so loved, and let the sun’s lazy rays warm her face.

Then, a gust of wind hit her back. She twisted herself to look.

Revali had landed with the same lightweight grace he left with yesterday.

“Chief Revali, pleasure to see you again.” She stood from her seated position to give him a crude head tilt. Unsure how to address a chief.

“Indeed it is.” She was unable to decipher by his tone if he meant her or himself. “I see you getting some much-needed respite from the self-important knight. I don’t blame you, quite frankly. I can only tolerate so much of his presence.”

Wow. “I actually don’t know where he is. He was gone when I woke.”

Revali brought his wing up in pondering. “I read the letter Master Impa provided. It’s very interesting, your situation.”

“What did the letter say exactly?” Zelda was curious what the contents of each sealed letter said, wondering how forthcoming Impa was with the information.

“Impa explained your situation.” Revali started to pace around her, as if a calculated predator to prey. “You, appearing out of thin air, having the same name as Hyrule’s crown princess, and what Impa didn’t mention, how similar you look to her, but of course she wouldn’t need to mention that for me to put that together.” Now he was behind her. “You and your gloried babysitter were to travel here to… encourage me, to provide you with any and all information my people have about similar happenings in history.” Now he stood directly in front of her. 

“And… do you have any information?” she asked.

He took a long moment, longer than necessary, just to drag it out. “You know why I loathe him, right?”

Zelda’s jaw tightened before easing. “He mentioned his knighthood tournament.”

Revali laughed. Actually cackled. “Of course he did, such a simpleton, your honored knight.”

“Why don’t you tell me then?” Zelda said. “It’s not like I have undying love and loyalty for him.” The words left a bitter taste in her mouth. She’d said it to get what she needed, but hearing the lie spoken aloud made her stomach twist with an unwelcome truth: she was already more loyal than she wanted to admit.

“It wasn’t that he won the tournament, it was his attitude afterward.” Revali stood proud, wing waving, “It’s his arrogance guised under his quiet demeanor. The contempt he exudes. He wins, what does he do, nothing. He keeps a straight face as though he’s holier than thou. At least show some emotion!”

She and Link didn’t get along, but that wasn’t an accurate summation of him. Stoic, yes. Professional, certainly. But arrogant and self-absorbed? That was Revali. “Are you sure you’re not misreading him?” Zelda didn’t want to upset Revali by disagreeing, but she wasn’t sure Link was getting a fair shake here.

“Maybe I am, but tell me this, did he ever make you feel bad under his watch?” Revali swung his head around to stare at her.

Her shoulder blades seized in answer.

“I’ll take it by your silence that I’m correct.” A flicker of satisfaction crossed Revali’s beak— a clear, small victory.

Before she could reply, Revali’s chest feathers puffed out, and he stood a little taller. “Ah, here’s the errand boy now.” Zelda whirled around. Link was heading towards them, his face a mask except for the hard glint in his eyes.

He passed by her and positioned himself just ever-so in front of her. Revali clearly accepted the challenge: “We were just talking about you, how fitting you come at the good part. I was just telling Zelda here about the truth of our sordid past.”

Revali rocked on his talons, practically vibrating with an energy he’d clearly been holding in since yesterday. “I thought it was strange you showed up here as a guard to this Zelda, not the Princess. I did hear Princess Zelda would receive a royal knight after the tournament. But then I discovered Master Impa sent you because you lost that position.” He tapped a wing-tip to his chin. “How fitting. Even as the best, you still don’t win.”

She could see in the corner of his face something of a flicker of disappointment. But he didn’t say anything. Didn’t deny it.

“How about this? I had planned to tell your Zelda what I knew about her predicament, but that’s too easy. We’ll play for it, a rematch.” He turned his back to both of them. “Let’s meet at the flight range, say, midday?”

“Fine.” And oddly, he turned to head back to the village without her.

“I told you, just wait and see.” Revali said as he glanced over his shoulder. Then he promptly took off in the same direction as yesterday.

What the hell just happened?

So much for a peaceful, solitary morning. Something’s never changed, no matter the time or place; men will still hold pissing contests leaving her in the dust.

She turned towards the village to run after Link.

When she finally caught up with him at the inn, he was grabbing his bow and arrows. “Link?”

He didn’t reply.

“Link, what’s the flight range?”

His eyes still counting his arrows, he said, “It’s the Rito training grounds. For practicing their aerial skills.”

Link did seem perfect at everything but flying; she doubted. “How are you supposed to fly?”

“They have gliders for non-Rito. I’ll use that.” Satisfied at the quantity of arrows, he hooked his quiver onto his side and slung a bow onto his back, followed by a thick, pale jacket. His fingers reached into the pockets and pulled out a rough, transparent crimson stone, no larger than a fingertip. It was held by a feathered string, adorned with earth-toned beads and a single feather.

“What’s that?” Her fingers instinctively went out to explore the glass-like stone but quickly pulled back.

“It’s a Rito headdress. The ruby helps with the cold.” He thoughtfully braided the hair that hung in his face and slid the emblem behind his ear. Not many could pull off a feather in their hair, but he looked… good. “It’ll take a few hours to get to the flight range; I’ll be back at dusk.”

“Wait, I’m coming,” she said, surprising herself.

He paused and looked at her, his mouth opening and closing once as if weighing a dozen arguments against her coming. Her own reasons were already lining up in her mind, ready for a fight.

He let out a short, frustrated sigh. “Fine. But dress warm; it’s cold there.” 

With her jacket already on, she slipped on a provided pair of gloves and tied her hood, and they were on their way.

After a solid few hours, they made it to the flight range. It was closer in proximity to the village— if one had wings to take the aerial path, which they did not have. So after saddling their horses, they made it there just as the sun hung in the middle of the sky above.

And it was a good thing the sun had been out, otherwise the frigid air would have made her bones freeze. It was significantly colder than the village. With fresh, untracked snow on the ground all around them, and it didn’t help that a strange, cold updraft pushed relentlessly from the cavernous space below.

Revali was already airborne as they approached.

He turned to soar over to the landing, his feet silently gracing the extended platform. His face was somehow even more delighted than earlier this morning. “You made it, took you long enough.” He noticed Zelda and smirked, “And you brought a witness to watch your defeat.” 

Every moment with Revali had her understanding Link’s long-standing frustration. 

“Rules?” Link had asked while unhinging his bow from his back.

“Straight to business. The rules are simple: hit as many targets as you can in one minute. In the unlikely event there is a tie, we’ll run it again in less time. Zelda can keep track.” He pointed to a stopwatch on the table.

“Deal.” Link grabbed an old, folded fabric that once he shook open, seemed to harden and straighten.

“I’ll go first, watch and learn.” She couldn’t hide her eye roll as Revali strutted away. Zelda counted him down, and he launched off the landing, cutting through the air with a sharpness that made it look effortless. Mid-flight, he tucked his bow beneath his talons to free his hands, then snatched it back up and loosed three arrows in a single fluid motion, each one finding its mark. This continued all surrounding the center spire. Before she knew it, the stopwatch had stopped, and his time was up.

All 25 targets had been hit.

He was impressive; she had to give him that.

Now Link’s turn. He readied himself at the edge of the platform. He turned back, finding her gaze.

Was it determination or pride that glinted in his eye? It was hard to read someone like Link. He hadn’t naturally been very expressive in his emotions to her since they met. He turned back, ready to jump into the abyss as she counted him down, and what followed after she said one, stunned her beyond what she imagined possible.

He dove off the landing. Her heart leaped into her throat, but then the up draft caught him, and he floated weightlessly. He unstrapped his bow, steady in the gale, and began to fire. Each arrow found its mark. As he moved through the air, angling for more targets, Zelda glanced at Revali. The Rito's smug smirk had vanished, his wings held rigidly at his sides. Link could actually win this.

As the last few seconds passed, she sounded the time for him to stop. He connected his bow to his back, angled the glider into the strongest current, and rode the up draft in a wide, ascending spiral. Honestly, it looked absolutely fun, if not slightly terrifying. He aimed himself to the landing and stuck it perfectly.

As they tallied up Link’s arrows, the final score revealed itself: Revali 25, Link 22.

Link’s face remained a neutral mask. He methodically slotted his arrows back into his quiver, his posture unchanged, not even sparing Revali a glance. He must have known this would be the outcome, Zelda thought, yet he’d stood his ground anyway.

“Well, isn’t that a shame? The honorable knight loses fair and square. Better luck next time.” Revali’s chest puffed proudly, as he turned on his heel. “Now, if you excuse me—”

“Wait.” Zelda instinctively reached her hand out to his wing. “Please, can you tell me what you know about my situation?”

Revali considered it. “Meet me back at the village. We’ll talk.”

A breath she hadn’t realized she was holding escaped her.

By the time they stored the horses and returned to the village, the sun was a dying ember on the horizon. A Rito guard informed them Revali was in the chief’s hut—at the very top of the spire. Each flight of stairs was a new layer of exhaustion, but Zelda pushed onward. When they finally reached the peak, another guard met them with a practiced, indifferent look. “Master Revali had an urgent matter to attend to. He has departed.”

Now Zelda had reached her limit with the bird. She was exhausted, and he was punishing them both for Link’s loss. A sore winner indeed.

She turned and took the stairs back down to the inn, eight flights, each step harder than the last. She had nothing left to say, no appetite, no patience. She wanted only to put this day behind her.

Surprisingly, Link spoke from behind her, his voice gentle. “I’ll make you supper.”

She snapped to him, “I don’t want to eat. I’m fried. I just want to sleep.”

“Please, then you can sleep.” Link ushered her to follow with a gentle touch of her elbow. She reluctantly obeyed.

They sat quietly around the cooking pot, just the two of them. Link was cooking a stew, throwing in the last of the ingredients before stepping away to let it simmer. All she heard were sounds of small bubbles popping and smells of fresh-cut herbs.

“Is this how it’s going to be, every step of the way?” She didn’t look at him, just rested her chin in her hand and watched the stew.

Link didn’t respond immediately. He crouched by the fire and adjusted one of the stones beneath the pot. “No. It won’t be.”

And that was the extent of their conversation before the food had been served, eaten, and her shuffling, defeated slide back to the inn. She changed into sleeping pants and a long shirt in the curtained-off alcove, and when she emerged, Link had left. She swore he had been behind her as she fetched her spare clothes before changing. But she didn’t have the energy to search for him as her hammock hugged her and darkness came.

She woke to the sun tanning her face, the warmth a delightful kiss upon the chill air. Link was already gone, or perhaps he never made it back. She changed and walked to the familiar pond as steam and fog rose upon the horizon. Except this morning, Rito children were surrounding the pond, excitedly spear fishing for anything that swam.

She watched them with a faint smile, the feeling on her face so foreign from the past week. They were chaotic and loud, their chirping voices and playful questions they leveled at her had a genuine laugh escaping her as she knelt to answer them, and the tight knot of yesterday’s frustration finally loosened its grip. She almost forgot about the events from the day before until—

“Master Revali!” A small pastel pink feathered girl said. Zelda’s shoulders sagged as she rose from her kneel, her smile turning opposite of the lift.

Somehow, his tall stature no longer loomed over her as much. Revali ushered the children to scatter. “Zelda, may we speak?”

She huffed an exaggerated breath but nodded her head. He held his wing out indicating for her to walk towards the bridge. After they were far enough away from the children, Revali opened his beak, “I apologize for yesterday; it’s not your fault you’re stuck with the dull knight.”

The apology, she realized, was just another weapon.

She eyed him curiously, her scowl fixed. He continued, “My people have no history that could help you. The Rito are a newer species— a superior evolution, you might say, born from the necessity of survival.” He paused, preening slightly before getting back to the point. “It is ancient history you need. I have heard stories regarding Gorons and the Zora. Their people have been around since the Hero of Time, another overrated Hylian hero that traveled through time, but it’s the closest situation I know of related to yours.”

The Hero of Time, perhaps Link knew more about this. Revali didn’t strike her as someone who was willingly learning about Hyrule’s history if it hadn’t related to him.

“Thank you, Revali.” She managed a small smile— an effort. She caught what she assumed was the closest thing to a blush from him, his feathers ruffling.

“You’ll be heading to Goron City next. We’ll provide you with provisions before leaving. I need to take care of something, but I’ll see you off this morning.” Revali proceeded to give her a bow and fly away.

How did he know where they were headed next? Still, a knot of unease tightened in her stomach. It felt like another piece of a puzzle she couldn’t see.

She drew a long, slow breath, letting it out with the weight of the last day. The knot in her shoulders finally eased as she watched the orange sky bleed into blue over the mountains. After taking a beat to enjoy the view, she headed back towards the village, but as she rounded the last bridge to the main island, Link trotted out of the woods and stepped into her path.

“Link?” She arched her head to where he approached from: a small group of pine trees hidden from view. “Is this where you’ve been every morning?”

He nodded. “Yes, I like to train early. This spot has privacy but a good vantage point leading out of town.”

“So you knew when I left the village every morning? Did you choose this spot for that reason?” She eyed him curiously.

His lips briefly curled upwards, barely noticeable before falling back into a neutral line. “Perhaps.”

She smirked. So he hadn’t just been training; he had been waiting for her. “So you must have seen Revali and me.” He nodded. “He finally told me something, though I’m not sure what to make of it. He mentioned a ‘Hero of Time’ and suggested we seek answers in Goron City.” 

“I’m glad he finally spoke with you. We should probably pack up and head out before midday—“

“Wait.” She narrowed at him inquisitively, cutting him off. “Why aren’t you more surprised?”

He gripped the hilt of his sword, the leather creaking under the pressure. “I spoke with him last night.” He wouldn’t meet her eyes, focusing instead on her boots. “I reminded him of his duty.”

His duty. The thought of Link scraping and bowing before Revali had her stomach clenching.

Still, she couldn’t suppress a wry smile. This small victory, at least, was theirs. “Well, it was a success, whatever you did to him.”

He chuckled, as he sheathed his blade, not before ushering Zelda back towards the inn to fetch their stuff, “I reminded him no one likes a sore winner.”

“I bet you did.” A hidden, proud smile formed before she could walk in front of him. “So, have you heard of the Hero of Time?”

“Every half-decent knight has.” His eyes were bright as he continued. “It’s a long story. I can tell you on the way.”

 

Chapter 11: Detour
Chapter Text
During their ride south, he felt the tension melt the further he got from Revali. He knew Revali wouldn’t know much; he would drop the line about his species being a hybrid of perfect evolution and so on, but Impa had strongly encouraged him to make that their first stop. He assumed correctly in how Revali treated Zelda, exactly how he treats everyone else.


The soft background sounds of Epona’s hooves made him ponder if Revali and he would ever bury the axe.


Probably not.


They had made their way down through the pass in good time, deciding to camp above Strock Lake in a familiar enclave. They would make it to Tabantha Bridge Stable by the following afternoon if they kept up the pace. He was somewhat relieved to have privacy again, just the two of them. Zelda had eagerly been waiting to hear about the Hero of Time Legend, and he promised to tell her once camp was set up.


She looked at him with an eager smile on her face, her elbows on her knees, knuckles on her chin. After he hammered the last post of her tent into the ground, he couldn’t help but smile to himself, “I’m pretty tired. Good night, Zel—”


“No wait! You promised me the story.” She stood from her seat.


“Alright, alright.” He grinned. It was too easy.


She sat eagerly in anticipation. He lit the fire between them and settled comfortably into his seat. “Do you remember the oath Impa had me repeat at my knighting ceremony? Particularly about the harmony of power, wisdom, and courage?” A small pink flush painted her high cheekbones. She nodded. “Before time began, there existed three Golden Goddesses, who descended upon the land to create Hyrule.”


“The Goddess Din created the land, the Goddess Nayru blessed it with the law, and the Goddess Farore filled it with life. The three represent power, wisdom, and courage, respectively. When they departed, they left the world colliding, and in the exact location they left the physical world created the Triforce, which resides in the Scared Realm. It is said that whomever touches the Triforce will be granted one wish, regardless of good or evil intentions. And the Scared Realm was created to protect this power. If and when evil came to corrupt it, a Hero would rise.”


Zelda was enthralled by the story, wide-eyed and pulling her bottom lip with her thumb. “A day came when an evil man by the name of Ganondorf schemed to enter the Scared Realm and lay claim to the Triforce. He had evil intentions of ultimate power over all of life. A young boy and the Princess of Hyrule aimed to stop him. They planned to open the realm themselves, and as they did so, they were tricked by Ganondorf. All was not lost, though. The Scared Realm had a fail-safe. Because his heart was evil and unbalanced, the Triforce split, and he was only left with the Triforce of Power. The young boy held the Triforce of Courage. He slept for seven years until he was old enough to wield the Master Sword, the blade of evil’s bane.”


Link continued while grabbing a handful of berries out of the pouch the Rito gave them, “During those seven years, the land became dark and full of despair. Once he woke, the Princess was nowhere to be found. He was instructed to search for the Seven Sages, who were said to have the power to bind evil and return light to the world. Through his courage and bravery, he found and awakened each Sage and in doing so brought peace to each region and their people. After the sixth Sage awoke, the Princess revealed herself from hiding as the seventh and final Sage and the holder of the Triforce of Wisdom. Except Ganondorf was cunning; he waited patiently for the Princess’ return and when she revealed herself to the hero, he captured her to lure the hero to him so he could control all three pieces of the Triforce.”


“The hero, with the assistance of the Sages, fought his way to the throne of the King of Evil. An epic battle ensued that ended with the Hero of Time thrusting the Master Sword through him in defeat. The Sages then bound him in the void of the Scared Realm to never return. Yet he still held the Triforce of Power, promising a time that he would return to cast down the hero and the Princess who put him there. Despite that, peace returned to the land and the people of Hyrule were saved.”


“Wow, you’re a good storyteller.” Zelda resting her face on her palm, “What happened to the Hero and the Princess?”


“The Princess used her powers to send the Hero of Time back to his age, just before pulling the Master Sword, so he could regain his lost childhood. Technically erasing all he had done, leaving the legend behind.”


“That’s… tragic. No one knew that he saved them?” Zelda said sadly.


“Yes, but true heroes shouldn’t do good deeds for recognition. They act because they want to prevail against evil. My fellow knights and I have heard this legend dozens of times in our lives, to remind us why we became knights, not for honor and glory but to triumph over evil and protect Hyrule.”


“I suppose that’s true, but,” Zelda paused, as if unsure if she should continue, her eyes anywhere but his, “weren’t you disappointed when you were not chosen to be Princess Zelda’s royal guard?”


He couldn’t contain the surprise on his face at her question. They never yet spoke on what happened that day that led him to this point with her. He was indeed disappointed, but he hadn’t really given it thought to the real reason why.


Actually, he knew why, but he wasn’t ready to share that with her. “Yes, I was. But perhaps what Impa said was true, we were destined for bigger things.”


He was grateful she sensed his reluctance to continue and didn’t press further. Instead, they ate their dinner in content silence and slept.

They made it to Tabantha Bridge Stable the next afternoon. As he checked them and their horses in for the night, the stable master indicated a messenger left word for him. He handed over a parchment, stamped with Impa’s personal seal.


Link, you are to head to Gatepost Town before departing for Goron City. There are two sets of flame retardant armor and an abundance of flame-resistant elixirs. Ask for Captain Viscan. 


He thought it a bit silly to travel out of the way towards Kolomo on their way to Goron City; it added at least three additional days into their journey. He had planned to stop by the castle to swap out the colder articles for the appropriate heat-resistant ones. But Impa was not one to waste time or energy, so perhaps the castle was out of reserves. He could certainly catch the necessary critters to produce them, but he wasn’t going to disobey Impa.


He frowned to himself; he wasn’t looking forward to it. It had been a few years since he last visited Gatepost Town Garrison. It was an offshoot military garrison south of the castle. Positioned strategically in the southernmost area of Hyrule Field and below the Great Plateau, close to the sacred buildings and better positioned to stall an attack on the castle from the east or west roads. The main garrison laid just an hour north and could easily send troops to help.


But, that wasn’t why he didn’t like it. He didn’t like it because the knights and soldiers positioned there barely knew battle, yet their laziness and entitlement certainly said otherwise. And he was sure that they all heard about Groose’s appointment as the Princess’ royal guard and would make that known to him.


But he would grin and bear it, stay silent until they departed. 


On a positive turn, his and Zelda’s relationship was much improved. After they left Rito Village, the tension eased noticeably between both of them. Zelda had been shooting him warm smiles, and he opened up more. She continued to ask details about the Hero of Time Legend and about the landscape they passed. And he was happy to answer her.


After two days, they made their way down along the Regencia River, passing Giant’s Forest, then Mount Daphnes until the path turned into large stone buildings, sticking out as a sore thumb against the flat green fields, with guards greeting them upon their entry. Zelda was clearly impressed, wonderment painted across her bright face as she glanced around. At least that was a sight to behold.


Hyrule Garrison was mainly military-related buildings and barracks housing. They had their own functioning economy outside the castle, with major trade to provide imports, and Gatepost town only a short ride away where senior military officials who had families lived. Kolomo had been that place initially, but over time, the buildings faded into ruins, now existing only as a scenic landmark.


They continued their descent past Lake Kolomo until the pristine buildings of Gatepost came into focus. The outpost was much larger, and just past the small clearing, most likely that’s where they’d bunk for the night. They dismounted, and Link spoke with the nearest guard, who pointed him towards where Captain Viscan was.


Link didn’t know him personally, but he knew of him. Despite Link’s distaste for the locals, Captain Viscan seemed to be a good man. Both he and Zelda reached the singular building. Link stopped.


“Uh— do you mind waiting out here?” He awkwardly said to Zelda. He hoped he didn’t come off as rude, but he explained, “Typically, non-military personnel do not address captains. I should be fairly quick.”


She smirked, delighted at his uncomfortable nature in asking her innocently. “Of course, I won’t move a muscle.”


He shot her a cheeky grin and headed in. The room had a long table greeting him, designed for military strategy amongst ranking officials, and doors on either side, one closed, another open. “Captain Viscan?” He called out.


“Yes, come in.” A voice from the door on the left. He entered, seeing Captain Viscan sitting at his desk. He was dressed in traditional military gear befitting a captain not in battle. He was younger than most captains he knew, maybe in his mid-thirties, despite the worrying wrinkles on his forehead. He pulled himself up from his paperwork. “Ah, Sir Link. What do we owe the pleasure?”


Link was surprised he knew him by name. “Master Impa sent me to retrieve flame resistance gear and elixirs you have in store. She routed me here on my way to Goron City.”


“Right, she sent a letter here mentioning that. We have to pull it out of stores. I’ll send a few men to do that. While they are preparing, you can stay in the Outpost Inn for the night.” 


“Thank you, Captain. That’s appreciated. I’ll leave you to your work.” Link turned and proceeded to exit. 


“I saw your tournament.”


He stopped in his tracks. Who hadn’t seen it.


“You were robbed. Anyone with eyes saw you were the clear winner.”


“Thank you.” Link gritted through his teeth.


“I’m assuming since you are here on Master Impa’s word that she has since assigned you?” Captain Viscan eyed him curiously. “I’m certain whatever it is is of utmost importance, as anyone would be unwell to decide against you safeguarding the Princess.” His facial expression remained the same bored look but he genuinely meant that.


Link didn’t really think about it that way. He kept his face in a neutral expression, trying to repress a small smile.


Maybe that’s true. Zelda was important. “Yes, important indeed. Thank you, Captain, for the kind words. I’ll make my way to the Outpost now and connect with you in the morning.”


He nodded and dismissed Link with a half-hand wave. As he exited the building, the captain’s words hung in his ear. He had been looking at his appointment of Zelda as an opportunity of chance rather than a skill in deserving. Sure, she wasn’t a princess, but she was important to him and Impa. 


As he exited, renewed with a sense of purpose, she was nowhere to be found. Slight panic rose in his throat, his mind flashing to the events with the Bokoblins that seemed like a lifetime ago.


Just as quickly as the thought came, he heard her laugh. Following the enchanting new sounds around the corner, he saw her. Her smile wide, beaming, white teeth visible, and eyes shining.


Was this the first time he heard her laugh? Surely not? They’ve spent almost every moment together over the past two weeks. He glanced at the person making her features glow brightly. It was another knight, who he knew well.


Purlo was facing her, leaning against the building, too close to her, beaming his white smile down at her, almost hauntingly as his eyes stared greedily at hers. He towered over her, dressed in his chest armor, polished into a mirror shine, and sword on his back that had probably never seen battle. What was he saying that was so funny?


Then he noticed Link, tilting his head to him, and his smile faded to a shit-eating smirk. “Ah, Sir Link, good to see you, kid.”


Link’s blood was boiling at the remark. Purlo had only been a few years older; they were knighted at the same time, except Link was younger when he was knighted and earned it, whereas Purlo came from a rich family and was given the title. “Sir Purlo,” Link thought his teeth might splinter as he gritted out his titled name.


“Have you met the lovely Zelda? I’ve just had the charming pleasure.” He turned and shot an arrogant smile to her. Surely she did not buy this rubbish he was saying? Yet her smile was still wide at his remark. 


He was certainly going to lose his cool. Before he could, Zelda spoke, “Link is my appointed knight. Master Impa appointed him herself to me.”


“Ah, that’s right, the tournament.” Purlo now stopped leaning and had been a solid few inches taller than Link. “I heard all about it. Your loss seems to have been for the better though, being charged to such a lovely lady.” He winked at Zelda. Link had to stop himself from unsheathing his sword as Zelda snorted. 


“Zelda, I have rooms for us in the Outpost, just a short walk away. Let’s head there now before it gets dark.” Link ignored Purlo completely. Childish, sure, but it was the only way to stop himself from splintering his own teeth.


“Of course, it was a pleasure, Sir Purlo.” Zelda said, giving him a faint head bow.


He picked up her hand and kissed it, “The pleasure was mine. I’m sure I’ll see you soon.” That smirk he shot her would haunt Link later.


“Sir Link.” He finished casually with a barely noticeable head tilt and walked towards the captain’s office.


Link was hot. As much as he disliked Purlo in general, he never felt so twisted over previous interactions with him. He thought back to his days just before he became a knight, the last time he saw Purlo before he was assigned here.


Purlo had come from a rich, noble family. He was objectively handsome, at least that’s how girls and women treated him. He had golden blonde hair, blue eyes, he was tall, and had a strong build. As if he was designed to be in the military, except he was talentless. Back then, some even mistook them for brothers or cousins at times. Besides the color of their eyes, Link never saw any resemblance and resented that comparison. Unfortunately for all the righteousness Hyrule likes to pride itself on, it was not immune to the shadow of nepotism in the military and otherwise.


He hadn’t seen him since then. Link stayed in the castle to continue training in his career, whereas Purlo was assigned to the Hyrule Garrison, as befitting someone who will never see battle. He forgot all about him until he saw him flirting with his charge.


Link grabbed their horses by the lead and walked toward the Outpost. Zelda seemed lighter and chatty. “You know Sir Purlo well?”


“I know him well enough,” he said coolly.


Zelda either ignored his curt tone or didn’t hear it. “He was telling me about the community. They have a tavern that has a famous bard play often, and everyone in the community attends. They drink, dance, and it’s positively festive. He said tonight the bard was playing.”


He grunted.


“Would you like to go? It might be nice for you to have some respite.” She smiled pleadingly at him.


He couldn’t help but soften. “I’d like that.” 

He got their horses stabled and checked them into rooms for the evening. It was dusk, and they agreed to meet outside her room door.


He wasn’t one to sit in anger or resentment. Honestly, he hadn’t even thought of Purlo since their knighting ceremony all those years ago.


Why did it bother him so much that Zelda was laughing? Her laugh was infectious; he wanted to hear it again, but at the command of his words, not another’s.


He knocked on her door and waited for her while giving himself a once-over. He decided to forgo his armor and weapons, knowing that any threat would be swiftly dealt with in the community filled with military officials. Plus, the tavern was close enough that he could gather his weapons in a few moments. Her door creaked loudly, catching his attention and making his eyes widen.


She decided to forgo her typical travel pants and shirt and instead opted for a simple linen skirt and corset. Her arms, bare yet subtly defined, highlighted her sharp collarbones. She tied her golden blonde locks into a low braided bun, revealing her naked neck while still partially covering her ears. The sparkles of her earrings twinkled back at him. She appeared modestly gorgeous, and every inch of her had his core growing molten.


“Is this okay to wear? I’m sure your taverns are a very different scene from what I’m used to.” She smiled and pursed her lower lip.


He continued to rake his eyes over her. Was it okay? It was certainly okay with him. He shamefully thought that he would prefer that she wore it elsewhere with just him, away from the eyes of hungry soldiers. And, she smelled of lavender; being so close to her, the scent filled his nostrils blissfully, making him forget the question.


“What?” He said embarrassingly late.


“Maybe I’ll wear a jacket.” She went back in her room, and he was sure his ears were red.


They walked into the tavern, which was already brimming full of guards and soldiers situated at the tables, all so engrossed in their conversations, none turned to notice their entrance. They made their way to one of the last empty tables and sat. A young barmaid greeted them eagerly. Link asked her for two ales.


“You only have one type of ale?” Zelda asked.


“Sort of, only Hylian ale is available around here. Other regions have specialty drinks based on what’s seasonal to their regions.”


He proceeded to tell her about the wider range of spirits and wines in the Zora and Gerudo regions. Rito typically didn’t drink, but in the northern Hebra region, they brew hearty lagers, and Gorons had fire water. She shook her head and countered that where she was from, they had millions of variations of spirits imported and exported all across their world, but she only partook in a few favorites of hers. She did enjoy a good ale and a nice wine.


The barmaid brought their ales with a smile for him. He ordered the kitchen special for the both of them, which was a rice and meat dish. They happily drank and talked about their respective homes. He hadn’t even started asking her where she came from and how drastically different it would be. He felt ignorant at that and made an effort to ask her about her life. 


She explained that what she had witnessed here so far was a similar to her world, but centuries before her time. Technological advancements had streamlined their way of life, but every new creation or improvement to aid humans only brought more challenges. There’s a constant balance in everything.


As their meals arrived and they began to eat, she continued. “—One aspect I very much enjoy here is how slow things are.” He lifted a brow at her, and she chuckled, “I just mean that there’s a serene calmness in every task. We are taking time to get to our destinations; we aren’t running at breakneck speeds, enjoying the adventure. It’s very different from what I’m used to.” Her eyes were staring in thought just past him, and he watched a faint smile pull on her mouth. “It’s not so bad being here a little longer.”


Right, can’t forget the whole point of this journey. Find answers to get her home. 


They finished their meals, and another round was brought for both of them. Any troubles that had been plaguing them were slowly fading away with each sip and bite they took. Link excused himself, and she teased with a smile, eyes twinkling, “Hurry back.”


Maybe it was the ale making him looser, but he felt real progress of a blooming friendship with her. The mysterious, unconscious woman who appeared out of thin air in strange clothes seemed like a lifetime ago now. Her appearing when she did, just before the tournament to decide his future, was perhaps fate.


There were worse things than adventuring with an attractive woman who also had a pleasant personality, he mused to himself.


He made his way back inside, head spinning at the thought of what his life might look like now, until he saw them.


Purlo, again, that fucker. He had one arm pressing up on the table, hovering over her. He was drinking in the site of her, with his unsettling smirk and predator’s gleam as he glared down at her. Had he been lurking in the shadows, waiting for him to leave to pounce on her?


Then, she laughed. The weightlessness he had felt a moment ago suddenly felt as if a boulder lay on his chest.


He begrudgingly made his way back to the table. The sight of her laugh made him feel ill.


“Purlo.” Short and cutting.


“Link.” He gave him a half-cocked nod, finally picking his hand off the table to flex his height over Link. “I just came in and was greeted by the beautiful Zelda sitting here alone. I positively had to save her from the loneliness she surely felt in your absence.”


Zelda huffed fake concern and smiled at the clearly fake flattery. “Oh yes, my hero.” She rolled her eyes with a smile.


As if the timing couldn’t be any worse, the band started up to the delight of the crowd around them. His gut sank knowing what was coming next. Purlo extended his hand to her and asked for a dance.


Zelda looked at Link, her head tilted just slightly, eyes wide, somewhat waiting for any indication from him. He didn’t give it.


She finally turned her gaze back to Purlo, “I’d be honored.”


Link sat fuming in his seat, trying not to watch them dance, trying not to react watching Purlo’s hand hold her back. Too low. He told himself it was because he didn’t trust Purlo, the guy was a snake. How was he supposed to accurately watch his charge if he allowed another he doesn’t trust to be near her? Might as well be dancing with a Moblin.


But that wasn’t true and he knew it. The lie burrowed itself deep in his spine. He tried to close his eyes or look elsewhere but Purlo’s smirk still hung in his vision.


After what seemed like an hour, the song stopped and they made their way back. Zelda was flushed prettily with excursion.


“Shall we refill and keep going?” Purlo said looking straight at her.


“We have an early day tomorrow, we should get going.” Link snapped without acknowledging him.


“If the lady wants to stay, I can escort her back, it would be my honor.” Purlo shot a wink at her. Link almost throttled him.


“That’s up to her.” He sensed her eyes on him, pausing for any indication he could give her. But he couldn’t look her in the eyes, shamefully.


“Sure, I’ll stay for one more, if that’s okay with you, Link?” Zelda said quietly.


“Fine by me. I’ll see you in the morning.” He didn’t want to be so biting with her, but the selfishness in him was rising quickly. Before he could see her reaction, he turned and left.


He walked back to his room thinking how could he be so distracted? He had to keep the task at hand in the forefront. He could not fail, remembering his vows. Honor Hyrule, honor the goddesses, and to be faithful, holding honor and courtesy above all else to his charge. He wasn’t holding up to any of those vows, instead letting his emotions get the best of him. He needed to become the stoic knight he’d been before her arrival. Determined to be the best, putting duty above all else.


But it wasn’t easy. He lay awake in his room, unable to sleep. Thoughts of her skirt twirling, the accentuated curve of her hips, and the scent of lavender spun around his head. He was only able to drift off for a bit after he heard her shut her door across the hall.

He was up early. Before sunrise. He had barely slept. He grabbed his sword and walked to Kolomo, passing by the yawning night guards, waiting for their relief to arrive. He walked by the crumbling buildings overlooking the lake. Just like everything else that isn’t properly maintained, it falls into ruin, leaving behind the visible scars of history past. 


There was a training facility in town, but he resolved to expel all the tension he held privately. The last thing he wanted to do was run into anyone else that knew him.


As the sun rose over Dueling Peaks, he continued lunging aggressively at the imaginary foe he just so happened to picture with blonde hair and shiny armor. He didn’t realize that hours had passed until Zelda’s figure approached in the distance, golden light shining behind her.


She wore her travel clothes again, her hair was down and pull to one side. She looked radiant. Daylight made human. Perhaps the bright smile she had been showing him lately was what tied it all together. “I was looking for you all morning. The guard said he saw you heading this way.”


He grunted in response, continuing his squat twist.


“How did you sleep?” She asked with trepidation. She was trying. Standing at a distance, a distance he put between them.


“Alright.” 


Her smile faded and her posture stiffened. “Is something upsetting you?”


He stopped, letting his sword’s tip drop to the dirt. “No. I don’t want to lose focus on the task at hand. I’m getting distracted.” He breathed deeply. He knew he shouldn’t have said what he said next. “Impa tasked me with helping you. I am to keep you alive and get you home, nothing more.”


“Right. OK.” She found his eyes, challenging him. “You’ll be the hero, safely guiding me to my destination.” She held his gaze, so intensely into his soul he was sure she’d see through him. “Why are you even doing this? Because Impa said?”


He paused.


She continued, “What are you hoping to gain?”


He didn’t answer. He was ready to be her punching bag if need be.


She scoffed. “Such a hero.” Her words like venom. “You are no better than everyone else. Doing heroic deeds to be remembered in your history books. I’m just sorry you were saddled with me instead of the Princess.” She stomped back towards town but not before stopping and throwing the last verbal punch. “Next time I’ll make sure to time my sudden appearance after you’ve been assigned.”


He wanted to stop her and tell her it wasn’t true. He was happy to be with her, that for the first time in his life he felt the heaviness of the pressure of his destiny soften. That the past few days have made him feel lightweight, free, and happy. That perhaps she was fated to appear when she did.


But he didn’t. Instead, he silently followed her back towards town.

 

Chapter 12: Fire
Notes:
I’m LIVING for all your engagement in this story. It’s keeping me motivated and moving, so much so that I’m getting ahead that I might have two for you next week— in the meantime enjoy the heated* tension between these two.

Chapter Text
She watched as a butterfly with red wings lazily flapped in front of her. She sat perfectly still in front of the communal cooking pot, observing the winged creature flutter about. She slowly held her hand out in an effort to let it perch, but it instinctively flew away.


How fitting, not even butterflies want to be around me. She thought.


They made it to Foothill Stable in less than a week. The journey had been quiet. Her jaw hurt from the tension of trying to keep it shut, which had been difficult because she liked to talk. Link, in no uncertain way, made it clear that this was a job to him, and he could get back to his life once she got home. 


It was hurtful. She had thought they started to develop a friendly relationship, since he shared the Hero of Time Legend with her. It was the most she ever heard him speak, and he had such a way about him when he was telling her. Pride, almost, beaming at the knowledge he held in kindred spirit towards the hero of legend. Her willingness to learn about their legends and folklore only inspired him more to open up and answer her questions. By the time they arrived at the Gatepost, they were exchanging smiles with each other.


That night in the tavern, she had hoped he would ask her to dance, but Purlo swooped in the second he left and proceeded to flatter her. His blatant attempts at said flattery were so over the top that it made her laugh. She had thought it was intentional in an effort to exaggerate, but rather he was serious.


Purlo was classically handsome, no doubt. He was built lean, tall, and had chiseled facial features, but he didn’t make her heart swell. Still, she was human, and catching the favor of a handsome young knight isn’t the worst thing to happen. 


It did cause Link to become shut off from her. After he left abruptly, she made polite small talk with Purlo and left shortly after he did. She wanted to knock on his door, let him know she was back and safe, but she didn’t.


She knew based on their Rito stay that he liked to train isolated each morning. She asked the guard on duty where the wheat-blonde knight went; he pointed to Lake Kolomo. As she approached him, the morning sun dancing off the water’s edge hit him just right; he was glistening. He used the rest of the day to prepare for their journey ahead: resting their horses, stocking saddle bags, and forging ingredients for heat elixirs. He picked up his salary from the treasury, his pay sitting untouched while traveling. The cranky treasurer handed over his purse, annoyed that he had to pay Link interest on the sitting amount. He carefully poured out the contents, and a number of silver, gold, and purple rupees sparkled at him. He counted the amount: two months of salary, but double what he had been paid previously.


If he had to guess, his silent promotion to royal guard almost doubled his salary. Knights were paid well, enough to comfortably support a family, a home, and sizable land, but royal guards could own large estates and multiple lands and homes with this rate.


Link didn’t much care or need money. He paid his fair share of taxes, but he resided in the castle, and whatever food he consumed was either provided for him or he foraged for it. During his and Zelda’s travels, he’d spent the most, opting to stay at the stables and purchasing meals for both of them. But he didn’t mind spending money on her.

She told him about a kabob she had in the castle town square after the tournament when she was wandering alone. How a woman gave her a free one, and it was the most satisfying meal she ever had. He was impressed; not often did vendors give free food, and he joked with her on what she really offered to the vendor. Zelda exaggerated a fake insult, mouth gapping and chuckling, her eyes sparkling, and she swatted at him in fake hurt.


He was fond of that memory.

His motives were selfish, primarily to avoid Gatepost Town. Additionally, he wanted to show her the grassy, mountainous views she had briefly mentioned about her own home. Something to make her happy, to see her brilliant smile again.

Impa also had a home in Kakariko Village, but she mainly spent her time at the castle.

“He mentioned that there has been an unusual amount of monsters around the city and that Death Mountain has become unpredictable, causing quakes and falling boulders more often.” Link paused and continued. “He also mentioned Sages.”

Kokiri’s Emerald, Goron’s Ruby, and Zora’s Sapphire.” Impa closed the book. He could read the title of the book, Hyrule Legends: Volume III. The Legend of the Hero of Time.

Impa pensively brought her hand to her chin. “Very interesting that this story was brought up. I’m assuming because our Zelda traveled through Time, they both immediately came to this conclusion. But I’m not sure.” Hearing our Zelda caused his stomach to twist.

He was ruthless in his pursuit of power. One Gerudo warrior defied him, aided the Hero, and became the Sage of Spirit. Ask Urbosa what they know about their history with the Evil King and the Sage.”

His gut flipped. He turned to her face, using every ounce of training to hold his emotions in check. “What?” Replying with a question seemed like the right move, even if Impa thought less of him for it.


“I sensed it from her. The moment I saw her face, I knew she was important. I don’t know why or how yet, but she’s meant to be here.” Impa stopped her sentence, but he knew she wasn’t finished. “And I think you’re meant to be with her on this journey.”


She’s important.


He knew that. He knew that from the moment he picked her up, all sun-kissed skin, white clothes, and golden hair safely wrapped in his arms. He knew she was important, but he didn’t know what that meant to him.


Her brows raised slightly towards her hairline. She tilted her head down in a knowing motion, “You’ll do well to remember to care for her. Not only keep her from physical danger but take care of her emotional state.” Impa was being as subtle as a hinox sleeping.


“I will.” He replied back, but couldn’t meet her gaze.

After Impa’s not-so-subtle advice, he decided to head to the stables. He’d make sure both their horses had fresh horseshoes and were cleaned for the journey.


Part of him hoped to see Ilya.


After they arrived back at the castle, Zelda had gravitated to Ilya, drawing the line in the sand for sides. He wondered if Zelda told his old childhood friend every detail about their journey. Ilya would scold him if she did, rightfully so.

“Link!” Her face warm and inviting, “I was wondering if I’d see you before you left again. I thought maybe you’d sneak out in the middle of the night without a word,” she chortled.

“I know, I’m only teasing.” She came to squeeze his arm, making him feel at ease. “I have both Epona and Storm all set to go. New horseshoes, they’ve been brushed and washed. I even had the stable hand fix your saddle.”


“Thank you, Ilya. You know me and Epona so well.” Link couldn’t help his deflated tone.


“You know, Epona and Storm are getting along surprisingly well. Epona has always been mild-mannered, but I wasn’t sure how Storm would interact with her since he’s feisty. But they just seem to work well together.” Ilya had clearly been hinting at something.


“Have you spoken with her?” They both knew who he meant.


“Briefly. She was tight-lipped about your journey. I’m sure it’s— difficult— for both of you.”


Clearly, Zelda had not filled in her new friend on the details of his overly watchful gaze on her. If she had, Ilya would be having a very different tone with her childhood friend.


“Link, it will get easier. You’ll continue to search for answers, you both will find your way. And you’ll learn to work together too.” Ilya now holding his hand, silently comforting him.


She misunderstood the true source of his internal struggle, but he wasn’t ready to share that. “I know, Ilya, thank you for the reassurance.” He pulled gently away from her. “I should get going.”


“She asked me about the Legends of the Hero of Time.” Ilya responded quickly, “I showed her the library, and she lit up. I’m sure that’s where she’s been.”


Ilya knew him too well, “Thanks.” He shot her one more knowing smile, which she returned.


The library was buried deep in the castle. The magnificent two-story room held every book anyone could possibly need. Books about science and technology, books about the royal family tree, or even storybooks, such as ones he read as a child.


He hiked all the way back to the castle; he was actually slightly tired from all the back and forth he’d done today.


As he entered the large room from the top floor, ceiling-length curtains hung throughout to give a sense of privacy amongst the genres and sections. There were also small reading nooks built off to the sides on both floors. Each nook was situated based on the need of the reader. If research was necessary, the room with the long table and parchment. If you were reading for pleasure, the smaller room with the couch might suit better. He couldn’t locate her from his first glance above, so he descended the stairs to check below.


He was quietly snaking around the sections. Peaking behind every curtain to try to locate where she may be. For such an open room, the castle decorator had done a good job making it seem private.


When Ilya told him she was probably here, he couldn’t help his quickening heart at the thought of her golden hair buried in a book. The idea that the Legend of the Hero of Time had piqued her interest so much that she wanted to know more. He thought back to their campsite near Strock Lake and how her face lit up as he told her the story. Green eyes wide with eagerness, brows perked at the sudden twists and betrayals, finished with a smile for the triumphant conquering hero. 


He hadn’t told her he was named after the Hero of Legend.


He wanted to. He would now, if the time was right.


He was resolved to explain his behavior at Gatepost and Goron City. He would explain his intentions, that he didn’t want to keep his distance; he was only envious. He would apologize to her and ask her forgiveness. And if she wasn’t ready to give it to him, he would wait, wait until she was ready.

She was there. She was sitting quietly on the long couch, relaxed. Her legs curled in, hiding underneath the black skirt she wore, splayed out against the red fabric of the couch. Her hair was styled in a loose braid on her side. She had a book in hand, smiling down at the pages in her grasp, eyes twinkling underneath long lashes. No matter what she wore or what she was doing, she was alluring.


He so desperately wished she were alone. 


Purlo sat next to her on the couch. He was smiling a disgustingly white smile down upon her. He had no book; he seemed to be just watching her while she read, annoyingly so.


Link stood at the threshold. The room was designed with a small entryway for privacy. He could see both of them clearly, but they hadn’t had a chance to see him. He was hoping to keep it that way and carefully back away.


Unfortunately, the goddesses had other plans, and Purlo noticed him.

Luckily, Zelda didn’t notice or care that Purlo had left her personal space; her eyes were still scanning the book in front of her.

“I’ve been assigned here temporarily.” He said slyly, “Since you and Groose are on assignment, I’ve come to fill your position. You know how hard it is to find good knights.”


Bastard.


“I needed to confirm our itinerary with Zelda.” Link emphasized our. He would not let him get a rise out of him today.


“Of course, you leave the day after tomorrow. Zelda did tell me that. I’m sure you’ll take good care of her, but I’d be happy to step in if you’d rather be assigned elsewhere.” Smugness oozed from him.

If you kill him, you can’t protect her anymore. He had to remind himself, she was more important than his pride.

His hand reaching under her shirt, touching her soft skin. Lifting up fabric, exposing her.


Fuck. He dropped the vial he had in his hands, shattering it.

What did he wish for? 


His gaze traitorously went to the adjoining door. He wished for a lot of things. Things good, honest knights shouldn’t want for.

 

Chapter 14: Shrine
Chapter Text
The bass was thumping in her rib cage. Pulsing and vibrating rhythmically within her. Surrounded by strangers seated at high-top tables, dressed in their weekend finest, she herself donned a matching beige silken bandeau and skirt. The cool night air caressed her bare shoulders. The café lights overhead cast a warm, flickering glow on everyone.


It wasn’t really her scene. Out in the city at a new rooftop bar, but Linda wanted to come, and she didn’t see her friend very often these days. They just finished the university year, so it was cause to celebrate. Unfortunately, Linda’s idea of celebration was with overpriced bottle service and vapid strangers.


The night air kissed her face and blew lightly through her already tangled hair. She reached for a knot near her neck and methodically began to detangle it.


“Stop doing that!” Linda hissed at Zelda. She swatted her hand away from the tangle she was working on. “Nobody is going to approach the girl pulling out stray hairs from her head.” Linda snarled, close enough for only her to hear but loud enough to cut through the house music.


“I don’t care about anyone else, I’m just here for you.” She countered. Linda cocked her brow. Zelda knew Linda couldn’t resist the attention.


“Fine. As long as you’re over that dickhead.” The dickhead in question she was referring to was Cole. And she was. Mostly.


She stared out past the open ceiling of the bar, her eyes landing on an old red brick building in the distance. The stained and discolored bricks were uneven and barely held together. She left Cole six months ago. She didn’t miss him, the person, but she did miss the companionship. She pondered that thought and compared herself to the bricks that barely held together the facade of the building. Beautifully imperfect.

“What! How do you know?” Zelda’s brows went high, mouth gaping.


“Well—” she dragged the word and paused in anticipation, “He told me he would.” She laughed.


“What?” Zelda asked flatly.


“We talk about it all the time. We’ve been together so long, and it was bound to happen sooner rather than later.” Linda took a long sip of her vodka soda. “Why should we wait? We know we’re meant to be together.”


For someone like Linda, whose whole personality was built on deep irony and ridicule of the world and everything in it, it was her undeniable love for Anton that made all her jaded feelings seem like cute remarks. They were destined to be together; it was obvious when they were children who played together. Their friendship grew from cute fondness to a deep, powerful love over their tenure. Zelda wondered if she’d ever be so lucky.
