Or she, she thought. Maybe this technology could get her home. Why hadn’t Impa or Link mentioned that? “Where is this shrine, exactly?” She pressed the merchant.


He explained throughly where the shrine should be. Back along the path they already traveled to Rito Village, with a slight deviation. Maybe a half-day’s ride, if they went fast. 


She finished her wine and politely excused herself from the merchant to make her way to stand above Link, whose blue eyes were meeting hers for the first time that day.


She always forgot how blue they were until he stared at her like this. Almost making her forget why she’d come over to him in the first place.


“That merchant mentioned a shrine near the ancient columns.” She whispered to him.


Link pulled his eyes back down to continue to work on his bow string, pulling it tightly towards the opposite end of the base, which was made of intricate blue and grey markings. “I’m familiar with it.”


“Maybe that shrine will get me answers about going home. Can we go investigate?” She tried her best to sound innocently pleading. It had been a while since she used that form of exploitation on anyone, and she was never good at it.


Link’s face unchanged, his fingers had successfully threaded the string through the edge as he set it down on his knees. “All shrines across Hyrule have stayed inactive since the dawn of history. I doubt it will open its secrets now.”


“But can’t we try? It’s only a half-day’s ride from here.” She pleaded her voice in a last-ditch effort, but trying not to sound desperate.


“We can’t. We have to stay on schedule; the Gerudo are expecting us.” He replied in his flat, unemotional tone. For a split second, she thought his mouth twitched downwards.


“What’s the point of visiting the Gerudo if the shrine works?” She said in a dry tone.


He picked his head up to stare deeply at her; she went breathless for a moment at the quiet intensity between them. His face looked sad, desperate, yet unfazed. “I’m sorry.”


She glowered at him, pursing her lips. Her batting eyelashes and sweet tone did nothing to persuade him.


Fine. She’ll find her own way. She grabbed an apple from his open bag next to him and shot him a cold look before stomping away.

After she retired to her tent, she listened as Link climbed into the hammock. He purposely positioned his hammock nearby, close if he had to get to her quickly but some distance if she had to relieve herself in the night.


Her plan was risky; for all she knew, he never slept. Everything he had shown her said he was a superior species; maybe he didn’t need sleep. Even if she slipped past him, she would have to lead Storm away quietly. Which would be a challenge, as he was appropriately named.


She was going to the ancient columns; she had to try. She had a horse this time, and she knew the path well enough. Last time they traveled, no monsters were blocking their path. There was a stable up ahead if she got into trouble. She didn’t need him. That much.


She quietly stepped out of her tent, in her same travel clothes. She didn’t risk peeking at him. She crept over to Storm, next to Epona, who looked at her judgmentally but kept quiet. She untied his lead from the tree and pulled out the apple she swiped from Link and started to walk backwards from their campsite. Storm followed, to her surprise, quietly.


After she felt far enough away from the campsite, Storm indulged in his apple while she climbed into the saddle and headed northwest.

Dawn had since come to pass, and she assumed it was still early as she led Storm up a steep incline. She had stopped travelers and merchants along her path to confirm her route; they assured her she was going in the right direction.


Link had to be awake by now, she pondered his reaction. He always awoke before her, but he may not realize her absence yet unless he peered in her tent or noticed the missing horse next to his own.


Would he be worried? Furious with anger over her misdirection? Would he be relieved? Tell Impa that she was insignificant and stupid enough to go on her own.


As she plateaued, old marble columns and archways stood epically in front of her. The sky still had remnants of pink from the sunrise greeting her. Even if the shrine hadn’t been the reason for her insubordination, this view was worth it.


She spotted what she could only assume was the shrine. A dark stone monument stood out of place from all the other ruins. Orange constellations decorated the outside curiously. 


She dismounted Storm, who was happy to rest and eat grass as she approached. The shrine was huge. She felt the immense power radiating from it. Perhaps containing the power to get her home.


For a better part of an hour, she examined every square inch of the shrine. She ran her fingers over the obsidian exterior, which was cold to the touch. She traced the orange lines that seemed to glow, despite no obvious power source. It had a pedestal with a mechanism that looked like it could be activated. She pressed her handprint to the cold stone, feeling for a button or lever, but nothing she tried worked.


She sat on the edge of the shrine’s surface, facing the curious old ruined columns. Elbows on her knees, hand on her temples, and pulled her face down in an effort to wipe away her growing frustration. She nudged a rock by her boot, picking it up. A worm left in the impression of dirt, twisting violently at the displacement she caused it.


She felt that. Felt like that worm. It had been minding its business, mindlessly carrying on in the cold earth, until someone disrupted its whole universe with one simple action.


Looking back at the shrine, eyes tracing the orange lines that glowed mysteriously by some magic.


That was it. Magic.


Her world had no magic, no monsters, no special ability foods or tonics. She didn’t belong here.


She still wasn’t convinced everything that happened to her was entirely real. She could indeed be dead or in a coma.


But weeks have passed by, and she still continued to dream. She didn’t escape her nightmares of possessed machines, still visiting her occasionally here. And the dreams of a gallant, handsome knight extending a hand to her. Her hand squeezed the smooth rock, trying to turn it into a stress ball.


She wasn’t special. She wasn’t magic. She didn’t belong here. Everyone at the castle knew it. Impa knew it. Link knew it. Maybe she didn’t belong anywhere. Her vision became blurry.


She threw the rock and screamed. A primal scream that was buried deep inside her.


She screamed for everything. But ultimately, she screamed because she was lonely.


She never had a lot of friends, but Linda was enough to give her what she needed. Marin’s presence helped her feel less lonely despite an apartment wall between them. Cole was an asshole, but he filled those holes, as best as he could. Everyone here had been welcoming enough. But she was so lonely for real warmth.


She let herself get lost in her despair. Hands buried in her face, hot tears running down her cheeks. It was the first time since she landed here that she let herself fall into this negative space. Her optimism could only bring her so far. The small ray of hope to see her friend’s face again now seemed impossible.


Then she heard it. Thundering hoofbeats sounded up the hill, instantly she knew.


Link’s familiar blonde head and his chestnut mare emerged. They swiftly made their way directly to her. She barely had more than a few seconds to pull herself together. She turned her back to his approach, wiping the salty tears off her flushed face. Despite her best efforts, anyone that saw her would know she had been crying.


Link swung off Epona in an always impressive display of strength and strode up to her.


She knew Link would be mad. She left him without a word in the middle of the night. She wondered if he knew immediately where she had gone. She wasn’t totally heartless; she did make a point to show her face at the Tabantha Bridge Stable before heading up here.


She braced herself for his wrath. Facing him down, her face unyielding to the potentially incoming anger that she had seen out in the field against the Bokoblins. She wouldn’t let herself be fazed; she had more tears to cry, but she wouldn’t let him be the one to unleash them. 


She steeled herself, knowing that he could have prevented this fury if he just took her here himself.


As he arrived mere feet away, he said nothing. Just fixated on her as her hand gripped the shrine’s pedestal. She braced. Waited for him to say anything.


But nothing came. He just stared at her.


His indifference drove her outburst. Her face red as she bellowed, “You didn’t need to follow me. I clearly made it here on my own just fine.” She stared him down in challenge.


Nothing, his expression unchanged. His eyes bright and mouth straight, clenched tight. It only fueled her rage more.


She yelled for everything she wanted to say for weeks, “I had to try this, try something! I know you hate me and wished for anything or anyone else to be assigned to. I’m sorry that Impa assigned you to me, for both our sakes.” Spit was flying from her mouth, her cheeks red.


She would come to regret her next words for a long time.


“The faster I get home, the faster we can be rid of each other, you can go back to your life of honorary service and noble deeds protecting princesses and nobles. Not having to watch over some common, insignificant person such as me.” Her fists were white and shaking with rage. Half-crescent moons dug into her palms. 


It wasn’t what she truly meant. None of it was. But it was better to be angry at him for his lack of emotion rather than try to let him in. She already tried to do that and he recoiled. She couldn’t take the rejection again.


She stared at him with feral desperation. He still said nothing. Unfazed by her outburst. Any reaction would have been something, a sign of care in some form of anger or relief.


She pulled her eyes away from his, instinctively back to the spot the worm had been, now vanished.


“I’m honored to serve you in any way you need and I will continue to do so until my last breath or until I am dismissed,” Link said, strong and unfaltering. She almost believed him.


She couldn’t manage to meet his gaze again. All she could do is jump back on Storm and trot away from the failed experiment. She heard his familiar grunt when he swung onto Epona. She couldn’t be bothered to look.

As they passed through the familiar canyon, this time, she led. Storm walking slowly, as if spent, his energy matching hers. She listened to the hooves echoing off the walls and drifted back into her daydream from before. The man on the rooftop bar. He asked her out and she said yes.


They went out to dinner a few nights later. He was devilishly charming with a perfectly white smile. He had a good job, a nice family, and lots of friends. He was funny, charismatic, and perfect on paper. As they laughed and talked through dinner, it hit her that something was missing.


Then she remembered why they parted the dinner as friends and why she never saw him again.


The spark. The physical attraction for him was there but she was lacking that instant chemistry. The feeling of forgetting how to breathe when first locking eyes with someone.


She dared to look over her shoulder in that moment. Link’s bright blue eyes found hers.

Chapter 15: Sand
Notes:
We’ve arrived to Chapter 15! I’m deeply grateful to everyone enjoying this story so far. Let’s pause for a moment and take a quick look at what’s ahead.

I’ve already outlined and drafted over 40 chapters. It’s a long fic. But I promise, it won’t drag. I have been marinating on this story for over a year, and for those of you waiting for that eventual E rating… we’ll get there. Just remember, the first tag is slow burn for a reason. So you’ll have to be patient. So patient. But hey, it is a virtue, right?

As for our two leads, things will definitely get messier before they get better. So settle in and enjoy.

Chapter Text
“Bugs for sale! Cold, warm, and electric darners! All you’ll need to survive the unforgiving wasteland ahead!” A traveling merchant with a straw hat boomed loudly to anyone listening. Link just sat in front of the cooking pot, fist on his cheek, paying no attention.

After what felt like a full year of traveling, they made it to the Gerudo Canyon Stable.

Zelda was inside resting. Link sat quietly and stared at the billowing smoke from the fire in front of him.

Their journey took a week from Tabantha Bridge Stable but felt much longer. They hadn’t stopped by Satori Mountain as he had planned just for her. She was completely shut down the whole ride here.

He found Storm gone and her tent empty just before dawn. The feeling of dread and panic, coupled with flashes of the memory of her terrified face from the night he found her in Hyrule Field, haunted him. He knew instinctively she went to the shrine. She made it clear she wanted to go home and would do anything, with or without him, to do it.

When he made it to the stable, a passerby mentioned a golden blond woman that looked like the princess asking after the shrine’s location. The tension in his shoulders eased slightly at his relief that they confirmed she had been alive. By midday, he made his way up the last incline towards the mysterious column ruins when he heard a scream. Every bone in his body went rigid, and he had already worn Epona out with his race to get her. But as if Epona was worried herself, she continued to thunder towards her.

As he leveled out, he finally took a long-awaited exhale, seeing her alive and physically unharmed. But as he approached, he sensed the heaviness in the air.

She screamed, not because she was in danger, but in agony and anguish. He saw her face red and flushed from crying, her features pulled into pained desolation, her bright green eyes empty and hollow. He saw the shrine just as all others had been, cold and unopened. And the relief he felt just a moment ago that he found her safe was replaced by deep wretchedness. Yes, she was alive, but this pain she held hurt him by extension. He could protect her physically from harm but spiritually.

He fell short, yet again, by not saying anything. He felt as though all he could do was make it worse. Any comforting words that were spinning in his head seemed hopeless to say to her in this moment. She wanted to go back to her old life, her family, her friends, her home, and all he wanted to say was he was glad of her to be here. He was glad he found her, glad he was sworn to her.

But that would be the last thing she wanted to hear. So he stayed quiet.

And her despair turned to rage, directed at him. Each word felt like a dagger. He took each blow until she called herself insignificant. He opened his mouth to yell, ‘You’re significant and special, don’t you see that?’

But she turned away from him, so he instead told her of his honor to serve her, in any capacity, hoping she caught the double meaning of his words. She either did and didn’t care or ignored him, and she hadn’t met his gaze again. They had been silent for two days until she asked to stop between stables.

The rest of the journey had been taut with tension. He barely slept each night, listening to the sounds of her breathing next to him. One night, he had the same retched nightmare that had recurred so often before. The one he came to realize had been Zelda, his sworn charge, lying in the mud, bloody, dirty, and broken. Her eyes full of the same despair he saw at the shrine. He awoke in cool sweat and shamefully opened her tent to make sure she was still there.

Maybe being in Gerudo Town would lift her spirits. The town was inhabited by strong, independent women. He didn’t know Urbosa well, only from passing by in the castle during royal celebrations but she was aware of their arrival from Impa. If he remembered Impa’s phrasing, she was rapturous to receive the mysterious woman.

He’d never traveled this far south or even seen a desert. The Gerudo ruled and thrived in this part of the world, only meant for the strong. The desert was unforgiving, freezing cold at night and blazing hot during the day. The vast plains of sand stretching farther than eyes can see, sandstorms disorienting routes, and elemental monsters, especially the deadly quick Lizalfos hiding under the surface ready to strike. And that was to only name a few of the many threats lurking just beyond this canyon.

Another reason why he had never come here was that he knew no males were allowed in Gerudo Town. Or voe as they called them. He hoped Urbosa would make an exception given his unyielding loyalty, or perhaps they’ll stay at Kara Kara Bazaar. It wouldn’t be ideal considering it would take them a half day to make it to town and back.

That was tomorrow’s issue. Tonight he would try to rest.

He walked into the stable, quiet and empty except for the far bed where he saw the familiar cloak hanging off the bed frame, curtains drawn, and heard her shallow breaths. He exhaled and climbed to the empty bed next to hers. Not bothering to pull his own curtain, he fixed his eyes on the curtains closed next to him.

Link squinted at the small beetle flying in front of him, buzzing noisily near his ear as he swatted it from his person. Zelda noticed the sudden hand gesture and glanced sidelong from her shoulder, locking eyes with him. He forced himself to remember to breathe as he fixated on the faint gold swirling in her stunning green eyes, eyes he had not looked upon for days. And just as fast, she pulled her gaze away and stared back at the opening of the desert.

Urbosa sent an envoy at first light to the stable. A towering guard found Link immediately, without so much as pleasantries being exchanged. She instructed them to meet mid-morning in Kara Kara and that Urbosa would greet them personally.

They paid to board their horses for a few weeks, packed small handheld bags for themselves, and made the trek on foot towards the Bazaar. They left at dawn and arrived a few hours later, now waiting nearby the small inn in Kara Kara. The weather was still crisp before the sun fully rose to beat down the heat to unbearable proportions.

As on queue, a small group of equally tall and powerful warriors emerged from the desert entrance. They were either equipped with large long blades or large curved daggers and shields. All had coppery and fire-red hair either braided or pulled up and back. Gold featured on clothing, weapons, jewelry, and shoes all complemented their dark, tawny skin.

Link couldn’t help but look to Zelda. Her hair was pulled to the side and cascaded in layered waves as her one ear was exposed. She kept her earrings the same since he found her: Pierced and decorated with gold and jewels. As if she had been thinking the same, she reached her fingers to fidget with the small hoop.

Amongst the small horde of warriors, Urbosa stood out. An incredible feminine energy of power and grace radiated from her as she sauntered towards them. Link had been known for his unwavering, stilled emotion in battle, but even the sight of the mighty Gerudo leader had him fidgety. 

He again shot another glance towards Zelda. She, like him, was in complete awe of the power the women held in front of them, but her face was more in delight rather than faltering nervousness.

Urbosa now stood in front of both of them. A wicked smile on her painted blue lips, eyes twinkling. “Vasaaq.” She looked directly at Zelda, paying no attention to Link slightly behind her.

She said welcome. Link had learned the general greetings and phrases back during his early page training.

Zelda smiled up at the woman who easily towered over her, only barely reaching her chest. “Sarqso.” Zelda said. Both Link and Urbosa could not contain their surprise at the phrase and both turned dumbfounded to Zelda. How did Zelda know the words for thank you, let alone welcome?

Urbosa boomed laughter at that. “I like this vai already.” She winked at Zelda in a warm show of affection. “I am Urbosa, Chieftain of the Gerudo.” She extended her hand to Zelda. 

Zelda extended her own, matching the strength in the shake. “I’m Zelda.” She smiled faintly, understanding the slight strain in revealing her name.

Urbosa pursed her lip. “I have heard about you and your situation. Let us talk out of prying ears.” She gestured towards the inn. Her entourage had quietly already cleared the room and bordered themselves around the perimeter. Urbosa waved her hand for Zelda to enter first.

As Link followed, Urbosa finally met Link’s eyes, as if forgetting he was there. “Sir Link, thank you for escorting her here. We have much to discuss.” She gave him a pointed glare. Link controlled his facial expression to cool indifference and nodded slowly. Trailing behind Zelda.

As one of her warrior’s had confirmed, the large open room had been cleared. There were couches in front of them and beds on their left. The beds had been carved into stone with small curtains allowing privacy. Zelda stopped in front of the couch, not yet deigning to sit until Urbosa ordered.

Urbosa made long and slow strides to the lone chair, leaving the long couch for Zelda. With a simple wave, Zelda sat. Link, like the well-trained knight he was, stood next to her, as a knight should to his charge. Urbosa noticed.

“Link, I understand that you are Zelda’s appointed knight and that honor says you must stand, but I insist you sit for this conversation.” Urbosa gave him a pointed glare. Her voice was powerful and commanding.

Link did not technically have to obey her. But he was in her territory where she ruled. It would send the wrong message if he did not choose his battles wisely. He sat on the long couch next to Zelda, making an effort to sit at the farthest spot from her. Offering her as much space from him as he could offer. Urbosa’s lip curled ever so slightly at the sight, but she did not say anything.

“Impa filled me in on your predicament, enough in a letter that if it was intercepted it would not raise alarms. Why don’t you tell me from your side?” Urbosa’s tone was demanding yet warm to Zelda.

And Zelda did. She mentioned her mysterious arrival, Link’s and Impa’s involvement, their travels to Rito Village and Goron City, with Link noticing the slight change in tone at the mention of leaving Goron City and the events that transpired. She mentioned the Hero of Time Legend that seemed to always linger in every visit and how or why it could be connected to her.

After the long-winded story, Urbosa crossed her arms and brought her hand to her face, resting her thumb and forefinger on her chin in quiet reflection. “Interesting.” She purred at Zelda. She continued to stare at the blond, like a complicated puzzle with missing pieces. “You look just like her.” She mused.

“I know, I look like the princess.” Zelda said, eyes pulled down.

“No, not her.” Zelda quickly picked her head up, brows raised, and met Urbosa’s stare. “Yes, you look like the princess, but I meant my old friend, the queen.” Urbosa was quiet, and a faint hint of sadness hung on her words.

Link’s eyes went wide at the omission. He searched his mind to picture the dearly departed Queen of Hyrule, Princess Zelda’s mother. She had died more than a decade ago, and he was just a child when that happened. He remembered musings of the court, speaking of her grace, her beauty, her thick blond hair, and green eyes.

“I’m sorry for your loss.” Zelda said, eyes full of compassion.

“Thank you, she was a great woman.” Urbosa said proudly. The silence stretched for a spell until she continued, “It is fitting you mentioned the Hero of Time. The Gerudo played a large role in that part of history. Not all in deeds we were proud of, but we have since come to rectify that.” She angled her head high, staring at the decorations on the far side of the room. Her sweeping fire-red hair perfectly styled to accommodate the swing of her head. Her large gold hoops rocked. 

She crossed her legs and continued, “During the time period of the Hero of Time, the Gerudo were a different people. They were a race of thieves, and relations with Hyrule were sour. Instead of honoring the royal family and goddesses, they worshipped the Goddess of the Sand and honored the traditions of Spirit. Back then, a male was born every one hundred years, and he was always the leader of the Gerudo.” Urbosa did not contain her scowl at the thought. “This male, Ganondorf, became King of my ancestors. He was destined to be evil, born to equally evil mothers. He was a power-hungry thief and sorcerer seeking to rule all of Hyrule and its people, by any means necessary. All my ancestors worshipped him without question, as was their nature, except one.” She smiled and gleamed. “Nabooru, an honorable Gerudo, saw through his ideals and would work with the Hero of Time to aid him in his quest. She went through years of torture and torment but eventually became the Sage of Spirit and helped defeat and drive back Ganondorf. After Ganondorf’s defeat, my people noted the sacrifice of Nabooru and changed their ways to who we are today. No longer do we practice thievery or adhere to male kings. We proudly support the royal family of Hyrule as one.”

Link knew that. He told Zelda of Ganondorf weeks ago but not the Gerudo involvement. He knew Ganondorf was a Gerudo, but that was eons ago

“What happened to Ganondorf?” Zelda asked.

Urbosa inhaled and exhaled a large breath. “It depends on who you ask and in what context.” Her feline eyes narrowed. “Things got interesting after the Hero of Time. Some say he unintentionally split the fates of our worlds into three separate paths. One of childhood, one of adulthood, and one of defeat.” 

The room felt as though all the air had been taken out. Link could see the goosebumps forming on Zelda’s bare arm.

“The path of childhood, he was sent back to his young form and warned the Princess of Ganondorf’s anticipated betrayal. The one of adulthood, he stayed an adult after defeating Ganondorf, rebuilding Hyrule and beyond.” Urbosa clicked her tongue before continuing, “And one of defeat, where Ganondorf won and the hero died.”

Link did not know that part of the story. He found his voice, “Why isn’t this written in history books?”

Urbosa barely looked at him this whole time, now her attention on him, “Because it’s not proven or was ever written by historians. This is pure speculation. But my people believe it. That we are just one parallel thread amongst many.” Now she turned her feline gaze back to Zelda, “This might explain how Zelda arrived here.”

Link went stiff with that heavy revelation. He couldn’t help but glance at Zelda, who had a vacant expression in her eyes as she stared past Urbosa.

“This is enough for one day.” Urbosa’s word was final. They would not talk more about the bombshell knowledge she just dropped. She looked to Zelda, as if silently commanding her to look at her, which she did. “I’d like to invite you back to my city to stay while we talk more about this.”

Zelda’s vacant stare turned to a warm smile, eager to accept. “I’d love to.” 

Urbosa gave a huffed snort, “Fantastic, we can leave right now if you’re ready.” She rose from her seat and started to leave the room. Link felt like he was completely forgotten, on purpose. Zelda shot him a glance, tilted her head in quiet consideration at him, but it wasn’t stopping her from going.

Urbosa suddenly remembered Link. “Ah Sir Link, as I’m sure you are aware, no man is to enter our city, one rule from the Hero of Time Legend that we kept in place.” She gestured her hand to nothing. “I will happily set you up here at the inn while Zelda is our honored guest. I can have my guards set you up with transportation, food, anything you need.”

Link couldn’t help the small scowl forming. He was not to leave his charge alone, ever. That was the oath he swore. He might as well have left her in the field to be slaughtered by Bokoblins. Urbosa noted his quiet fuming.

“It’s up to Zelda. If she would rather stay here with you, we’ll set you both up here. But as my guest, Gerudo Town will be safe for her.”

Zelda looked absolutely delighted at the prospect, her eyes twinkling. “I would love to stay in Gerudo Town, Lady Urbosa, thank you for the invitation. Link will stay back.”

She was all too happy to say that. He didn’t bother to look at her. Instead, he said, “I’ll camp near the town, just in case.”

Urbosa shot a brow towards him and clicked her tongue, “it’s unnecessary. My guards will protect her with their lives, but— if you insist for your peace of mind, I will not object.”

He felt Zelda’s gaze on him. Perhaps he was blurring the lines between honorable dedication and overbearing protectiveness. Neither he nor she knew which was which anymore.

Urbosa led them both to the town perimeter. Giving Link one more curious look if he wanted to really stay in the uncomfortable elements rather than the inn, but he shook his head in protest. Zelda shot him an unknown look as she was permitted through the entrance beyond.

Urbosa was at least kind enough to have her guards bring him a tent, sleeping roll, and male voe clothing. He hadn’t packed anything to sleep on before boarding his horse back at the stable, so he was grateful for that. 

The night was cold, but he appropriately prepared for it with a Rito ruby headpiece. However, sleep eluded him due to the twisted thoughts of Ganondorf and the Hero of Time’s threads of fate. And as always, Zelda.

The next morning, a guard greeted him with a traditional breakfast of rice, fruit, and spices, and afterwards, he swiftly changed into the clothing Urbosa had provided him. His left side was covered in a spaulder that offered little bodily protection for his right side, while thick armor covered his forearms and a baldric lay across his bare chest. Small sapphires adorned the guards, harnessing the magic of cooling to bear the hot desert days.  The trousers were at least more modest, made of loose, breezy fabric with golden shin guards and flat shoes better for navigating desert terrain.

He wondered if Urbosa sent him the clothes as punishment rather than convenience. No knight he knew stationed at a castle would leave their most vulnerable parts open to strike, but he mused that it would be rude to ignore her gift. Voe clothing was more of a novelty rather than necessity.

He awaited any or all instructions at the front gate, unaware of how this leg of their trip would play out. He pulled out his sword as he did every morning and trained.

An hour had passed as he routinely trained, and he noticed between sets, Gerudo women of all ages peeking out over the town entrance at him. Some giggling, cheeks pink and flushed or both. They rarely see men, so he tried to ignore it. But the latest ogling him was a large guard heading directly towards him. He stopped his lunge mid-strike.

“Urbosa would like to meet with you at the Lookout Post by mid-day. Do you accept?” The guard had on traditional Gerudo guard gear, including a face covering, only her brown eyes visible. A stern and no-nonsense attitude exuded from her.

“Yes.”

“I will inform her of your reply. She has set up a sand seal for you to use on the west side of town. Head there and mention to the attendant it’s for Link.” As she punctuated her last word, she was already turning back towards the town.

He gazed towards the horizon, guessing it was mid-morning. Might as well head there now, at least to pass time.

The attendant gave him the basic rundown of sand seals and sand seal sledding. The common mode of quick transportation in the desert as horses nor carts would work on the desert sand. After adjusting his balance, he felt comfortable and urged the sand seal on its way. 

He had taken a detour to the lookout post, enjoying the scenery around him as he mastered the ebb and flow of the seal’s trajectory. Again, looking towards the horizon, the sun had almost reached above him, indicating midday.

He reined in his sand seal and tied it to a post near the isolated building. The lookout post triangulated between the Bazaar and the city, the only point that stood between the unforgiving desert and civilization. A guard was already posted, either there on permanent duty or because their chieftain was approaching. She gave him a slight nod to wait inside.

After a short time, Urbosa appeared, alone. The alarm on his face was obvious.

“She’s safe. Back in the city with my best guards.” Urbosa gave him a feline smile, “I thought it best you and I chat. Alone.”

His shoulders went limp at the comment, yet the edge still present, knowing how far away he was from the city if something happened.

“You care.” Urbosa said as she took a seat across from him.

“Of course, she’s my charge.” He said while taking a seat, staring straight into her.

“More than that.” Urbosa flicked her hand upwards in a lazy motion. “This goes beyond duty.”

Link was quiet, carefully rolling over the response in his head. But before he could reply. She did first, “It wasn’t a question to be answered.” Her face was a mixture of concern and satisfaction.

He tried to find his inner stability at the comment. There was no good to come out of letting his emotions free. He must always be the stoic knight he was trained to be. As hard as it was to keep his emotions in check around Zelda.

Urbosa, no doubt, intentionally decided to give him a reprieve and change the subject, “It’s no coincidence that she’s here. That she looks like the princess and the royal family. And it’s also no coincidence that strange powers are at play at the same time.”

“We’ve visited Goron City, and Daruk said the same. Monsters are becoming more frequent.”

She moved her hand to her chin, contemplative, “There is a force at work. I sense it, as if it were born here. There were an unusual number of monsters littering the desert. And worse.” She trailed off.

Link shot her a curious brow.

“An enemy clan has risen, in defiance of the royal family and all that they represent. An offshoot of the Sheikah clan. Their base is here deep in the highlands.” She looked angry, a fire building in her eyes. “They’ve been slightly more than an insect that we’ve been able to stomp as they poke their heads up, but…” she now stood, hands fisted, “it’s starting to become a nuisance that has to be dealt with, by firstly containing it to the desert.”

Link didn’t know Urbosa well, but if this proud leader is telling him about her concerns, it must be a problem.

“The Yiga. The cowards that they are hide under masks and use ancient Sheikah training to carry out their bidding. Their vision is to overthrow the royal family, to wipe them out, and rule Hyrule under a guise of evil.” The bite in her tone was apparent.

The quiet stretched on between them like heavy fog, unable to clear.

“Zelda needs time. I spoke with her yesterday. She needs time to collect herself and adjust to her new reality. It seems Impa and you barely gave her time to adjust before shoving her out into this path.” Urbosa cocked a brow at him.

Link startled a bit. He never thought about it that way, but Urbosa was right. She barely had time to settle before they forced her out with a stranger to learn about something no one has ever seen before. Even though he was the stranger and would never harm her, he never asked her how she felt; he just assumed she’d adjust.

“I’m guessing by the look on your face, you know I’m right.” Link was quiet; he couldn’t meet her gaze. “I thought so.” Urbosa clicked her tongue.

“We’ll give her a week to do as she pleases. She is safe in the city with me and my guards; you have my word on that. You and I will meet to discuss what we know while she is surrounded by my people and pleasures. Let her be a vai; let her have autonomy over her decisions, all she’s had is you until now.”

That stung Link more than he had anticipated, but she was right. He reluctantly nodded his agreement.

“I set up a room for you at the Bazaar,” she trailed off, “but I’m guessing you’ll continue to stay where you camped?” Her eyes rolled as he nodded.

“Okay, boy. I’ll have my guards bring you food and whatever you need until she’s ready to leave.” Urbosa smirked, “You just need to be careful; once the young Gerudo vai find out who you are and what you look like, you’ll be wishing you stayed back at the inn. Or perhaps you can let off a little tension yourself while you’re alone.”

Link’s face heated; Urbosa laughed a deep belly laugh at his squirming, but it quickly faded back to their original concerns.

“When exactly did Zelda land in this realm?” Her back was to Link.

“Over two months ago.”

Urbosa held her hand to her hip, her neck twisted to meet his gaze. “That’s what I was afraid of.”

Link left the lookout post a few hours later, with more questions than answers.

The Yiga. He wondered if Impa knew. He felt more on edge than before, especially not being able to see Zelda, knowing he wouldn’t be able to protect her outside the city walls.

At least Urbosa was already fond of her. He knew her close relationship with the matriarch of the royal family and her daughter. This Zelda reminded her of that, maybe even more so than the Princess had.

The next morning, he was greeted with steamed fruit, eggs, and rice. All rich in spices. He resolved to make the most of his days while here. He changed into the Gerudo Voe Spaulder, tied his hair up, and got to training.

By mid-day, it was brutally hot. The sun burned into his bare back; he knew he would be red soon if he didn’t get in shade. Luckily, a pavilion was erected nearby, probably for the men who tried to enter the city and now needed respite before journeying back. 

He sat on the cool, shaded sand and drank water. Before he could finish the last gulp, a handful of young Gerudo women were making their way to him.

They all giggled and stared at him, cheeks flushed in tones of pink and red, with golden colored eyes and long lashes. They were in traditional Gerudo wear; thin, loose, colorful fabric similar to his. Their chests were barely covered with toned midriffs exposed. His thoughts briefly went to Zelda and wondered what she would look like in this garb—

“Sir Link?” The young self-appointed leader spoke to him, her red hair tied half up, bright purple lip stain, and her feline eyes decorated with kohl and colorful lids. She, like the rest of them, was stunning. Most likely a few years younger than him, not quite ready to venture out into the world beyond.

He snapped out of his trance and gave her a half nod.

She gave him a devilish smile. “We were watching you train, you were spectacular. It’s not often we see knights of Hyrule Castle around here.” She purred as the rest of the girls snickered behind her.

“Thank you.” That was all he was able to muster, as he fixed his eyes to the leader.

“We know that you’re here for Zelda, and while she’s inside, we’ll be happy to keep you company. My name is Gilda, that’s Tatti, and Rigena.” She pointed behind her back at the eagerly smiling girls.

It was the same ogling he received at the castle, except these girls were bolder, more transparent in what they wanted. Perhaps not being around males made them unafraid.

“Anyway, it’s nice to properly meet you, Sir Link. We’ll be back later.” Gilda shot him a seductive wink followed by a bright laugh. She turned back towards the city entrance, practically skipping. As he watched them, they petered off to avoid another figure standing at the entrance. When the trail of red hair and tawny skin disappeared, he was left with a better image than his daydreams had ever allowed.

Zelda stood there, staring at him, arms hung at her side, face unreadable. He had only moments ago wondered what she would look like in a Gerudo dress, and she was before him in the same outfit the young girls had approached him with, except… better.

Her outfit was green, to match her eyes. The color also fit her skin tone perfectly, like a jewel mounted in gold. Her figure was hourglass-shaped, her waist and hips bare, not as toned as the Gerudo women tended to be, but flat and well-defined. Her neck and collarbone he had come to memorize from their first meeting, also bare, but he hadn’t noticed back then that her shoulders were perfectly squared and proud, inadvertently pushing her breasts against the small piece of cloth holding them.

Her hair was braided neatly to her side. It was golden like a ribbon, but as the wind blew, it caused small pieces to escape. Her one ear was exposed, showcasing the earrings she arrived with, and just as he thought back then, they perfectly complemented her new outfit. Her jawline was sharp, even sharper at the tension she clearly held there.

The Gerudo usually wore eye stain, liner, and lipstick in bold colors, yet Zelda stood out wearing nothing. Her natural beauty accentuated her already pink, pillowed lips and hazy, green eyes. The sun had kissed her cheeks and left faint freckles in its wake.

She looked like she belonged amongst the powerful warrior women, and he should be so lucky to be in her airspace.

They locked eyes, and it felt as if time stood still. In that moment, it was only them in this wasteland. He had forgotten about the heat, the sand, the Yiga… until her eyes narrowed at him. He was gawking.

She crossed her arms, and something bright bloomed in her eyes as she returned the look. But before he could register it, she turned back towards the town.

He wondered if Urbosa read it the moment she saw him, knowing he was already doomed.

 

Chapter 16: Dismissal

Chapter Text
She awoke from another nightmare. This one was different from the horrid machines. This one was endless sand with not one landmark to guide her. Fire burned around her while her body convulsed with electricity. Sand pelted her skin painfully as the hot wind blinded her vision. Her hands scraped and bled, her clothes torn. No one was there to save her.

Her nightmare haunted her as she sat alone in her quarters, staring at her breakfast of ripe fruits, spiced meat and rice, unable to get the smell of burning flesh out of her mind to choke it down.

Urbosa greeted her early and mentioned that she had business to tend to and that Zelda was free to do what she wished in town while she was away. She did urge her, strongly, to speak with Link. To have him fill her in about their private meeting she wasn’t invited to.

She resolved to do that, walking just outside the town’s entrance until she came upon a group of young girls, no more than eighteen years old, flocking around him. After they cleared, she immediately knew why they had large smiles plastered on their faces. 

Despite the town not allowing males inside, he was dressed in Gerudo colors and fabrics, somehow magically tailored for him. 

His chest was bare, except for armor and a baldric hanging off his left side. His defined, lean muscles from shoulder to V cut were glistening with sweat from the midday heat. Somehow from the distance, his skin was soft yet rugged at the same time. She’d seen him with his shirt off before, but this, this was… magnificent to behold. The image of little armor with sweat dripping off his firm, naked, tanned body did something to her core.

She was drooling, and he was staring at her.

For a brief moment, she thought his eyes blazed back the same desire she felt for him. He gripped his sword in hand, knuckles white.

Before she turned into a puddle in front of him, she cowardly backed inside the sanctuary of the female community.

She hurriedly went back to her room, under the throne room, complete with privacy except for Urbosa’s prized sand seal in the shared courtyard. Her breathing ragged as she stared in the small mirror.

Her pupils were as large as moons despite the sun. Her chest heaved unevenly. Shivers ran down her bare arms.

He affected her, every time. On her balcony, in the small Goron shared cave, in the hot springs. She had never reacted to anyone that way.

He was the most captivating man she ever laid eyes on. He was perfect: his face, his eyes, his body—

Despite all logic, her body betrayed her at the most inconvenient moments. Her breast swelled against her top. Her body went limp. She reached her hand to her neck, lightly stroking her pulse and trailing to her jaw. She imagined it was his calloused hand firmly holding her, angling her as he wanted, gently yet fervently. His thumb brushing over her lips, opening just for him, as her tongue would guide him…

“Fuck.” She shook her head in the mirror and covered her face with both hands as she snapped back to reality.

The heat was getting to her. She needed to dunk her head into an ice bath.

She’d been here almost two weeks. Enjoying the feminine energy all around. It was unlike anything she ever experienced: a community of only women, all supporting, trading, and bartering with each other. She fit in immediately, perhaps because she was Urbosa’s honored guest, but she’d like to think that all the women would have treated her the same way, regardless of her status. It was exactly what she needed: to clear her mind.

The seamstress offered her decadent clothing, which she proudly wore, nicer than any article of clothing she’d ever owned, even if it was slightly revealing for her taste. It was a very small, very tight bandeau with matching emerald pants that were made from light, flowing fabric. The cut sat low on her hips and gathered at her ankles. Threads of gold decorated the seams along with a thick gold belt. It was flattering and comfortable in the dry heat of the desert.

Next, the jeweler squealed in delight at her earrings, amazed at the uncommon number of holes she had and wished she had thought of it. In thanks for the new idea to sell more earrings, she gave her a sapphire headpiece, similar to a crown. Zelda had refused; she couldn’t accept such a prestigious gift, but the jeweler insisted. Aggressively.

Each day, the trade tents would be displayed with weapons, fruit, food, and more. And each day they would offer her whatever they had, even as she started to give them a wide berth.

Now, she sat in her isolated room, unable to accept more gifts. She wouldn’t be able to ride her horse back if she continued to receive them; she would have to ask Link to take some of the load.

Her mind drifted to that. It was the first time today she thought about him, thinking of their return trip back. She hadn’t seen him in almost a week.

She knew he was outside the town walls, waiting for her to be ready, sleeping on the sand in the cold desert air. She felt a pang of guilt, yet every day as she passed by traders and townspeople, she heard things that made her change her mind.

All the young girls and women could not stop talking about the strapping Hylian knight just outside of town. Girls would giggle when talking about him, wondering out loud if all knights looked like him. And if they did, that when they came of age, they would go to the castle to find a knight to marry. Universally, they agreed he was extremely chivalrous for waiting outside of town for his charge. They were more than happy to keep him company day in and day out.

Every day they would head outside the town gates and practice their flirting that they learned on him. They would come back with large smiles and pink blushes decorating their cheeks. She even heard whispers of a bet with the younger woman trying to bed him.

Of course, he was free to do whatever or whomever he wished, but she couldn’t help that parts of her sank at the thought.

“Sav’otta Gabora,” Zelda already learned some Gerudo phrases while visiting, knowing this one was good morning. Urbosa had been thoroughly impressed with her picking up the language so quickly.

“Urbosa is requesting your presence,” she was blunt and unyielding in her tone, as all Gerudo had tended to be. They did not ask; they told.

She never ceased to be in awe of the powerful woman who stood mere inches from her. Urbosa radiated fierceness, yet held her people in tender regard. She was stunningly glamorous, effortlessly unapologetic and her movements calculated and feline by nature. Always ready to pounce, if necessary.

She warmed to Zelda immediately, and she to her. She was the only one to truly ask about her life before Hyrule. She seemed genuinely interested in her stories and her life. They would eat at least one meal together every day. If Urbosa wasn’t asking about her life, then Zelda was asking about hers and learning about the Gerudo history.

“Zelda, good to see you this morning.” Urbosa smiled, her bright blue lipstick and white teeth contrasting in the morning sun.

“Sarqso Urbosa, likewise.” Zelda returned the smile.

“Your Gerudo is getting better. Soon you’ll be mistaken for one of us.” Her hand motioned from Zelda’s feet to her head.

The guards had stayed back, but Zelda knew they were close, yet out of earshot. Not that Urbosa needed guards. Tales of her heroics were on the tongue of every citizen Zelda spoke to. They loved their chieftain and honored her with tales of brave deeds.

The trails and journey you have faced, I know, have not been easy, and lesser people would have gone mad over it.”

Urbosa smirked and winked, “I know you will.”

My duty.

An all powerful aura radiating off of her as she spoke, “I know you’ll keep an eye on her, but watch her especially close.” She looked grave, as grave as the confident warrior woman would let herself be. “I‘ve heard rumblings of— what we spoke about.
