Even if he hadn’t agreed, she would tell him anyway. He nodded for her to continue.

“I’ve only spent a brief time with Zelda, not nearly as much as you have, but I do know she needs to have some semblance of control over her destiny. Put yourself in her shoes and what she’s been through. Protect her, but also let her find her way. I don’t want to see the fragile peace you’ve built crumble so soon.” She gave him a knowing glare.

“I will. I won’t take her or this posting for granted again.” And he meant that, and more. More he wouldn’t share with Urbosa.

“I will be visiting the castle during Farore’s Spring celebrations. I hope to have learned more to share with you both then.” She turned to exit, “Sav’orq, Sir Link.”

“Sav’orq, Urbosa.”

Chapter 18: Ambush
Chapter Text
It was winter by the time they arrived back at the castle.

But it wasn’t winter weather she had been accustomed to, no snow storms or shorter days, but it was still cold. It left the castle rooms and halls drafty, and her digging through her chest for extra blankets and warmer clothes.

They arrived just the day before. Taking the better part of a week to journey back. It hadn’t felt strained as their journey south had been, they happily held pleasant conversation throughout. They finally found a way to coexist.

She learned about his life, directly from him this time, not Ilya or Fledge. He intentionally or unintentionally skipped over his childhood but went into great detail about his promotions from Page to Knight. Enthusiastically answering every question she had.

He even asked about her life. She intentionally skipped over her own childhood and covered her schooling, her community, Linda, Marin, and her apartment. Link had seemed thoroughly confused about her living situation. The concept of a landlord was hard for him to wrap his head around. It was funny considering that was the one concept he had trouble grasping, not the plethora of modern technology and advancements she mentioned.

But then again, she didn’t question the unexplained magic of Hyrule either.

She continued to ask about Hyrule’s traditions and history. Eager to learn everything she could about her surroundings. Besides already visiting the Rito, Gorons, and Gerudo, there was still the Zora she still had yet to meet, and in addition to regions of specific species, there were communities of Hylians littered throughout Hyrule, such as Hateno or where Impa held her personal home in Kakariko Village.

She had more to ask about, but before she knew it, they were leading their horses into the royal stables. Ilya excitedly greeting them.

They arrived back to their apartments, with faint hesitation in separating from one another. A month ago, she would have darted to her room unspeaking; now, it felt strange to be alone.

She looked around her elegant room and caught herself glancing at the joint door. And suddenly everything felt deafening, the quiet she now hated.

Everything shifted in Gerudo. He saved her without one thought for everything she had said to him. He hadn’t abandoned her despite her treating him poorly. He was a good… knight.

Or was it something more?

This was unfamiliar territory for her. The line blurred between duty and more. She lay on her silken bed, staring at the ceiling, contemplating.

He was the most alluring man she’d ever met. Not only was he good looking, he was loyal, honorable, courageous, and even had a sense of humor. And watching him in battle, how his muscles flexed and stirred. How he inhumanly moved. Woof.

No wonder Ilya, the Gerudo girls, and every handmaid and castle employee wanted him. She toyed with her lips thinking about it.

‘No woman who has ever pursued me has interested me.’

What did that even mean? He left it ambiguous on purpose. Likely he has pursued women or possibly men? Surely he’s had relations with someone, just look at him. He wouldn’t even have to try. Her stomach flipped at the thought.

He said they could have relationships, but did he actually have or ever want one? With anyone…

She was spiraling. 

She awoke the next morning and for the first time since she arrived in Hyrule, they had no immediate agenda. She took care to lazily wake and clean herself and dress in an extremely warm, green, chunky sweater that had been provided for her in the chest of clothes.

As she brushed her hair, styled in its natural soft waves, a knock sounded, and she instinctively smiled.

Link stood in front of her, dressed gallantly in his traditional red tunic, beige pants, and brown boots. His hair was neatly pulled back with his blue tie, still slightly wet from the bath he’d surely just taken. Her throat dropped to her stomach.

It was like she was seeing him for the first time.

“Good morning, Zelda.” He held his face neutral yet there was some softness apparent. “Impa would like to see us this morning.”

“Good morning, Sir Link.” He rolled his eyes as she smirked. He was a titled knight but he mentioned to her on their journey back that he never liked the title and formality. “What time do we need to meet with Impa?”

“I believe her exact words were right now, but if you’d like to grab breakfast with me first then we can head there?”

“I’m famished, so yes.” She cooed as she shut her door and they strode out together.

They arrived at the dining hall and besides a few head turns from soldiers and castle employees, most ignored their presence. Except for Fledge, who animatedly gestured them over. They walked along the narrow space between the impractically long tables and benches, heading towards him.

Link gave Fledge a small grunt of hello as Zelda warmly greeted the fawn of a man. 

“I heard you both were back, how was Gerudo Town?”

Link was already shoving a large piece of meat into his mouth so Zelda opted to speak for them both. “Gerudo Town was lovely. The town itself was incredible, full of wonderful women, arts, and trade. Though Link can’t say the same as he only saw outside town walls.”

Link huffed through his chewing. 

“They didn’t make an exception for him as your personal knight?”

“No, they did not. But he did get very familiar with his Gerudo fan club.” She dragged out as she looked sidelong at him.

Link looked visibly uncomfortable. Fledge looked confused, and Zelda laughed.

“Never mind. We did learn a lot from Urbosa, but no solid leads yet. We’ll regroup with Impa after breakfast.”

She decided not to mention him saving her life; that felt too personal to share with Fledge, oddly, since that was his job.

“That’s good,” Fledge said with a hopeful smile.

“What did we miss here?”

“Nothing much. Groose and Princess Zelda left to head to Goron City; she’ll start her official tour. But everyone’s been a little on edge lately because of it.” Fledge’s already high pitch voice somehow rose more.

Link stopped chewing. “Why is everyone on edge?” He had a slightly authoritative tone in his ask.

“Well, there’s been reports of more monster attacks. Not just the typical stray ones you’d find near roads but larger, more organized groups starting to get closer to the towns and villages now. Impa and Auru have dispatched more soldiers to stand guard. There were even a few that made it into Mabe Village.”

Zelda recognized the name; Ilya mentioned that had been Hyrule’s largest farm and mainly used to feed the castle. Coincidentally, it was the closest settlement to the castle.

Link’s jaw tensed visibly. “Has anyone been injured?”

“No serious injuries, a few minor incidents. But it’s definitely set the advisors on edge.”

Zelda tried to grab Link’s gaze, but he looked down and went back to his food, unspeaking.

They finished their meals after changing topics. Then Link and Zelda walked towards Impa’s quarters.

They stood in front of Impa in her study. She sat at a modest desk, finishing her correspondence. Large floor-to-ceiling bookcases loomed over them both behind her. Zelda would have bet that Impa had read every page of every book, at least twice.

“What have you both learned?” Impa hadn’t bothered to look up from her writing, but she did wave her hand in a gesture for them to sit at the two creaky wooden chairs in front of her. It reminded her of getting called to the principal’s office as a child.

Link led, his voice was almost robotic. A knight reporting for duty. “Urbosa mentioned Ganondorf, the evil king from the Hero of Time. She mentioned the Sage of Spirit, Nabooru, and their triumph over evil. When I asked what happened with Ganondorf, she mentioned something interesting. She said he was defeated when the Hero was an adult, but no one knows what happened to him when the Hero was sent back to be a child.”

Impa stopped writing immediately and picked her face up to look at him, then to study Zelda, then back to Link. Her face was unreadable. “Tell me everything Urbosa said.”

Zelda was surprised at her tone. There was a small, very tiny shred of what seemed like concern. She couldn’t help but fidget with her ring as Link relayed every word Urbosa spoke to them, with Impa listened intently.

Zelda couldn’t help but feel they were off topic. They had been searching for similarities between her, for all intents and purposes, time traveling here, but now were discussing an evil villain from a millennium ago.

She wouldn’t say that, after all, what did she even know about Hyrule’s history or time travel?

After Link had finished, Impa sat quietly for a solid minute. Face tense. But she did not ask or say anything further.

He continued, “There’s one more thing.”

She looked at him to go on.

“Zelda was… pulled, again to something unknown. It happened her second night here in Hyrule Field and again in the Gerudo Desert.”

Impa’s deep, red eyes found hers, and she immediately felt compelled to explain.

“It’s an odd feeling. It feels as though a string is tied to my core and is yanking me in an unknown direction. It feels unsettling if I don’t follow it, like I’m going to be sick.”

She caught Link’s eye. He looked concerned.

“What did the pull lead you to?”

“Well, the first time it called me out into the field. It felt… like all the answers I was looking for would be answered if I followed the beckoning. As I got closer towards the feeling, it stopped when the Bokoblins noticed me. I ran from them, but they cornered me around a tree. It was maybe a solid few seconds before Link intervened. The second time I was inside Gerudo Town, and I saw a small child in the distance. She looked so young and helpless. Every available guard in town was dealing with the molduga, so I went to her. When I made it halfway, the Lizalfos spotted me. They attacked me and surely would have killed me had it not been for Link rescuing me, again.”

“So you had not made it to the destination you had been pulled to, but in both instances, monsters had been nearby and intercepted your path?”

Zelda grunted and nodded.

Impa turned her face from them and stared out the small window. The only source of natural daylight in the small cramped space. “Next time you are pulled, you fight it with everything you have. You wait for Link to be by your side, and then you follow it. If monsters are near, your knight will defeat them, and you continue on.”

“Use her as bait? That’s unnecessarily dangerous to put her in that position.” Link was cutting in his response. Zelda couldn’t hide her surprise. She never expected him to speak to Impa that way.

“It is. Perhaps she should train to defend herself if you feel as though you are not well equipped to protect her on your own.”

Link’s face was of stone.

“You two are to head to the military training camp, get Zelda equipped with proper equipment, and she will be trained by the best knight in all of Hyrule, who just so happens to be her personal guard.”

Zelda’s brows shot up. She tried not to gape at Impa.

“Take this time to prepare yourselves and then plan to go to Zora’s Domain in the new moon.”

The next day, they arrived at the military training camp by late morning.

They boarded their horses at the nearby stable and walked the rest of the way. Zelda was winded by the time she scaled the steep hill from the stable. Link, of course, was not winded; he never was.

As she caught her breath, she viewed the massive obstacle course in front of her. Large wooden structures as tall as 5-story buildings. Thick ropes and bridges snaked throughout, all built above a lake. She viewed young boys and men in the distance running, jumping, heaving. She equated it to a pay-as-you-play obstacle course she passed at home near the ski resorts, except the young military men probably felt the opposite of playing.

“You trained here?” She asked Link, trying not to be more impressed than she already was with him.

“Yes, every knight has had to train here. Six weeks of nonstop moving and fighting. Every day you wake up at dawn and train until dusk.” She gawked at him, he shrugged, “Honestly, it wasn’t that bad, except the food was terrible.”

“Why is it not surprising that not having a good meal would be the worst part for you?” She shook her head in pretend disbelief.

“Hey, good food is what I need to stay sustained. How do you think I stay so fit?” He cocked a brow at her.

A shameless thought popped into her head. His arms were crossed, and his powerful stance flexed every lick of muscle. Let him eat whatever he needed in that case.

But she quickly went back to reality, “You’re not leaving me here for six weeks?” She tried to stamp down the growing panic creeping on her face.

Link huffed a laugh, “No, definitely not. As much as I’m sure you’d enjoy that, it doesn’t work that way. You need to be a ranking military member to train here. We’re here to get you fitted with guards and wooden weapons.”

Zelda was relieved, she tried not to let it show as she nervously grabbed her hair to pull to the side. “They don’t have that at the castle?”

“They do, but not practice or starter gear. That can only be obtained by training here.” Link gestured for her to follow him with a frank nod as they circled the perimeter of the lake.

They made their way to the sullen captain off in the distance. He was yelling at some younger boys to pick up the pace. He noticed Link and her approach and his scowl deepened.

“Do you mind staying here while I go speak with the captain? He’s… not pleasant.”

Zelda nodded and watched Link confidently stride up to the sour man. Link spoke out of earshot of her and she saw the captain’s scowl become deeper somehow. Link stood unfazed awaiting the man’s reply. Finally, his hands went up in defeat and he turned back to the boys who only had a moment of reprieve before more screams came out of his mouth.

As Link smoothly walked back towards her, she asked, “What did you say to him?”

“I told him you needed training weapons and guards, to which he had an undesirable reaction. But to which I reminded him that it was per Impa’s request, so he relented.”

Zelda’s brows went up, “Does everyone respect Impa’s word?”

“Everyone fears Impa.”

Her brow cocked, “Do you?”

“What do you think?” He eyed her knowingly.

They walked towards the small storehouse on the edge of the training grounds. The building looked worse for wear but she supposed a closet for practice weapons and second rate armor probably didn’t need a fancy building. As Link pulled open the double doors she wondered out loud to him, “Why was the captain so agitated?”

Link didn’t look at her as he turned to the shelves of endless wooden weapons. He scanned the shelves for what she could assume was the perfect weapon for her. All in various lengths and weights from what she could gauge from the doorway. He picked up one and weighed it in his palm, his voice clipped, “The captain doesn’t believe women should be in the military, let alone learn how to use weapons.”

Zelda scoffed, “Honestly, that’s not surprising.” She should have known she would encounter someone with that mindset at some point. “At least where I’m from, women can serve in our military— perhaps one day Hyrule will be as progressive.”

Link was already onto the next set of shelves, pawing through the guards and measuring for one to try on Zelda. He still hadn’t made eye contact with her, but she saw a sly smile form. “I’d like to see that one day. I’m sure your military is formidable.”

She suppressed her smile as they exited the dusty building.

After fitting her with shoulder and arm guards traditionally set for young boys, they headed to the stable to sleep.

They awoke the next morning and planned to head back to the castle after breakfast. They sat at the communal cooking pot and ate what Link purchased for them both. The day was clear and cool. The trees that surrounded them were in various stages of hibernation. Leaves bright green to brown on the ground.

She lifted her fork to her mouth, the perfect bite of potato and eggs. She savored the freshness as her boot grazed against her new wooden sword that lay next to her.

“I didn’t realize it would be so heavy.” She tilted her head to the wooden sword. She had grabbed it yesterday and her arm embarrassingly dropped like a stone in a lake at the unexpected weight.

“It has to be like the real thing. Real swords are much heavier.”

Zelda didn’t really think of the strength needed to be a soldier or a knight. Carrying around not only a sword, but a shield, bow and arrows, armor. No wonder they all looked so… fit. Link had agreed to train her in the privacy of the castle gardens rather than near the barracks.

She eyed the familiar leather-wrapped handle that lay next to Link, analyzing it. “Have you always had that sword?”

He looked at it then to her, “No, we are given standard-issue blades based on our rank: soldiers’ swords, knights’ swords, royal swords. I’ve had this one forged to me personally. Most blades need some customization before someone can weld it. Balance is the key.”

She instinctively looked past the military training camp at the dense, mysterious forest beyond. A cool wind blew from the north. Covered in dense trees and fog, no one could see beyond. “I suppose I’ll have to train to build my muscle.” She said between bites. She had the Scimitar Urbosa gifted her, but strength training her arms, core, legs— basically everything— would need to be first priority.

“You already are fit, shouldn’t be too difficult.” Link said as he shoveled his last bite in his mouth, plate practically licked clean.

“I’m already fit?” She gawked at him.

He coughed up whatever he swallowed, she continued staring at him, enjoying his sweat. “I, uh— your legs and arms seem toned is all. From what I’ve seen.” He muttered as a pink blush swept across his cheeks ever so faintly as he looked anywhere but towards her.

She shot him a wicked smirk, “Ah, I didn’t realize you were paying such close attention to my level of physical fitness.”

“Well, you are my charge. What type of knight would I be if I didn’t take notice of certain things?” Regaining his composure, his deep blue eyes challenged her back.

Was he flirting? Now she had to stop herself from blushing. She let her smile fade slowly as she returned to her meal.

After their meals were finished, they started preparing their horses when suddenly it hit her.

The pull, the same pull as before. It twisted in her stomach, and she audibly gasped.

Link immediately dropped his bag and turned to her side. “What happened?”

She felt her breakfast churning within her. The bile rising. She likened the feeling to a roller coaster she rode as a child.

Her breath quickened, and she held her stomach. “I’m getting that pull sensation, the same as before.”

Link’s face turned to stone, and he grabbed his sword and bow and arrows. “Put on your guards.”

She didn’t argue with him as she buckled them on. Link already had his shoulder and bracer on, ready to cut down anything that harmed her.

He was now in front of her, facing her, “Where is it telling you to go?”

“This way,” she turned her face towards the red, rocky mountain looming over the stable.

They left their horses behind. The rocky terrain was not stable for them to continue. She continued to hike up the steep incline. Red dust swirling behind them as she shuffled her feet. Link stayed as close to her as he’d ever been, practically interlocking arms. His head was continuously swiveling around them. Any slight sound caused her to jump.

They hiked for hours, finally stopping at the highest peak. The pull had ceased. There was no person or monster in sight, and the only way to them was the path they just took. If it weren’t for the creeping dread rising in her belly, she would have marveled at the sight in front of her.

They overlooked the training grounds. The afternoon sun was reflecting off the still waters of the lake as small figures ran and jumped on the wooden bridges. To their backs, that mysterious forest lay. A permanent shroud of fog sat lazily amongst the density of the trees. All magically green, unfazed by the winter weather. The castle in the distance looked almost comically small from this height. Behind them was the fiery Death Mountain. Over the hazy heat and steam, she could almost make out Goron City from the angle. 

She tried to slow her heart rate, to enjoy the serene landscape of Hyrule from this altitude, but the last time she was in this situation, she almost burned to death. Link stood next to her, sword unsheathed.

“Link?” She whispered his name. “Are you nervous?”

His eyes never stopped moving, carefully trailing in front of them. He simultaneously moved slow and fast, preternaturally so, “I’m not nervous for my sake.” He was quiet for a moment but continued, his voice soft, “I’m nervous you’ll get hurt over something we can avoid.”

Somehow that made her feel better, and she wanted to return the favor to him, make him feel at ease. “I know you won’t let anything happen to me.” She instinctively grabbed his arm, hooking it between them to hold onto him tightly. “I never— I never thanked you for accepting.”

“Accepting what?” His head still on a swivel.

“For being my knight. Being swearing to me in the first place. I… thank you.”

He stopped moving and turned to face her, he grabbed her arm tight with his non-sword hand. She wanted to throw up, part from this pull feeling, the other from being so vulnerable in front of him.

He stared into her so intensely she thought she might burst. “Zelda, you never have to thank me for that. If anything I’m thankful to—”

He was cut off by a horn.

His face went pale.

“Zelda” he whispered, gripping her tight, as if afraid to let go. “I need you to hide behind me, behind that rock. Please, do not come out until I say it’s safe.” His voice was pleading.

She nodded and did as she was asked.

A small rock jutted out from the peak, it wasn’t the best place to hide, but it was the only place. Link had marched slightly out of sight down towards where they came, trying to give a buffer between her and the impending threat. She could still see him while squatting behind the red rock. He stood tall, courageously against the unknown.

The unknown revealed itself. The familiar pig noses and glowing eyes of bokoblins. There were more than a dozen of them. Cold fear ran through her blood. He easily cut down two of them that first time, but he had the advantage of sneaking upon them. Now he faced them head-on and their myriad of crude weapons.

He didn’t hesitate; he immediately sprang into action and started feinting and slicing. Cutting down two within seconds and heading for more. She saw his route he planned, starting on his left and dancing in a half circle to the right to finish them all off one-by-one. This strategy helped ease the burden of taking on too many in one go but, also provided a buffer between them and her.

By the time her mind caught up, he took down ten more; there were three left, blue and black with white markings.

Stab. Block. Swing. Parry. Chop. Twirl.

It was horrifying to watch such violence, blood spraying, limbs cut, bodies dropped… but hauntingly mesmerizing.

She was in awe. Never fearing him or his instrument of death. She’d seen him before with only the few monsters. He’d cut them down as if he were swatting a fly. Now he was composing a song. He was the conductor, dancing. With death. The quick slice of his blade was mercy.

Until there were none left standing.

She finally let out a breath of relief. Until the earth shook.

Link dared not look back at her. He stood tense, sword firm in his grip. Posture strong. He looked like a painting. A moment captured in time.

She thought the lizalfos were a twisted nightmare made real. She placed her hand to her mouth to stop herself from letting out a shuddering breath at the horrifying sight.

Her mind could barely register what she saw. They were plucked out of a myth. From the history books her mother had of legendary creatures. Three massive horse-man creatures trotted in front of him. They were larger than their own horses by at least half; they were pure muscle with four legs and two hulking arms each. Their eyes glowed the same pure evil as the other monsters. There was no mistaking these for friendly creatures.

All she heard was the quiet, ragged breaths Link had been expelling before all chaos unleashed.

As if a switch flipped, Link was running in a zig-zag pattern, and she saw why. The far-off creature shot off its bow with three arrows, all straight up and surely pointed where Link had been just standing. The closer one held out its massive sword, as wide as them both and almost as large. The middle one roared, shaking the earth. She thought the sheer force of it was able to shatter the mountain they had been on.

Link darted, and as the other continued to knock arrows, the closer one decided to lunge at him. It was quick, far quicker than the bokoblins, but not as graceful as Link. He dodged its sword by a hair and cut its ankles deeply, causing it to buckle under itself. It roared in anguish. The sounds vibrated in her ribcage, clattering her teeth.

Before Link could finish it off, he continued to move as more arrows landed within inches of him. The second one, now charging with its massive sword and shield in hand, aimed to swiftly remove his head from his body.

She grew sick at the thought, not because she would surely be next if he fell, but knowing she led him to his demise.

But she hadn’t to worry, yet.

He dodged again with a perfectly timed jump and slashed wildly at its legs in the same strategy as the first. Disabling it from moving again. Except after its legs buckled, he swiftly struck his sword under its throat. These creatures seemed to have similar arteries as them, as it drastically started to gush dark crimson, or rather, black liquid. 

It slumped with a weak roar and fell to its side. This promptly incited the other two into a mad rage.

Link hadn’t had time to stop. With the first disabled, he moved to the further one.

It knocked more arrows, Link barely dodged. Timing had been on Link’s side as he made it to the beast before it could draw more. This time, Link swung into its back, and its eyes went wide.

Link had to be a mad man.

It bucked and jumped to try and launch him off. Link held and between bucks, drove his sword deep into the back of its neck. The bucking started to subside slowly as the familiar black liquid poured out.

One more to deal with.

Hope started to bloom in her chest. They were going to make it out of here.

He slowed his movement to the first one. He was able to catch his breath finally. Surely his stamina had been almost depleted. 

He made it back to the first, planning to be an easy slice to end it’s existence but fate had other plans. Perhaps it had been ill-fated. Perhaps the adrenaline coursing gave him focus to avoid such dangers, but now it had slowed.

The creature had been laying in wait. It promptly swung it’s weapon and managed to nick Link. 

Zelda screamed as he fell. It sliced into his sword arm and he dropped it. The sound of metal against rock rang in the canyon as it fell from his hand. The monster could not move it’s legs but it’s arms had been fully mobile to dish out the blow. He fell, as the creature had, buckling under himself.

They had hope, they were almost free. This can’t be how it ends.

She watched in horror as the creature started to hold it’s arms up to swing down on him, and this time there was no doubt, that swing would end his life. She acted without thought for the man who had saved her more than once.

She ran towards the nightmare creature and flung her blunt wooden sword at its chest with every ounce of strength she could muster. The wooden weapon soared through the air, propelling directly at the beast’s chest.

Now it’s glowing eyes directed at her.

She had no more weapons, she just needed Link to snap out of it in time to cut it down while she pulled it’s attention from him. Except Link hadn’t snapped out of it and the creature pulled out a bow from it’s back.

“Oh fuck.” She breathed. She hadn’t thought it had a bow, she turned to run, zig zagging as she had watched Link do. She gasped in terror. She could only run back to her hiding place and even there she had no cover from it’s precise aim straight into the sky.

This had become familiar to her, quickly making peace at her potential end.

She managed to look back to gauge the short time she did have left. Link was gone from sight. The creature still focused on her. And suddenly a feral yell sounded, echoing all around.

Link had crouched and jumped into its back and jammed his sword into its head. An ugly sight unfolded, followed by the creature’s large body thudding to the ground.

Quiet flooded them both. She dared not even breathe if there had been more coming to surprise them. After a pregnant pause, Link buckled under himself again. Without thought, she bolted to him.

“Link! Are you okay?” She was frantic, already dropping into the dirt next to him, dust floating up around them. She still hadn’t seen how badly he’d been cut.

He held his hand to his forearm, his bracer already lying next to him, along with his sword, pressure holding against the dripping blood. 

She scrambled to move his hand to apply pressure with her own. The wound was deep and unsettling but not fatal at a glance. A wave of relief flashed in her eyes, water pooling she tried to desperately blink away.

She tore her own shirt sleeve and promptly wrapped it tightly around his arm to stop the bleeding. As she worked she felt his stare on her. He still hadn’t said anything.

What was there to say?

“Thank you,” he said weakly, in a whisper, managing to find her eyes as his head lolled.

She barked out a laugh. “Thank you?” She must have looked mad. “Link, you saved my life. I don’t know how you did it but somehow you took down an ungodly number of horrifying monsters while I hid and you’re saying thank you to me?” She had been delirious. “I need to thank you.”

He looked so earnestly into her eyes. “You saved me, throwing your sword at the lynel. Had you not done that, it would have surely ended me. I got lazy on my way back to it and made a mistake.” His own words wounded him, cutting deeper than the lynel had.

So those things were called lynels, even their names were straight from the depths. 

She placed her hand on his cheek. She couldn’t help it. She just wanted him to know how incredibly appreciative she was. His own breath hitched as they started at each other, one moment lasting what felt like an eternity as their faces were inches apart. His pulse was wild under her fingertips. Her own heart frantically thundered at the heat she felt from his skin. Or was it the heat radiating from the active volcano at her back?

She wanted to kiss him. Just lean in and plant a sweet kiss on his chiseled lips. Perhaps because of the heroics of his actions. Perhaps the adrenaline. Or his impossibly blue eyes staring at her weakly.

But she stopped herself, tore that thought from her head. It wouldn’t be fair of her to do that. He saved her out of duty. He was sworn to protect her, in honor of the Hyrule royal family and the goddesses and all that pomp and circumstance. He never made any indication he felt any other way.

She dropped her hand from his cheek, breathed a noticeable exhale, and her eyes fell to his arm. 

“It doesn’t look too bad. Can you walk?”

He nodded.

They both stood from their position, shaking on trembling legs. Him, slightly wobbly from blood loss, her from whatever it was that she just felt. She held onto him, picking up his sword.

It was heavy. He noticed and laughed.

“I told you it was heavy.”

She grunted, “I can’t believe you swing this thing.” She held it pointed end down on the rock face, “You make it look easy.”

He did, and she regretted not kissing him.

Chapter 19: Drink
Chapter Text
“Fuck!” He hissed.

He sat, frozen at the desk his room, holding his breath, hoping Zelda had not heard his outburst.

No indication she had. He exhaled deeply.

He was applying the ointment provided for him from the infirmary to the deep laceration the lynel gave him. So deep it nearly severed the muscle. It was in an unfortunate place to have a wound, on his sword arm— every time he swung, it stung and bled. Not only that, the sliced tendon made the connection to his grip weak.

It nicked him under his bracer, on the soft part of his forearm next to his main artery. He mused he was lucky it hadn’t nicked him a millimeter closer, as Zelda would have buried him on top of that mountain rather than carry him away.

That wasn’t why he was angry; he had gotten lazy and sloppy. How was he to properly defend her if he had gotten tired?

The bokoblins were a breeze to dispense with. He cut them down with ease, hoping that would be that. Each time Zelda was tugged on the invisible string, there had only been two monsters to deal with. Fifteen bokoblins weren’t so bad.

Then pure terror ripped through him once he heard the lynels roar. Plural. As in more than one. Their roar shook his ribs, threatening to hurl his breakfast back up.

He’d taken down one lynel before, and that was a challenge. Now he had to take down three.

All thoughts in his head revolved around Zelda. He was driven by the fact that if he failed, she would die. They were alone; there was no backup. Images plagued his head of the lynels grabbing her by her golden blonde hair, pulling her skyward, and swinging their brutal weapons down—

He needed to focus. He wouldn’t let that happen.

Every monster had a weak point, so he went to work. Cutting their ankles, disabling their powerful legs. He strategically dispensed the farther of the two, knowing he only needed to land a surgical strike on a main artery and watch them fade away.

After the second one was dead, he was tired. All the running, jumping, and thinking almost depleted him. There was one left that he already had disabled, so he decided to slow down, catch his breath.

Which happened to be the almost fatal mistake.

His captain had told him countless times, never, ever, slow down in battle. The second you slow, you die.

It’s sharp blade sliced him, and he lost his grip on his sword, buckling beneath himself at the sudden shock of it. Zelda screamed.

He’d been wounded before. His body had litters of scars from his arms to his legs. All small, innocuous cuts. Now only puckered white flesh left behind. Each one he remembered and felt shame. Each one a reminder he wasn’t perfect. But this one would never scar. It would never close and heal.

He couldn’t look at Zelda. Knowing he had failed her. Failed his vows. Failed Hyrule.

He wondered how long it would take for Impa or a search party to find their bodies. The crows would have their fill by the time anyone managed to track them all the way up here. His teeth almost cracked at the tension he held at the thought of her heavenly face decaying.

As he prepared for the final blow, he regretted that he never would get to kiss her, hold her, taste her. He imagined it in that brief moment, for his dreams could bring him peace. But instead, a wooden object came flying at the lynel’s chest.

He managed to look up, Zelda in front of them, her wooden sword clanging on the ground. She had distracted it from its killing blow. For him.

The relief he felt quickly faded to horror as he realized it had pulled out a bow and aimed it directly at her.

He willed every inch of him to move, adrenaline building. He had all about five seconds to strategize before it let off its arrows. He crouched and shot himself up, yelling through the pain. He stuck his sword directly into its head. 

Rotting meat for the vultures.

He huffed out a breath. Zelda matched his motion, frozen in the distance, waiting for more monsters to attack. But they never came. 

Then he let himself fall. Buckling under himself, and she came running. Taking care of his arm, he tried to hold back the pain he felt in front of her. He thanked her; had it not been for her actions, they’d both be dead. And she laughed. Laughed.

Her laugh was chaotic, wild and unhinged. But so damn delightful to his ears. He could stop his small smile.

She thanked him, deliriously. Holding his arm up to stop the bleeding. He knew she was staring at him, urging him to look at her, but he couldn’t. He couldn’t meet her eyes knowing he had failed her.

Then suddenly, her warm hand caressed his cheek. He had willed his heart to slow down, release some of the adrenaline he had, but he couldn’t. His heart rate jumped under her touch.

He looked into her green eyes. He couldn’t breathe with her so close. Inhaling her scent.

Somehow, she continued to smell of lavender, despite it being a rare herb. Her eyes trailed to his lips. Was she going to kiss him? Her mouth parted slightly, her pupils grew.

But she pulled away. Focusing on his arm.

She had not felt that way about him. They had just built peace amongst each other. She never made any indication otherwise. She had hated him up until a few weeks ago.

But had he not been so stuck by her, he would have grabbed her neck in return, leaned in, and kissed her pillowed lips. Tasted her deeply.

It would be better than all his fantasies.

Instead, she helped him up; they made it back to the stables, slowly. They found the medic at the training grounds, and he patched him up, gave him instructions to clean and wash it, and enough supplies to get them safely back to the castle. 

Which was days ago.

They made it back after a slow journey. Zelda had been so concerned about him the whole time. Each time they stopped to rest, she checked his wound. Holding his arm firmly as she examined it, she felt his head for a fever with the back of her hand. He observed her closely, the meticulous and attentiveness she directed at him and his wound. Her surgical focus surpassed anything he had done for her after the lizalfos attacked her.

He shrugged it off to her, he didn’t want her to worry, but he knew it was a troublesome wound. He needed to hide it; the last thing he wanted was her being assigned to someone else because he was wounded.

She checked on him multiple times a day after they had been back. Each time, she knocked on their adjoining door, which they had never used up until then.

He would open the door, show her his still bandaged arm, and reassure her that he was okay. She would either roll her eyes, offer a quiet smile, or purse her lips and leave.

And each time he wished she would stay.

Impa summoned him. This time just him, without Zelda.

Perhaps she heard about what happened. She wanted to scold him, tell him he wasn’t good enough. That she made a mistake in choosing him. He would fight to keep his charge if she tried to reassign him. There was no way he would live and let someone else watch over her.

Before leaving, he felt the urge to tell Zelda where he was going. So he knocked on the adjoining door.

She swiftly answered it, her golden hair swept to her side, cascading down her shoulder. She was wearing a grey skirt with a large white chunky sweater, and despite the muted colors, it did not dull her. She was incredibly bright.

She smiled widely at him, eyes twinkling with a sense of surprise and he couldn’t help but return the sentiment.

“Link. How are you feeling?” Her eyes immediately drew to his arm.

His head swam at the sound of his name on her lips. “I’m good, better than yesterday.” A lie, he wasn’t healing as fast as he hoped. But he didn’t want her to worry.

“I’m glad,” she purred. 

In effort to not drool over her, he pulled his eyes down, eyeing a book in her hand. She noticed.

She lifted it to show him the cover, “I’ve been reading about the Hero of Time. This book is very informative.”

He wondered if her interest in Hyrule’s history and their stories was pure curiosity, or if it was because it offered clues to help her return home. He didn’t ask, though, because he didn’t want to know the answer. “Impa has summoned me. I’m going to speak with her.” He hesitated, and before his brain could catch up to the words spilling out of his mouth, he asked, “Afterwards, would you like to meet? We can get a drink in town?”

Her brows went up, surprised at his ask, but quickly faded when she quirked her mouth, “That would be great. I’ll meet you here?”

“Sounds like a plan.”

He noted a wicked gleam in her eye as she shut the door. He didn’t hear the lock click after.

He asked her on a date. He hadn’t even realized he had done it. Did she realize? If he hadn’t realized, then she probably didn’t. They had spent so much time alone together. This was no different. He didn’t need to make it as such. She just looked so… luminous. He couldn’t help himself.

He didn’t want to be as happy as he was when visiting Impa. He took a few moments to calm himself before facing the most fearsome woman in all of Hyrule. The last thing he’d want is to face her with a stupid smile on his face.

“She was pulled again,” he said, sitting in front of Impa in her small, dark study.

Impa, this time, had not been distracted by letters or otherwise. It was as though she expected something like this to happen on their brief journey. She sat and listened intently.

“What happened, exactly?”

“We were at the training camp. We slept at the stable. The next morning, we were sitting eating breakfast as normal, readying our horses to leave, when she suddenly gasped and said it felt as though her stomach twisted. We followed it towards Death Mountain, up a steep cliff overlooking Goronbi River and the Training Camp. It was deathly quiet when we arrived, and then we were ambushed by a horde of bokoblins, then three lynels. We were completely surrounded with nowhere to flee.”

Impa’s brows had slightly raised, the most animation he’d ever seen from her. “You defeated three lynels?”

“Yes, but it wasn’t smooth.” He flexed his right hand, his sword hand, the pain radiating through every flex of the joints. It was out of Impa’s eyeshot.

But she immediately looked to his arm. He had his traditional red tunic on, long sleeves covering his wound, yet somehow she knew. Thankfully, she didn’t push further.

“Was it a trap?” Her red eyes on his own. No hint of an emotion behind them.

“I hadn’t thought about it that way.” They still weren’t sure what this pull was and why it was happening to Zelda. The first two times it happened, he had not readily been there. This time he was, and the monsters were tenfold.

Impa scowled, “I’m not sure we’ll ever know. It’s too dangerous to have her test the theory alone. The monsters seem to be after her and lure her accordingly.” She brought her hand to her chin, “It’s odd, the range of monsters is different each time, but are increasingly more dangerous. If she is pulled again, you do not let her go.”

He nodded in absolute agreement. He would gladly protect her, but it was safer to not put her in those positions to begin with.

“I want you both to go to the Royal Laboratory. I have briefed Purah and Robbie on the situation. They politely reminded me that I should have consulted them when she first arrived.”

Link could sense the disdain in her tone. Purah happened to be her sister, but they could not be more different. 

“Go tomorrow. Spend as much time as you need. Then you’ll come back and head to Zora’s Domain for the last leg of your journey.”

Link stood and gave her a slight head bow in confirmation and left.

He walked back to his apartment thinking about what Impa said. 

The pulling sensation she felt was a trap. But why? Who or what did they want with her? 

He didn’t intend to ever find out.

He thought about the Royal Lab; it was a half-day’s ride. Purah and Robbie, despite the King’s permission to work anywhere inside the castle, sought a secluded spot. Their reasoning remained unknown but they chose an abandoned fortress close enough to the castle. The Princess, known for her love of knowledge and curiosity about technology, visited them frequently.

He hadn’t heard much about the reclusive pair. Only that they were… eccentric. And they experimented with Sheikah tech, known to bleed into other aspects. He didn’t care that both Purah and Robbie were respected; if they over stepped in any way, he’d yank Zelda out. Regardless of Impa’s orders.

He made it back to his apartment with enough time to wash himself and be presentable before fetching Zelda for their non-date, date.

His stomach churned with bits of thrill and nervousness. But he told himself he needn’t be. Things had become easy between them. The tension that had been fraught now faded into his own different type of tension when he was near her.

He stripped off his clothing and slid into the porcelain clawfoot bath. The warm waters embraced him, easing his anxiety. He dipped his head down, wetting his hair, using his fingernails to scratch and rub the earthy soap into it. A slight pain lanced through his right arm, radiating towards his shoulder. The soap burning the open cut, he slowly flexed his fingers, praying he wasn’t doing more damage with his stubbornness to heal properly.

He stood slightly dripping in front of his long mirror, taking in his reflection. Something he wasn’t accustomed to in the barracks, since military men shouldn’t care what they look like. Mirrors were only provided for higher-ranking officials, so they could make sure their uniforms were as sharp as their weapons. 

His blue eyes— his mother’s eyes— stared back at him. But everything else was his father. His round face, his lean build, his nose, lips. Even his sandy blonde hair. He combed and tied it back as he’d always done with his same worn blue hair tie. Two pieces fell into front of his face, too short to tie back again the long, shaggy back.

He actually couldn’t remember the last time his hair wasn’t long. Ilya cut it for him usually; he would ask her to go shorter, it was easier to manage, but whenever the scissors were in her hand, she would just trim it, because to her, his long hair suited him.

He dressed back into his red typical tunic, lest the guards and weapons. Except for a small dagger he always kept sheathed on his side, never to be completely unarmed. He shrugged in the mirror at his typical appearance.

He shook out the nerves that were twisting his insides and knocked on their adjoining door. Holding his posture upright, preparing to be knocked breathless by whatever she chose to wear, surely looking much better than him.

But she never came.

He stood for a few more moments, his heart thundering in his chest. Perhaps she hadn’t heard? He knocked again.

Nothing, not a sound. Nervous energy coursed through him as he flexed his fingers at his sides. He debated whether to open the door; he knew it was unlocked. But he ultimately decided against it. He already had caught her in precarious positions before that hadn’t faired well for their relationship. Instead, he headed out of his apartment, trying not to worry where she could be or why she hadn’t answered.

As he opened the door, he was greeted by the darkening sky in the east, pale blues mixed with the darker shades of winter’s grey. It was supper time.

He scrubbed at his face. She was safe in the castle. She had free reign to go where she pleased, and she was familiar enough with all the locations. She could be in the library. Or perhaps she was with Ilya at the stables. Or perhaps in the dining hall eating, since he only asked her for drinks.

He straightened himself, throwing back his shoulders, and the creeping worry. He decided the latter is where he’d go.

While heading to the dining hall, he passed Fledge along the way.

“Link, good to see you.” Fledge gave him his classic nervous smile with a small wave.

“You too. Have you seen Zelda?” He was barely able to separate the two sentences.

“Yes, she’s in the dining hall. I just left her. She’s still there.”

A small smile bloomed on his face he couldn’t help to contain. Fledge noticed. “You two have been getting along now?”

Link only nodded. He didn’t feel like getting into details with Fledge. And Fledge sensed that and went on his way.

He walked into the dining hall, packed with servants, soldiers, knights, and more castle employees. He scanned the dark room for the golden-haired stunner. His eyes landed on her at a distance, but he stiffened.

Purlo was next to her, large and looming. He almost forgot he was now stationed at the castle, to his dismay. Fledge didn’t mention him, as he was sure he would have. He must have waited for Fledge to leave her side and pounced. Link’s knuckles were white.

She looked soft, quietly gorgeous, sitting next to him. With a small smile and hazy eyes while listening to him speak. His heart sank.

He did hear that Purlo wanted to court her before they left for Gerudo Town. Not from her directly, but from whispers. He didn’t know what her answer had been. He’d been too nervous to ask. He wasn’t going to let this destroy what they’d built. Last time, he ruined it with his jealousy. She can be with whomever she chooses, including large, undeserving assholes if she so wished. He wouldn’t let his feelings affect their new friendship. 

So he left.

He was a whirlwind of emotions as he walked aimlessly, his feet carrying him to an unknown destination. It was ironic, considering he usually prided himself on being stoic and unemotional. But ever since she entered his life, a pile of white linens, tanned skin, and golden hair, he’s been fighting against his very nature.

As he made his way around the bend heading towards town, completely unaware of his surroundings, Ilya ran smack into him.

“Link!” She clutched her chest.

“Ilya, I’m so sorry.“ He instinctively reached his hand out to grip her arm. “Are you alright?” He shook his head, shaking out the image of Zelda to focus on his friend in front of him.

She laughed, her lighthearted, familiar laugh. “Yeah, I’m fine. But we have to stop running into each other like that.” She tilted her head in a knowing way.

His face was tight, and his eyes wandered past her face to the horizon. “I’m sorry I was distracted. I’ll let you be on your way—“

“What’s bothering you?” She cut in quickly. He focused back on her eyes, sparkling with concern.

Link exhaled loudly, unintentionally. She drilled into him, which she never did. He was clenching his jaw, unable or unwilling to share, even if it was with Ilya.

“Come with me.” She promptly hooked her arm through his and led him back towards the dining hall.

Before he could object to where she was bringing him, not wanting to see the image again of Zelda and Purlo, she instead led him directly to the kitchen. 

They entered the large room, still humid from cooking dinner. The humming of the chefs and servants cleaning and prepping for the next day echoed throughout the stone room. He hung back at the doorframe as she spoke with one of the chefs out of earshot, who gave her a bottle and a wink. Ilya turned to hold up the bottle to Link. He huffed a laugh once he recognized the contents. 

It was wild berry wine. He hated it. But it was a private joke between them. When they were younger, living in Hateno still, they both snuck away from their mothers to indulge. They ended up completely sick; their mothers were furious with them both and punishing them with double the amount of chores for the month. When his father came back a week later, he thought he’d be punished further, but he only said the hangover was punishment enough.

He’d since been able to handle his liquor, but the overly sweet taste did him no favors. But the sentiment counted.

Ilya led them to the pavilion garden, the same place he found Zelda just months prior. It felt like a lifetime ago. They sat on a marble bench against the wall, in direct view of the old oak tree. Dense vines of orange flowers decorated the trellis above them as the sky deepened it’s dark hue above them.

The air smelled of winter— no blooms of flowers coating his senses, only that damp air with the hint of smoky soot, the faint wafts of the charred wood from the hundreds of castle fireplaces being lit. It was chilly, but not cold— a mild winter. Ilya was in her stable gear, brown pants, long riding boots and a jacket. Her ears slightly pink from the wind. She must have been heading to supper after a long day of work.

Ilya opened the bottle and handed it to him, just as they did when they were children, without any fancy glasses. He took a large swig; the tart fruit hung on his lips; he held back a scowl. He passed it to Ilya as she took a more delicate chug.

Ilya puckered her lips at the tartness still lingering, “So what’s wrong?”

His gaze was on the old oak tree. He knew Ilya was starting side long at him. “Nothing is wrong.”

“Link.” She challenged back with a hiss. He rarely heard her like this. Serious and commanding.

He grabbed the bottle again and chugged. He set the bottle down and couldn’t help but continue to stare at the tree. Imagining Zelda underneath it. Ilya noticed.

“I heard you are getting along now?” She spoke in barely a whisper.

He knew who she meant, “We are.”

“Isn’t that good? Makes your journey less strained?” Ilya was urging him to look at her, craning her neck further into his vision.

“Yes.”

Ilya exhaled an exaggerated breath, “Link. I’m trying here.”

She was right; he’d have to stop being so moody. She was trying to cheer him up; he didn’t mean to bring her down. “I’m sorry, I—uh, I asked if she’d like to go for a drink tonight. But she’s with Purlo.”

Ilya was quiet; she took the bottle and sipped slowly. “She told me you saved her again. Twice.”

He nodded.

Ilya shrugged, “Link, she’s different now. Perhaps in the beginning of your travels things were.. rocky, but you’re both in a good place it seems. You have a common goal. You do remember what that is, right?”

Unfortunately, yes, he had tried to forget. He kept silent but nodded.

“She’s been here a few months and adapted well; that’s the best scenario. But I’m sure she still misses her home, her family, her friends.”

He knew deep, deep down that was true. It’s the reason he’d been assigned to her in the first place. It had just gotten blurred in the past few weeks. She barely mentioned her home since Gerudo Town, not with sadness, but rather as if she was recalling a fond memory. She seemed to be adapting to Hyrule and their culture, enjoying it— thriving in it.

“Link, can I ask you a personal question?” Ilya took another swig as Link grunted his yes. He tore his gaze from the tree and landed on Ilya’s face. Her cheeks were pink, probably from the alcohol. “Have you ever thought about being with anyone? Romantically?”

“Yes.” He didn’t hesitate with that answer, because he had. He fantasized about it wildly.

She swallowed. “Why haven’t you done anything about it?”

He felt a lump in his throat at that. He had almost done something, but a part of him had held him back. He continued to gaze at his old childhood friend who looked at him fondly, albeit with a slight sorrow in her eyes as he gripped the edge of the bench with both palms.

He sucked in his teeth, “Who is to say I’m worthy of it?”

“Link, you deserve anything you desire. You are the best person I know. Anyone, and I mean it, anyone would be lucky to have you.” She looked at him, through him, as she gently covered his hand with her own.

And he returned the look. Analyzing his best friend. His oldest childhood friend. Her heart-shaped face illuminated under the dark sky, the shadows of the moon highlighting her beautiful features. It would be easy to love her. Convenient even. He wondered why he never felt that way about her.

Ilya wrapped her arm around his and rested her head on his shoulder as she whispered to him. “Know your worth.”

They sat there quietly, finishing the rest of the sickly-sweet wine, and he wondered if the former of Ilya’s words were true.

Chapter 20: Tent
Chapter Text
They passed pockets of trees, the bare branches covered in new growth. Bare no more. Spring was near.

She rubbed her nose with her knuckle, which was running. Perhaps she had a cold, or her seasonal allergies followed her here.

The sky was littered with clouds in the distance. Above them, it was light blue and clear, but in the distance, it was darker, grayish-navy. She noted where the two skies met, clouds blending with bright blue. A storm was on its way.

She closed her eyes and breathed in the crisp, cool air while atop Storm. It smelled sharp. Of fresh grass and budding flowers— and pine. She instinctively looked over at Link, who was astride Epona, trotting behind her at a distance. Wondering how he always seemed to smell the same no matter what region they traveled to.

He didn’t notice her twisting her neck as his thoughts seemed to be elsewhere.

Their ride was mostly silent on their way to the Royal Tech Lab. Link had been quiet; something was clearly bothering him.

He apologized for missing their outing, as he called it. She would have called it a date, but she surely misunderstood.

While he was meeting with Impa, she was hungry and went to the dining hall, assuming he’d meet her there at some point, knowing his gluttonous eating habits. She spotted Fledge, who warmly invited her to join him. She told him about their journey with an unmasked fondness in her tone. About the Gerudo, about the lizalfos, about their reconciliation. Fledge listened quietly, nodding his head, feigning shock, and smiling along. Zelda was winded after her hour-long tirade, and Fledge looked tired from listening.

She decided to sit and wait for Link, not wanting to go back to their apartment and risk missing him. But after Fledge left, Purlo found her and decidedly invited himself to join her.

She didn’t mind, but all he spoke of was himself, of his time in the castle, of his time at the Gatepost, of his supposed victories. He was quite— boring. And full of himself. She sat politely and smiled as he spoke. Initially flattered when he asked to court her before her departure for the Gerudo desert, she couldn’t fathom enduring a date with him if this was any indication of how it might go. So, she just nodded politely to his incessant rambling and immediately started to think of excuses to get out of it.

Perhaps months ago, she would have been more inclined to give him a chance, however, after the events in the Gerudo Desert, she couldn’t see past her rose-colored lens for another. Another who was courageous, honorable, kind, generous, handsome…

After she was able to excuse herself from the arrogant knight, she went to find Link, but his apartment was empty. She was so bold to even check that he hadn’t fallen asleep by opening their shared door. After hours of waiting, she laid in her own bed and only later did she hear his door open and shut, well after the moon was high in the sky.

The next morning, a knock on her main apartment door had her scrambling for the possibility of seeing Impa, Fledge, or Ilya until he presented himself in front of her, dressed in his full gear; tunic, guards, and sword. She couldn’t hide her surprise at the newfound formality, as they’d been communicating through their shared door since arriving back from the military training camp.

In additional to his apology for missing their outing, in which he didn’t elaborate on why, he said they were instructed to go to the Royal Tech Lab, to leave by mid-morning.

She transformed into her beloved travel attire—black pants, a crisp white shirt, and the corset. While initially she found the corset oppressive, now she reveled in its flattering fit, accentuating her curves and enhancing her bosom. She also found joy in styling it with various colored shirts. It was her very own accessory, a piece of self-identification.

She packed a light bag, as Link mentioned it wasn’t far from the castle, but it could turn into an overnight stay depending on how late they stayed. So she packed her favorite nightgown, the one that fit her like a second skin, and a warm, chunky sweater made of sheep’s wool.

Oddly, she was excited for this impromptu trip. She had come to enjoy traveling outside the castle. Of course, her apartment was lovely, and she was grateful to have it, but being out in the wild, breathing in the air, and seeing the glorious landscape. It was refreshing.

And it seemed to be the only other time she could speak with her… knight on a more informal basis. Even if threats happened to lurk nearby, she was never truly afraid with him at her side.

They arrived early afternoon to a large gatehouse, only a few hours of light riding from the castle. It had to be four stories tall and similar in architecture to Castle Town’s guard post, except this one had a large telescope on the roof. She mused that since this was royal property, they certainly made it obvious with the grandeur of it.

Blue flamed lanterns guided their steps as the gate opened for them. A chill ran through her and she tried not to shudder.

“Have you ever been here before?” She whispered to Link. She wasn’t even sure why she whispered, it felt as though she had to.

“No, I’ve passed it countless times but never been inside. You need an invitation from a royal family member or a high-ranking Sheikah.” Link hadn’t looked at her when he answered. He had been carefully scouting around them for threats, there was clearly an uneasiness he held, evident by the tightness in his jaw.

They entered the small stone courtyard and dismounted from their horses. Men dressed in tight, slick outfits with matching grey hair and red eyes greeted them. The men said nothing through their covered mouths, fabric pulled to their noses as they took their horses’ reins to guide them to the small stable with others. Zelda glanced nervously at Link. This place was very different from the castle.

Link gave a tight smile in reassurance, but part of her knew he felt the same unease.

Ilya did mention to her that the Sheikah were a sub-race of the Hylians. They served the royal family but in tandem operated on their own. Some Hylians had negative prejudices against them, citing their natural abilities in stealth as sneaky and shady. Zelda’s only encounter was with Impa, who despite her tough exterior, she felt a sense of protection and sanctuary in.

She was pulled from those thoughts as she and Link were escorted through the building by a young Sheikah woman, she lead them down an impossibly long hallway. 

They finally arrived at massive double doors to which the young woman pushed open. Zelda held her breath as the large, dark room yawned open to them. She couldn’t get her eyes to focus on one area for longer than a second.

Large piles of discarded metal pieces decorated every corner of the room, all illuminated by an unnatural glowing light. As if this room alone was the dumping ground for all the kingdom’s scraps. Papers, some untouched and others crumpled in balls, scattered across the floor. Chalkboards bore indistinguishable scribbles on either side of the room. Odd claw-like arms hung from the ceiling, which she shuddered at, the same chill she felt when she arrived coursing through her. The only part of the room completely free of clutter was a large, tall table in the center, bathed in a bright light that cast a slightly ominous glow.

“CHECK IT!” She heard a soft, female voice yell on the opposite side of the large room.

Check what?

“Hold on!” Now a gruff, melodramatic voice sounded from an unknown direction.

Link and she turned to each other. Both their faces painted in complete confusion.

A small blue light exploded on the far side of the room, followed by “Oh shoot.”

A tall, white-haired, red-eyed woman stumbled out from the corner, coughing and mumbling to herself, something about charging ancient technology. Then she noticed them.

“Who are you two?” She spoke with complete disinterest in her tone.

Link spoke up, “Impa sent us. I’m Link, a knight in the royal guard, and this is Zel—”

“OH YES, Zelda—” she said her name as if it tasted funny on her tongue, “—the one that appeared out of thin air and resembles our royalty.” The woman hurried to close the distance between them. Her eyes were large and eager under her thick red glasses, fixated on Zelda, as if she were a shiny new toy she was able to play with. “Robbie! The girl who time traveled is here!”

Zelda opened her mouth, shut it, then opened it again. “I don’t know if time traveled is correct.” She trailed off by the time the woman reached her.

She practically pushed Link out of the way to examine her. Her familiar red eyes trailed every inch of her from toes to crown. On the other hand, if she had to describe the Sheikah Master, methodical, cunning, and composed were just a few words to describe Impa. Two very different sides of the same coin.

“What is it?” Link asked.

His googles still on and moving wildly, she could only assume his eyes were red as well. “To summarize, more monsters have been documented since your arrival. We’ve known this, we’ve gotten reports from every region, which all started the same week you arrived.” He pulled a rouge paper from the floor, apparently in effort to show said report. “The pull started the day after you arrived, which was unsuccessful to either hurt you or capture you as Link intervened. But then you felt it again in Gerudo Desert, except that time, a mirage of a child lured you, which turned out to be not real. Then the latest, you were lured to a peak where you could not flee with a horde waiting to ambush you.”

The first time, the bokoblins surrounded you but did not immediately attack. The second time, the lizalfos subdued you, but it’s unknown if they would have maimed you or otherwise.” Link glared at Robbie at the insinuation that the lizalfos would have done anything other than kill her, but he continued, ignoring him, “The third time, Link was by your side, and the monsters that appeared were tenfold.”

Zelda nodded.

Robbie puckered his mouth and brought his fingers to his chin to drum on in nervous anticipation, “I suspect something or someone is orchestrating this. Controlling monsters to capture or hurt you, but still unknown as to the intention.”

Zelda let out a shaky breath as Link stiffened next to her. “But I’m no one. I’m not the Princess or even anyone important here. Who or what would want me?”

Link turned his face to her ever so slightly. His blue eyes looked despondent at her. As if her words hurt him somehow.

Purah stepped up and grabbed Zelda’s jaw, jerking her head to have a better look, “You share their family name and you look eerily similar to the Princess.” Purah paused, considering, “Actually, you resemble the late Queen more. If you assume that is correct, then it makes sense why something would want you.”

“Our research has concluded they don’t reproduce, but they magically appear when evil is near. Evil commands them, and they don’t tire or die unless slayed.” Robbie explained as if he was talking about the weather.

She wasn’t ready to touch that one yet; luckily, Link interjected. “How can something control monsters?”

“It’s not widely documented in research because it has never been proven. Past ages when good and evil have faced each other, there are assumptions—“ Robbie started.

“Based on facts!” Purah interjected, her pointer finger held up.

“Yes, yes, based on facts, that when a true evil rises, it controls other evil. Heroes of legend have faced hordes of monsters when facing off against evil. Once good triumphs, the monsters fade.”

They were standing at a high table but she couldn’t help but dramatically place her elbows on the table and cover her face with her hands. All three went quiet.

How could she be related to royalty from a line that didn’t exist in her world? Could they have been named something else? Why hadn’t her own mother ever mentioned it?

The notoriety wouldn’t have mattered to her. But that there might be family that she might have out there. Family she might yet still know when she thought all were lost. Her heart ached.

And monsters. And evil beings. There were plenty of figurative monsters where she came from, but not literal ones. She hadn’t even put that much thought into their presence in Hyrule until now. How insane it was that there were living, breathing beings with a sole purpose to kill. It was as though she had buried that logic and rationality deep inside herself. That last lingering thought that perhaps even after all this time, this entire experience had been a dream, had finally vanished.

She swore she now tasted that odd metallic smell in her throat.

“We don’t know for sure, so there’s no reason to panic. You have the best knight in all the kingdom protecting you.” Purah said softly. As if now realizing their frankness had been too much for her to handle.

Zelda paused, wondering if she should even bother to ask, “What about getting me back home?”

Link’s jaw feathered and his eyes slid from her own to Purah’s.

Purah slid her glasses up to rest upon the crown of her head. Zelda then noticed the intense red eyeshadow to match her red eyes as she stared into Zelda’s green ones, “We will look into that too, whatever we find out, we will let you know.” Purah’s voice sounded almost comforting.

Zelda believed that. However, something changed. A part of her hadn’t even wanted to ask because she knew they probably wouldn’t find anything or that they had bigger concerns than her needs, among other reasons. She gave them both a half hearted smile, “Thank you, both of you. We should go, try to make it back to the castle.”

“Our offer stands. If you’d like to do further evaluations, we can help!” Purah said too eagerly as they turned to leave. Link turned and shot them a glare she couldn’t see.

As they left the lab, she seemed to finally exhale, she winced at the sharp pain from the amount of pressure she suddenly felt on her chest. 

Link noticed. “It’s going to rain. Do you want to stay here for the night so we don’t have to rush back?”

“No. I— I don’t want to go back in there. Can we stay outside?” Her eyes were pleading and her hand was gently rubbing her chest.

“Yes, let me speak with the attendants. They can hold our horses.”

Link rushed off to make preparations as the gate opened. She instantly felt better breathing in the fresh air and grass. Yet everything came crashing over her.

How can everyone around her be so casual about everything? Purah and Robbie all but said out loud that she was of royal blood. The Princess Zelda might as well be her distant relative. How did that not shake them as it had her?

And on top of that, they theorize that something evil is the puppet master inciting the monsters to attack? How are they not batting down hatches or lowering the gates in response? 

But why would this mysterious presence want her? Even if she believed she was related to royalty.. why wouldn’t they go after the Princess instead? She was the obvious choice.

As her breathing quickened in panic, her vision was starting to blur and her hands began to shake, Link found his way quickly back to her with their saddle bags. The sight of him gallantly walking towards her calmed her nerves before he could ask her what was wrong.

He escorted her out and started to walk towards a lone tree far enough away from the lab. The anxiety she felt in her muscles eased. She felt better with each step.

He set up their camp, as he always did. Her tent, his hammock, he unpacked the food he brought and they ate quietly as they watched the sunset bleed orange, navy and purple in the distance. Rain was coming.

The pain in her chest had subsided, but she had barely been able to eat. All the things she thought she knew churned in her gut, threatening to be sick if she forced it. Her only recourse was distraction. Finally, she mustered up the courage to say, “I was disappointed that we didn’t have our drink yesterday.” She lifted her head from the bowl of food to meet his gaze. She hadn’t wanted to discuss royalty, monsters, or evil; only them.

His brows shot up, earnest surprise. “Really? You were?”

“Of course, you did ask me to go, and I said yes.”

His mouth twitched up slightly. “I swear on all my honor, I will take you out once we are back. Even as early as tomorrow if you wish.”

Her stomach flipped, but for different reasons. “Oh honorable knight, to care about my thirst as such, I am so honored.” She proclaimed dramatically waving her hands to cover her heart in exaggeration.

He rolled his eyes and huffed.

After they finished their meals and packed away their supplies, she managed to climb into her tent and change. The weather was temperate, so the feeling of her favorite silk nightgown in combination with the sweater she had the hindsight to pack was delightful.

What was not delightful was the clouds rolling in and Link lying out in the open in his hammock.

She opened the tent. Link was already in his hammock. She couldn’t bear the thought of him trying to sleep in the rain, so she bravely asked. “Link, do you want to sleep in my tent tonight, to avoid the rain?”

He turned to face her, as graceful as he could in a hammock, slightly taken aback by the suggestion. “I don’t mind. Your tent is small.”

“There’s enough room for both of us.”

“Really though, it’s meant for just you.”

She pushed past her wounded pride and went for honesty. Purah and Robbie certainly were unapologetically blunt, why couldn’t she be?

“Link, I don’t want to beg you, and I won’t push if you insist because of decorum, but I don’t mind at all. We spend every moment together. Sleeping next to each other is more than okay with me. Plus, if you stay out there, all I will be able to think about is you trying to sleep with rain pelting your face and how uncomfortable you’ll be in wet clothes.”

He was quiet for a moment. She did not want to be desperate, but the fact was true. He saved her life and protected her, and she couldn’t possibly sleep comfortably knowing she could do this small service for him in return.

“Alright,” he said, twisting out of his hammock. He grabbed his sword to bring into the tent as she slid over to make room. He entered, taking his boots off, leaving his socked feet at her eye level until he laid down. He still had his tunic and pants on, sans his guards and belts. He laid on his back facing the ceiling of the tent, his sword near his dominant hand as she laid on the opposite side, her head propped up on her elbow.

There was an unexpected tension between them. She hadn’t thought it weird when she initially asked but now he was a mere breath away and she still thought him incredibly desirable, but she could manage to sleep next to him in complete mutual respect for one night. 

Yet the tension continued to stretch unbearably until she interrupted it. “You mentioned in Gerudo that knights can have relationships. What does that exactly look like?”

She barely finished her sentence as a whiff of pine filled her nostrils. The tent grew warm. Maybe it wasn’t the best question to ask in the moment, being so close, but she was curious.

He turned his face to her, propping his head up, mirroring her, which did little to calm her. “Knights can court nobles or servants. Really anyone except royalty. Most marriages are arranged from the fathers directly with the knights. If a knight is interested in someone specific, they can court them but if it’s a noble, then they need to get permission from their male relative. If they’re not noble, then typically permission isn’t needed, but it’s considered polite to ask anyway.”

“Have you gotten proposals?”

“Yes.” He replied quickly.

She was shocked and did not hide it on her face as her jaw unhinged.

He smiled and shook his head. “I’ve gotten a few proposals since I’ve been promoted, but I turned them down.”

That creeping chest pain was coming back, but for different reasons, “Why?”

He clicked his tongue. “They were nice-looking women, and I’m sure they were kind and loving and would make a good wife, but I don’t want an arranged relationship. My parents didn’t have one, and they had the best relationship.” His voice grew more distant as he trailed off.

She knew that feeling, not personally but in similarity to her own parents’ relationship.

She pivoted around the subject of their parents. “What does courting entail?”

He pursed his lips, as if trying to think through whatever he was going to say appropriately. “Courting can be outings, such as walks or strolls outside. It can be picnics, riding, dancing. Usually supervised, but again, it depends on the rank.”

“What about getting drinks?” She dared with a suggestive smile.

He grew slightly fidgety. “Not exactly courting, that’s more— forward.”

She laughed. “That’s very different from what I’m used to.”

“What does courting look like for you?”

“It… varies.” She paused as he looked at her bright eyed. She wanted to phrase it as traditionally as she could. “Some couples take things slow, such as your courting, doing activities together, getting to know each other. Then others can have intimate relations the same night they meet. But no one needs permission from their parents.”

Link looked stunned as he swallowed. “Have you… courted that way?”

She couldn’t help the heat in her cheeks, as the blue in his eyes seemed to darken, “No, not that forward. I’ve been on dates, but it’s been very casual, just dinner or drinks. Never went further than that.”

Something eased on his face at that admission. She didn’t feel like sullying the conversation with talks of Cole. He had only asked about courting, not full-out dating.

Sure, it was semantics, and perhaps one day she would tell him that story.

Cole felt like a bad vacation from a long time ago. Surprisingly, she had just now realized that she hadn’t thought about him more than once since she arrived here. Cole never deserved her, and he certainly doesn’t deserve her thoughts of him. This experience made her appreciate everything that had taken those negative feelings away from her.

She twisted to lie on her stomach, her legs lifted and crossed, but she kept her arms under her chin, still gazing at her too-good-looking knight. “So back to your courting, you’re telling me all couples don’t kiss or— more— before getting married?” Her lids were hazy as something stirred within her.

“Not exactly…”

“Ah, the catch.”

“Rules dictate strict enforcement; it’s more strained on the women, unfairly of course.” He facial expression conveyed that he meant that last statement, “—but men can get away with being… rakish.” She swore a faint blush colored his cheeks.

“That sounds about right.” She rolled her eyes instinctively, “What about you, are you rakish?” She was feeling bold, the smell of his scent, grass, and pine, lingering all around her as she let the word drip off her tongue.
