Mipha watched him carefully as he sat and explained, quiet and focused on the healing in front of her. Once he finished speaking, Mipha looked at him with her deep, expressive eyes, so gold it looked like living candlelight. She was looking at him the same way as when he was a child.

She asked the question he’d been asking himself since Zelda arrived: what does all this mean?

He had never thought it nor said it aloud. Was Zelda here for a reason? Or was it all a coincidence and meant nothing?

But as he pondered, even if it was the latter, it still meant something to him. It was too late to be meaningless. His life and path were significantly changed forever. Months ago, all he wanted was the honor to protect the princess. He was plagued by regret and bitterness, but now he couldn’t fathom any other outcome. Despite the detour that had derailed his career, he no longer cared. His sole purpose now was Zelda’s safety and well-being.

As he concluded his retelling of the past six months, his arm had been completely healed. The dull pain he had endured for weeks vanished, as if it had never existed. Mipha’s large eyes turned downcast, and he sensed her concern as she tensed next to him.

He had shared too much. Despite their long friendship, he rarely expressed his feelings to anyone. He preferred to silently endure, never wanting to burden anyone. But all she said was perhaps they could spend some time together once this was all over.

And that made him tense.

He hadn’t thought about when this would be over. He’d sworn a vow, until his death or duty fulfilled, to serve Zelda. He never thought about the fulfilled portion of that vow. Even when she dismissed him in the desert, he still lingered nearby to protect her. But if she went home, his service would end.

He would get an honorable discharge. He could continue his knighthood in high ranks. Training others to become like him. His salary would be substantial; he could afford a nice house in Castle Town. Or he could ask to be stationed somewhere else, such as Zora’s Domain, and then Mipha and he could spend time together.

But those thoughts were unnerving. He hadn’t thought about what comes after. He had even forgotten what life was like before.

After Mipha and he returned, Zelda had been preoccupied ever since. She seemingly made herself scarce, reading by the pools or gazing out from the balconies. She had even been asleep that night before he slipped into his own bed, and the next morning at breakfast she was already there with Mipha and Sidon.

He had no reason to think anything happened; they engaged in polite conversation during their journey back to the castle, but it felt… strained. She seemed distant; she wouldn’t meet his eye, and the flirting and light banter they had shared in recent weeks was absent.

He couldn’t place what had occurred to cause this sudden shift in her. Had it happened before his departure to slay the lynel or after? Perhaps that had triggered traumatic stress in her, or perhaps the prospect of facing King Dorephan’s latest information may be even more terrifying than the reality of returning home.

Worse for him or her?

So here he was, days later trying to train, hoping to distract himself from his thoughts, but he was failing miserably. If he were still in the barracks training with the rest, Auru would have had him on night watch for a month had he seen how absentmindedly he was handling his blade.

“Enjoying the view?” He shouted to her. He would try being cheeky once more, his heart racing, hoping her reaction would be different from the past few days.

“Yes, the flowers are looking quite vibrant today.” She said straight-faced, yet he swore he saw a ghost of a curl on her lips.

It was something.

“Would you like to join me on a morning walk around the gardens? I’m finishing up here.” He wasn’t going to be able to train efficiently until he spoke with her anyway.

“Sure, I’ll be right down.”

He hurriedly retied his hair back, smoothing it as best he could. He used his forearm to wipe the beads of sweat from his forehead, using the motion to check his scent discreetly. And just as suddenly as she left, she appeared before him, looking refreshed and bright. A contrast to his disheveled and tired appearance.

“Did you have a good rest?” He asked sheepishly.

It was a lame question to ask her after everything they’d been through. His confidence now blown to smithereens with her standing in front of him, softly gorgeous against the morning light.

“I did.” She tilted her head ever so slightly, “and you?”

“Yes, I did.”

He felt foolish. He hadn’t been this tongue-tied around her before. He wouldn’t be able to think straight until he learned what troubled her. “After you.” He promptly sheathed his sword and extended his hand for her to follow the path out of the plaza. She tilted her head in acknowledgment, and they started their walk.

They quietly strolled on the narrow path, leading them to one of the castle’s many public gardens. Filled with marble statues of ancient Loftwings, Hyrule crests, and famous royal family members. Her dainty fingers gently held the maroon flower as she stared down at it. “That’s incredible.”

He stared at her, as she stared at the flowers. He wanted to ask her outright what had been troubling her, but he had to wait for the right time. Whenever they were alone, they confided in each other, sharing their innermost thoughts and deepest secrets. Perhaps bringing her to the royal gardens would open her up.

“What did you talk about?” She averted her gaze, looking down at the stone path as she continued. “If you prefer to keep to yourself, you don’t have to tell me,” she said.

“No, I don’t mind.” He glanced sidelong at her, “About the last few months, about you and me.” He paused at the joining of them in sentence form, “about your arrival, our journey. If Zelda had been looking at him, she would have seen his face twist in distaste, “Zelda, I love spending time with my friend, but not seeing her has nothing to do with you.” His tone was commanding, urging her to look at him.

She did, her eyes half hooded, sad, a faint twisting of her lips, “Aren’t you both… involved?”

Link took a second to register what she was asking. His brain finally caught up a moment later.

Zelda thought him and Mipha were dating?

“Mipha is my friend, my good friend, but nothing more than that.”

Zelda took a breath, her features already less tense, “She hadn’t mentioned a tunic or measurements to you?”

Link shot her a raised brow and shook his head.

Zelda shook her head, “Never mind” and finally a small smile painted her soft features. He’d been dying to see it for days.

She went back to staring at the flowers next to her. As they navigated around the private paths, she touched every colorful flower or herb along the way asking him for the names and properties of each. He was happy to indulge her, especially as the distance between them melted away. It was as if every bloom she touched, the color’s vibrance and life force was rubbing off on her, waking her out of her haze. 

After spending an hour or so in the garden, they walked back to their apartments. It was getting warmer, and he needed to bathe. They both seemed to linger at his door.

“Do you want to grab breakfast? Then we can head to Impa’s afterwards?” He said coyly. He was trying to avoid all things Impa and Zelda’s future, but Impa would just come to them, angrily, if they didn’t go to her first.

He watched her go, hesitating at his door. It was as if his eyes didn’t want to tear itself away from her. Her long blonde hair swung with her hips, distinctly visible against the tight fit of the skirt. The view of her backside was just as incredible as her front. Every curve pronounced and perfect.

He quickly lowered his heart rate and told Impa all. About the Spiritual Stones, specifically the Zora’s Sapphire. Using that with the other two opens the Door of Time at the Temple of Time— as the legend went.

Impa was quiet. She stood from her seat, smoothing her typical grey garb and adjusting the red belt around her waist. Impa, still her back turned to them as she glanced sidelong out her small window, said, “Pray is a loose term. You are to go into the Spring and kneel, ask for the goddess’ blessing.” She paused, perhaps for dramatic effect or just choosing her next words wisely, “See what comes of it.”

Zelda stared into Impa’s eyes, her jaw clearly tense as she thought through her answer. Contemplating. Link felt invisible between the two women.

“I might never go home. Maybe we should be trying to… fit my life into Hyrule rather than trying to find a way out.” Zelda breathed a shaky breath. Her shoulders fell, and her gaze lowered from Impa’s. 

As much as he hated the thought of her leaving, he hated seeing her this way more. He looked away, unable to stomach it.

Zelda was quiet for a long moment. She looked to Link, her face looking to his in silent question, pleading. But what question was she trying to ask him? Should she continue her journey or stay? He remained neutral, giving no indication of his personal feelings on the subject.

It had to be her choice.

She looked to Impa, followed by a large exhale, and said quietly, “I’ll do it.”

“No, good luck, Zelda.”

He didn’t need to be scolded about thoughts he had. He hadn’t acted on them— yet.

“I suspect.”

The Faron region had always been sultry, no matter the time of year. Balmy, wet, hot, and muggy. Vastly different from the temperate climate of Central Hyrule. Link estimated they’d be gone for the better part of a week, and when they arrived back, Spring festivities would be starting, mainly, the annual Spring Ball to welcome and give blessing to the goddess for a fruitful season ahead. Hosted by the Royal family, the King and Princess Zelda would be heavily featured, along with the region’s delegates, including Mipha, Daruk, Urbosa, and Revali. Then, of course, the royal guard and knights were in attendance as was expected of high-ranking military, then filled out with other nobles or notable families.

Link always dreaded these events. He had to attend given his station. He usually asked Ilya or would attend alone and spend his time catching up with Mipha. It was the only time in the past few years he could catch up with the Zora Princess. But then, as all balls went, knights were expected to dance in a group setting at some point in the night. His thoughts were growing bolder. He had thought of Zelda all day, every day as of late, but increasingly his thoughts became more explicit, barely able to hide his desire when facing her. He would have to do the next best thing: train.

“I—uh— I’m going to train. Just over the hill. Will you be okay here for a bit?”

“Can I come with you?”

“Your dedication to training is incredible.” Her voice was as gentle as the rain around them.

“No, I don’t think so.” She pulled her knees to her chest, hugging her brown boots that went over her black pants. “I’ve heard rumors about you before I even really knew you. You are one of the best knights that ever graced Hyrule’s walls. Your fellow knights, captains, soldiers, and even the majority of the castle staff know it. Plus, I’ve seen you in battle. Link knew that. He knew that story because the noble offered his daughter’s hand in marriage to his father afterwards. In that moment, I knew I wanted to do the same thing as her. I wanted to absorb every ounce of knowledge about the history of our world.”

She looked over at the horizon, to Lake Hylia’s still water, her green eyes distant— as if she was back in her world, remembering. “When I was particularly obsessed with a time period or theory, I would spend every waking minute for weeks, learning about the societal influences or pressures that inherently were depicted at the time. All I wanted to do was learn it all. For those who do not remember the past are condemned to repeat it. As they say.”

Link turned to face her. Her eyes now staring down at the weathered book closed next to her, she placed one hand over the cover delicately rubbing her fingers over the engraved title letters.

“And so I did. After my parents died, I went to university and studied hard. I double-majored in history and liberal arts. I wanted to honor my mother that way. I still hope to.”

Link knew in that moment why she said what she said. She would be okay in Hyrule if she had a purpose. Knowledge to learn and pass down, to enrich her own soul, to inspire others. He felt the same. All he wanted was to be a knight, like his father. To serve and protect. He was probably the only other person that knew what she meant, down in his marrow.

He sheathed his sword and walked towards her and knelt. He was good and soaked from head to feet, but he wiped his hand dry as best he could and placed it over hers, still over the book cover. She looked at him under her long lashes, reflectively, as he stared back at her. It was the first time all day he could look at her, past her beauty and into her true self as he said, “I will ensure that you do. Regardless of what happens next, you will honor her. I promise you that much.”

So he amended his vow he made to her all those months ago. Until his last breath, he would do everything for her, so she could do anything she wanted.

They woke early from the inn at Deya Village and started the trek to the Spring of Courage. He took her pack and slung it over his shoulder, baring the weight of it all. Link had told her to pack light as they wouldn’t be taking main roads, but he also still carried his sword, which was heavy enough without the extra weight.

No wonder he was as toned as he was. The endless training and moving. How could anyone compare?

Link led the way; the hills weren’t impossible to scale but considerably steep enough. He always found his footing, then turned to her. Extending his hand out to grasp hers and pull her up. His calloused fingers grazing hers sparked something through her nerves every time he touched her. She tried to keep her wits about her, but imagining his fingers elsewhere kept her distracted during the climb.

As they peaked on the foothills, the landscape turned from temperate Central Hyrule grass, shrubs, and trees to more tropical life in front of them. Thick, dark, lush palms and large leaves were the canopy above them, completely shading the ground below. Every time she visited a new place in Hyrule, she was completely enthralled by its landscape and how vastly different a few steps made between regions.

They carefully made their way down the hill; the air was already thick with humidity from the arid climate. Loud insects sang all around them, welcoming them to their home. She swore she even heard monkeys laughing.

She knew they had arrived near the spring; despite not knowing where they were, all her senses were screaming at her. The jungle had grown quiet as they stepped on the stone path; the air was hot, but she felt a cool breeze, leaving goosebumps in their wake. Nothing.

Not one flaw to be had, almost as if it was freshly polished or newly forged, not sitting in muddy water for centuries. It was a deep, transparent green with bright gold encasing it. The gold twirled around the gem like a vine. It was the most captivating and magnificent thing she’d ever seen.

She felt that otherworldly weight settling into her palm. An unfamiliar presence of power. It whispered to her, a spell. A trance veiled her; she was frozen to its existence. She wasn’t supposed to ever know such a feeling but meant to be at the same time. Wrong, but so right.

“What? Are you okay?” His eyes scanned her body up and down swiftly, then darted nearby for threats. Finally, satisfied she was not in immediate danger, he saw her hand and the large gem she was holding.

“What is that…?” He straightened his spine. Tension laced his voice.

“I don’t know.” She said, shaky. “I did what Impa asked, and suddenly it glowed in the water afterwards. I just— I just picked it up.”

He looked uneasy. “May I?” As he sheathed his sword.

She nodded and handed him the large stone.

He looked it over attentively, rolling it over in his hands, holding it up to examine it in the small sun ray poking in from above them. The refraction danced on the stone that was vibrant green, fresh, and rich. Then he placed it gently back in her hands.

“I’m not entirely sure, but that may be the Spiritual Stone of Courage. Also known as the Kokiri’s Emerald.” He said so matter-of-factly, straight-faced. This was a known phenomenon?

“What does this mean?” She tried not to let the panic rise in her tone, but her head was spinning.

He took a minute, looked at the goddess statue, then back to her face, and shook his head. “I don’t know.”

He said it calmly but his expression was telling. He was worried. 

She stared at the goddess statue, half expecting her to answer for him. But she remained unmoved. Smiling at her. Taunting her.

Here, take it. I have no use for it anymore.

How? How could this appear to her? Her, out of all people? Impa said royalty is only allowed in the sacred springs. Royalty can only speak to goddesses. She wasn’t royalty. She was no one. She was a mistake. Not because of some divine intervention.

“Link.” She was shaking her head, her chest heaving. She sucked in a breath, and pain greeted her in her ribs. “I— I— can’t. I can’t do this.” She lifted the stone up in emphasis. “This is a mistake. I shouldn’t have come here. They made a mistake.”

Water filled her eyes. She had completely given way to the spiraling feeling growing in her center. All the times she told herself this was a fluke, she didn’t want this type of responsibility. She resolved to live here content with a rudimentary life. She was not some divine being or part of some spiritual destiny. She couldn’t— wouldn’t be.

Before she let the tears fall, he pulled her swiftly into his chest, into a firm embrace. Her hands went under his arms, and she held him tight. Her wet dress pressed against his hard body. The air was warm, but he was warmer. She let out a timid breath against his shoulder. Opening her eyes to see in her blurry vision the emerald in her hand behind his back.

They stayed like that until her breathing regulated. He pulled away from her just far enough and reached his hand to her neck, tilting her face towards his with his thumb. The touch shot crashing waves coursing through her body, and their faces were mere inches apart. Had she not felt so unhinged, she might have risen on tipped toes to press her lips to his.

“Let’s go.” He said, gazing at her longingly, eyes hazy. 

“Where?” She managed to croak.

“A surprise.” His hand left her neck to her disappointment but grabbed her hand and held it as he led the way out of the dragon’s maw.

They walked for hours. Unspeaking.

Link grabbed her, the stone, and their pack and led her out quickly from the altar. The further she got from the goddess statue, the better she felt.

He mazed through the thick jungle, seemingly following the river as they went. She hadn’t asked where they were going, but deeper into Faron Woods was a good guess.

They emerged on a clear path hours later and continued onwards. She heard water crashing in the distance, then saw a stable tucked beneath a canopy of lush trees.

Link went to speak with the stable owner as she stood a distance away. A passerby shot her a puzzled look, and she realized she was still in the prayer dress, now mostly dry except for the layers of sweat glistening on her skin.

Link walked back after his conversation. “We’ll stay the night here if you want to get changed while I cook for us. After, we’ll go on a— small excursion.” He laid his hand on her arm and gently squeezed it as he trailed. 

She could melt from him. His touch, his care, his thoughtfulness. He truly was a good, earnest knight. A rare breed. A good man.

She gave him a forced smile, the best she could muster, and marched into the stable to change.

As her dress loudly slapped against the wooden floorboard of the stable, stripping off the prayer dress made her feel loads better. She’d never been so happy to wear her travel clothes. The binding lace of the corset felt freeing in contrast.

The stone was in Link’s possession, and she was starting to feel like herself again. She tried to smooth her now frizzy hair as best she could but opted for a messy ponytail. Perhaps his surprise was a bath for her to enjoy.

She meandered out of the stable to where he sat by the cooking pot, dishes in both hands. As she sat, he extended one out to her, and the smell of spicy paella nearly had her crying.

They ate in relative silence, besides her happy grunts of approval at the flavors dancing on her tongue. She wondered about her last few bites how he managed to get his hands on the ingredients needed to make this dish so delectable. But before she could ask, he stood and extended his hand for her empty dish.

“If you’re ready, we need to go. I’ll clean this up later.”

She handed over her bowl, and he set both down on a table nearby. She raised an eyebrow at him. “Where are we going?”

He smirked, his blue eyes shining, and he was so handsome when he did. “It’s a surprise. Unless you don’t want to find out.” His voice playful, daring as he walked away from her towards a bridge.

After realizing he was leaving her behind, she quickly caught up with him. Crossing a vast wooden bridge, a breathtaking landscape of red rocks and cascading waterfalls on either side unfolded before her eyes, leaving her in a state of silent awe. This was a delightful surprise.

Except he kept walking. All the way to the other side of the bridge.

The roar of the water crashing kept her senses loaded; it delayed her reaction to notice the colorful tropical plants that she had in her old apartment. The same types of purple and pink against the fresh green. Before she could think about digging in the ground and taking one with her, Link kept a fast pace heading towards the waterfalls against the rich red rock face.

There was a small carved stairway built into the rocks, leading upwards. They climbed and climbed until they reached the top, plateauing on a grassy foothill. They were so close to the waterfalls that she could feel the droplets and mist on her face, but he continued forward, finding another carved staircase and climbing up, up, up.

By the exhausting last step, she wondered if this surprise was truly worth the burning in her muscles. Would her legs give out before they could make it? She was so used to horseback riding and hadn’t walked this much in ages.

Before she could protest, they were at the top of the cascading waterfalls, so very high they practically touched the sky. If she hadn’t been trying to catch her breath, the view would have taken it away.

Link had stopped nearby, finding a spot in the middle of the flat landscape and sitting down. He was barely winded. He nudged his head for her to join him. She would have hated him for this had he not looked effortlessly perfect. His red tunic, his thick hair pulled back, water and sweat mixing on his face. He was the perfect balance of rugged and beautiful.

As she walked over to him, she turned towards the view of the sunset in the distance against the tall canyon. It was a challenge to tear her eyes from it. The word, epic, came to mind as she looked over the precipice of the falls.

She sat cross-legged next to him, tightly wound, in contrast to his casual appearance; legs stretched outwards and arms behind him, pushing himself straight as his sword hung from his back. He looked completely relaxed and satisfied, staring at the pool of water in front of him.

“Did you just make me climb all the way up here for my health, or is this the surprise?” She couldn’t hide the displeasure in her tone, trying to steady her breathing.

He grunted, eyes still on the water in front of him, “The surprise. We should have made it in time. Just need to give it a few minutes.”

She narrowed at him, trying to scan his face for clues, anything to hint at why he had brought her here. After an impatient minute, he relented.

“Legends say he only appears to those who are worthy and pure of heart. Others say he only appears when you need courage the most.” Link tilted his face up. The sky in answer had become darker, storm clouds swirling above them. 

Zelda looked to Link, his face unbothered by the impending storm that seemed to brew in front of them. 

She started to nervously fidget, wondering if at any moment they’d be soaking wet from the inevitable rain. Until…

A large, glowing yellow horn poked through the water’s surface, followed by a large scaled face and even larger body. The creature was shooting straight up into the sky, lightning pulsing all around its body and head.

She flung herself back, scrambling to a crouching position, readying herself to bolt, but Link stopped her with a gentle grasp on her arm. She could barely manage to choke out, “What is that?”

“That’s Farosh, he’s the Great Lightning Spirit Dragon, protector of this region.”

“A— A dragon?” She would have screamed in disbelief if she hadn’t been so stunned by the sight.

He faced her, “I’m guessing you don’t have dragons where you come from?”

She scoffed. “Only in stories or myths.” Her face was fully angled towards the sky, watching Farosh’s massive, crystalized body start to twirl on itself.

A dragon. Months ago, she would have believed herself in the asylum. Now— 

“He decided to bless us tonight.” Link took her hand in his, and she tore her gaze from the unbelievable sight of Farosh to his alluring face. But he was staring at their hands clasped together until he lifted his gaze to set on her, his deep blue eyes full of desire. She whimpered at the look. “Because, Zelda, you are worthy and you are courageous. Farosh does not appear to everyone. I’ve stood on this mountain with others who have not seen him while I did.”

Tears welled in her eyes at his words as her nose flared. She was worthy. She was good. She was courageous. He knew it before she saw Farosh; he knew without a doubt that dragon would appear to her. He saw her for who she was, beyond the pain of her past, beyond whoever she is now. He brought her here to remind her of that. No matter what lies ahead. Having a stone and whatever that means for her and her future, she would be brave and courageous in facing it.

She returned the look. Deeply burning for him, gazing longingly into his eyes. Their faces both barely lit by the flashes of Farosh’s lightning against the dark sky, but she could see his eyes land on her mouth. He moved his hand to her face and brushed away a piece of rogue hair that fell from her ponytail, delicately tucking it behind her ear. Then his hand stayed, but drifted to her neck, the same perfect spot he’d been before, his calloused fingers lightly twirling on her nape.

Every sense in her buzzed at the mere touch of his fingers on her bare skin. Her heart plummeted to her core, her eyes hazy and full of fire stared back at him, silently encouraging him to make the move.

She wanted this man. This good, perfect, handsome man. Parts of her always wanted him, even when they weren’t speaking. But she held herself back, unsure of the line between duty-bound knight and potential lover.

Now it was clear: he wanted her as much as she wanted him.

He parted his lips slightly and pulled her face towards his, gently. She closed her eyes and licked her own lips, awaiting the feeling of his hot kiss. The real thing, better than anything she had imagined.

A sizzle.

Then another.

Then a crack sounded next to them. She opened her eyes to see Link an inch away, pulling back from her. The sudden emptiness at the lack of friction quickly faded to panic. His sword was still strapped on his back, and it was charging with electricity.

Farosh had seen to it to ruin their moment as he descended down the waterfall, bringing his pulses of energy next to them. Anything metal within his radius would have sparked, including Link’s sword. He stood quickly, unsheathing it and throwing it a distance away from them. Immediately after it landed, a loud thunderbolt struck it down. If he hadn’t acted a moment quicker, they might not be standing here.

Before she could beg him to come back to her. To that moment. The rain came, down-pouring on the both of them with such force that they were drenched within seconds.

Zelda laughed, a belly laugh from her seat on the ground. Link must have thought her insane.

She had wanted him so badly that they almost died over it. Link grabbed her hand and lifted her from her seat quickly, and went to collect his sword. They hid in a small rock overhang, away from thunder and rain, temporarily, while Farosh continued his path.

Zelda continued to laugh, “Great timing.” She said to him.

Link didn’t look as amused as she did. His gaze was feral.

Despite it all, Link had effectively saved her from breaking. He showed her what he saw in her and reassured her of what she already knew—about herself and her feelings for Link. Their moment was coming soon enough.

Chapter 25: Swim
Chapter Text
He never thought he’d be so sour with a spiritual deity.

The humid air was visible. His tunic clung to his skin in the sweltering heat, and he was already in a foul mood as he settled into the hard, old wagon.

They started their long trek back to Deya Village to obtain their horses and rest for the night before returning to the castle. He hadn’t thought the long walk through when he rushed Zelda out of the spring yesterday, but luckily a passing merchant with a wagon took pity on them and gave them a ride shortly into their trip.

He was rolling over the events from last night as he sat on the back of the creaking old wagon. It was all he could do to resist the urge to reach out to Zelda now, in broad daylight, as she sat opposite of him.

Instead he reached for her in his memory. Her silky neck, her pulse wild under his fingers as his thumb rubbed over her soft cheek. She was staring into his eyes so intensely it made his breath catch. Her eyes— so bright against Farosh’s dark sky, so close he could see the gold flecks near her pupils. He’d drawn her closer, soft but sure. She licked her lips and closed her eyes. Permission.

Had he only been a second faster?

It was his own fault; he took her to see a dragon that pulsed with electricity; he should have opted for a different weapon.

But the second he saw the emerald in her hand and the terror on her face, he knew he had to get her out of there quickly, before she spiraled.

He had shamefully hoped praying in the spring wouldn’t send her home. The last thing he expected was for her to end up with an apparent Spiritual Stone. But he didn’t care who she was or could be. None of that mattered to him.

By morning, Zelda had seemingly forgotten all about the spring and the stone that weighed heavily in his pack. Her smiling face and bright eyes caught his every chance he looked. This ride couldn’t be over soon enough. 

By mid-afternoon, they crossed the bridge of Hylia and turned north to be dropped off at Deya Village’s entrance. Seeing the harsh stone buildings in contrast to the lush jungle brought him swiftly back into reality, dreading and longing for their return to the castle in equal measure.

Impa would be delighted about the fruitfulness of their trip. She knew something that she was playing close to her chest, and Link would demand she tell him upon their return. He would not bring Zelda to another spring or planned location if Impa continued to withhold information that could potentially put a target on her back. Damn his career or the consequences.

But he didn’t want to be dramatic, so he hoped it wouldn’t come to that.

They arrived as the sun was hovering above the horizon, greeted by the sounds of the cicadas and smells of minerals and musk. They thanked the merchant and hopped off the cart.

Link noticed immediately there was a heavier presence of soldiers posted, and the pad was completely full of horses. He scanned the walkways as village residents quickly shuffled by and promptly headed to their destinations. Heads down, feet quick.

Something was off. His eyes shifted and darted around them, and his hand itched towards the pommel of his sword. Zelda noticed.

“What’s the matter?”

He clicked his tongue. “I don’t know. There’s an unusual amount of military presence here.”

Zelda tensed and straightened. She too remembered where they were and where they had just come from. Let alone the fact that if anyone discovered a so-called sacred gem in their possession large enough to purchase an entire village. Or perhaps even the castle itself.

“I’m sure it’s nothing.” He said to her reassuringly, making the lie sit in his shoulders uncomfortably. “I’ll go talk to the innkeeper about rooms for tonight if you want to wait a moment.” He instinctively reached his hand out to cup her arm.

She leaned into his touch and visibly relaxed. The air seemed to shift around them. Her breath hitched, his hand warmed against hers. The arousal between them was a living flame. Each breath, each touch; feeding it, growing it.

He couldn’t help it. Every time he was this close to her, smelling her scent in her golden hair, her eyes so green they put Faron’s lush jungle to shame.

What if it grew, enveloping everything in its path until they acted upon it?

He was cut off by the sound of his own name getting yelled from the distance.

“Sir Link!”

He whirled around to his surprise to see Fledge, waving wildly and walking over to them. He dropped his hand as if he burned it.

Zelda stiffened again as she glanced between him and Fledge. He trusted Fledge with his life, he kept Zelda a secret when she first arrived. But this was bigger than that. It was best to keep the stone between themselves for now. So he had to come up with an excuse fairly quickly as Fledge closed the space between them.

“Sir Link, Zelda, what are you doing here?” Fledge asked in his soft, melodic voice. He was so happy to see them.

“We were just coming back from Lurelin Village. Impa sent us there to speak with the elder.” Link said smoothly. Another lie ripping from his lips, corroding his soul.

Lurelin was far enough that it would be highly unlikely for anyone to press or question that story further. As Fledge nodded, accepting this lie, Link pivoted. “More importantly, what are you doing here?”

Fledge huffed a chuckle, “Well, seeing as you don’t need a squire anymore, I’m finally training to become a knight. The elder here said there’s a monster horde lingering close to the village. It’s starting to cause issues for the merchants trying to get supplies in. He requested that the castle send a party out to track and clear them. After asking enough times, Auru finally assigned me.”

That explains the increased military presence. Link’s shoulders eased, oddly grateful it was only monsters putting everyone on edge. “Who else is here?” He had to assess who else he’d have to repeat his Lurelin story to.

“About ten of us, some of the older knights: Cawlin, Pipit, Grante, and Purlo…” Fledge trailed off.

Link scowled. He had never explicitly said to Fledge he hated Purlo, but Fledge was sharper than he looked to pick up on his distaste for the knight.

Zelda sensed his displeasure and threaded her arm through his forearm. “Fledge, we’ve had a long journey. Do you mind if we catch up with you at dinner? I would love to relax and change, and I’m sure Link would as well.”

“Oh, sure, we’ll be in the tavern later if you two would like to join us. I’ll hopefully see you then.” Fledge said excitedly before heading back.

Zelda’s hand lingered on his forearm. A brand against his bracer. He turned to her and gave her a weak smile. “Don’t worry about Purlo,” she said, smirking. “I don’t think people like him as much as he thinks they do, at least a certain person.” Her eyes looked at him under long lashes, positively telling.

He never asked her outright about how she felt about him, but hearing that veiled answer made him feel instantly better. He relaxed his jaw. “Good to know,” he said interestingly. “Let’s go check in.” 

After the sun had set, he knocked on Zelda’s door for dinner. He’d forgone his usual guards and belts, wearing only the sword across his back with his red tunic. Full gear seemed like overkill with the large military presence in the village; this was as safe as the castle at the moment. 

The door opened, and he tried to swallow the sudden lump that formed in his throat.

She wore the same green skirt and grey corset she wore when they stayed at the Outpost so long ago. The corset was enhancing her curves in all the right places, and the green of her skirt brightened her eyes even more than he thought possible. Her hair was styled so casually, tied up and out of her face beside a few stray pieces that accentuated her high cheekbones and sharp jaw. She somehow always managed to look stunning even in the plainest of clothing.

“You look beautiful,” he blurted out, a flush spreading across his cheeks.

Screw the game they played for months. He would lay his soul bare before her if she only asked.

She returned with a pink blush of her own and a crooked smile, “Thank you. You look handsome. As always.”

And perhaps the most significant aspect was their discreetness. Ilya had even mentioned something similar about low-ranking women, as long as it was done in private, everyone looked the other way.

She wasn’t royalty, as Impa had mentioned, so she essentially received a free pass to do whatever she pleased. However, she wasn’t about to clarify with Impa what she was allowed to do with her knight.

Either way, that wasn’t what bothered her.

“Love casts long shadows.”

Love felt like an exaggeration; lust was a more accurate description of what they both felt. Zelda admitted to herself that she liked him, but love?

Link stopped mid-groping to fight monsters. He had made a vow to her to protect her, and he would always prioritize duty. That’s just who he was.

At least, that’s what she told herself.

She exited the garden and embarked on a short uphill walk back to her apartment. Despite the distance, thoughts of love, duty, and the upcoming ball continued to swirl in her mind.

The ball. Link hadn’t mentioned it to her. He hated royal gatherings, but he was always duty-bound to attend. Did he not want to bring her?

He would bring Ilya or Mipha on past occasions. Maybe he couldn’t bring her. As far as everyone knew, she was still Ilya’s cousin, a delegate. She could attend—

She walked straight into a wall of muscle.

“I’m so sorry, Sir—” her eyes went wide as she stared up at the familiar face. “Link?!”

He gripped her shoulders to steady her as she backed away enough to fully get a good look at him. His hands were heated weights on her it was hard to focus. He greeted her with a warm smile, his bright blue eyes gazing at her languidly. Red tunic, full guards, and his sword hanging on his back. He was dirty, mud and blood smeared across his body. “Distracted?” He playfully quipped.

Despite the dirt and grime, he looked good.

He had been all-consuming in her dreams and thoughts for days, and now he was standing in front of her. She ignored the quip and scanned him for injuries. “When did you get back?”

“Just now, actually. I was looking for you. You weren’t in your apartment, so I figured I would try the dining hall first.”

“Hmm, perhaps that would be the place to go if you were looking for yourself.”

He smirked, sinfully. An expression she’d never seen before. “True. I am known for my eating habits.”

Oh. My. Gods. Goddesses. Whatever. She was going to burn right here in the garden. Taking every flower with her.

She couldn’t articulate what she wanted to say— standing so close to him… fully clothed. She tried not to imagine the length of him grazing her thighs just days ago. She needed to make sure he was okay. “Are you hurt?”

He looked down at the obvious blood stains and shook his head. “Not my blood. There were more monsters than we anticipated, that’s why I’m back so late. But they’re dealt with, with no casualties on our end.”

She let out a sigh of relief. “Good.”

“Have you been worried about me?” He teased. “Do I consume all your thoughts? Is that why you almost knocked me over?”

Yes. He did.

She scoffed. “Of course not!” As she playfully swatted his insanely hard chest at the truth he revealed. He let a chuckle escape.

“Well, you were all I thought about.” He said, voice dropping lower, his eyes blazing on hers. He lifted his hand to tuck a loose piece of hair behind her ear. The brush of his fingers at the tip had melted her.

How could someone do these things to her? It was too public to kiss him, as much as she wanted to jump into his arms. To hell with the blood and mud. To hell with being discreet.

His smile slightly faded as they both seemed to realize they were unfortunately in public. “Where were you just now?” 

“Impa summoned me.” His smile gone now as Zelda hesitated. “I told her everything. Everything relating to the stone.”

Link was quiet. He scanned around them. “She summoned me as well. Perhaps we can speak later about it when it’s just the two of us.” Zelda nodded in agreement.

“Anyway,” Link continued. “I was looking for you for a few reasons. The main one being about the Spring Ball.”

Her heart fluttered. “What about it?” 

He smiled. “I suppose someone had told you about it.” He seemed so much calmer than her as he continued, “I was wondering if you’d do me the honor of being my date?”

She was a puddle. It was hard to hide as she tried to contain her wide smile. “I’d be honored to attend with such a prestigious and honorable knight such as yourself.” Her playful spin on pomp and circumstance that she knew he adored.

He returned her acceptance by quickly grabbing her hand and planting a kiss on it. It was completely corny, but she was swooning over the gesture. His hand lingered in hers after it dropped. Long enough had anyone been watching that they would have noticed how she wished for that hand to be elsewhere.

She changed the subject awkwardly. “What does one wear to a ball?” She had no formal clothes except the engagement party dress she arrived in, and that did not seem appropriate.

“There’s a seamstress in Castle Town. She’s actually expecting you. I told her you would be stopping by.”

Zelda’s brows went up. “That’s certainly presumptuous of you. I just said yes.”

His jaw ticked. He leaned down to her ear and whispered, “Well, I did hope that swimming naked with me guaranteed an acceptance.” He pulled back, only inches from her face to meet her eyes. “And, I can’t imagine asking anyone else, especially no one more beautiful than you.”

With two sentences, he successfully drenched her. She managed to let out the breath she’d been holding. “Honorable knight indeed.”

He straightened. “Her name is Greta. She’s expecting you this afternoon. Her shop is in the middle of the town square. You know your way there.”

“You’re not coming with me?”

“I could, but, I’d rather be blown away on the day of the ball than seeing you in your dress beforehand. Plus, I should probably bathe this blood and guts off me. I haven’t had a proper bath since the pond.”

He was being uncharacteristically cheeky. He certainly had the upper hand.

To try to win back some semblance of respect, “That’s true. I wouldn’t want you to blow it before the big day.”

He scoffed. “Me? Blow it? I would never, unless someone gave me a reason to.”

Zelda floated down from the castle to the town square, high on their exchange. If anyone spoke to her, she didn’t notice. 

She stopped in front of a bright orange sign that read “Castle Town Seamstress”. A bell chimed as she entered, and she was greeted with  colorful, vibrant hues of purple and pink decorating the interior walls. Cascades of fabrics draped from ceiling and floor on either side of the small entrance.

An older woman, who looked to be in her late forties, appeared from the back of the shop. Her hair was like stained walnut with small streaks of grey lined into a messy bun. She had on glasses that looked to be too large for her small face, and she was wearing a long blue dress with an apron stuck with pins on either side.

The woman stopped in the hallway and locked eyes with her. “Zelda?” She said, surprised.

Zelda closed the door. “Yes.”

The woman crossed her arms and lifted her hand to grasp her chin. “My, my, Link certainly wasn’t exaggerating. You are quite stunning.”

Zelda opened her mouth to disagree, to reject the compliment, but instead quietly replied, “Thank you.”

“I’m Greta. Now, come, dear, we have much to do in a short amount of time.” Her voice commanding, no nonsense, as her hand that was resting on her chin now beckoned her down the hallway.

Zelda obeyed, following the woman into a large room with countless mirrors in a semicircle. On either side were dresses in every color, length, and style. Crystals and stones glittered against the sun’s rays from the small window. Greta immediately ushered Zelda to the center of the room, snagging her attention away from the captivating dresses.

Greta caught her gaze. “No, not those, those dresses aren’t suitable for you. Hold still.”

Zelda’s mouth fell open, and she couldn’t help but be hurt by the comment as Greta disappeared into another area behind endless curtains. Those dresses were some of the most exquisite pieces of fabric she had ever seen. What could compare? Were they only held for nobles and royalty? In which she wasn—

Greta returned, an emerald gown in hand.

Then she realized how wrong she had been. 

Zelda couldn’t stop the gasp escaping as her eyes scanned the dress from top to bottom. Held on a wooden hanger with straps so thin they were almost nonexistent. The bodice was sculpted to honor and flatter the female form, with scattered crystal embroidery and illusion mesh to fit and shape. From the waist, glittered beads and crystals burst and scattered down past the hips and thigh, framing a sensually cut slit. The overskirt was layers of tulle that fell in ethereal waves, drifting out. The entire dress looked to be spun from Hyrule’s own landscape, radiating otherworldly grace.

It was— everything. And then she thought of how unworthy she was to be wearing something so finely crafted, so regal, so perfect.

But all she could manage to say, “Is it appropriate to have a leg slit for formal occasions?”

Greta rolled her eyes, “Only on the right person. The Princess could not get away with something so provocative but you certainly can. Try it on so I can make adjustments. We only have two days before the ball.”

The ball was in two days? Of course he waited until the last minute.

The dress fit shockingly well. The straps were a bit loose and the length was a tad long but she emerged for Greta to take final considerations.

Greta’s brows went up, “Wow. He has good taste.” It was the longest she took to pause before pointing at her to step onto the pedestal.

Her waist was snatched and her breasts hadn’t been that lifted in ages. The straps lightly dusting over the curve of her collarbone. The skirt’s delicate layers were a living thing, dancing around her legs. The gems catching in the sun and sparkled in her reflection. They were somehow magically sewn into the fabric, as if they were floating, tied on with invisible thread.

This dress… it would ruin her relationship with every piece of fabric that touched her forevermore.

“I’m very good at my job dear.”

“Huh?” Greta snapped her out of her trance as Zelda looked down at her pining the bottom with expert speed and efficiency.

“It’s one of my best dresses. Perhaps thee best. But I am the best seamstress in all of Hyrule.” She said with no hint of humbleness in her tone.

Then her head caught up, “You said Link has good taste? Did he pick out this dress?”

Greta had a pin between her teeth. She promptly stuck it low before raising herself up to examine the straps. “In a way. If your concern is money, he already took care of it. He paid handsomely for the dress, my services today, training tomorrow, and for someone to style you the day of.”

Of course, he did. Not that Zelda had any money, but he had always been generous when it came to her. “Training?”

“Yes, you’ll need it.” Greta said with an air of snobbery. “He mentioned you’ve never attended a royal ball. Nobles train for years in courtly traditions. Not that one day will get you to that level of proficiency, but she’ll teach you the basic rules of etiquette and at least one waltz.”

Greta turned, already finished with the left strap, now facing Zelda to work on the right. Her glasses were low on her nose, her chocolate eyes drilling into hers. “You should ask him. As you probably already know Link well enough, he would have you choose whatever you wished, but this dress was special, and I insisted.” Greta turned and squeezed the strap to her skin as she said gently, “I was good friends with his mother. If that boy needs anything, I am happy to help him.”

“What was his mother like?”

Her eyes still on the strap. “Incredibly kind but fiercely protective. She was dazzling in a quiet way. And loyal. She loved deeply and was deeply loved.” Greta’s voice thinned softly, “I miss her.”

Zelda thought carefully about what she wanted to say next.

“Link takes after his mother then.”

“That he does.”

Zelda left about an hour later. Greta was pleased that the dress needed minimal hemming, considering how little time she had. She told Zelda to be back early tomorrow for the last fitting and then off to her assistant to squeeze years of lessons and etiquette into one night and day. Then the day of, the same assistant would dress, style her hair, and handle her makeup.

Link only spoke about his parents briefly. Like herself, they found a kinship in each other. Loss made the memories a delicate archive. Her scent, the clothes she wore, was her eye color the same blue as his own or more sky blue?

What would she have thought of his knighthood? This vow to her? Would she have liked her or disapproved of a foreigner for her only son?

She was rounding the corner near the dining hall as someone called her name. She recognized the deep, masculine voice.

“Yeah, we didn’t. I heard you were on the monster control party. How did that go?” She said politely, clipped.

“Great, it was easy for me to dispatch of those wretched monsters. Stupid beasts really.”

Zelda tried not to roll her eyes. Her patience had been tested each time she spoke with him. He always found her when she was alone, as if lurking, a snake in the grass. Sure, he was attractive, but all he talked about was himself and how amazing he was at any and every activity he could bring into a conversation. She realized after their second meeting that going on a date with him would feel like a punishment.

“I did hear that. I’m glad to hear there were no casualties.” Hopefully, curt answers would end this conversation quickly so she could find the knight she really wanted to see.

He smirked at her comment, “As I said, I’m glad I ran into you. I wanted to ask you something.”

Zelda’s throat dropped to her stomach. She knew instantly what he was going to ask.

He straightened his already tall frame even longer. He spoke with as much authority as he could, “Would you do me the honor of attending the Spring Ball with me?”

Somehow his ask sounded more like a demand than a genuine question. She tried to sound and look as sincere as possible as she replied, “I’m so sorry, Purlo, but I already have a date.”

He bristled, his features going dark, “Link?”

Zelda nodded.

He didn’t bother to hide his scowl. Somehow he had seemed to grow even taller in front of her and Zelda’s gut was telling her to go. “I’m sorry, I’m sure whoever you ask will be thrilled to attend with you.”

His scowl deepened as he spat, “I don’t need your pity.” Zelda couldn’t hide her eyes going wide and raised brows at the curt remark. “You enjoy yourself with that spineless knight of yours.” And before Zelda could reply, his back was already turned and stalking towards Castle Town.

She stood there completely stunned at the exchange. She had never seen someone’s demeanor change so drastically, and his words sounded like a threat as he glowered over her. Even if Link hadn’t asked her, she wouldn’t have gone with Purlo. She could barely tolerate the last few minutes talking to him, let alone a whole night of his incessant bragging and boasting.

Only one of those grounded her.

Then she heard her name yet again, this time from a sweet, melodic voice.

“Zelda! It’s been a while. What have you been up to?” Ilya asked sweetly as she pulled Zelda into a warm embrace. 

What hasn’t she been up to would be easier to list.

“You know, this and that. It’s quite boring, really. Just standard visits with villages and towns, trying to still understand how I got here.” Zelda tried to nonchalantly convey.

Zelda tensed. “Yeah, I heard about it today.”

“Are you going?”

“Yes…” Zelda trailed. Hoping Ilya would drop it.

Zelda reached for the right thing to say, “I think he just asked me because I’ve never attended a ball before. He wants me to see everything Hyrule has to offer.”

It was lame as excuses go.

Ilya shook her head, “No, Zelda, that’s not why. I do appreciate your excuse, but there’s no need. I love Link, more than he’s ever loved me in that way, but at the end of the day, I want him to have happiness in his life. And you make him happy.”

“Sure,” Ilya said, eyes hazy. “Tell Link I said hello. I’ll see you around.” And she walked away.

Guilt burned inside her as she watched Ilya’s bright aura dim. She looked back towards the stairs in front of her and she desperately wished she was a few moments earlier. She could have avoided Purlo and Ilya altogether.

Finally, she made it to her apartment. Her limbs heavy. She couldn’t face the dining hall.

She fell back onto her bed and before the events of the day could consume her, she drifted swiftly into a deep sleep.

Chapter Text
The anticipation of seeing Zelda was killing him. 

It was the morning of the ball, and he hadn’t seen her since he asked her to attend with him two days ago. They kept missing each other between her fittings and training. He only hoped for a quick glimpse of her on her balcony this morning during his own training.

He gripped his pommel, his calluses rubbing against the leather.

He’d been outside since dawn, and it was harder and harder to stay focused on his self-appointed drills. He reached for water, and the mere thought of the substance had a warm wave churning within him.

To the night he almost had her.

After he sent Zelda back to the castle with Fledge, he had barely been able to listen to the group strategize on the best approach of attack. Her scent clung to his tunic, lavender and something distinctively her. Every time the scent lifted, it filled him with a heady buzz. He closed his eyes so he could see her— straddling him— his hands trailing every surface of wet skin, her perfect body under his fingertips, pulling back from her swollen lips, tasting the soft cord of her neck. 

It was hard to think about anything else.

They took off for the hills where the scouts had said the monsters were. He kept catching Purlo staring at him, a deep scowl plastered on his face. As if he knew where Link’s hands had been, where his mouth was, just moments ago.

By the following evening, they had found the monsters. There were more than they anticipated, but they dealt with them cleanly, with no casualties. Afterwards, they regrouped at the village before dawn. While some stayed to rest, he and a few others gathered their belongings and horses and rode for the castle. He didn’t bother to bathe or change; he wanted to reach Zelda as swiftly as his horse would allow him. And, he had to make a stop first.

He had known Greta his whole life. She had a small shop in Hateno when he was a child. She dressed the whole town, and even some nobles traveled from Castle Town for her one-of-a-kind gowns. She was friendly with his mother, and whenever his father had to attend royal events, Greta would dress her. Greta’s gowns made his mother look more regal than the queen. But, after his mother passed, Greta moved her shop to Castle Town and promptly became the go-to for formal fashion for nobles and the rest alike. Coincidentally or not.

He arrived at her shop early, and Greta greeted him with a smile, then swiftly reprimanded him on why he hadn’t seen her in so long. After his heartfelt apologies, he handed her a fat pouch of rupees and instructed her to let Zelda pick out whatever she wanted. As he turned to leave, she stopped him. Questions about Zelda’s hair color, eye color, and skin tone. He answered as neutrally as he could, leveling against Greta’s pointed stare. She paused, disappeared, and returned within a beat with a glittering emerald dress.

He tried not to gape, imagining her in that dress. 

She specifically had it set aside years ago; and that his own mother had commissioned her to design it. It never felt right to sell it, so Greta kept it.

It was fated. Threaded into existence long ago.

But he told her not to force it. Whatever Zelda wanted, he’d be happy to get for her, even if this dress was practically sewn by the Goddess for her. Walking back towards their apartments, that scent fluttered into his nostrils, and the thoughts of seeing her consumed him. He twisted his neck, alighting every nerve within him.

He had never felt this way about anyone before, and he couldn’t fully articulate what it was. He desired her, definitely, but it wasn’t solely that. He missed talking to her. His fellow knights were fine company, but with her— their laughter, the banter. He was more open, more confidently himself. 

When he finally saw her, the pathway slowed beneath his feet, an arrow tipped into his heart. She was distracted, her head down, in her own realm of thoughts as he let her collide into him, and when she finally locked eyes with him, all air left his lungs. How he managed to banter with her, let alone ask her to the ball, he didn’t know. Perhaps Farosh’s courage still lingered in him.

And now, the day of the ball, he hadn’t seen her since.

He wiped the sweat from his brow. It was still early yet; he had time before he had to pick up his dress clothes, and he wasn’t getting any productive training done, so he sheathed his sword and grabbed his shirt, but not without one last glance at her balcony.

He stared at his perfectly pressed attire for the evening. A pine green pleated tunic, black trousers, white leather boots, and gloves. He sighed, looking at the matching beret, fairly undecided about that choice of accessory.

The outfit, modeled after the royal guards’ gear, was new. However, he had chosen green to match the spring theme of lush growth, hoping it would complement Zelda’s dress.

He detested this type of clothing; he preferred his armored tunic, but this one offered greater mobility. Good for dancing, in which he didn’t particularly enjoy either, but this time would be different. He was going with someone he… liked.

But he still planned to keep a dagger in his belt. A ball didn’t negate duty.

He changed into his clean, Hylian tunic and pulled his hair back into his signature ponytail, still wet from his bath. As he slid on his boots, he noticed a piece of parchment on his desk that wasn’t there before he left to train this morning.

He opened the folded note to reveal elegant cursive handwriting:

Link,

I saw you training this morning but did not want to distract you. I am off to Greta’s for a final fitting, and then I’ll be back to prepare for tonight. I don’t want to ruin the suspense, so I will meet you at the bottom of our apartment hallway steps just before sunset.

Yours, 

Zelda

P.S.  I cannot wait to see you.

Impa continued, “I fear it is no coincidence that she is here. Confirmed with the first stone, but we cannot unwind the clock; she needs to obtain the other two stones. They may be the only explanation of what’s to come.”

He nodded to Impa. Ignoring that new, cold stab in his spine.

“Next is the Spring of Power. You should leave after the ball.”

As much as he tried to stay relaxed. He straightened in the chair at the mention of the night to come. He quickly scanned Impa’s face for any trace of knowing, but she was as still as stone.

“We will. Are we finished?”

“Love and duty.”

A dam broke in his veins as his blood warmed him. Every sense screamed at him to retort, deny it.

But he hadn’t bothered to reply.

He would always do his duty, to her.

The sun was starting to lower in the horizon.

He glanced ahead in his mirror, noticing the misbuttoned, pleated tunic and the crooked fabric. He rolled his shoulders back, shaking away the tension that had built up. As he unbuttoned each button on his dress uniform to try again, Impa’s warning rattled around his head.

‘Love and duty.’

He shook it away.

He finished the last button, then adjusted the collar that structured his neck. He tucked his dagger into his belt on his side, carefully concealing the short blade in its sheath but placed within reach if needed.

He scowled as he stood in front of his mirror and placed the beret on his head. What a ridiculous piece of clothing for a knight, what was the point of a hat that didn’t even sit straight?

He slid on his pristine white gloves and smoothed his hair back and gave himself one last look. He shrugged.
