He nodded.

“You are one lucky man.” She said with a smirk. “I barely needed to style your date. She’s a perfect canvas, and that dress.” She blew out a breath. “You have exquisite taste, but looking at you, it makes sense.” She said in an air of confidence as she hit the last step with a wink. Heat rose to his cheeks.

The stylist, Greta, sent to help Zelda dress. His heart beat wildly at the mere mention of her.

“I’m Sasha, the stylist.” She said with a swing of her short-chopped bob. “You both may be the most handsome couple in all of Hyrule tonight. She’ll be down in a moment.”

“Thank you.” He choked out, willing his heart to slow.

She tilted her head in acknowledgment. “You paid well enough, but truly she needed little. Enjoy yourselves.” She said as she slipped out of the building.

He braced himself, looking to the top of the steps, his fingers clenching so hard the leather of his gloves squeaked.

And then a door closed.

He held his breath.

Nothing prepared him for the sight that appeared before him.

He gazed at her, and time held. There were no words, none worthy enough of her magnificence.

He raked his eyes over her from head to toe. The floor-length emerald-green gown he saw days ago looked drastically different on her. It warmed to her skin. Her bare shoulders were squared under the thin straps. Her curves exquisitely shaped as crystals and beads sparkled down from the lift of her breasts to her feet. The dress simultaneously flowed yet hugged her. She was the goddess, and this dress was the forest canopy of lush tree leaves, all bowing to her greatness, giving her life.

Every thought, every sense, failed. It wasn’t possible for someone, anyone, to look this good.

She descended the staircase, her smooth bare leg flashed through the front slit, revealing the soft skin he had gripped greedily days ago. White jeweled heels caught his eye, making her a few inches taller, now eye level to him.

Her normally loose blonde hair was pinned up, with soft strands framing her face. The noticeably large teardrop emeralds in gold hung from her ears, the only pieces of jewelry she wore. And thick braids wrapped from each ear pulled to a low bun, shining in the candlelight.

He wanted to claim that skin on her bare neck.

She reached the bottom, and he took in her face.

It was as if her face was the sun. But he wasn’t blinded by her; only he had been granted a glimpse. Just this once.

The assistant was right; she didn’t need heavy makeup; only little color dusted her cheeks and painted her lips. With a wash of gold to her eyelids, enhancing her already sharp features, making her eyes sparkle an impossible shade of green. As if her eyes had been gifted from the Spiritual Stone of Courage itself. All she needed was a crown.

She stared at him over long lashes. Her lips moved. “Link?”

He hadn’t been listening. He had been busy imagining his hand under that silk.

He could skip the ball, scoop her up in his arms, carry her back upstairs to their apartments, and rip the dress off her—

“Link?” She said more sharply.

“Huh?” He blinked back at her, lost in those eyes.

“Do I look okay?” She asked with a sheepish smile.

He pulled on his glove, the leather tight as it slipped from each finger. He reached for her neck and drew her to him. He greedily devoured her mouth with his own. She smiled into it and met his motion, opening to him, letting his tongue find hers.

They moved together. His other hand found her lower back and pulled her closer. Clothed, unclothed, in water— he could never get enough. Goddess, he missed her.

After a long moment, she pulled back, hands on his waist and shoulder. They caught their breath. “I guess that’s a yes then.” She said breathlessly.

“You look—” he stuttered. “There are no words worthy.”

She blushed, the pink on her cheeks blending with the color already dusted there.

He must have looked unhinged as he matched her lustrous gaze. He was still holding her neck, as he leaned to the shell of her ear, “We can just stay here. We don’t have to go.” He whispered, trying not to sound desperate.

She chuckled, “Don’t tempt me, my honorable knight. We have all night, and haven’t you learned, good things come to those who wait?”

He hated that lesson right now. Truth was, he waited for twenty years for a night like this with a woman like her. As much as he didn’t want to wait a second longer, he knew this only sharpened the desire. He’d just have to somehow control his hands all evening. “I suppose…”

She shot him a wicked smirk, her tongue rolling over her white teeth, “I’ll happily make it up to you later. With pleasure.”

Goddess help him.

They left the privacy of their apartments and made their way to the sanctum, the highest point of all the castle grounds. The same room he had been knighted in, and where royal balls were hosted. The royals believed the higher they were to the sky, the closer to the goddess they were.

He offered his arm to her, in which she smiled as she threaded hers through and they walked through the large doors.

The room was massive, at least six stories high. It was always decorated differently, always immaculate. Tonight, the room was covered in candles and lanterns, setting the mood: bright enough to see the fine details but still dim enough for intimacy. A long buffet flanked the far wall. Only the best the royal chefs could cook, from roasted fowl to heavenly pastries and breads, along with infused spirits from every region.

Hundreds of guests were already mingling; Hylians, Rito, Gorons, Gerudo, and Zora. Their entrance went mostly unnoticed.

Zelda’s eyes were wide, gripping his arm tightly, her head tilted back to marvel at the gold and green tapestries hung up in honor of Farore’s Spring. Each one ran from ceiling to floor, stitched with a completely different story of Hyrule’s founding legends and conquests.

“What is that?” She asked, pointing to the tapestry displaying the story of the Hero of Twilight, both in his wolf and Hylian form, with ancient symbols decorating the border.

“That’s the story of the Hero of Twilight,” he said. “He was changed into a beast when Hyrule fell into twilight. He and Midna, the princess of Twilight, fought to bring light back into Hyrule and rescue the princess.” It was the take he favored most. Becoming a wolf at will had a certain appeal.

Her mouth was slightly agape as she analyzed every tapestry’s intricate story. He knew she would be asking him about them all throughout the night. He steered her towards the buffet. He needed a drink if he was going to survive the whole evening with her on his arm.

Near the table, the scents rose to his nostrils— rich spices, rare butters. He grabbed a flute of bubbling champagne and handed it to her. She took it with a raised brow, knowing she wanted him to do the same. He grabbed one for himself.

She tapped his glass with a delicate clink, “Cheers to us, for making it here.” She winked at him and took a small sip. He took a steadying breath and downed his.

He scanned the room. Twin staircases curved up to the center balcony where the royals would sit. Two chairs, one for the king and another for the princess, sat empty. Which was typical; royalty always arrived last and left first. Zelda and he had arrived late; so they should be arriving any moment.

He spotted Daruk, who fondly waved to him. He finished his conversation with other Gorons and lumbered over.

“Little guy! Tiny lady!” Daruk beamed with his megawatt smile. He spared Link’s back a bone-breaking slap and offered a crude bow to the both of them instead.

“Daruk, lovely to see you again.” Zelda chirped with a smile.

“You too, tiny lady. I’m not up to snuff on Hyrule’s fashions, but you look absolutely shining. Like freshly mined ore from Death Mountain.”

Zelda laughed at the odd compliment, which was high praise from someone like Daruk who barely wore clothes. Link watched her as she laughed, catching Daruk’s eye and his knowing smile. Daruk had seen the way Link looked at her months ago, before Link even had words for it.

“I see you two are getting along now. Maybe those healing Goron hot springs helped, huh?” Daruk’s booming laugh drew attention from those closest to them.

Zelda blushed a deep pink, Link’s eyes widened. Daruk meant it in earnest, but Link met Zelda’s gaze. They shared a knowing smirk. That misadventure felt like a lifetime ago. Maybe on the way back from Akkala, they could swing by the hot springs and—

Royal trumpets sounded. Calling to attention that the King and Princess had arrived.

He whispered to Zelda to bow when they passed. She nodded in acknowledgment.

The room went still as the King escorted Princess Zelda, arm in arm, through the parting crowd, Groose following a few paces behind. Both royals were clad in the royal blue and gold. The king in his doublet and crown and the princess in a floor-length gown and a tiara. 

All three of them bowed as they passed. 

It was strange to see Princess Zelda and— his Zelda, in the same room. Side by side, the resemblance was uncanny. The Princess was undoubtedly beautiful, so desirable in fact, tales of her beauty were sung and praised across all of Hyrule. But his Zelda… glowed, in a way he couldn’t name.

Both royals ascended the staircase and took their places. The room was silent, waiting on baited breath for the king to speak.

“Thank you all for attending tonight. We honor and welcome Farore’s Spring and usher in another successful growing season.” His booming voice rattled and echoed through the chamber. “My daughter and I wish you all good fortune. Now please, enjoy.” A command, as he waved to the musicians. A rousing jig began and the whole room resumed their conversations to the sounds of flutes and violins in the background.

Link fetched Zelda another glass of the bubbling spirit but decided not to partake himself. He wanted to stay sharp for more than one reason. Instead, he made friendly conversation with Daruk about the latest happenings near Death Mountain.

After the band finished their jig, they started up immediately with a striking melody of a song Link recognized as a popular waltz. Couples around them started to make their way to the center of the room. Zelda watched them in youthful wonderment.

“Well, that’s my cue to clear out. I don’t think this room can handle my dancing.” Daruk joked in his gravelly voice. “I’ll catch you both later.”

Link watched the large, gentle Goron exit to the far side of the room. He then did something completely uncharacteristic of himself. He extended his hand to Zelda and asked, “Will you honor me with a dance?”

Zelda returned the question with a nervous smile. “I might be bad. I’ve only had one day of lessons.”

“That’s alright. I’ll lead and you can follow. Just as we danced in the tavern.” He said as charmingly as he could. It was unlike him to want to dance, but he was itching to touch her.

“Then I’d love to.” She said as she set her glass down and took his hand in hers. Even though the wretched glove he wore, he immediately felt the spark of fire connecting them at their fingertips.

He led her to the floor amongst the other couples. As they faced each other, he nudged her to place her free hand on his shoulder as he grabbed her waist and free hand. The violin picked up on cue and he nodded for her to follow. He stepped forward, back, then to each side and repeated the steps, weaving through the other couples.

Her trepidation eased as they stepped in unison, and his grip on her waist tightened. She stopped glancing at her feet and instead trusted his lead, her eyes on him. She looked at home, as if she were meant for this, for him. Her bright smile flashed as he spun her outwards and back into his chest. Her heat back into his.

The song was nearing its peak, and he whispered in the shell of her ear, “Do you trust me?”

She nodded, her earrings swinging.

As the violin crested, he drew her closer, so close their lips were a hair’s width apart. It was risky to do in public, but he no longer cared. He placed one hand firmly on her lower back, the other still holding her hand as he dipped her slowly towards the floor, leaning with her. Her lips parted, and her breath caught as she arched herself; his lips grazed her neck; he could taste her scent on her skin. So close, he could see every pore, see every muscle work her swallow.

The song had ended, and other couples around them watched, silent and their eyes wide as he held her still.

There was no room for disconcert. He was the one who had been able to hold her while others merely watched.

He finally lifted her back upright, his eyes never leaving hers. His hand was still holding her back, and she was gripping his shoulder. Lust blazed in her eyes. “I hope you save some of that for later, Sir Link,” she whispered.

The title on her tongue set him alight. He opened his mouth to answer—

“You two certainly know how to make it all about you.” The nasally, sarcastic tone chimed in as both their heads whipped in the direction of it.

It was Revali. Unfortunately.

He was dressed in his typical aerial armor and scarf but in the theme of greens and golds. He stood, arms crossed, with his characteristic scowl.

“Revali.” He said by way of greeting, as civil as he could.

“Knight.” Revali curtly replied. He turned to Zelda and made a show of taking her in. Link’s jaw-ticking. “Zelda, you look absolutely… glittering.”

“Thank you, Revali. You look very regal yourself.” Zelda politely replied.

“Will you do me the honor of a dance?” He made a show of bowing before her and extending his winged hand to her.

Zelda glanced at Link and smiled, then turned back to Revali. “Of course, Revali. I’m sure my date can spare me for just a song or two.” And she grabbed his hand in hers.

Link kept his face neutral and did his best to be civil as he moved off the dance floor. He hung to the wall as he watched the preening Revali exaggerate his placement of his hands on Zelda, holding her waist just as he had mere minutes ago. He knew Zelda was being polite. It wouldn’t be surprising if some of his fellow knights had asked her to a dance. She was dazzling, especially watching her glittering green gown fan outwards as Revali spun her. She looked like a human sparkler.

“Link?” A soft voice at his shoulder. Someone had quietly joined him near the wall.

Not someone, but Mipha. He looked at her and gave her a bow. “Princess Mipha, it’s nice to see you again so soon.”

He usually did not greet his old friend so properly, but they were in public, and she was royalty. He scanned her from head to fin; she wore a sea foam blue dress made of pure silk. It blended perfectly with her skin tone, making her look like she was water itself. “You look absolutely magnificent, Mipha.”

She blushed a faint pink. “You also look very handsome tonight. I see your date is otherwise occupied.” She nodded towards Zelda, still spinning with Revali. “Would you like to dance with an old friend instead?” She asked gracefully.

Dancing with Mipha was better than seething in the corner. “I would be so honored.” He extended his own hand for her to grab and lead her to the dance floor to join the rest as a new song started.

They found a space between a Hylian noble couple and two Rito. Zelda and Revali were a few couples away, and Link angled himself so he could keep them in view. Probably unnecessary since Revali’s bark was worse than his bite.

He took Mipha in hand and waist as she gripped his own. Mipha was smaller than Zelda. Her arm was angled quite high in comparison as they started to spin.

He watched Revali and Zelda carry on in conversation. Revali’s face was smug, and Zelda’s head was tipped in interest at whatever Revali was saying. He wondered what could Revali be saying to her. The last Zelda saw him was in Rito Village, and he only tolerated her, treating her slightly better than how he treated him. Now he wanted her attention? 

His view shifted as the dance required it, and Mipha tracked his eyesight right to Revali and Zelda. “He’s just trying to get a rise out of you.” She said in her soft, melodic tone.

“You’re right.” He felt foolish. He resolved to catch up with his friend rather than let Revali get under his skin. His gaze shifted, and he gave her a smile. “Tell me something good, Mipha.”

She lifted her face upwards to drill into him. Scanning his face as sorrow blanketed her large amber eyes. “You love her.” She said, almost to herself.

He couldn’t hide his surprise. His gut twisted. “I swore to protect her.”

“It wasn’t a question.” Mipha’s mouth tightened. “I’ve known you your whole life. You are one of the better, if not the best, Hylians I’ve ever met. I— I— always hoped that you would find someone who deserved you. I just didn’t realize it would be a woman you were sworn to protect.”

He didn’t respond. There wasn’t anything to say. He instead held Mipha close, and they finished their dance in silence. All the while, Mipha’s words swirled in his head.

He loved her.

Was it love? He’s never loved anyone. Where was the line between swearing an oath and love? He had blurred those lines the moment they kissed in that pond, if not long before that. She dismissed him even, back in the desert, but he stayed. Was that duty or something else?

The song ended, and Mipha offered him a weak smile and a small hug. “I will always be your friend,” she said as she slipped away, blending into the crowd before he could articulate a response.

The band took a breather. Zelda, his Zelda, walked towards him, eyes shining, and his thoughts eddied from him.

“How is Princess Mipha?” She asked.

“She’s well—” his eyes slid to Revali, smirking at him from the opposite wall next to Rito guards. “How is Revali?” He tried not to sound bitter as he asked.

Zelda rolled her eyes. “He’s fine.” A curious look. “I think he is a bit obsessed with you.” She reached for a small crystal cup off a server’s tray as he passed by. She took a long swallow, thirsty from the back-to-back dances.

He kept his face neutral. “Is that so?”

“I can only imagine why.” Zelda said, smirking, glass at her lips.

The band returned to their positions on the small stage, indicating that they were about to start up again. Link had already had his limit of dancing for the evening. He was ready to whisk Zelda out quietly, damn royal protocol. Then, familiar sounds from the pianoforte’s gentle notes stilled both of their ears.

Zelda looked at him. He didn’t even have to ask as he extended his hand to hers.

Zelda’s Lullaby was not a waltz, but more of an intimate sway. Couples deeply in love or courting gathered closely around them. Zelda gripped his collar, her fingers curling in his nape, her breath tickling his ear. He held her lower back close to his front.

Link trailed Zelda’s gaze. She was looking up at the dais to glance at the princess. She paid no mind to them as she sat on her throne in perfect posture, watching her subjects below partake. No indication if she particularly even liked the song or not.

“She’s not allowed to dance unless the king approves her date or dance partners. Most are too afraid to ask, so she rarely dances at any ball.” Link told her, reading her mind.

“That’s— sad. Can’t even dance to the song dedicated to her.” She pulled her face back, meeting his stare. “Did I ever tell you about what this song means to me? More than my drunken tavern recognition?” She asked him.

“No, you didn’t.”

“When I was little, my mother played this song for me. I don’t remember the specifics, but she told me later in life that I wouldn’t sleep as a child. I would have nightmares, or would be so scared of the nightmares I wouldn’t want to fall asleep. One night, she brought this large, clunky electric piano into my bedroom. It took up the whole room; it was so large—” he felt the warmth from her smile as she vividly described it. “—and she started playing this song. I remember it like it was yesterday, the calm of the melody luring me to sleep. It was the first night I slept in ages. She continued to play for me every night for years. I couldn’t fall asleep unless I heard her play it. Even my father would try, but it wasn’t the same.”

She was quiet. He knew why. It was the same quiet he felt whenever he thought about his own parents. The kind that opens locked rooms.

“I never thought I would be happy again after they died. I’d been content, but never honestly happy, because a part of me died the day they died. Then I heard this song, in the tavern with you—” she pressed her fingers warmly into his nape. “—I realized then how lonely I was before and how alive I was to be here. I truly never thought I would feel that ting of happiness that I lost, especially after everything we’ve been through, but that night I knew.. Hyrule is.. special. And so are you, to me.”

Emeralds that were her eyes bore into him. He was a mess. He froze, had it not been for the gentle swaying to the soft piano rhythms that held her to him. He would have thought himself a statue. He couldn’t articulate what he wanted to say. He could only manage in a breathy whisper, “Zelda, I—” he stuttered on the words he tried to get past his lips.

She smiled, bringing the daylight into the room. “Me too,” she said.

Hours past that seemed like minutes. After they peeled apart, they spent the rest of the night drinking, eating, and dancing. Everyone was full of merriment, even his fellow knights loosened up and partook in the spirit, and spirits, of the evening. Except Purlo, Link kept catching his ugly glare from across the room. His eyes would rest on Zelda in a menacing sneer, then on Link, until he made eye contact.

Link wasn’t one to be smug, but knowing Zelda was here with him rather than someone undeserving felt good.

His latest view of the seething knight was blocked by a familiar tall, tanned woman. Urbosa. She was dressed as she normally was in light armor, showing her muscular frame with a long green skirt to match the occasion. Not the type to conform to feminine fashion in lieu of battle ready attire.

“Sav’saaba, Sir Link and Zelda.” She said in her typical swagger. “Enjoying your evening?”

“Urbosa, it’s great to see you again.” Zelda beamed. Urbosa was the one leader that Zelda got along with the best out of all their travels. And it seemed to be mutual as she hugged Zelda in return. “How are things?” 

Urbosa clicked her tongue, “Things are fine with us Gerudo.” She waved her hand off. “I’m more interested in your travels and how you’ve faired.” She gave both of them a curious look.

Link and Zelda looked at each other, Zelda’s smile slowly fading.

Before they could respond, Urbosa waved her hand again, “Your silence tells me enough.” Zelda nodded.

They were cut off by the king and princess standing from their chairs, the room quieted as quickly as a door slamming. They had become restless or bored or both, and that meant the night was nearly over.

“I must go see the princess out before they part. Let’s catch up before I leave. I’m staying in the castle for the next few days. We’ll talk then.” She winked at them both and glided away. It was no secret Urbosa loved the crown princess, but on nights like this, the dais was only reserved for Hylian royalty.

“I’m assuming that means our evening is almost over?” Zelda asked after Urbosa left. It was the first time in hours that it was just the two of them.

Link straightened himself, “It means the ball is over, but it’s up to you if you want the evening to end.” He said smoothly.

“Well, if I get a choice in the matter—” she paused and leaned in, her breath tickling the shell of his ear, “Preferably, I want our night to continue— just us. Either in your apartment or mine.”

His blood was roaring. She pulled back with a wicked look, and goosebumps littered her bare shoulders. He met her with unconfined lust, “Well, in that case, I’m obligated to do whatever my date desires.”

She let out an exasperated breath, “Be careful what you wish for, knight.” 

They both bowed as the king and princess passed. Link had been trained in patience his whole career, but he couldn’t wait a second more to leave. 

Before he could be so lucky, Fledge approached.

“Sir Link, Zelda.” He nervously addressed them both and Link in his proper title. They had already seen and spoken with Fledge earlier, so a formal address meant business. “Captain Auru would like you to speak with him immediately. He’s waiting in the barracks.”

Link frowned. Why would the captain want to speak with him tonight, in the barracks of all places rather than his office? Link noted Auru’s attendance earlier in the night. He had been a hair over the line with Zelda, but nothing so scandalous that he would be punished for.

“Did he say why?”

“No.” Fledge said, stone-faced.

He was desperate to leave with Zelda, but he couldn’t ignore a summons from his superior officer. He slumped his shoulders. Somehow, every time, something came between them. “Alright.” He said as he turned to Zelda, “I’m sorry, I’ll try to be quick.”

She fidgeted with the large emerald dangling from her ear, “Take your time. I’ll be in my apartment.” She angled herself between him and Fledge so he couldn’t catch the subtle wink she gave him.

Link exhaled and watched her walk out the doors of the sanctum, her dress floating her out on a phantom wind. He resolved to run if need be to reach the barracks if he had to.

As the cool night air hit his face, he took off the beret, letting the crown of his head get air. Fledge kept pace. “I’ll keep you company,” he said cheerfully.

The cold air was already cooling his blood. He didn’t need company, but the distraction would help. He nodded to his closest comrade, and they swiftly marched down the path.

About halfway through their walk, Fledge asked, “Are you courting Zelda?”

Fledge was not one to be blunt, ever, so it took Link by surprise, where he wasn’t sure how to respond. “I wouldn’t call it courting, exactly.”

“What then?”

It seemed that everyone either wanted to know about their relationship or warned against it. “I don’t know—” And he didn’t. “—I just enjoy spending time with her.”

“It makes sense,” Fledge said, uncharacteristically frank. “You two are always traveling together. She’s pretty, fun, and kind; it would be easy to fall in love with her.”

Link turned to his old squire, brows up, ready to deny or brush off the insinuation, but before he could say anything, he realized he was right. Everyone around him knew it, and while it wasn’t exactly the best example for a knight to fall for his charge, it did happen occasionally in the history books and legends.

“It’s as easy as swinging my blade with her. As easy as breathing.” 

Fledge smiled. “I’ve always liked Zelda. Maybe she’ll decide not to go home, and she can stay here.”

That sobered Link. Every time he thought he could be truly happy with her, that crushing reality hit. They were still ultimately trying to find her a way back home. To her home. Where he wasn’t.

Before he could sink into that thought, they arrived at the barracks. The large common room was dark but for the fireplace giving off the only light. Link and Fledge both lit the lanterns, highlighting an empty room, no one in sight.

Link took a lantern in hand and walked up the steps. Perhaps Auru was up in the small office on the second floor, but by the time he scanned the space, the whole floor was empty.

He met Fledge entering the common room from the sleeping quarters, lantern in hand, and shook his head. Where was the captain?

“When did he instruct you to inform me?” Link asked.

“He didn’t directly tell me. He told Purlo, who told me.”

Link’s stomach dropped. He frantically ran out of the common room into the cool spring air, Fledge behind him. “What is it?!”

It was a trap. Purlo sent him as far away from their apartments as he could. But to what end?

Link shuddered to think as Zelda was alone and unprotected. He grabbed Fledge. “Find Grante, Cawlin, and Pipit, whoever you can find as quickly as possible, and meet me at my apartment as fast as you can.”

Before Fledge could acknowledge his demand, Link was already sprinting toward the castle.

And he knew right in that moment that it wasn’t duty driving his fear.

It was more.

Chapter 28: Culmination

Chapter Text
Zelda floated out of the sanctum. The cool, night air hadn’t fazed her as it hit her face and bare shoulders. She needed it to steady herself on her walk back to her apartment.

The ball was magical; nothing she had ever experienced came close to it. Her own prom seemed like a knockoff in comparison.

The finery of the room— the décor— a crystal chandelier with millions of diamonds. The hundreds of candles lit and suspended in the air. The gold-plated trim, threads, and dinnerware. She had never seen anything like it, as if it had been clipped out of her favorite fantasy novel.

And her dress… she had never worn a piece of fabric so elegant in her life. With her namesake and blood in her veins, she felt like a princess. The princess.

When Greta’s assistant, Sasha, showed up at her door earlier that day, she hadn’t even asked Zelda how she wanted to be styled; all she asked for was to trust the process as she got to work braiding and sweeping her hair into a low bun. She teased a few pieces to frame her face as she admired her bone structure. She then ever so faintly painted her eyelids with gold and her cheeks and lips with the same pink cream.

Zelda never thought herself to be gorgeous, but as she looked in the mirror at Sasha’s work, she barely recognized herself.

Afterwards, Sasha helped her into the emerald gown, which now, thanks to Greta’s quick and efficient hemming, fit like a second skin. She stood in front of the mirror as Sasha buttoned her in; she locked eyes with her and scandalously commented that she may need an additional hand to help her out of the dress later. Zelda’s core sank at the insinuation, and she hoped Sasha hadn’t noticed the tension as her body locked, stamping down that physical hunger.

Sasha brought a case of jewelry to complement her gown, apparently already taken care of when Zelda asked about prices. She explained that Link had apparently given Greta enough money for ten dresses had she wanted it.

Zelda’s reluctance was noted, taking jewelry to put on his tab hadn’t sat right, but Sasha dug into the case and pulled out one pair of teardrop emerald earrings. Her insistence that these were the only pieces she needed and was a must to tie the outfit together. Anything more would be unnecessary.

Sasha packed up her styling kit and the rest of the jewelry as Zelda took out her own gold studs she had continuously left in her ear and replaced with the heavy emeralds that matched her own eyes.

Sasha bid farewell with a remark, “I’ve never seen a more exquisite work of art.”

Zelda used this quiet moment to stand and take herself in. The last two days had been a whirlwind of fittings, training in etiquette, and dance lessons. She hadn’t had a spare second to appreciate the situation.

She was dressed in the most elegant fabric of her life, melted to her— her curves on display but the outer fabric flowing and living around her. Her blonde locks styled in a flawless do, leaving her shoulders squared and proud under the thin straps of her gown.

And she was about to meet her date, her knight, the most attractive man she had ever laid eyes on.

She was beautiful. She was worthy. She was forunate… to be here, to be dressed in finery of magic threads and fabric. To be styled by someone other than herself. To attend a royal ball, with the man of her dreams.

She exhaled the last shreds of anxiety that lingered in her nerves as she heard Sasha speaking with someone at the foot of the stairs.

Link.

She emerged into view and it took everything in her to not pant at the sight of him.

He looked so different. He matched her in a pine green pleated uniform, it was perfectly pressed and tailored to his hard chest and toned arms, a stark contrast to his usual attire. As she descended towards him, she caught the sounds of his leather gloves fidgeted from behind his back, matching his white-as-snow boots. His hair was pulled back in his familiar style, but a flat beret sat atop his head, and she couldn’t help but smile at knowing how much he probably disliked the whole outfit, despite how handsome he looked.

She finally met his gaze, latching into the blue of his eyes— her favorite color amongst a canopy of green.

Then he lunged and pulled her into a passionate kiss to her shock and delight. She missed him. The heat of that kiss alone tempted her to skip the ball and run upstairs with him.

But she wanted to be in public with him, to be on his arm. To be his. Not just for the night.

They entered the sanctum, hand in hand, and it was a blow to her senses. Chapter 31: Crossroads
Chapter Text
‘I don’t belong here.’

He felt like he’d been stabbed. The words cut sharper than a blade.

Actually, this was worse because he’d been stabbed before. A small flesh wound on his thigh during a sparring match. His mind had raced to catch up to how his body reacted. Blood poured from the wound before the pain swelled.

But how would he patch this wound—the wound he never saw coming? The one with no clear entry or exit?

He finished his training earlier in the morning and went to wake Zelda. As he sheathed his sword, the tent was a dark silhouette against the welcoming rays of dawn, his heart raced and he smiled like a fool. Not from his exertion but from recalling the night they shared. He turned to leave, but froze as he heard her say it.

“I don’t belong here.” Her voice clipped as she slammed her fists into the surface, hard enough to splash the statue.

Everything was rushing through his vision, a carousel of portraits.

The day they met. White dress. Emerald eyes. Golden hair. Picking up her limp body. Glimpsing her in the colosseum stands. Rescuing her from bokoblins.

Their journey. The icy chill thawing from Rito Village, drinking in the outpost, Goron hot springs, the heat in the desert, the rescue from Lizalfos.

The shift— The lab and the night they shared opening up to each other, the dance they shared in the tavern, how she rescued him from the Lynels. When he showed her Farosh. When he found the courage to kiss her. When he asked her to the ball and would have fallen upon his sword to see her in her gown again had she only asked.

The night they shared, and all the days and nights after.

They just slept anyway; he held her close, memorizing the golden color of her hair. How it was silken but formed into a delicate natural wave. How her skin was tan, and small sunspots littered her shoulders. He brushed his lips upon the space between her ear and her neck and watched goosebumps rise in his wake.

It would eviscerate him when she’d go. Deprive him of something that had become so essential to his life.

But it was her choice. It would always be.

He struck his sword into the soft ground, unable to concentrate, so instead, he stared out at the horizon.

Zelda’s mood was much lighter when they sat for breakfast. The revelations she shared were cathartic; her face wasn’t hollow anymore, and her body seemed looser, more relaxed, but her eyes were still unfocused.

It was heavy, what they had spoken about. She either stayed here, shutting the door to her old life— the known and familiar. Or she’d leave Hyrule— the unknown and thrilling. But even if she had wanted to leave, there was no guarantee she even could.

It was a mess, no matter how he looked at it.

So he distracted himself. When he wasn’t sharpening his sword, eating, or packing their belongings, he spent the day doing chores for Impa and the community. They bartered with him, trading Sheikah specialties for completed work. The local tailor traded him silent Sheikah gear for helping her sister and grandmother. He helped Impa’s guard collect his missing chickens in return for stealthy elixirs.

Zelda busied herself with the children of the village. Keeping them preoccupied, surely to allow Link time to help their mothers and fathers. By the time he was done, the sun was starting to set.

“Good deeds don’t go unpunished.” Impa said to him as she appeared next to him silently. Everyone in this village seemed to sneak up on him.

“I would have done what they needed without a payment.” Link said to her coolly.

“I know you would have. You are an honorable man.”

It may have been the first time Impa complimented him.

“Walk with me.”

It wasn’t a request.

They made their way to the Sheikah graveyard down the narrow pass. He couldn’t help but glance at Zelda before moving out of view. She was laughing at a toddler brandishing a wooden spoon as if it had been a sword. A small twitch of a smile formed on his mouth. Before he could hide it, Impa noticed it at the corner of her eye. He didn’t care; they just kept walking silently towards that small encased area.

The colors were the same as the day before, as they overlooked the horizon of Lanayru’s swamp lands. Impa stared at him, not in disappointment but concern? He could never fully read her.

“I warned you. But it seems it fell on deaf ears.” She said, not unkindly. He didn’t have to ask her to clarify what she meant. “I won’t ask if you broke your knightly chivalric vows because I know you won’t lie to me, and I already know the answer.”

Of course, she knew; anyone who knew Zelda and him from the start could see the shift in their demeanor. He didn’t react; perhaps only a faint red blush decorated his cheeks.

“But that’s not what worries me.”

Link’s brows furrowed.

“You love her.” It was not a question, as she asked in an unfamiliar, soft tone.

Link was silent. All but giving her the confirmation she already knew.

She exhaled, but not in anger, maybe disappointment.

“My duty to her and you has not changed.” He said firmly.

Impa laughed. Laughed. More of a cackle if anything. “It already has, by listing your duty to her first rather than the task at hand.”

He closed his lips tightly.

“Despite it, I do understand. We’ve always been loyal to the throne, putting our own interests second. But when you meet someone worthy, your oath suddenly feels… negotiable. No matter your countless years of dedication and service.”

He could not contain his stunned look.

She huffed a small chuckle. “You are trying to imagine me with a partner? It may come as a surprise to you, but I have loved.” She paused and corrected, “Love.” She turned away from him, as if the realization hit her just as deeply. “I know the sacrifices it entails.”

Link stared at her, dumbfounded. He had never imagined Impa as anything more than a cold, calculating servant to the throne. Certainly not someone who had compassion for anything less than perfect, especially people stupid enough to fall in love. She noted his reaction. “I know. It’s hard to imagine. But I did warn you, you cannot serve two masters. That wasn’t just some carefully crafted language I pulled out of thin air.”

She continued to stare at the serene scenery in front of them. “You need to choose, the crown and everything you worked your whole life towards. Or… her.”

It was easy to answer.

Before he could, Impa’s hand shot up. “Please, just go to the spring tomorrow and then we’ll talk. I can’t stop you from your own choices, but there’s more at stake than you know.”

“What else?”

“The Yiga Clan has been attacking small parties of soldiers.”

He had heard of the Yiga Clan; they were Sheikah people that rebelled against the crown and worshipped a deity far more evil. He asked, “Why now? They’ve barely been more than a whisper for countless years, nothing more than an inconvenience, robbing trade routes mostly.”

Impa had cold rage in her eyes; being that they are Sheikah, this was personal. “They’ve grown more bold. They have killed soldiers on patrol, leaving only one left alive to report back.”

“What have they taken in these attacks?”

“Nothing.”

Murdering without reason. An icy chill went down his spine. “Do we know why?”

“No. I can only suspect they are targeting Hyrule’s soldiers for one reason. To have less when the time comes.”

Impa turned to him, her red eyes almost glowing. “I said you both have a choice, but something is coming, a culmination. I ask that you go to the spring, retrieve that last Spiritual Stone, and promptly return to the castle. Be on your guard. Only I know your true mission with Zelda, but that doesn’t mean you haven’t been being watched.”

It was his turn to be enraged. The thought of them getting anywhere near Zelda— he refused to deepen that thought.

He nodded his head in agreement. One more stone. Then Zelda can choose. And he would stand by it, even if it finished him.

Chapter 32: Wisdom
Chapter Text
The trees were bare. No leaves decorated the dark, thin branches. They silhouetted in contrast against the fading light on the horizon.

Except for the lush pines.

She watched a large red bird—as conspicuous as a drop of blood against snow—fly between branches. Two squirrels chased each other up a tree, twirling around from the base, up and up and up, in a race to the top.

Everything smelled new and sharp. A reset on the land.

Except for the scent of pine.

The land of perpetual snow. There was a fresh blanket of it as far as she could see. It was cold and getting colder the more they climbed. That bitter, bone-biting cold, where the moisture settles ice into the soul.

And it was quiet. A spooky, yet serene quiet as snow gently fell. As if she thought too loud, the mountain would listen and retort.

The holiest of treks to the peak, to another goddess statue, and inevitably, another stone.

She gazed over the mountainside; they were about halfway to the top. Angry cliffs jutted behind and beneath them like monstrous teeth. Out of all of their traveling across Hyrule, this one felt the least forgiving. The kind of terrain that didn’t care about her destiny, only that it was a challenge to fulfill.

The trail started easy enough. Careful architecture led to a small green valley, then a snowed valley. But then they ascended. Her thighs had been burning, both from the incline and trudging through the snow— both old and new. She’d been in the best shape of her life since traversing Hyrule, but this trek was a test for her newly honed body.

It wasn’t lost on her. How she needed this type of journey to center herself. How the cold lifted the fog. Made her sharper and honest.

She sat on a discarded log from a fell tree near the now raging fire. She stared at the flames, the white and orange and red, hypnotic enough to blur her vision, reminding her of the sunsets they left in Kakariko Village. She should have known the tone shifted as they walked through Lanayru Promenade; there was an eerie sense of dread building since they stepped on the ancient stones.

But… she had felt better since their conversation.

She was feeling sorry for herself when they arrived back at the castle from the Spring of Power. She hadn’t realized she missed Linda’s wedding until then. The final nail in the coffin of her old life.

She had been so busy in her discovery of herself and her infatuation for Link for all those months, a beautiful cotton candy dream that she had harshly woken from. She hadn’t even thought about her old home in months, but it all hit her at once. And she had done what she had done before, and dove headfirst into the pool of self-pity.

But Link beheld her for who she was and is. And did not look away.

Her protector, her lover, her match.

She laid heavy realities upon his ears. Truths and anxieties and vulnerabilities she had never confronted. Her shaky fingers cracking open the safe inside of her, turning the knob to the left, and the right, back to the left. Each gear clicking closer—

Click.

Click.

Each sound made her hesitate to show him. What she planned to unlock. Fear—that he may not like the woman she was underneath it all.

But it was never too much. Her pain, her past was never too much. She just never shared it with the right person. Who earned the right to hear her story. Who didn’t sneer or curl their lip in disgust. Who didn’t act like she was inconvenient.  The perfect, shiny trophy they wanted her to be— but that she was nonetheless still precious underneath the smudges and the dirt. Luminous and proud despite the small chips and scratches. Perfectly imperfect.

As she warmed her fingers near the fire. She glanced to where Link was under lowered lashes. He was kneeling over the pack he brought, looking for food or something or other. He wore a hood to cover his head from the elements and a drab grey jacket. Similar to her own muted colors, to attract less attention but still thick enough to keep warm in the harsh environment. Despite the layers, she could see the muscles in his arms and back flex as he rooted through his belongings. His sword hung from his back, his bracer and guards still strapped to his person, ready for anything.

Her protector, her lover, her match.

She dreamed that night. Not of the horrid death machines, that hadn’t plagued her in months; instead, she relived her own memories through glass she never saw.

She was in a department store, the smell of new plastic and fake linen burned her nose. The fluorescent lighting was too bright, too flat, turning everything shades of grey and beige.

Her parents had just died.

And she needed… something or other, she couldn’t remember.

She did remember the feeling of walking down the aisles like a corpse. She glanced at everything, multiplied items in various colors and sizes. Things. Things that would bring so much joy and longing and excitement. But it was pointless and useless. Things people didn’t really need. Or maybe they did, and it just seemed so insignificant to her now. She hated it. She hated all of it. It was all so meaningless. How could she want for things when all she wanted was her parents back?

A child threw a ball down the aisle at his brother. Laughing and yelling as he landed his mark.

A middle aged woman on her cellphone was asking the other line which a person would like better, as she judged two sets of essentially the same thing.

A young man looked bored as he followed a young woman with her cart.

She wanted to scream and cry and yell at everyone in the store. How could they continue their lives as they did? Why were they so oblivious? She was as alone in the aisle as she was in life. The world kept moving when all she wanted was to rewind.

But she didn’t scream and cry and yell. She swallowed the building sob—painfully choking back the blades of hurt. In defeat, she turned to the doors, expecting to exit to the grey and drab concrete lot; however, grass greeted her.

She froze. Her body on edge.

The air smelled fresh and pure. A small stream sounded next to her, the water glacier clear. Mountains in the distance against the bluest sky. Her spirit felt free as she breathed in the wild, tasting pine and grass on her tongue.

It was Hyrule.

She turned to glance back at the aisles of things, the muted colors. Turn back or go forward.

The choice was easy.

She walked forward. Toward home.

The sky had laid a delicate blanket of snow while they slept. The white untouched and pure. No dirt, no fluids polluting it—only animal tracks as proof of life. The shimmering cover against the trying sunlight was a sight worth her most precise memories.

Still bone-biting cold—even colder with the whipping wind. She knew her nose was red without being able to see it.

The elixirs Link provided kept hypothermia at bay. Each vial he produced for her seemed to manifest out of air, the constant fussing he was doing over her—she hadn’t actually seen him take one since they started their ascent.

She barely grazed a small tree as the snow gave way from its young branches. A flurry of white glitter fell over her, smooth and gentle. She should have shivered having the cold, wet perspiration fall onto her bare face, but instead it felt like a jolt. An awakening. Of something yet to come.

Link hiked behind her. Not in front. Not next to. It gave her a chance to run those tunnels in her soul. Taking stock of everything she was before. Asking herself the question, what if I never went back home?

Her apartment was mostly filled with replaceable, material things. Her parents had left her their house and everything in it when they died, but she couldn’t bear to live in it without them, so she sold it. She couldn’t look at any of the pieces of furniture without feeling sad, so she sold those too. Anything that she had a somewhat sentimental attachment to, which wasn’t much, she packed into storage. Everything except for the gold triangle ring she wore on her finger. She could do without the rest.

Technology. She could do without it. She hadn’t realized how easy it would be. She had more meaningful interactions in person. There had been technological advancements here that even transcended her modern time. Nothing was inconvenient or too far from her reality. It gave her the opportunity to open a book and learn or see nature as intended.

But Linda and Marin—that would hurt.

She missed Linda terribly. All her fire and loyalty and sharp love. But she missed Marin too. She had become a guardian figure to her; showering her with warmth and stubborn care.

She wondered if she missed her too? She had always come into her apartment completely disregarding her boundaries, but she was always kind and loving. She loved Marin’s backyard, full of greenery and flowers. But everything outside of that was hard pavements, ugly buildings, pollution, and garbage. Everything was richer here. The smells. The colors. The taste. The air she breathed. Her spirit flourished.

And her life. Her career, her goals, and dreams. If she had to be honest with herself, she hadn’t given anything much thought since her parents had died. She planned to go back to school. But her Dreams? Goals? At the time of her departure, the most she strived for was a direction, a purpose, something that never came.

But she could see it as undiluted as the snow next to her. Her working in the castle library— cataloging the books and volumes of histories while Link joined her when he could. Sneaking out from duties to cozy up to him in a hidden alcove while she read him poetry— or about the heroes of legend.

Or the lab. She could work with Robbie and Purah, sure they were eccentric but their obsession of the unknown she shared. Link could be stationed nearby or perhaps he could share a horseback ride back to their nearby village where they resided.

She saw a home. Laundry snapping on a line in the wind that smelled of the sea. A weapon rack full of mismatched and assorted steel. Smelled the onions and the rosemary steaming and crackling in a pan in the kitchen. She saw Epona and Storm in their own pen. She saw a pond, the deep blue and yellow fireflies in perfect harmony with each other.

And Link.

She forgot where she was. She tripped over a jutting rock and lost her footing. Her palms instinctively breaking her fall. Her hands covered with thick gloves but she still felt that icy plunge into the snow.

Then strong hands were immediately behind her, hauling her up.

Link’s expression was tight, carved from worry as she dusted herself off. She couldn’t identify what caused his concern; her fall, this trek, the cold. Take a pick. 

“Are you alright?” He asked low and careful.

She nodded, avoiding licking her lips for fear of the icy cold coating.

“We’re almost there.”

She continued the slow ascent, easily slipping back into her thoughts that had distracted her.

That even if she wanted to return home, there was one she couldn’t ignore. And as much as she wanted to make this decision purely on her own independence she could not ignore that he was… 

The love of her life.

The universe was funny that way. She didn’t plan it; love was the last thing she needed or wanted when she came here, but here he was, the man of her dreams. Brave, loyal, kind, thoughtful, passionate, handsome—and a hundred more adjectives to describe his perfection.

And she loved him, and had probably loved him since the moment she laid eyes on him.

He never took away her agency. She was under no illusion that she could traverse Hyrule on her own, that she hadn’t needed a protector, a sword. But he never once made her feel that she owed him for his service. For every monster’s life he took. Never indebted. But rather she had never felt more confident and strong with him at her side.

And he unknowingly built her back up from the shell she was.

But was he enough for her to stay? To build a life? A home?

If he felt the same.

They may have started in lust, but did he grow to share her sentiments? Did the lines between being her sworn protector and lover blur? Or was she simply… pleasure. A bright, impossible thing that was thrilling to have while he carried out his duty?

She wanted to know, wanted to confess to him everything she felt, but she was scared. Terrified. She could live in Hyrule without him if she had to.

But she didn’t want to.

They arrived at the spring late in the afternoon. The sky was already dark and mixed with fog and falling snow that she couldn’t see more than a few yards. Only the goddess statue was visible as she stood carved on her throne of crystals with a holy basin at her feet. Somehow placed here by a divine being, challenging anyone’s commitment that wanted to worship her.

And the silence that followed was bizarre but welcomed. Beautiful in that haunting manner. Not an animal, critter, or soul to sing with nature—only the sounds of Link setting up their camp for the night.

After they ate a cold meal, they curled up in their shared tent. They made love in the small space, unhurried and lazy. Their hands grasping into each other and eyes roaming. It had been weeks since Akkala and their night under the moon.

She made a conscious effort to memorize every inch of skin on him, noting the raised scars that littered his torso and arms. The one in particular on his forearm from the lynel he fought to protect her from. She kissed every one as he drove into her.

The straw color of his hair, how it was thick but straight, and how pieces fell from his hairband no matter how many times he tied it back. Her hands threaded through, catching small knots.

His face. His handsome, perfect face. Her fingers traced his perfectly carved cheekbones downwards, to the faint stubble decorating his strong jaw, then his lips. A shade of dull maroon, too full and flawless for a man that killed monsters. He greeted her fingers with light kisses and bites.

His eyes, though.

She could never forget his eyes.

Blue as a lagoon. Or as the depths of a glacier. Deeper, richer than the sky. Her favorite color. Even when she became ash on the wind, she would remember his eyes, as they would coax her home. She gazed into them as he held her face tenderly, and they both shattered around each other.

Her lover. Her partner. Her other half.

She would pray and pray not to let the fates take her from him. From Hyrule. From her home.

She made her decision.

Morning came, and she changed into the white prayer dress she’d come to loathe. Somehow the white was too white. Too pure for a mere mortal such as herself. Too angelic for her imperfection. 

The air was frigid, but manageable, as Link had given her another elixir to keep her warm. The cruel air still carried a chill on her skin, but it was no more than jumping into a lake in the peak of summer— sharp and temporary. 

Link had been restless all morning. Training in this horrid cold, cutting logs to keep their fire going, cooking or prepping. Moving like he couldn’t sit still.

She glanced at him again before walking into the waters. He looked tired, with bags under his eyes, and his complexion was wan against the grey landscape. She supposed they both hadn’t slept, but he had looked especially depleted.

She gave him a weak smile, which he returned and then turned his back to give her privacy. The cold biting steel strapped on his back— she was sure the metal bit into his skin, unbearable to hold in this weather.

Say it and leave.

She dipped her toe in the water, expecting an unbearable temperature to greet her, but no. The water was cold, but not as awful as she anticipated. She stepped further and bent her knees, submerging herself to the waist.

She instinctively looked back at Link. His back was turned from her. Then her gaze turned hard to the statue.

She would not cower. She breathed out a breath and repeated the prayer aloud.

She waited, hands clasped painfully; she was cutting off her blood supply.

Nothing.

She repeated it again, louder, in case the inanimate statue hadn’t heard her the first time through the wind and snow.

Waited.

Waited.

Nothing.

Her face scrunched in disbelief. “Really?”

Despite the growing satisfaction that the stone had not appeared, she couldn’t help but mutter, “Now you deny me?”

Silence. No glow. No stone.

She scoffed, her warm breath visible. “I met your sisters, I poured every ounce of fear, shame, and disappointment into their listening ears. They gave me their stones, much to my dismay. Now I come to you resolved of that, and you give me nothing?”

No response. But what was she expecting? A frank conversation with a goddess from a myth that may or may not be real about the wishes and whims of a mortal young woman?

She rolled her eyes.

“Is it because I’ve come to terms with my fate?” She swallowed. “I want to stay. I don’t want to go back. I want—” she tried not to choke on her declaration, “I want to build a home here. A life.”

She snuck a side-long glance at Link to see if he heard her. He made no indication.

“He is my true love. The one who has healed my shattered soul. He has shown me the beauty that lives in every pore of the land. From the greenest grass to the hard, untouched earth, to the unfiltered waters that run clear, to the heat in the sand. This world—this place—is everything I couldn’t even begin to imagine. And I want to explore every inch of it, with him by my side.”

A tear slid down her cheek, not in despair but for the first time in her life, she felt blessed. Truly blessed. She didn’t look at what happened to her as an adversarial event. No, it was a blessing. It may have been traumatic but it brought her here, where she was supposed to be.

“I don’t want your stone. If I am to receive it, they will use it to send me home. I don’t want it. I will make my way without it.” She smiled to herself. “We will.”

And that was the truth. Impa said the stones would send her home. She didn’t need it or want it anymore. They could build their own life without it. Her fate was sealed because she willed it that way, destiny be damned. She huffed and rose from her knees and started to walk out.

Then, a bell-note trembled through the fog, thin and horrible as a finger circling a cup’s rim. Her breath fogged as she let an exhalated breath lose, as that familiar glow radiated from the water.

She crumbled beneath herself, not caring that she was met with a hard stone that felt like it shattered her kneecaps. Her fists clenched on her side and her head hung low.

She sat frozen for what felt like forever. The glow taunting her. She hadn’t dared reach in to retrieve it.

There was no denying it. Her destiny. They had all three stones. To be used in some unknown ritual.

Never hers to make.

A silent sob worked its way up her throat.

Suddenly, she felt strong arms around her middle. The far-away smell of grass and pine filled her space. He kissed her behind her ear, his warm breath giving her life again. He lifted her out of the water, tender and slow, almost afraid he’d break her if he jostled her further. 

“No more cold for you today.” He murmured as she sat up on her own two feet. He reached in to grab the stone.

It was a sapphire, sapphires. So blue it looked black against the moisture and fog. Three identical large pentagon gems fit within the impossibly shiny gold encasement. Sharp daggers jutted outwards from the center, making it awkward for Link to hold.

He led her back to their campsite. Her hands were biting, aching in pain. Link took them in his hands, inadvertently pushing his warmth into them.

She was trembling as Link practically shoved her into their tent to change. He handed her another elixir and demanded she drink it. She hadn’t realized the first one had worn off sometime ago. How long had she sat in that water?

She emerged from the tent in her warm clothes. Link was standing outside, waiting. His features were schooled into an anxious look as his eyes looked her up and down. He looked satisfied enough as he grabbed her shoulders, forcing her to meet his gaze. “We’re leaving. Give me a few minutes to pack up, go stand by the fire and warm up.” He said curtly before letting go and getting to work on dismantling their campsite.

Link had been quick; she had barely warmed her fingers by the time he had the tent and their belongings in his pack. Without speaking, he kicked snow onto the fire and placed a hand on the small of her back to lead her away.

Her feet mindlessly moved towards the familiar path until a firm pressure directed her in a different direction.

“We’re going a different way.” His eyes were so clear, so full of determination. She just nodded numbly as he escorted her down.

The frozen peak had turned into a grassy mountain, as if cut and sewn together. A cool sea breeze caressed her face. She glanced back at Mount Lanayru. She wasn’t sure how they were able to descend that steep mountain so quickly, let alone at all.

They didn’t speak the whole way down. Link led her through hidden caves and paths opposite the way they came. Holding her hand on the more treacherous parts. As they emerged from a cave, the sun was low and the sky painted in swirls of orange and purple. They had been walking nonstop for the better part of a day.

“Where are we going?” She managed to croak. Her voice raw.

“Home.” He said without turning back to her.

She hid her disappointment.

He led her into a dirt path. They were still on a mountain but less threatening than Mount Lanayru. Her breath caught as she looked down. The winding path they were on was leading them down to a bustling village, but it wasn’t Kakariko.

It was large, buildings with orange roofs cascading down the mountain, full of people and farm animals. On her right, cows, goats, and chickens ran freely near a pond. On the left, homes, shops, and a large windmill turning slow and steady. It was the largest village she had seen so far in Hyrule, all nestled in between mountains smelling of the sea.

Link led her through the dusty street as it opened. People smiled at him as they passed. As if they knew him.

They passed the inn and continued on. Would they camp again?

They were at the edge of town, or perhaps the beginning, when Link veered off to the left, up a small hill. She was too charmed by the village to notice how her legs had started to feel like jelly beneath her.

They crossed a small bridge, and a lone house lay ahead of them. It was a modest home and looked well taken care of. The property was large and private; whoever lived here had taken care to landscape with choice flowers, shrubs, and she scented it before she saw it—

Lavender.

Below on the small hill, a pond dotted with fireflies was starting to glow against the darkening sky. It was so enchanting, it made her want to cry.

They approached the front door, but instead of knocking, Link reached directly for the handle. He didn’t see her brows shoot up as she stood behind him. He held it open for her as he gestured for her to enter. It was bold to assume whoever’s house it was would be so inviting.

She moved to the center of the room. The home was cozy, like a warm embrace. There was a large kitchen, a vase of fresh-cut flowers with sprigs of pine and herbs sat near the basin. The open living room was bare with little to no decorations besides a guard’s armor and an assortment of deadly, used steel. A short staircase leading to a loft and what she assumed was a bedroom from this angle.

She turned back towards Link, “Whose house is this?”

Link had shut the door and met her eyes with such voracity, his eyes pinning her in the middle of the room. “It’s mine.”

Chapter 33: Home
Chapter Text
“It’s mine.”

Zelda’s eyes went wide, caught between disbelief and wonder. “Yours?”

“It was my parents’ home, the house I was raised in.” The words grated on their way out. “But when they died, it became mine.”

He could see the gears turning in her mind.

When he lifted her out of the spring, she was a frozen shell— staring at the glow in the water as if she moved, the very floor beneath her would swallow her whole. He knew she needed a beat, and Kakariko was the last place he wanted to be. Impa would make them rush onto their next task with three stones in hand. So instead, he brought her to his own sanctuary—or at least it used to be.

Zelda crossed the room slowly, examining the bare walls and plain rafters. He hadn’t returned since his mother’s death five years ago.

He had removed his mother’s artwork and most of his father’s belongings and stored them in storage, only a few choice weapons lay on mounts around them. Weapons, more like relics— that held some sentimental value to him but were impractical in combat. They were in various shades of bluntness and dullness, desperately needing a polish and shine. It was fitting—considering.

He waited with bated breath for her to say something.

Zelda pawed at the edge of the kitchen table. “Everything is so… clean. Considering you haven’t visited in some time, unless you somehow teleported here.”

He had still been glued to the front door. “I pay someone to clean and maintain the house and the property. I—I haven’t been here in years. My parents loved this house, but I never wanted to come back. I didn’t want to stain the happy memories I had with my grief. I only ever wanted to keep love in this home.”

Zelda was toying with a small carved spice box on the table before snapping her head to him. Freezing him with her glittering eyes but no smile on her face. “Why now?”

“Because—” he hesitated, as if afraid of startling her if he stepped closer. “You needed a sanctuary.” He paused, swallowing the nerves. “And because I need to tell you something.”

She remained still, frozen to the table, patiently waiting for him to continue.

He unbuckled his sword belt and bracers to set beside the small table next to the door.
