The smells of natural tannins mixed with sweat and blood made her want to gag despite her closed mouth. She couldn’t see their face, but she knew this was no friend of theirs. Their other hand was around her middle, yanking her further from Link, who was still fishing, unaware of her kidnapping.

For one terrible heartbeat, time stopped. She was helpless, dragged backward like a caught animal.

Then her instincts roared.

She slammed the heel of her foot down to stabilize herself, then with the other angled it backwards as hard as she could, and on cue her attacker groaned in agony while simultaneously dropping his arms around her, freeing her mouth to yell.

Link was moving before the attacker’s knees hit the ground, sword in hand, charging towards her with a look on his face she had only ever seen when that sword was in his hand—pure rage and purpose.

Zelda bolted towards him and quickly froze as two masked figures dropped in around Link as if birthed from the air itself.

Both were dressed in the same uniform of red leather with metal guards on their shoulder blades. Equipped with only curved blades and the sinister-looking white mask that had the Sheikah symbol painted on. The Sheikah symbol, but warped.

Link made quick work of the demonic masked figures, cutting them down with ease. But then two more appeared between them.

They weren’t wildly attacking, they were herding him. To separate them.

As Link feinted and weapons clashed, her original assailant was on their feet again. Advancing towards her with a feline sort of caution. She backed herself towards the rock wall, heart pounding wildly; it was radiating pain to her shoulder blades.

She didn’t have a weapon on her, nor did she ever learn to fight all that time ago. She was utterly useless. She glanced to Link. He had cut down another for two more to take their place.

She made use of what she had: a large rock at her feet that she threw at the assailant, which he dodged with grace. But instead of riling him, it just amused him. “That won’t help you, Zelda.” His voice was vicious and cold, chuckling at her.

How did he know her name?

“What do you want?” She snarled. She couldn’t fight her way out of this, but perhaps could talk her way out.

“You’ll find out once we bring you to our master.”

Master? Her eyes flicked to Link; he cut down two more, but four took their place, a nightmare that kept replenishing itself. She never, ever doubted Link’s abilities to fight and protect her, but they were purposefully overwhelming him and depleting his stamina.

She couldn’t watch him die. “If I go with you willingly, will you let him live?” Words that she never intended to speak ground out of her.

The masked figure cocked his head slowly at her. Serpentine like, as he hissed. “No.”

Her face twisted in horror. They had to fight or run. She took a steadying breath and bolted. Perhaps running would deter some of Link’s attackers to her direction instead, giving him a reprieve.

She made it all of a few meters as another red-clad figure appeared in front of her. As he raised his hand above her, she saw Link fall, surrounded by an outrageous amount of masked assailants. She cried out his name as one struck him hard enough to send him motionless to the ground.

Then she was surrounded by pain and darkness.

She awoke; her head was throbbing.

A cool dampness pressed against her cheek. She was sprawled on a cold stone floor.  As if thrown there and left to rot.

The air smelled dank, like mold and wet earth and copper. There was a rough-looking bed, chamber pot, and nothing else. The door was solid metal, with a small barred window at the top, much too high for her to see over. It was the only source of light streaming in, which was abysmal.

She was in a cell. Caged. But where? For how long? By whom?

The red-clad assailants.

Her head was pounding red-hot. She lifted her hands, her nails full of dirt as she squeezed, trying to slow that pulsing pain. The left side of her skull hurt. She was hit with something heavy, but that seemed to be the extent of her injuries; besides her clothing being ripped and dirty, she was fine.

She rubbed at her temples, forcing the memories to come back through the haze.

Link.

He had fallen; she watched him fall, circled by at least a dozen of those masked assailants after he’d already cut down a dozen before. Her attacker had promised he wouldn’t live before he knocked her out.

She let out a small sob.

“Zelda?” She heard that muffled, familiar voice say.

“Link?!” She stood up and tried to jump up to the barred window to see. No luck.

“Zelda.” His voice was coated in relief. “Are you hurt?”

He sounded so close but so far, like trying to listen under the water’s surface. Perhaps across the hallway behind a similar door. “I’m alright, my head aches from where they hit me, but otherwise I’m all right. Are you okay?”

Link swore. “I’m all right.”

He was lying. She knew it instantly. He had to be in rough shape but wouldn’t want to worry her. She wanted to push, but her head spun with missing pieces.

“Where are we? How long have we been here? Who were they?”

A pause, a sound of metal scraping stone. “I’m not sure where we are, but it resembles the castle’s lockup.” He paused and quietly finished, “As for time… judging by the color of the bruise on my arm, I’d say two days.”

She’d been knocked out for two days?

“And who were they?”

“The Yiga Clan.” He spit out.

“Yiga Clan?”

“Sheikah traitors to the crown. They were trained as Sheikah warriors but defected from the crown to serve evil instead. They are organized… and ruthless.”

Evil. That’s what he said. Served evil, not a who. Who could be so evil they are nameless?

She stood, trembling. The reality of her new room was starting to hit her. “What do they want with us?”

He spoke softly, not because he was far away. “I don’t know. They took the Spiritual Stones, but if it had been a robbery, they would have just killed us on the spot. They went to the effort to bring us here, to lock us up.”

Every possibility eddied in her head. They worshipped evil. Impa had said on their first meeting all that time ago that something was coming, something terrible. And how did her attacker know her name? To Link’s point, if they just wanted the Spiritual Stones, wouldn’t they have just killed them? Or perhaps they went after the wrong Zelda, thinking she was the princess and wanted to hold her for ransom.

This was a bad dream. This was not reality.

Nausea riled her low and swift. She sucked in a steady breath as she tried to focus on anything else except that churning sensation.

She looked at the bed, essentially just stumps of wood barely off the ground, sheets that may have been white at some point but were now a stained collage of brown. No food. No water. Horrible chains hung on the far side of the wall, manacles at its end for some unholy type of torture she never wanted to experience.

She ran to her sorry excuse of a chamber pot and vomited.

Her brow was slicked with sweat. The icy spread of dehydration was rolling on her skin. Link had not said a word. Hopefully, he had not heard her retching.

She exhaled a shaky breath, careful to breathe back in through her mouth. “I was so scared for you. My attacker said they would kill you.”

“They said the same to me about you.” Rage laced his voice, “they distracted me before they knocked me out.”

They knew.

They knew that they were… more than a knight guarding his charge. How long had they been watching them? Had they seen what they’d done in Akkala at the Spring of Power? Her head felt warm and she was nauseous all over again.

What lengths would they go to break them now knowing they could use their pain against them? Link was the most honorable man she’d ever known, but what wouldn’t he do or say to protect her?

As if he read her thoughts, “I won’t let them hurt you.”

She curled into a ball on the uncomfortable, disgusting bed, hugging her knees trying to hide the sorrow in her voice to say, “I know.”

Days had passed.

Maybe. It was hard to tell. The faint firelight shining through her cell door was always lit from a lantern or sconce. There were no windows to tell when night came. The guards brought food at random intervals, perhaps to purposely disorient them, or perhaps because they didn’t care when they needed to eat. Not that she was hungry; the food looked inedible, so she stuck to the stale pieces of bread instead.

The only constant was the smell of organic copper and raw earth.

They made no mention of torture or interrogation for either of them. They just were seemingly leaving them to rot or leaving them alone long enough to break them.

Link and she had spoken throughout the days, keeping their voices low and conversation light. Nothing personal or strategic, in case someone was listening.

He asked what book she took from Hateno.

She asked what his favorite season was.

He asked what she’d name the black cat if it stays.

She then asked who he was speaking to before they left Hateno. A laborer of sorts, evident by the tool belt hung from his waist. She had been at the market buying provisions for the journey, and when she crossed the worn bridge to their home, Link was speaking low to the man and pointing towards the back of the house.

All he said was that the house needed repairs.

She was tracing the mortar lines, a mixture of mud and fine gravel against the charcoal stone, when she heard boots.

Not the light, quick steps of the guard. These were heavy, slow, and deliberate. Even the scurrying rats seemed to halt.

Then, an ominous pause; she sensed their presence taunting her behind the cell door.

“The infamous knight and Zelda. I did not think I’d need so many men to capture you, but I have to say I underestimated you.” The stranger’s voice was deep and rough, but not raspy— confident.

Neither of them replied.

“You’re wondering why we brought you here. Why we kept you alive.”

They didn’t take the bait.

He laughed at their silence. “You should have seen yourselves in that tidy little yard. Your heads to the sky, no weapon in sight. As if all the world was forgotten except for you.”

She quickly covered her mouth with both of her icy hands. She hunched down, hiding her gasp. They were watching, planning it all.

“No matter. You two have done well in getting our master what he needs. But there’s no reason to keep you both around.”

She heard Link snarl. Fear coursed through her, leaving goosebumps in their wake as both of their cell doors opened. 

She stood, trying not to let her knees wobble from under her. The guard that was taunting them was massive, broader and taller than the other guards that captured them. His frame towered over her cell door as he opened it. He had the same white mask and a similar red leather uniform but more refined than the foot soldiers. It was hard not to notice the large sheathed blade hung at his side. The blade underneath had to be as tall as her.

As he stood in the doorway, and even behind the mask, she knew he was smirking at her.

She should have felt enraged. Or sad. Or terrified. Instead, she just felt shame.

Foolish for thinking they could be happy. That she could be happy. They used it to lure them into a sense of safety. They had spent that week in Hateno, such as regular people. Chores, cooking, cleaning— enjoying their days off. Link hadn’t even worn his sword the whole of their time there. They could have attacked them at any moment. But they waited until they were completely ignorant and blind.

“Zelda, you have been a challenge to capture. Longer than you know. Who knew we just had to wait until the perfect moment when you were both so disgustingly distracted by your profound infatuation, it was easy to overpower you both. It’s only fitting you should see him one last time.”

She tried not to be sick at his words, as his large frame moved out of the doorway; the sight almost had her retching up whatever little bits were in her stomach.

Link was on his knees across the hall, shackled and bruised. His handsome face was mottled in shades of purple and swollen. He had cuts on his arms and legs, and blood crusted his hair. They must have beaten him after they captured him and continued to do so. Why hadn’t he told her?

Tears swelled in her eyes. He had to be in immense pain. He looked at her with such sorrow and regret. Her lip quivered so hard she bit the inside of her cheek.

“Pathetic.” The large guard spat. “Since you do not bear the holy sword, you are of no use to us.”

She braced herself for him to unsheathe that mighty blade at his side on her. She would be brave. It was horrible to end this way, but at least she would go to her death knowing Link loved her, and he knew she loved him too.

“I’ll grant you this one mercy, girl.” And he shut her cell door, sealing her behind the heavy door with a ringing crash. His heavy boots walked across the hall. Link’s cell door had not been shut.

No.

No. No. No.

“Any last words, knight?” The brute asked, his voice coated in venom.

Zelda was already launching herself at the door, pounding her fists. She screamed and shouted, clawing at the barred window. This was no mercy.

This wasn’t happening. Her head swelled, her brain becoming a churned sea. Waves crashing in her skull. Logic and reason getting carried away with the tide.

She could accept dying, but not him. Not after everything they had been through. He loved her. She loved him. They were supposed to have longer. She just found him, found this happiness.

She jumped and her hands clasped the barred window. She tried to pull herself up by leveraging herself against the door. But she couldn’t against the smooth surface. Her boots slipped, and she slammed her body against it.

“Zelda, I love y—”

A blade zinged, then a heavy thud hit the ground.

She screamed.

Chapter 35: Destiny
Chapter Text
His body hit the stone, wet and stiff. The loud crack of chains followed. Liquid splattered. Copper carried in the air.

“Please— please.” She was whining, begging, her voice unrecognizable. The tears already warming her cheeks.

But only the cold, dampness of nothingness answered her back.

Then the scrapes of dragging.

Her knees struck the ground first. She wailed, ignoring the screaming pain in her knee caps. An ungodly shriek escaped her, as if she were an animal. Her fists clenched and banged on the door. Her unkempt, knotted hair fell forward and stuck to her wet face.

She might have yelled his name.

No voice replied.

This wasn’t real. This wasn’t happening. It was a nightmare.

But alas, she hadn’t awakened.

Link was— he was—.

“Pl— please.” Her voice was small. Far away, as her body seized in trembling agony. “Don’t leave me.”

She couldn’t think it, say it.

She wept so loudly that she didn’t even hear the guard leave.

Time did not exist.

Only the emptiness of a void.

She stopped counting how many meals she received. She stopped counting footsteps that sounded down the long hallway. She stopped pretending she could count without the sun’s beams.

She wasn’t eating anyway. Her despair fed her better than food ever could.

She tunneled into her own pit of misery. Greeting the bottom of that well inside herself like an old friend. She curled around it, let it swallow her, trying to grasp any scrap of comfort she could find.

But there was none to be found.

She remembered this. She knew it well.

She barely made it out alive when her parents died. Linda had to force her to move, to eat, to bathe. In her stages of denial that then moved to anger. She started to destroy her parents’ house. She threw foolish things that meant nothing anymore at frames with them pictured and posed, happy and alive.

Then Marin came and told her to live with her, in the empty apartment, with no happy people smiling at her, mocking her heartsickness. With no reminders of them in every object crushing her.

But they weren’t here this time.

She had no one. Only her old friend, grief.

And she finally admitted it: he was dead. Link was dead. The only man she loved was dead.

Loved.

She sat in the middle of the room, hugging her knees, on the too-cold stone that was warmer than the air. She couldn’t bear to be near a wall, for fear the shadows would swallow her whole.

She was left alone in the dark, so darkness she became.

“Get up.” 

The voice snapped like a whip.

She was curled up in the middle of the floor, trying to be one with the stone, trying to ground herself to some reality where she wasn’t here.

She managed to open her swollen eyes to a squint at the direction of the voice. If she had a mirror, surely red veins would stare back.

A guard stood at the threshold of her cell door, arms crossed, agitated. As if her imprisonment was a personal annoyance to him.

“I’m not going to tell you a third time. Get. Up.” He seethed.

Zelda thought about ignoring it, letting them drag her if they wanted her. They already did the worst thing to her.

But a small voice unburied itself deep inside of her, Linda’s unyielding voice matching it. Telling her to move, to keep going.

She rose on shaky legs.

She was freezing, weak, and could barely stand. But she would not give him the satisfaction of faltering.

The guard grabbed her hands painfully behind her back and led her down the hallway. Relieved in a sick way because otherwise she would have collapsed at the glance at Link’s cell door. A small shred of hope that he was still there, that she had heard wrong.

But the door was open, blood splatter they hadn’t bothered to wipe away, coated the stone floor of the empty cell. She would have shed a tear, but she hadn’t the energy to let one fall.

The long, dark hallway opened to a large room; there were guards everywhere. Some sitting and relaxing, others sharpening blades, playing cards, one even eating a banana. Such casual acts for men of evil.

Some wore their masks, others didn’t bother. White hair, red eyes. They looked so normal— as normal as everyone in Kakariko Village had looked. She wouldn’t have been able to pick them out of that crowd had she wanted to.

The guard hadn’t spoken a word as he marched her up staircase after staircase. Only huffing an exasperated breath each time she stumbled. Each room was larger and uninviting than the next, dark with no sunlight and little firelight. Guards of all sizes littered throughout but all in the same red uniform, that she could still see in the shadows.

Darkness birthed them, raised them, nourished them.

She thought about escaping. Pulling the move she had with the guard before her capture, but there were too many others around to easily recapture her. And she was kidding herself with misguided hope that she could even run, let alone escape. Instead, she scanned every room, making mental notes on the path they took. He hadn’t blindfolded her, which either meant they were confident she would never escape or this would be her tomb.

They walked for what seemed like forever. Her legs were barely able to continue as they climbed a seemingly endless amount of stairs. She had put on considerable muscle while in Hyrule, but days, or weeks, in her cell had atrophied her, and not eating didn’t help. She was rotting away from the inside.

As she was about to beg the guard to give her a break, they stopped. She lifted her heavy head to gaze above her.

A large man with tawny-grayish skin sat upon a throne. Shades were drawn on the windows, and a red carpet was lining the staircase to where he sat in the middle of a second-story balcony. The room smelled of copper and rot. The smells of death seeped into the stone.

The room struck her with familiarity; it disoriented her. But she’d never willingly be in a room so foul.

The guard pushed her shoulders to the ground. She slammed to her knees. As her palms hit next. She bit back her wince at the pain singing through her limbs.

“Zelda,” the large man said her name like a caress as his amber eyes drilled into her. “Good to meet you, finally.”

His voice was deep like the ocean, but cruel and wicked. His flame-red hair was pulled into a low ponytail, meticulously in place. He was adorned in gold, from the circlet on his forehead to earrings and a necklace. He wore black clothing that draped over his shoulder and waist, leaving the opposite bare with no armor. He didn’t need it; the sheer size of him was monstrous and built of pure muscle, enough to deter any foe that took one look at him.

Yet, despite his dark appearance, he was dangerously… alluring. There was an air of casual arrogance, something that could be considered attractive.

She couldn’t take her eyes off him.

He smiled. Perfect white teeth glittered in the dark room. “Leave us.”

The guard scattered faster than hunted prey.

It was just them. Her on her knees and a living weapon on a throne. She wasn’t bound. And she didn’t need to be as she laid her hands flat on her thighs, in an effort not to focus on the pain.

“You are probably wondering who I am and what you are doing here.” He drawled. “I am most intrigued to meet you after so much time. And that is… telling, considering I don’t care for most.”

Zelda hid her confusion, her face a mask of nothingness as she tried to focus on him rather than her aching limbs.

“Of course,” he continued, irritation flickering, “it would have been easier and quicker for us to meet had she not made it so difficult every step of the way.” He snarled.

Impa?

He held his hand up, catching his own composure. “First, let me introduce myself properly.”

He stood, his frame towered over the throne. “I am Ganondorf, Rightful King of Hyrule.”

She couldn’t hide her shock as she blanched. King of Hyrule?

Where was the king she had bowed to the night of the ball, Princess Zelda’s father?

And his name… it sounded so horribly familiar. The name old and hateful. She searched the cobwebs of her sanity to where she had heard it. But like her muscles, her mind had become soft.

“By your expression, I’m sure you are confused. Let me start at the beginning. We have some time before we need to begin.” He sat again, this time she didn’t miss the large curved sword on his right. Anything or anyone that crossed that unsheathed blade was now dead. There was no doubt in her mind.

“I am Gerudo born, the first male in a century. I was born to lead my homeland, to rule. When it was my time, my ideas were deemed too extreme, too narrow-minded. Those who opposed me kept my throne from me. I was excommunicated and cast out of my home.”

He continued, as if he were reading her his favorite bedtime story. “They thought I would sit and take it. But alas, I honed my power. I sharpened my mind to better understand my enemies. I discovered sorcery— ancient and runed within me, that forced monsters to obey me. I encountered those who were like-minded, and they all bound themselves to me. I used this to position myself with Hyrule, as an ally, an equal.”

She was too weak to hear him right. No person leverages monsters and an army to position themselves as a friend to the crown.

“The useless fool who sat here before me? He was weak. He didn’t see my vision for what we could have been, the greatness that could have been Hyrule, so he cast me out of his hall.” He angrily spat. “So to prove him wrong, I infiltrated this castle in mere days, killing him as punishment.”

Zelda’s eyes were wide, she fisted her hands to stop from shaking, and her nostrils flared, holding back a sob at the realization. The room was familiar because she had been here before. They were in Hyrule Castle, in the Sanctum, where Link and she had danced.

And then she noticed the pattern on the center of the floor, the three symbols, the three stones. The tapestries were pulled down and discarded. Every candle was unlit.

The thought of him and that night had her painfully swallowing. 

He laughed. Laughed at murder. “Now I sit upon his throne. My throne as king. All who oppose me are dead, or soon will be.”

She dared be brave as she managed to look him in the eyes. “What does that have to do with me?” If he thought she was Princess Zelda, let him continue that belief. Protect her, protect the last shred of hope Hyrule has, for the land Link loved so much.

He smiled, slow and cunning. “Because, to assure my victory, I will use the Triforce to make my wish, and because you are the goddess reborn, I need you to do it.”

She hid the scowl forming but not what came out of her next. “Are you unwell? I am no goddess.” She spat back at him, uncaring for his wrath; she had nothing more to lose.

But rather, he delighted in her defiance, his features serpentine. “The goddess Hylia, always so bold.” He smiled to himself. “And always reborn at the time Hyrule needs her most.”

Zelda looked at him like he was insane, but he continued in a playful tone, “I forgot you don’t know Hyrule’s legends and lore, being from a different era. Let me explain, it’s only fair you know why and who put you in this retched position.”

He knew.

He knew she was not the princess. He knew where she came from. Chills coursed through her, waiting on baited breath for him to continue.

“After the Golden Goddesses created our world and the Triforce, the Goddess Hylia was entrusted to protect it from my kin, Demise. He almost had it in his grasp, until she sent it away to the sky. A great battle ensued, and she defeated him, but he mortally wounded her. In her last act of defiance, she shed her divinity and power to transfer her soul to the body of a mortal so that she could use the power of the Triforce when the time came.” He audibly scoffed, presumably at the Goddess’ sacrifice.

He rose from his throne and started to slowly descend the staircase towards her. “For millennia, each time one of my ancestors rose to capture the Triforce, the Goddess and the Hero were reborn. Each time he was met with defeat at the hands of those two. You see, only the Goddess can obtain the Spiritual Stones to open the door to the sacred realm, and only the Hero can obtain the Master Sword, and both can only be reborn of the same line of ancestors. For the Goddess, that is the royal family of Hyrule. The Goddess reincarnated has always been the princess. But she was clever this time, as if she sensed that I was better, more determined than my previous forms.”

His bare feet smacked the floor as he stepped off the last stair. He had not bothered to wear shoes in his own throne room, his long shaw flowing on the floor behind him on a cruel wind as he stood directly in front of her. His giant form was endless as his amber eyes found hers. Then he turned his back to her, as if the mere sight of her disgusted him. She was but an insect, a pest.

He drawled, “She hid not in Princess Zelda of the present as she’d done before. But instead, she found another, deep within the line. She used the realm’s connection to time to find her, someone no one would have ever suspected, someone with no title, a nobody, only a drop of that royal blood.”

He turned to face her, his amber eyes glowing with malice and satisfaction. “You.”

Zelda had stopped breathing.

“I searched and searched for years. She was clever in her attempts to hide from me, but I was better. I found her on your 18th birthday. The day she cannot hide, the day she exposes herself as part of her new mortal shell.”

“I am no goddess!” She snapped and stood with unknown stamina. “I am not special, nor powerful. I would know if I was.”

He hadn’t flinched at her outburst. “That’s where you’re mistaken. The Goddess only exposes herself at times of need and when she enters the body, fusing to their soul, it causes a bit of a blowback.”

She searched her memories to that day. For any indication of a divine being merging with her. It had been like any ordinary July day, warm and balmy.

He waited, almost breathless as it hit her, like a blow to the gut.

She had fainted that day. She was standing in her bedroom. Blinding light overtook her vision, but only for a moment, like lightning, and then she was suddenly sick. She awoke on the floor minutes later as if nothing had happened. She hadn’t even told her parents. She didn’t want to worry them. She didn’t want to ruin the day.

Her face gave it away as Ganondorf wickedly smirked down at her. “I see you remember now.”

Had that been the Goddess? She had no way of knowing, so how did he? She couldn’t help her curious mind as she engaged in this lunacy. “How did you know?”

“I felt a nudge. A pull.” He tilted his head. “We are all connected.”

A pull.

“You’re the one who lured me to those monsters trying to kill me?”

He tightened his lips, his brows lifted in impressed delight. “You’re smarter than you look. Yes, that was me. But they weren’t supposed to kill you, just to bring you to me. But your hindrance of a knight made that near impossible, so each time I sent more. And it was clear when he slaughtered my most wicked beasts for you and how close you two had become after that. It made me rethink my strategy. Letting you and your knight fall in love, it was the perfect chance to capture you. So disgustingly distracted by each other, you never saw me lurking in wait.”

Link. Another brief moment she forgot he was dead. Her heart ached. He watched them for weeks, months, slowly falling for each other.

“Why couldn’t you have just captured me that day the Goddess showed herself?” She was angry, furious. Had he just captured her then, Link would still be alive.

“I tried the next day to capture you, but your wretched father stopped me.”

Zelda was gritting her teeth so hard, but she managed to breathe. “What?”

“I sent my minion to get you then, just as I did a year ago. This time, you fell through the portal to our world, except you didn’t fall where I intended. You fell in the middle of the castle.”

It was never an accident.

Ganondorf continued, ignoring that she placed her hand to her heart. Wildly, erratically, beating— it was the only place she could grasp to avoid caving into herself, as a bug would to defend itself. “The first time, the portal was open, but your father blocked you from going. So I killed him. And your mother.”

Everything was piercing. And silent. Her heart stopped. She knew because the thumping ceased and went to her head instead.

He said it so casually as if he was talking about a particularly annoying fly. The world started to spin as her heart resumed it’s beat in this horrible world her body existed in. She was barely able to continue to stand as water blurred her vision and she choked out in a whisper. “You killed them?”

He smiled. Smiled. Down at her from across the room. “Of course. Your mother knew of your destiny, of the Goddess. There were many things she hid from you, but I’m sure she told your father. That day I sent my minion to retrieve you, I had it all planned perfectly. By sending that beast to disorient you and your parents, that’s when it would drag you here. But… your father intervened. Causing me to have to wait two more years for my plan.” He gripped the hilt of his sword tight in frustration.

She met his stare, so intensely that an emotion she had never felt before bubbled to the surface. Tears escaped her but not from sadness, rather the raw anger she felt. “What did you do?” 

He was more than happy to continue. “Your father, so noble, like your departed knight-errant. He saw the beast and altered his course. He knew it was at the sacrifice of himself that you and your mother would live. Except your mother tried to protect you, as she knew of your destiny, perhaps she had always known. She didn’t have the Goddess’ full blessing but she did have enough to protect you. Her small golden light encircled you and my beast couldn’t touch you.” He paused and smirked. “So, I killed your mother in retaliation.”

All the air left her head. Her beautiful mother, so pure, so loving. Her smile could light up any room. And he stole that from her. All of her strength wavered as she yelled, “I would have gone with you willingly if you let them live!”

He chuckled, slowly, his deep voice echoing off the walls of the sanctum. “But they had to die. They would have ripped the worlds apart trying to get you back.”

He was the reason everyone she ever loved was taken from her. Her parents, Link. She fell to her knees, her hands hit the cold stone, biting into her palms. This time she welcomed the pain. She hung her head low, trying to stifle the sob working its way up her throat.

Her father, so strong and noble. She hadn’t realized it but Link was so much like him. He loved her. And her mother. And not in the basic way a father should love his family. He would have gone to the ends of the earth to protect them. He was good and righteous and honorable. And her mother… too good for this world.

All of it made sense. It was the final missing piece. Her mother knowing Zelda’s Lullaby. Calling her ‘my little goddess’ as a fond nickname throughout her childhood. When she was upset, she told her about the golden light inside of her, there to protect her when she could not. Even her name, Zelda, her grandmother’s name, and hers before, a long line of Zeldas for the goddess to choose from.

Zelda closed her eyes, violently cracking open the memory of her parent’s last moments. The memory she suppressed deep inside of her. The one buried in that well she never tapped.

The car was upright. Then sideways. Then upright again. The smell of ethanol stung her nose; it was hard to gasp air. Her eyes were heavy, too heavy, but she managed to open them, the darkness of the night stark against the harsh fluorescent light from the car. Her head was pounding, as if a chainsaw was cutting through it. The car was smashed, the roof caved in. Her head swam as she tried to gasp her surroundings. Her father lay in the driver’s seat. His head at an impossible angle. One that no one could survive. The beast— now she knew to be a lynel— it’s thick arm retracting from where it was on her father’s throat. She stalled as her mother was gasping her last breaths in the passenger seat, blood everywhere, matting her short yellow locks. Her matching green eyes locked onto Zelda’s. They were pleading. Every ounce of strength zapped from her. Zelda looked at her own body as she lay sprawled in the back of the car; there was not a scratch on her. She was in a bubble of golden light. She looked back to her mother, that beast rounding the car to seal her fate, the same fate as her father. She hadn’t heard her mother’s last words then, but her soft voice, chimed in her head— or maybe the bubble distorted it, ‘You are the light when everything is dark. Let your wisdom guide you when all seems lost. Remember you will always be Zelda first.’ The world went deathly still as the beast lurched and her mother took her final breath as Zelda passed out.

Zelda clasped her hands to her mouth to strangle her cry, but a small, broken noise escaped. The room pulsed around her, the rate of her heartbeats. She sucked in a harsh breath as she opened her eyes; the grey stone floor was blurry in her vision. She had blocked everything from that night out of her head. Too painful to face.

She wondered if death would be easier. To know peace, then to know this horror.

She lifted her head to face the monster who had stolen everything from her. The rage and the anguish mixing within her soul made her numb as he smirked at her. She had not thought in that moment as she lunged from her knees and charged at him. To do what, she didn’t care. Have him cut her down, end her misery.

He was much, much larger than her.

But she charged.

As she got close, he cranked his arm back and swung. She went flying across the room.

The pain of her body hitting the wall was welcoming. At least she still felt something.

“Foolish.” He spat. He hadn’t even tried to throttle her, but his brute strength was far beyond the pale.

Every muscle in her body ached, blood filled her mouth, and she may have broken her arm too. But she would not give him the satisfaction of laying broken; she managed to sit up with her good arm while the other hung limp. “Kill me then and be done with it!”

“I admire your courage, but no, I have no plans to kill you. Yet. I need you alive; I need you to open the Sacred Realm. You hold the Triforce of Wisdom. And holding you will lead the holder of the Triforce of Courage right to me. It’s destiny.”

She spit blood. “You killed the only man worthy of that title. No one will come.”

Link. Link would have been.

A scowl formed. “If that was true, then he was no worthy opponent. But alas, he was not the holder of the Master Sword; the keeper still has yet to reveal himself.” He narrowed at her, faltering for barely a second; something that worried him had crossed his mind, but he quickly resumed his glare. “Guard! Take her back to her cell. And make sure to bring her food and watch her eat it or force her if you must.” He had started to ascend the staircase back to his throne, his back turned to her. “Can’t have you trying to starve yourself before your time.”

A guard, maybe the same one that dragged her in, lifted her up, surprisingly tender, for how he had treated her earlier. He especially seemed gentle with her broken arm as he ushered her out of the sanctum.

As he led her back to her cell, and as she descended into each corridor, she noted the Hyrule crest littered in every detail. Carved, stitched and stamped. They were in the castle, in what was her home. Her apartment she shared so many memories in, only moments away from where she currently stood. Everything that was once vibrant and bright, now dark and cloudy. A permanent filter on the new world.

She arrived at her cell; the guard let go as she shuffled into the center and shut the large iron door. His voice was quieter than the others. “I’ll be back with food… and clothing.”

She moved to the wall, her broken arm burning and listened to the drip, drip, drip in the dark.

She didn’t bother to reply.

Chapter 36: Acceptance
Chapter Text
They had brought her new clothes— if they could be called that, calling them rags would be generous.

But she pulled them on anyway, hands moving without thought. The fabric scratching on her waist, the seams wrong. She didn’t bother to fix them.

She hadn’t had a bath or wash since she arrived. Her hair was losing its yellow color, turning ashen. Matted and full of knots, so thick her fingers snagged on the rat’s nest, she hadn’t tried again.

They’d brought her two, horrible heaps of what she guessed was food, but she hadn’t cared. She ate just enough to quell her rolling stomach.

The cell reeked of metal and mold. Damp earth. Rust. And beneath it all, copper, faint and lingering. Link’s blood baked into the stone. Taunting her.

The deafening silence sung to her, loudly. She tunneled into her own pit of despair, greeting the bottom of that chasm inside herself like an old friend. And as she dug deeper than she’d gone before, she looked to the walls, so high and so steep, desperately trying to grasp any scrap of comfort she could find, searching for the memories that brought her joy.

But there wasn’t any to be found.

She tried hard not to swallow. Not to think of the truth of her parents. Of Link. Any sob was too painful, more painful than losing them. The lack of water magnifying it.

Minutes turned into hours, hours into days, days into weeks. She lost count. There was no light to guide her. Despite what her mother said.

She slept, because at least in her dreams, her heart did not ache.

In her dreams, she was whole.

And he was still alive.

She dreamt that she was walking barefoot outside Link’s home—their home, the grass still wet with morning dew that she almost slipped on. The sun was shining, warming her face. The song in the air: of birds chirping, bugs singing, the wind blowing. Link came up behind her and wrapped his arms around her middle. He smelled of pine and home. She closed her eyes and smiled, letting her head fall back onto his chest. He grabbed her neck and tilted it towards his lips, kissing her deeply, savoring it, like they had all the time in the world.

She hadn’t known that would be the last time they kissed. The last time she would feel the warmth of his lips. The last time she would brush away his hair, the color of sand, yet so much softer. She turned in his embrace and met his eyes.

His eyes… she would never look into his eyes again. The blue that was not as light as the sky but not as dark as the ocean. Bright, cerulean, impossible. Like something the world shouldn’t be allowed to make, and yet had, just once, for him.

Maybe that was the dream all along.

She awoke to tears streaming down her face. The salt coating her lips.

She dreamt of an island floating in the sky. Vast stone, wind and strange, unfamiliar birds carrying people with pointed ears. Hylians. A large goddess statue guarding a temple. A sword calling to her. Looking for her.

The sword felt right in her hands once before. She crafted it of legends and steel that was not of the earth for the hero, her hero.

She was free falling, piercing the veil between sky and land. Forest, Mountain, Desert, no—oasis. Temples. Gates. A long, long sleep.

She felt the weightless position her body held in but she could not see, or smell, or feel.

She dreamt that she was there. Not dreaming, and not imagination... memories she never existed in. She had been there before, long, long ago. The images were like looking out of a foggy window.

She dreamt of her mother. Her golden hair. Her radiant smile. She was younger than when she last saw her. Zelda was little, her short legs didn’t touch the floor from her bed. She had a cut on her leg, a deep red gash, from falling off her bike. She was sweating from crying, her face hot and blotchy.

Her mother sat at the piano after bandaging her wound, playing a song Zelda didn’t know the name of, but her body knew it. The song is so hauntingly familiar. But not her lullaby. A slow, somber one, the tones dark and sad. Yet how the melodies were so tragic, yet captivating.

She gazed upon her mother, her eyes closed as her deft fingers pressed each key from memory. A lone tear traced the curve of her cheek.

The song of healing.

She said when she’s finished, kneeling to her eye level, cupping Zelda’s leg, ‘to heal, you first need to break and sometimes breaking can be beautiful.’

Liar.

She dreamt about the ball. The transcendental emerald dress, the gems sparkling like stars in the candlelight, the fabric hugging every dip and hollow. She had never felt more stunning, more belonging.

Her hand lay on his shoulder, his hand on her waist. He twirled her in and out, his hot breath searing her neck. He pulled back with a smile of desire and need and love. She so badly wanted to kiss him on that dance floor, for all of Hyrule to see. He was hers and she was his.

Then later, the most magical night of her existence. His hands running up her thighs, the delicious pleasure of his touch, his mouth, his tongue. His smell of pine and leather lingered in her lungs as she knocked her head back and cried out for him. The sounds of her dress, her exquisite dress, hitting the floor as she turned bravely to face him.

The look on his face was indescribable as she laid bare before him. As she was the goddess he wanted to worship. His warm body flushed with hers as she buried her face in his neck, breathing him in and crying out for him yet again. Gasping for air against the white-hot rolling in her core as he pushed into her.

She rudely awoke, heartbreak feeding her despair at realizing that she would never know his touch again. Never feel his kiss, how he had always placed a hand on her face before he lowered his lips. The way his hands were steady as they slid on her, rough but soft. She let a sob escape her; she didn’t care who heard.

She sensed his presence with her now, his spirit still chained across the hall.

Don’t go.

She dreamt of a field full of fresh snow and boot prints. Lines of pine trees— Christmas trees, in neat rows. Her small legs were running, full of excitement, searching and searching, holding out her hands, brushing on each of their branches, watching the snow tumble in glittering dust.

A male voice— powerful, yet gentle, yelled for her. Calm and patient and kind, with a hint of worry.

Her father.

She found the perfect tree, and he found her.

Zelda threw a snowball at his head.

His short, russet hair dusted with the feathery light snow. His matching eyes found hers with a smile as he shook it free. A sight that was soft and rare. He should have smiled more. It suited him. It matched his soul.

A traditional bow saw slung over his shoulder. Asking her if this is the one. The right one that she chose each year for them. Their tradition.

The man had a calming stillness about him. Reserved and wise but strong and protective.

He pushed and pulled the saw at the trunk. The sap was coating the blade.

And surrounded by pines, their tree’s scent filled the space, smelling of kindness, love, and safety.

She dreamt of a land blanketed in amber and gold. Dusk. 

Twilight.

The hero was a beast, aided by her dark counterpart. The same sword locked in an ancient forest. Singing. Begging, to be found.

It was as if she was there, viewing her kingdom from high above.

She was locked up tight in the castle until she gave part of herself away, handing something precious to the Twilight Princess. To save Hyrule, to save the hero.

When she awoke, her arm was healed.

Or perhaps it was never even broken at all.

She dreamt of the beach. Her boots were off in the grass. Her bare feet in the sand. The rough beads tickled but delighted her feet. The wind rustled and lifted the stray sand and pelted her skin. The salt air was absorbing in her hair, becoming thick and wavy.

They were walking back, and a storm caught them. They hid in a tree, and the abruptness of the weather was in tune with her. She wanted him; she wanted the sand from his skin to mix with her own.

He said, “I love you,” between pants. But his voice, the tone slipped away. She couldn’t remember if it was more of a medium pitch with a low whisper, or if it was strong and clear. Or how he finished on “I love you,” was it more of a croak or husky and breathless? She couldn’t remember, and she played it out in her head.

She was forgetting his voice. Forgetting him.

Where does that grief go when not resolved?

She woke hugging herself, balled up against the cold wall, sobbing into her knees.

She dreamt that she was in disguise as a young man. Hiding from Ganondorf’s reach.

Her gut told her, as a child no more than ten, that he was evil. She tried to tell the King, her father, but not her father. He wouldn’t listen. Ganondorf was an ally, securing trade deals with Hyrule; he wouldn’t betray him.

But he did; he killed him, causing her to flee the castle, to flee her home.

She hid for years. Seven long years deep in the sanctuary of the forest. Then the hero awoke, and she aided him in disguise. Disguised as a Sheikah. Watching him complete his tasks, watching him save the people of Hyrule, her people.

How could the Goddess do it each time? Not fall for this new hero?

She dreamt about university.

Philosophy class, gazing upon her professor’s salt-and-pepper hair as he turned his back to them in the lecture hall. He was writing on the chalkboard one word: Balance. His voice was hoarse and wet, like rubbing water on concrete, from years of smoking as he spoke to the class, ‘When you are joyous, look deep into your heart, and you shall find it is only that which has given you sorrow that is giving you joy. When you are sorrowful, look again in your heart, and you shall see that in truth you are weeping for which has been your delight.’ The quote from Kahlil Gibran.

In order to live a full life, a person needs a balance of joy and sorrow; it’s impossible to have one without the other. It is everywhere we are and see. Light and Dark. Yin and Yang. Two sides of the coin. If you have not known pain, you do not know joy.

Her professor continues, ‘for he who neither enjoys much nor suffers much, because he dwells in that grey twilight that knows neither victory nor defeat.’

She burst as the icy air wrapped around her, rousing her from her dreams. Reflecting on that subconscious memory, the key.

She was living in that grey twilight. She lived in it for years. Her parents had died. She suffered. And ultimately she feared to accept it and move on, to find happiness. For fear that she would lose it. She kept herself closed off until she came to Hyrule. Until she met Link.

Her heart was ripped out of her chest; the pain of losing him was so great, because their love was extraordinary.

It was greater than anything; it defied time and space. It was fate. Goddess or keeper of the Triforce of Wisdom or just a vessel, it didn’t matter. Her love for him transcended it all.

And something strange bloomed in her.

Gratitude.

She was grateful, realizing that she would have rather known him for a moment than never at all. She would rather endure this inexplicable pain of outliving him than to have never seen his face, spoken his name.

Grief was an ocean, coming in waves, ebbing and flowing. Sometimes the water is calm, and sometimes overwhelming. All she could do was learn to swim. She knew enough about loss to realize that she would never stop missing them. She just had to learn to live around the gaping hole of their absence, to not fall in and drown.

To walk this earth, this land without him, the sleepless nights, the sorrow, she would carry him in her heart. She would live for him.

This time, she awoke from her dream but without pity.

She would not rot in misery like before with her parents. It took her two years to dig herself out of that hole, and yet with every lift of her shovel, she knew it would never cease. She had to adapt rather than bury it.

She survived monster attacks, she survived Cole’s betrayal, she survived Link’s death, and she would survive this.

She wasn’t strong. But she would be brave.

She opened her eyes, fierce determination laced the lines of her face as she thought to herself.

I am resilient.

I will fight.

 

She pressed her spine against the cold stone, knees drawn in tight to her chest, and she stared at the flickering light through the barred window. Somewhere beyond, the drip, drip, drip sounded in steady intervals as she replayed every cruel word Ganondorf said to her, trying to weaponize anything against him.

If he had killed the King, where was Princess Zelda? Was she dead also? Or if she was alive, would she rally her allies and try to fight back? How many perished in these very halls once he took the castle? The same knights she smiled and laughed with at the dining hall? When did he overthrow and storm the castle? While she and Link spent their time in Hateno? Had they been less distracted, would they have avoided capture? Had a fighting chance? Where was Impa? Were Fledge and Ilya safe?

The questions were swarming her. And she was too weak to logically press on them all.

She had to focus her mind on the things she could control.

She glanced at the small, dainty ring on her right hand. The golden band gleamed on her finger, a bright contrast to her dirt-streaked skin. The triangle her mother gave her on her eighteenth birthday, the only piece of jewelry she kept. Her mother’s words ringing in her head: ‘Knowing yourself is the beginning of all wisdom.’

Perhaps the key was in those words. A riddle that only the Goddess could solve. Being a divine being brought endless wisdom upon oneself… right?

A divine being trapped helplessly in a cell.

She had never felt any different; she scoured her memory for any shred or spark of the goddess’ divine power lurking in the depths of her soul.

In her haze of grief from the week’s past, she dreamt of a sky island and Hyrule coated in twilight. But they weren’t dreams— they were… memories. Memories she herself had not lived but rather squinting through a fog, familiar yet unfamiliar. Could that be the Goddess’ own memories of time past?

Ganondorf mentioned this had continuously happened for eons. The Goddess, the hero, and his hateful spirit in battle, each time the former rising to defeat his incarnation. A hero would rise and aid the Goddess. Even as the formidable force she once was, capable of leveling entire battlefields, it wasn’t enough for her to face him alone.

She straightened herself, her spine painfully digging into the stone. That was it.

She could defeat him by finding the hero of legend. Perhaps this hero unlocked her power; they were stronger together.

But that grief stung her throat as she tried to force it down, churning her stomach. The only person that was honorable enough to be the hero was Link.

She shook her head and swallowed, inhaling the copper and iron.

Instead, she stood on trembling legs and came up with a plan.

She paced around her cell for hours. Her plan was shaky at best, but it was what she had given her resources.

No, her plan was mad. But a plan, nonetheless.

A guard came at least twice a day with food, and every few rotations, new clothing. They would open it enough to see her on her sad excuse of a cot and take whatever food she left. Because the door locked from the outside and swung inwards, they left the door open until they left. Only ever one guard at a time, trusting she was too weak, too broken to try anything.

They would soon find out how wrong they were.

She would hide behind the propped door while a guard entered her cell. By the time they realized she was not on her cot, they would check behind the door, and she would be at the ready. She found a small rock from the sad state of her cell, not big enough to do damage on its own, but with enough force, she might be able to stun the guard long enough to disarm them from their weapon.

Each time a guard visited her, they were outfitted in the same red leather uniform and sheathed either a sickle or dagger at their hip, but either would do—as long as she didn’t cut herself in the process. After disarming the guard, she could lock them inside her cell and have ample time to escape. Even if the guard yelled or screamed, no one would hear them in the secluded hallway until another came in rotation.

It was far-fetched and completely absurd, but it would have to work. And if she failed, Ganondorf wouldn’t kill her. He needed her alive to open the Door of Time.

At least she repeated that to herself; it was the only thing keeping her newfound courage from faltering.

So she waited, behind the door for her chance to strike.

A sound echoed off the hallway. Footsteps approached.

She couldn’t tell how long she had waited. The silence put her in a trance, a meditative state.

The heavy footsteps approached closer, closer, stopping at her cell door. The key rattled in the lock. Her heart was hammering, so loudly she was sure the guard would hear it. She thought of Link, his bravery, his courage. She would do this for him.

The door creaked open, and the guard paused at the threshold. She held her breath, waiting for the perfect moment. They had to enter the cell for this work.

A black boot stepped into the cell, and they turned towards her hiding spot. Except she was crouched down, taking the guard a split second more to realize and react. But before that, she was already striking, one hand punching that rock into his groin and the other going for their weapon, this one being a large dagger sheathed in leather.

The blade was bright in her palm, as the guard fell to his knees, letting out a loud groan at the unexpected pain. She pointed it at him and edged around his body. She would use the dagger if she had to, but taking a life of an unarmed man was not the way she wanted this to start. However, she recalled Link’s severely battered state and realized that this one might have contributed to his suffering, and she could plunge the blade deep, if she had to.

She slammed the cell door shut, locking the guard inside. He hissed and swore something at her, but she didn’t hear him as she was already running down the hallway to freedom.

Except she didn’t know where she was going. She had never explored inside the castle before, only ever the exterior. She headed the opposite way of where they first led her to Ganondorf, as she recalled that first room looked to be a guard’s chamber. And while she might have a weapon now, there was no way she could take on one, let alone ten guards.

A larger room opened to her, lined with barred cells. These were coated in thick iron from ceiling to floor, allowing her to see their inhabitants.

Endless breeds of monsters caged behind them. Some she recognized and had previously encountered. Such as the lizard-like Lizalfos she unfortunately met in the desert, except these were in various colors of white, black, and blue. Something as tall as the ceiling inhabited the other cells, some with long noses, surely able to smell their prey from miles away.

They immediately clocked their glowing eyes on her, snarling, menacing.

She ran down the pathway; it was too late to draw less attention to herself, all dancing and screeching at her presence.

She turned down a hallway, and it was a dead end. As she turned back, a guard’s voice echoed off the walls.

A narrow crack in the wall was all she had to hide behind. She slipped in between the rough stone, ripping her already tattered clothing, to discover a hidden room, no larger than a small closet.

She held her breath, only hearing the monsters wailing and footsteps. Firelight shone through the crack. She willed the piercing deafness in her head to cease.

Silence. Every one of her senses frayed.

Then a crash. The rock wall that was sheltering her was gone. A guard stood in front of her. “What do we have here?”

Fuck.

Despite not being able to see his face through the haunting white mask they all wore, she was sure he was smiling underneath. Amused at the attempt she made.

She still had the dagger. She refused to die in her cell. She would not aid the man who had killed everyone she had ever loved. She would fight and die or escape. No other option. She lifted her chin and her dagger, willing herself not to shutter. To be brave.

She had never even held a blade to a position. The blade Urbosa had gifted her, she had never been trained with it. And she vowed in that moment that if she made it out of this, she would. Until her palms cracked with calluses and welts.

The guard stepped forward.

But before she could lunge, he fell.

A dagger plunged directly into his heart from the back. And he fell like a towering tree, gasping a wet cough before falling silent in death.

Another guard stood in front of her now, identical to the last. Unspeaking, he lifted a finger to his lips, to not say one word.

And before she could react, he was pulling the guard into the small area she was found in and covered his body with rocks.

He made quick work of concealing the body, then turned to her. Only muttering two words from under his mask, “Trust me.”

His voice was quiet and familiar. He grabbed her waist, holding her powerlessly against the wall of the small chamber as he positioned himself to be flush with her body. He smelled of leather and something ordinary. Yet before she could open her mouth in defiance, two guards silently appeared in front of them through the narrow slit.

She stiffened as they paused. Her captor—or perhaps her savior—eased his grip on her waist. All but suggesting that he was helping her.

 The two guards disappeared back down the hallway just as they appeared.

The guard holding her eased and backed away. But as fast as lightning, he grabbed her hand and led her down the same pathway. He was stealthy like the others, only hearing her own steps on the wet stone before turning down the lock-up that held the monsters. He guided her down an alternative corridor. Not the path back towards her cell.

After minutes of walking, the tension she felt radiating from him as he gripped her hand started to relax. He was nervous but still had not muttered a word. He was built like the other guards, wore the same outfit, but there was an unexplainable warmth to him. Nonetheless, she still had her guard up, but something in her told her to obey.

The end of the corridor led to a large passage equipped with a railway and cart. Perhaps this mode of transportation had always been here, part of the secret passageways of castles this size, or perhaps her rescuer had planned this. He let go of her hand and motioned for her to get into the cart. She climbed in, stiff with suspicion, dagger still tucked in her hand. He followed her and cranked a lever as the cart lurched forward, rattling loudly through the dark channel.

After gut-wobbling twists and turns. Light appeared ahead. Grey light, but still brighter than what her eyes had become accustomed to in the past few weeks as she squinted painfully the closer they came. Wind hit her face, real air at last, not like the staleness of her cell. But it was coated in carrion and smoke.

She was able to adjust her eyes to see water. Moat water, dull beneath a dead sky. Before she could truly register her surroundings, the cart was plunged into darkness yet again.

It twisted down another narrow passageway and stopped. The guard ushered her to quickly follow him down a hidden path, rocks freshly laid around as if they had been blown up for this very purpose. The urgency in the guard’s body language had told her everything about the risk he was taking to get her out.

They reached a cliff’s edge, with nowhere to go but up.

The mysterious guard cocked his head for her to follow him as he ascended the cliff, a small rope dangling for support. She barely managed to hold onto the rope as she grabbed the next level of rock; her muscles were barking at her, so weak from her time in her cell. She hated the fact that she wallowed in her own despair for so long rather than keep her newfound strength up.

Her hands were bloody and burning by the time she hung on the cliff edge, trying to pull herself up. Her rescuer helped her the rest of the way as she barely made it the last few feet, snaking his arms under her shoulders to lift her. The touch felt wrong and foreign.

He set her down as she recoiled. He quickly dropped his hands as she glared at that unfazed white mask. He made no mention of the effort as he nodded his head for her to follow down the narrow pathway against the cliff face.

She was able to get a better look at her outfit in the overcast light. Similar to her usual travel garb, except dirty and ripped. She supposed Ganondorf didn’t need her to look good as she rotted away in her cell. The colors were muted and blended well enough against the landscape, much less noticeable than the red leather of her rescuer’s uniform. They carefully followed the narrow path, climbing up or down as needed, until the rescuer stopped abruptly.

They were now under the Hyrule drawbridge, the shadows from the rock face shielded them from any aerial view. As she got her bearings and caught her breath, the guard took off his mask, and she knew the face that greeted her. A young man with grey hair and blood-red eyes.

Grante.

Link’s fellow knight who competed against him in the tournament, long, long ago. The same knight who dined with them on many occasions.

She squeezed her eyes shut and opened to be sure her mind hadn’t lied to her as she stared at her savior in disbelief.

But he was not paying attention to her; he looked beyond her into the darkness and spoke softly, “You don’t have much time before they realize she’s gone. Head towards Kakariko; they’ll be waiting for you.”

She then felt the presence of another, cloaked in the shadows. A figure stepped forward, quiet and controlled, dressed in raven black and hooded. She could not see their face, but against the stark contrast of the darkness, a glowing blade in their hand. It was majestic, ethereal. Its hilt was pale indigo and adorned in gold.

The figure stepped forward into the light, too still, too measured, and her knees nearly buckled.

Their face was covered, except for their eyes, and she would remember those eyes anywhere. She’d been dreaming about them for weeks.

Link.

Chapter 37: Destiny p.II
