But the truth was, it just wasn’t where I wanted it to be, and I couldn’t bring myself to post and not give it the attention it deserved first. I so want to petition AO3 to have an “update from the author” feature.

That said, this chapter is an extra long one, and it comes from the point of view of our missing lead. I really hope you enjoy spending time with him again. Thank you for your patience, your kindness, and for still being here. I’m hoping to settle back into a shorter posting schedule again soon.

Chapter Text
His head throbbed, and his body felt weightless as a soft, spun fabric grazed his nape.

The smell of groundwater, musty and moldy, burned his nostrils. The sounds of cracking and popping, then faint voices that neared closer. Metallic grit scraped his teeth and traced to his lungs, which were full of daggers and acid. Something had been forced down his throat.

The ceiling above him was crowded with blue torches, their glow splintered across the rough stone.

He shifted his body. Ignoring the stiffness and soreness in every joint, every muscle. He was on a bed. A cot. In a cave.

He looked down at foreign clothes and bandages surrounding his legs and hands, tight enough the throbbing matched his head. Anything not covered was littered in bruises turning shades of brown and purple. He adjusted himself, suppressing a wince from the gnawing pain.

Then he caught sight of his wrists.

Deep lacerations lay on his skin. Raw angry flesh where rough iron rubbed him. Manacles that held him.

The memory hit him like a drop to the depths.

They were ambushed by the Yiga Clan. He tried inch by desperate inch to reach Zelda, but they strategically overwhelmed him, creating a wall between them. A sea of red and white against the backdrop of the perfect afternoon. He’d never seen them fight before, the traitors to the crown, but they were inhumanly quick and splintered out of thin air.

He cut down one after another, but each time he defeated one, two more appeared in their place. They fought like Sheikah masters, hard to defeat in practice, let alone a dozen monopolizing him.

Then he chanced a glimpse at Zelda, just as she folded over herself, her hair whipping as she fell and the blunt end of the foot soldier’s sickle over her head. And before the cold rage flushed through his veins could thrash, pain surged through his ankles. The innocuous-appearing gash was bleeding profusely on the sandy shores of the river as his knee hit the ground. And everything went dark.

Only the repeating sound of her cry haunted his subconscious before he awoke in a cell.

At first, he didn’t know where, but the dank stone walls slick with condensation and the ancient Hylian runes carved above the archway marked it unmistakably as the Hyrule Castle lockup. Reserved for high-priority prisoners, traitors, and those awaiting royal judgment, it had no bars to rattle, no windows to gauge the passing of time, only a solid metal door with rust-eaten hinges and a sorry-looking bed with a sagging, mildewed mattress.

He jerked his arm, but resistance pulled. He was chained and sprawled out on the dungeon floor.

Pain slammed into him like a wave, as if it had been waiting for consciousness to return before unleashing its full fury. Every inch of him screamed in protest, the mottled bruises painting his skin, the eye swollen so tight he couldn’t see through it, the raw cuts where his own teeth had torn into his cheeks. His ankle throbbed beneath a mess of half-dried blood, and by the watery feeling pulsing in his other leg, he knew it was broken. He couldn’t recall the beating that had left him this ruined.

Yet the most pain was the image of Zelda’s head bouncing off the ground.

Then— a muffled, broken sob hit his ears. It was her, she was alive. In the cell across the way.

Relief hit so hard that it was quickly replaced by shame and disappointment. He had failed her. Captured by the enemy Impa warned him about just a short time before. He didn’t deserve her, but he would get her out, save her, even if he had to gnarl through his own flesh.

Days passed, and his body barely healed. He spoke to Zelda through the walls and kept his voice steady, kept his pain grounded. He hadn’t wanted to tell her about the scent his own body started to ooze. How the smell had him choking. Decay, infection, disease. All probable and possible.

Then the guard opened their cell doors. The look on her face broke him far worse than any of the injuries he already had.

The guard threatened to kill him; he shut her cell door, and Zelda screamed, screamed his name, as she clawed at the iron door.

He rubbed his brow, trying to remember what happened. Clawing at his own memory, with as much ferocity as she had.

His head was hung down, neck exposed, his arms in chains. The Yiga Blademaster lifted his Windcleaver to deliver the blow. He tried to tell Zelda he loved her. But before he could swing—

The Blademaster was falling, a dagger plunged into his heart. By another guard, who then promptly covered Link’s mouth, and he passed out.

He shot up from the cot; he remembered it all. But where was he? Where was Zelda?

“Link.” A voice echoed nearby in the small cave.

He turned towards it.

Impa.

She was standing near the blue, smokeless fire, arms crossed, and dressed in Sheikah military gear. She looked as rough as he felt, dirt on her face, her clothes splattered in blood, her hair a frayed and tangled mess. He noticed two other Sheikah guards who had lifted their heads from a map drawn out on a flat rock and promptly returned to it under the flickering light.

“Impa,” he rasped, barely recognizing his own voice. “Where are we? Where is Zelda?”

“We’re in a cave in the Crenel Hills. A Sheikah safe house, of sorts.” This Impa had never let emotion get the better of her, but a slight tightness flexed in her jaw as she continued, “Zelda isn’t here.”

“Where is she?” His voice was lethally calm.

“She’s still in the castle, held as a prisoner.”

Dread, followed by panic and wrath, washed over him in a cold sweat. He recognized the castle lockup, but why? The Yiga had infiltrated the castle? Where was the king? Why were they targeted for capture? Why hadn’t Impa rescued them both?

So many questions, but he didn’t care except for one. He had to get Zelda out. He swung his legs out from the cot, his ankle was heavily bandaged, but the pressure seemed to hold as he scanned the room for his armor and sword.

“Your sword and guards are gone. We hadn’t managed to get those out.” She paused, “Don’t even think about trying to leave half-cocked. We need to talk first.”

“I need to get Zelda, that’s first.” He said, still looking around the room for any type of clothing and weapons he could find.

Impa marched over to him, her hand gripping his shoulder in the exact spot he’d been bruised, the pain flaring. “You are in no shape at the moment, and I already have a plan to get her back.”

He jerked his shoulder out of her clutch. “I don’t give a shit what your plan is. My plan is to save her. I won’t leave her in that cell a second longer than she needs to be!” He roared.

Impa was tense and calm, at odds with each other. “Leave us,” she said, still staring at Link as the two guards grabbed the map and hurried away up the single pathway.

“I know you love her, and love makes you do preposterous things, but you need to take a few minutes to listen to me first. Then, if you decide to go off and get yourself and her killed, that’s your choice, but my conscience will be cleansed.”

He hated her in that moment, more than he hated himself.

But he relented.

Impa crossed her arms and sighed. She looked tired, as if she had been on her feet for days without rest. “The castle was breached six days ago by the Yiga clan and a horde of monsters, working together. We were—” her voice was clipped, “—underprepared. I had sent out groups of soldiers to track the Yiga’s movements beforehand. However, I had never expected it was a trap, to lure our forces out.”

“I had been in Kakariko awaiting your return when I got the news. I only had a handful of Sheikah guards with me, so I sent them to search for you while I made my way to the castle. I made it down the northern pass when I had gotten word you and Zelda were captured. My guards saw the whole thing: how you were camped at the river bend and how the Yiga overran you.”

“We tried to cut off their path, but they were considerably quicker than us. Instead, I sent Grante to infiltrate and report back when he could. After a few days, he reported the worst. The king was dead, slaughtered in the sanctum after a brutal fight. Princess Zelda was missing, along with Sir Groose, with only vague reports that they had managed to flee, unknown to where. Most of the knights and soldiers still stationed in the castle were dead or imprisoned, and you and Zelda held in the royal lockup.” She let out an exasperated sigh, “And to make matters worse, we were in contact with each region’s respective leaders, but they had gone silent. Seemingly, every person in power was wiped away or disappeared.”

Link was almost afraid to ask the name of who could have orchestrated such a strategic coup, “By who?”

Impa’s face was tight with regret and fury. “Ganondorf.”

His hands gripped the sides of the bed, furrowing his brows in confusion, “That’s impossible.”

“It isn’t.” She said flatly, “I don’t know how he’s here, but I know why.”

Link didn’t ask; this time he was actually hesitant to hear the reply.

She looked at him pointedly. Telepathically trying to tell him everything he already knew. “He came for her. The Goddess Hylia reincarnate: Zelda.”

His stomach sank. The floor started to spin at his feet. If he hadn’t been gripping the bed, he would have fallen over.

He knew it in his bones, in his soul. Zelda, his Zelda, was the Goddess Hylia. The Goddess Hylia was Zelda. He buried that deep within him so long ago that he hadn’t bothered to consider how much danger she was in. Each time she obtained a Spiritual Stone, it led her closer to this disaster, this mess he left her in.

He hung his head in shame. His mouth was dry, but he managed to croak, “What does he want with her?”

Impa sat on the nearby chair across from him, unable to stand under the weight of the truth anymore. “He hasn’t revealed himself to her yet, but I can assume he means to open the Sacred Realm. And as you know from legend, he needs all three of the Spiritual Stones and the Triforce holders to do it. He already has the Spiritual Stones— plucked directly from you. He is the Triforce of Power and he will leave her— the holder of the Triforce of Wisdom— in captivity, hoping the Triforce of Courage holder will rescue her.”

He slowly lifted his head, the stillness stretching in the room as he met Impa’s red eyes. He silently urged her not to say it.

“Link, you need to go to the Great Hyrule Forest.”

“It’s not known if it’s even there.”

“It is.”

“I am not… that.” He snipped.

“I believe you are.”

He stood up, ankle screaming as he pushed past the barking pain. “I can’t be the Hero of Legend. I couldn’t even—” he choked on his next words, “—I couldn’t protect her.”

Impa watched him as it sunk in.

He couldn’t breathe. The pressure in his ribs ratcheted tighter with every word. Hero of Legend? The sword in the woods? The stories of that hero and his legendary sword that had been told to him since he was a boy. The same sword that every respectable knight wanted to claim but did not because the price was too high. The price of wielding it in a time of desperation— a price too steep.

“I don’t even know where it is. No one does. Anyone who enters that forest is never seen again.”

Impa was too calm. Too steady and rational that it made him want to rage. “It’s there. Guarded by the Forest Spirit. Only the hero is able to navigate the woods, the first trial, then once arriving at the sword, only they are able to draw it.”

He sat back down. The air eddied out of his head. The blade of evil’s bane. The Master Sword.

“I know you believe you are unworthy because of what happened,” Impa’s voice was firm yet soft, “but you embody everything that is the essence of the reincarnated soul of the hero. You are an exemplary knight, bound by honor and courage, and you have the mastery to take down any foe. Not to mention, chosen specifically by the Goddess Hylia. Isn’t it fitting you and Zelda already chose each other?” Impa rose from her seat to walk towards the map. “I was so focused on her, on Zelda, and those Spiritual Stones, I forgot about the Master Sword and its master. Destined to fight evil, together. The bearer of the Triforce of Courage.”

It just— couldn’t be.

His head burned. His hands shook. He tried to will it away, to find some handhold of normalcy, but every breath was sharp. Him, the legendary hero chosen by the Goddess Hylia— by Zelda. His Zelda. Servant and master, destiny bringing them together.

“He will use her to open the Sacred Realm, to manifest the Triforce, to destroy our world. He’s already unleashed hordes of monsters and the guardians across Hyrule, all controlled by malice. We can’t fight them on our own; all we can do is hide and pray.”

Link snapped his head to her at the word. Guardians.

The Sheikah technology they unearthed years ago. Meant to aid Hyrule in their time of need. But they left them buried, not needing them, either because of ignorance or belief that the world was good. The horror he felt churning in his gut, remembering the sheer power of those machines.

More than killing power. Annihilation-type power. And Ganondorf has control of them all.

“All the more reason I need to get her now! If she is the Goddess, I need to protect her from him.”

Impa turned from the map, the frustration palpable on her face. “You clearly haven’t been paying attention. If you go to her now, you risk the very thing he wants: to capture you both. You do not wield the Master Sword; trying to stop him now is a death sentence for you both.” He felt the exasperation in her voice, “Sometimes you need to lose the battle in order to win the war.”

He closed his eyes. And although his eye had been swollen shut at the time, he could still see as clear as an autumn day, the agony on Zelda’s face as she looked upon him in horror from her cell. The grey stone and rusted metal dimmed her radiant light. Her scream echoed as the guard shut the cell door, mistaking his execution for a real one.

He shook his head, the memory of her face as the door shut clawed at his insides like a wild animal trying to escape. His lungs felt crushed beneath the weight of his failure. He couldn’t leave her there, alone and terrified, while he sat here safely discussing strategy.

His voice emerged as a ragged whisper, not to Impa but to anyone who would listen, “How can I call myself a knight, let alone a man that loves her, if I am willing to turn my back on her?”

As if Impa were personally privy to the war he was fighting, she quietly stepped in front of him. “I know you were coming back to ask for leave with Zelda, to live in Hateno with her, to return to your parents’ house. I want that for you and her. I want you both to have a long, happy life, but you will surely die if you continue on your current path. At least with the Master Sword, you give her a chance. You give yourself both a chance to build that life together.” She gently lifted her hand to his shoulder. “I have Grante looking after her. He will ensure her safety while you do what is necessary. All I am asking for is time while you obtain the sword, so you can rescue her and fulfill your destiny together.”

He locked eyes with her, every fiber of his being yearning to defy her, but she was right. He had to give them a fighting chance at happiness, at the life he had promised her.

“I’m going now.” He said deflated.

“I would expect nothing less. Come.” As Impa led him to the map on the table to discuss the trip. And he wondered even if he rescued Zelda and she forgave him, could he ever forgive himself?

After hours of planning and discussion, he headed north, still bandaged and bruised but able to walk and swing a sword.

Impa provided him with Sheikah gear and weaponry. The tight, quiet fabric would help him evade the guardian stalkers that were crawling over the main roads, and a hood and mask to help disguise him from any Yiga Clan members that were actively looking for Hylian knights and soldiers. The dagger and short sword were not what he was accustomed to, but it would do the trick if he encountered any monsters in his way.

By the next day, he stood before the Woodland stable—or what remained of it. The once-welcoming structure loomed skeletal against the stone-colored sky. Overturned pails of hay lay scattered, while abandoned clothing hung limp from posts. Silence pressed against his ears where there should have been the comforting sounds of people and horses. They must have fled when news of the castle’s fall reached them, either east toward the unforgiving slopes of Death Mountain or south to Lanayru.

Keeping to the shadows, he slipped past a group of bokoblins too busy fighting over a bone to notice him. The military training camp appeared on the horizon, or what remained of it. 

His throat tightened. He’d spent his boyhood here, running drills on those wooden crosswalks, now reduced to charred splinters. Swords and shields lay half-buried in mud, their owns nowhere to be seen. A guardian’s handiwork, unmistakable in its terrible efficiency. The attack must have Come without warning. 

How many brothers-in-arms were buried forever entombed under the rubble? He pushed past the anguish and continued on.

He knew he was close to the forest as the air visibly shifted in the shallow valley. Gone was the sulfur and carrion and smoke, and a deep, heavy fog rolled over the path. Everything had gone quiet, deathly silent. He swore he heard faint laughter echoing in the distance. A coldness seeped into his bones as he squinted his eyes to see.

Crows perched on the bare tree branches, glaring at him, daring him to continue.

He had entered the Lost Woods.

A single lantern burned in front of him, and a torch. He turned to his right to see more lining a pathway. He followed the clear sign without instruction.

After navigating through the lit fires, there were no more to guide him.

His brain felt heavy; he had barely rested since he left the hideout in Crenel Hills. He wouldn’t let Zelda sit in that cell any longer than necessary, even if it cost him his sanity from lack of sleep. But he had to be careful; no one who entered these woods ever came back.

The obvious path may have been straight north, but something in his gut told him it couldn’t be that simple. He examined his surroundings: the trees with their faces carved in spooky, twisted delight, daring anyone to enter; the fires lit by an unknown force; the spirits floating on the phantom wind.

Then he looked at the torch. The wind blowing was unnatural; following the torches before the wind was at his back, then his side, then his face. No natural wind would change directions that way in an open forest. He lifted his head up and watched the sparks float away and turned in that direction.

He continued to follow that spark until it unexpectedly switched to a new direction. Then again, and again. Only the haunted trees littered throughout, forever laughing and taunting him. The fog was becoming heavier but hadn’t swallowed him yet.

He tried not to think about the stories of this forest. Of those who were swallowed by the hostile fog. Becoming angry and bitter shells of themselves, their aims to slaughter and kill. Malevolent spirits. But that was legend. The same legends of the hero… and the sword.

After about an hour of cautiously following the wind, he started to wonder if he was truly lost and how stupid he was to think dying embers in the wind were the key. Until the fog started to lift against a small valley of rock. Golden light spilled through the thinning mist, revealing a path bordered by wildflowers. The position of the sun, which was directly overhead, told him he’d been wandering the woods for hours.

He slowly approached, his hand reaching for the dagger sheathed at his side, ready for anything to test him. And in the corner of his eye, he swore he saw a movement, a shadow of a small creature.

The elusive koroks that served the forest. All but a myth of a whisper.

Only those pure of heart can see them.

He entered a tunnel, and the slope dropped off into a glen. A gasp escaped through his mask at the sight below.

Rocks, shrubs, and healthy trees were sprinkled throughout the glen. And a cherry blossom tree larger than anything he’d even deemed possible stood tall as a pillar to the sky in the center of it all. It had to be eons old, there for millennia. It was the most serene scene he’d ever discovered.

His heart squeezed thinking about how Zelda would love it here.

And in the middle, a pedestal and a glint caught his eye.

A sword.

The Master Sword.

It was real. It was here. Impa was right.

In a trance, he approached the sword. It sang to him, in an ancient and otherworldly tone. In a language only he could understand. He stood in front of it, and by gazing upon it, he knew it was sharper and deadlier than any other blade he’d ever wielded, or perhaps existed. The magic of it glowing, calling to him, beseeching him to take it.

He carefully extended his hand to grab the hilt. The impossible color of the indigo hilt gleamed and was held in a thread of green. As he wrapped his hand around it, he was struck with visions as vivid as in the moment itself.

It first flashed to a sky temple, the blade manifesting into a physical guide. Then he saw a child grabbing the same hilt, and suddenly waking as an adult. Another vision passed, and it was surrounded by the sea, flooding all around. Then buried deep, deep in a temple with twilight blanketing the horizon.

He stumbled back, dumbstruck.

An ancient voice spoke, startling him, “Who is that?”

He looked up to where the sound rumbled from to hear the lazy stretch of a yawn; the tree was yawning.

Not just a tree. The Great Deku Tree. The guardian of Hyrule. Not just another legend that had been passed down.

“Well, well,” the old voice drawled, its tone in clear amusement, “it’s you. You finally decided to come here; better late than never.”

Surprised striped his features as he craned his neck up to reply, “You know me?”

“Of course I know you. I have been watching your journey for some time.” Its voice was sincere, not a hint of mockery, “I am the Deku Tree. I have been here since immemorial, watching over the blade of evil’s bane.”

He should have known the Great Deku Tree would know all; surely the spirits of the forest reported directly to him. “Then you know why I’m here.” Link looked down at the Master Sword.

The Deku Tree chortled in that kind and ancient voice. “Of course. But you should know before you claim it. That is the weapon created by the ancient Goddess. The sword that seals the darkness, that only the chosen knight can wield. What you saw was your counterparts, the heroes of old, wielding that very same sword.”

Link’s brows shot up, “You— you know what I saw?”

The Deku Tree shifted his features, as much as a nod as a tree could muster. “As you are now, I cannot say if you are worthy. You will surely lose your life where you stand if it does not deem you so.”

The small forest creatures, Koroks, peeked over roots to look at him, their curiosity getting the better of them.

Link positioned himself in front of the pedestal, his stance ready and extended, both hands gripping the hilt. Life in the grove seemed to stop in anticipation.

But he hesitated. His hands tightly wrapping around the warm hilt, his knuckles turning white, his fingers pulsing painfully, unable or unwilling to pull the blade.

“Do you hesitate because you do not feel worthy at this moment? Or because you do not trust that you are the chosen one?” The Great Deku Tree inquired of him.

Link could not lift his gaze from the blade to look at the Deku Tree. Instead, he shut his eyes. The first image to cross his vision was that of Zelda and her rotting in that cell. Followed by her screams that rattled inside his head.

“Yes.” He admitted in a whisper, more to himself.

“I see all that you have done. I have watched your journey with the Goddess. With your Zelda.” The Deku Tree’s voice deepened, resonating with the wisdom of countless centuries. “Remember this, young hero: courage is not the absence of fear, but acting despite it. You have both grown and come so far, and though the burden lies heavy, your shoulders have strengthened beneath it. The Goddess does not pick lightly, nor does she test beyond what can be endured. She chooses those with pure hearts, for only they can recognize darkness without becoming it.”

But does she choose failures? 

With a heavy heart, he positioned himself again in that familiar stance and grabbed the hilt and lifted.

The blade slid out of the pedestal, the edges snagging on the stone, sharpening it as he raised it further. And with a held breath, it was loose, and he was still standing.

He dropped his left hand, welding the Master Sword in his right. The blade was made for him, the weight was a perfect balance to his own. It felt right, better than any other blade he’d ever welded—an extension of his own limb. He tightened his grip to swing and stab and slice, cutting the air itself.

He swore the blade hummed to him, happy to have its master returned. He raised it skyward, closing his eyes, that silent prayer. To serve and honor the Goddess, but above all, to Zelda.

‘I love you.’

‘I’ve been in love with you since the moment I laid eyes on you.’

‘I’m yours. Forever.’

His eyes still closed, reciting that silent prayer in his head, the Deku Tree interrupted. “She continues to fight, her spirit trapped deep within the confines of Hyrule Castle. Her heart wells with grief for you, believing you are gone from this realm. But she resists, not only against the grief to swallow her, but against the evil design of Ganondorf. You both must fight more than one battle to be victorious.”

He nodded, sheathing the sword on his back, but before he could turn to leave the forest, the wise voice continued, “She has a smile like the sun. I would surely like to see it again.”

Her smiles— he closed his eyes, savoring each from memory. That first kiss in the pond, how her lips had curled up at one corner before meeting his, the water droplets catching moonlight on her lashes. The way her mouth had fallen open at the sight of Farosh, her eyes widening with childlike wonder before her teeth appeared, bright against her glowing eyes. After the Gerudo Desert, how her trembling smile had broken through fear, her shoulders finally relaxing as she’d reached for his hand. And in his kitchen— their kitchen— her smile so tender it had made his chest ache, as she’d whispered “I love you too.”

He wanted nothing more than to see her smile again too.

It had been 17 days and 16 hours since he saw her last.

Impa remarked that he had been in her care for over a week before he awoke from his injuries. Between the healing and the trek to the forest, another week had bled by.

And Zelda had been in that lockup longer.

He would have been able to go faster if he had a horse, but it was too risky. He was running himself ragged to get back to her. Barely stopping to rest or eat. His needs and comfort took a secondary priority to the hell she was in.

He was passing by the military training camp, cinders still smoking after the rain, as he headed southwest to take the quickest path towards the castle. The sun rose behind a dead sky to his back. At this rate, he would reach her by dusk.

But that’s when he froze, detecting the threat by Helmhead Bridge.

A guardian. The monstrous six-legged Sheikah killing machine, now effortlessly possessed by Ganondorf. Leveling villages and encampments, just like the one he passed, with just one blast from its single eye.

He froze, yet the Master Sword vibrated at his back, singing to him to unsheathe it.

He was not afraid of dying nor being bested by this monstrosity, but he was afraid that if he fell, Zelda’s horrible fate would be sealed. If he could avoid capturing the attention of it, he would be able to get to the castle and risk the delay.

But as he tried to slip away, the spinning head of the machine stopped, focusing its eye directly on him.

As if a fish to water, or birds to the sky— the guardian headed straight towards him— its only purpose to execute. Moving faster than anything he’d ever seen. He wasn’t even sure how it was possible.

He quickly reacted to his surroundings to prepare a defense. There was barely a tree standing that he could fit behind, so he withdrew back towards the leveled settlement with only broken foundations left. The guardian pursued him swiftly and possessively. Closing the distance to him within a matter of seconds. He heard the metal clanking and whirling the closer it came. As if in response, his back vibrated again.

The Master Sword.

He unsheathed the legendary blade, and it was zinging and gleaming with holy light.

The guardian’s sharp claws were mere inches from his hiding spot. He steadied his breath, waiting for the opportune moment to attack. Strategizing on how best to destroy or disable it. Listening to its head twist away. He’d have a few seconds to strike.

He took it, running out from his shelter to charge. Aiming that blade directly for the eye, but the machine found him quicker. Immediately aiming for him while simultaneously backing away at lightning speed. It was putting itself further away from him in its own defense.

It was sounding down in warning, and he was running as fast as he could, and within a split second, he swerved. The laser fired, just missing him by a hair as the ground behind him exploded. Dirt and rock rained down upon him, as he was thrust forward from the blast.

But he began again, that legendary blade giving him the courage— pushing past the burning in his legs, the ache in his ankle. The machine froze for a split second, just enough time for Link to lunge. He twisted his body mid-air, the Master Sword whistling as he brought it down in a vicious arc and before he could wonder what damage could be done.

He realized he did not wield an ordinary blade.

Metal screamed against metal as the blade cleaved through the guardian’s leg joint. Sparks erupted around him, sizzling against his skin as the severed limb crashed to the ground.

He continued in a semi-circle, not giving the machine a chance to catch up. Ancient gears and wires exploded outward in a shower of sparks that singed his forearm. The sword sang with each slice, as if it had been restless for too long and thrilled to perform.

The last chop had the machine slamming to the earth, disabled. And before the eye could whirl and focus on him, he was driving the holy blade into it. Ending its existence, as it effectively shut down, powering off for good.

He jumped back, pulling the blade from the socket. The ethereal glow now shut off like a switch, saving its charge for the next battle. And it was still just as sharp as when he yanked it, not at all dulled from cutting the legs off the guardian.

He looked off into the distance, and three more guardians scattered across the plain like spiders. And as much as he felt the heady power of adrenaline from this victory, he knew he barely succeeded in destroying this one. He wasn’t under any illusion he could triumph again so soon, let alone against three at once.

So he turned back.

He found himself back in the familiar rolling hills of Crenel. The path was clear through the foothills towards the castle; pockets of trees that offered him shelter between guardian stalkers and the castle.

But before he could start his descent, two matching Sheikah guards silently revealed themselves, ushering him to follow. A considerable part of him wanted to continue striding by, but he begrudgingly understood that information was more valuable than brawn— and most likely Impa had something for him before he fetched Zelda.

So he followed the two mute guards as they led him back through the maze of the cave where he initially woke up, directly back to Impa.

And she somehow looked worse. Exhaustion leaking out of every movement of her body, and the profound bags under her eyes indicated she had slept probably as much as he had this past week.

“I see my suspicions were correct.” Was all she said as she eyed the hilt that peeked over his right shoulder. Her arms crossed, neither pleased nor dissatisfied with the outcome.

Link only responded with a tight flex of his jaw.

“I will send word to Grante, who will break Zelda out when the timing is right.” She turned back to the desk with the map.

“That wasn’t the deal.” He said to her back, “I don’t need your permission to rescue her. I had not planned to even come back here, but guardians deterred me.”

“I know you don’t need my permission.” She said quietly. “Come here, take a look.”

Did wielding the blade elevate him to a higher rank than her? Or perhaps being a Triforce holder had. Either way, the part of him trained in obedience over the course of his youth yanked him to the map.

A realistic representation of Hyrule was drawn on parchment, with red flags and blue statues littered throughout. Large X’s crossed over the Castle Square, the Military Camp, Mabe Village, and Kolomo Garrison. The Outpost had only a few blue statues with more red flags approaching from the north.

He didn’t need Impa to explain what each symbol meant. X’s meant the location was lost to the enemy. Blue statues were Hyrule’s military still fighting, and red flags were the enemy. And there was an unsettling amount of red compared to blue bleeding on the parchment.

“This is what we know of, this is what we control.” She circled a finger around Central Hyrule. “We still haven’t heard much from each region.” She pointed at the Hebra region first. “The Rito are dealing with a deadly storm. We cannot get a clear correspondence out of that region past the Tabantha Bridge. The Gerudo have been hit with intense sandstorms and unprecedented Molduga attacks. We have not heard anything from the Gorons since Death Mountain erupted. The Zora—” her finger landed on the heart of the Lanayru region. “all we know is scouts saw hundreds of electric Lizalfos entering and no word from King Dorephan nor his children.”

Link’s stomach sank. Mipha was his friend. Daruk and Urbosa were good people. As much as he had differences with Revali, he was part of Hyrule. Each region was struggling, if not already fallen to Ganondorf’s plan. He was so mindlessly focused on Zelda that he forgot why he joined the military in the first place.

“I have sent word for Hyrule’s forces to pull back from the outpost and head towards Fort Hateno.” She used her pointer finger to slide the path from the remaining blue statues to the location of the fort. “That fortress will give us a better advantage and keep the soldiers protected from guardians.” Then her gaze lifted and flicked to the Master Sword. “You managed what none of my scouts could, taking down a guardian. Even with that legendary blade aiding you, it must have required considerable skill.” Her voice dropped. “And perhaps some fortune.”

He didn’t want to ask what happened to those men.

“So, Sir Link, you have my blessing to march to the castle. If you are able to get past the countless guardians in the field, then the monsters crawling throughout the razed town, and somehow still manage to slip by unscathed into the castle to get Zelda and slip back out again, please do. Otherwise, I’d like to help you strategize.” She turned to glare into him, her red eyes flaring. “If Zelda is all you care about, that’s fine. But I care about everyone, everywhere, and you and her are the only two that can stop him.”

He nodded, finally able to see past his own desires, realizing the big picture that had been displayed before him. “What do you need me to do?”

“Ideally, I’d like to send you far away from each other, to avoid Ganondorf getting his hands on you both again, but I’m not stupid enough to even ask.”

Link huffed a breath, “Thanks, I was getting tired of saying no to you.”

She clasped his shoulder and walked by him to the lone chair in the corner to sit. She rested her elbow on her knee as she rubbed her face. “Grante is currently deep undercover within the castle as a Yiga guard. He’s been watching over her since and examining the rotations of the guards. He will break her out and quietly smuggle her out of the castle, where you will be waiting to take her away. You can bring her to Kakariko Village where we will rendezvous with Robbie and Purah. They have been interpreting and researching legends and tales for weeks, we might finally have a way to defeat him and stand a chance against his army.”

“Easy enough.” He said sarcastically.

Impa huffed, a first he’d ever seen from her. “If everything goes according to plan.”

“Then I’m off.” Link turned to head out of the dimly lit cave.

“Hold on, I have something you’ll want.” Impa rose from the chair and out of sight down a pathway. When she returned, she was holding a pile of clothes and guards that she shoved into his hands. “Put these on and meet me outside when you’re done. Keep your hood.”

He promptly undressed the Sheikah gear he had been wearing for the past week and outfitted himself in the clothes Impa provided. It was similar to his traditional Hylian gear but dark as night. The fabric was exceptional, and the bracers and guards seemed to be measured to his size.

As he walked out of the cave, greeted by the leaden sky, Impa stood holding the reins of Epona. He let a small smile form seeing his favorite companion; it was the happiest he had allowed himself to be since before they were captured.

“You’ll need to get away quickly once you have Zelda.” He walked over to his loyal steed, brushing his hand on her snout. She greeted him with a familiar huff as he bowed his forehead against hers in welcome relief. “Epona and Storm were left in Kakariko as you remember upon your ascent. Storm is still there, if Zelda is feeling sentimental.”

If any horse can get him out of the guardian stalkers’ dodge, Epona could.

“Good luck—” Impa was sincere, perhaps hopeful in her tone. “I placed some items for Zelda in Epona’s saddlebag. I’ll see you both in Kakariko; we’re packing to head there now.”

He swung himself onto Epona’s saddle, the familiar leather creaking beneath his weight. With a gentle press of his heels against her flanks and a low whistle, she reared slightly before lunging forward. The wind whipped his hood back as they thundered across the field, hooves pounding rhythmically against the earth, heading straight for the looming silhouette of Hyrule Castle.

Straight to Zelda.

He weaved Epona between five guardian stalkers in Hyrule Field. He should be relieved; he’d made it this far, but part of him almost wished for the fight, for something to unleash his fury upon. Epona snorted softly beneath him as they approached Mabe Village, now just a silhouette behind curtains of smoke.

Two stalkers guarded the front gate as he detoured east, the familiar bustle of the town replaced by a hush that made his skin crawl. As the fog cleared, his stomach dropped.

Where the east gate once stood was a gaping hole in the stone, and what lay beyond was razed to the ground.

The whole town beyond was nothing more than a graveyard.

The silence hit him first. The grand cathedral that stood was gone, wiped away from memory; if the foundations hadn’t been visible, he would have doubted it even existed. All the storied homes and businesses that colored the town were gone. And if one was still standing, it was smoldering from a fire. The scent in his nose burned of ash and death.

He dismounted at the center; at the fountain’s broken pipes, where water sprayed onto the cobblestones rather than the basin it was designed to be in. Market stalls lay in charred heaps, food lay rotting on the ground, flies and maggots swarming.

He led Epona towards the only area with grass, spotting a doll near the bridge, its painted face half-melted, a tiny dress still perfectly intact. His nostrils flared, his mouth tight and choked.

Everyone was just gone. Yet all he could do was send a silent prayer that they had escaped. However, he knew that wasn’t true.

He concealed Epona behind a substantial boulder near the bridge. It was an endeavor in and of itself to conceal her from view for a swift escape; her chestnut fur stood out starkly against the dull surroundings. He descended beneath the bridge, where Impa had indicated that Grante and Zelda would meet him. He maintained his concealment, becoming the shadows; the dark clothing and hood he donned aided in his disguise.

Hours had passed, and the sky was getting darker, as was the tension he held. With only his thoughts and the smoke billowing from Castle Town for company, he was on the verge of acting irrationally and storming the castle himself—

Until he spotted a red-clad guard and ashen hair in the distance.

His muscles seized while his knees nearly buckled beneath him. The sight of her alive ignited a spark in his chest that collided with the crushing weight of what they’d done to her.

It was Zelda. She was alive.

He observed her gingerly scaling the cliff face, Grante assisting her as she went. As she drew nearer, he didn’t recognize the clothes she was wearing. They must have given them to her, but they were barely better than rags. Her trousers had several rips and torn bits. Her shirt was dirty, covered in dust and debris. The fabric did little to conceal the bruises that littered her arm. The yellowish-brown coloring indicated that the injury had occurred at least a week ago. A bubbling sensation of rage crawled up his spine, tightening every fiber in his body.

He caught a glimpse of her hair— the gold now ashen, matted, and dull. Her skin was pale and wan, the almost permanent sun-kissed coloring gone. Her face was sunken, and her body was so thin that it appeared as if she had barely eaten in weeks. Her muscles had wasted away, the healthy glow she once had, deteriorated.

He wanted to sprint to her side, yet simultaneously dissolve into the earth all at once. Tearing out his heart and offering it in forgiveness at the sight. Knowing he had done this to her, not coming sooner, he had left her to rot away in the hands of the enemy. She was frail and battered and broken. The woman he loved, his soulmate.

He didn’t deserve her, perhaps he never did. He had already failed her one too many times. The lizalfos almost killed her, the lynel on Death Mountain would have if she had not bought him time, and now the Yiga Clan and Ganondorf. 

She now stood mere meters away, Grante revealing himself to her surprise, her green eyes locked onto his face. And though dark spots lined them, there was still spirit behind them. Buried under the darkness and the gloom.

She still had not seen him, shadowed by the dark, as he tried to mask the pain in his own eyes at looking upon her.

Then Grante’s red eyes found him, sensing his presence. “You don’t have much time before they realize she’s gone. Head towards Kakariko. They’ll be waiting for you.“

He barely heard her labored pants against the pounding in his chest. She was unable to catch her breath, as her gaze drifted in surprise from the familiar, quiet guard to where he stood. He forced himself to step forward, placing each foot as if treading on ice that might crack and swallow him whole. Her eyes found his face in the shadows, widening as they traveled over his features. Recognition dawned slowly, and when his blue eyes finally met hers, the broken sob that escaped her lips seemed to shatter something in the air between them.

Chapter 38: Reunited
Chapter Text
“Link.” She breathed, followed by a broken noise that escaped.

He was there, in front of her. Alive. Whole.

Seeing him hit her like a physical blow, her knees wobbled as she willed herself to stand and look at him.

He looked different. If it hadn’t been for his blue eyes blazing into hers, she would have questioned if it was even him.

Before her head caught up to her heart, she was running to him, jumping into his arms. She didn’t care how appalling she was or why he seemed so closed off; she had to touch him. Feel the warmth of his blood. Her arms swung over his shoulders, her face buried in his neck. She almost knocked him over with the sheer force of it.

She nuzzled into him, breathing him in. He still smelled of pine, grass, and— ash. But he was alive.

He reluctantly returned her embrace, clutching her tightly, almost afraid. One hand on her back, the other cradling her head.

His lips brushed against her ear, sending a shiver down her spine. “Zelda,” he whispered, his voice cleaving on the second syllable. His fingers trembled against her back, and when he finally spoke again, the words came out broken. “I’m so sorry.”

She pulled away, shaking her head. She knew why he was sorry, but he had no reason to be.

Before she could ask how he was here and not at the bottom of the Hyrule moat, Grante’s voice interrupted. “You need to go to Kakariko now. Zelda’s… untimely escape— moved up my timeline. You have a clear window at the moment, but that won’t last.” He was fastening that unseeing white mask back on. “I need to get back; there will be a manhunt for you soon.”

A blink of surprise at Zelda’s own escape was the only semblance of real emotion Link let slip towards her. But he quickly turned to Grante, nodding to him, and Zelda added with a grateful smile, “Thank you.”

He returned the gesture, and within a flash, he was gone.

“I’ll explain everything later; let’s go.” Link grabbed her hand and led her outwards.

She wanted to stop and talk as all the questions burned in her throat: Where he was. How he got out. How was he was even alive. Where did that mysterious, familiar sword come from? But they remained unasked as they raced forward. When they reached the cliff face, he gestured towards a dangling rope, a silent command for her to ascend before him.

She climbed, almost faltering as her shaky hands struggled to grab the flat top of the bridge. She hadn’t felt the small pieces of rock engrained in her palms, only feeling his touch propelling her up. The heat of it igniting her, pushing her beyond her physical limits.

She waited for him as he swung himself up effortlessly, but before she could remember to be impressed by the feat, he was grabbing her hand, yanking her to a shallow rock face. He crouched behind it, as she mirrored him, and in the distance, the chestnut coloring of Epona stuck out to her. Her reddish mane a stark contrast against the grey backdrop.

Before she could register where they were, Link was tugging her towards the loyal mare. Running swiftly, his dark cloak blowing in the sulfur-scented air.

Black was not his color.

As they approached, he grabbed her waist and thrust her onto Epona within one propelling motion. He swung up behind her, grabbing the reins. Zelda barely was able to lock her legs into place as he kicked his heels and yelled for Epona to run, throttling her back towards his chest.

Then it all registered. They were galloping through Castle Town. Or what was left of it.

Zelda couldn’t contain her gasp at the carnage. The whole town was reduced to rubble. Whatever was left was on fire or smoking.

The town she once was lost in lay obliterated before her eyes. Where grand, ornate buildings stood tall, now only blackened frames remained, allowing her to see both mountains on the west and east. The tavern, its dim glow with festive music, where Link had laid his hands on her waist as they danced— erased. The fountain where children laughed and she had savored sweet kabobs now held ruined water. And the homes with children’s clothing hanging on the laundry lines and toys littered on the ground were under a pile of rubble.

But what happened to those people that lived in those homes? She willed her lip not to quiver as tears lined her eyes. Her nostrils burned, the scent of smoke and ash— and death. 

Link had not said a word. She couldn’t see his face as he willed Epona to run, run faster than the wind itself out of the decimated town, but she was sure he was equally, if not more so, devastated.

They had not stopped until they made it to a small cropping of trees at nightfall.

Epona needed the rest. The mare’s chestnut coat was dark with sweat, her sides still rising and falling rapidly from the desperate gallop that had carried them both to safety. The castle only a small speck against the dimly lit horizon. Yet, the smell of death had left the air; it still lingered in her soul.

Link jumped off first and made to help Zelda, grabbing her waist, placing her gently on the earth. His hands lingered longer than necessary, and she met his gaze. He quickly jerked them back, balking at the touch. She suppressed her hurt at the motion. She had not been as put together, or as clean, as she once was.

His fingers twitched as he ran his hand along Epona’s neck, murmuring something too soft for Zelda to hear. The mare’s ears flicked back at his voice, and she nudged his shoulder with surprising gentleness for such a powerful creature before turning to gaze.

“How long?” she asked.

His hands busied in the saddlebag, his shoulders lifted and tight, hiding his face from her, pretending not to notice her watching him. “22 days,” he said in barely a whisper.

It had felt like months, while she lay in her cell, curled in on herself. But that’s what grief had done: hours blended into days and into weeks. What was the point of keeping track of time when she had nothing to live for? But here he was, alive and seemingly well. Except for the massive gulf between them. “How are you alive? Where did you get that sword?”

“Why don’t you get cleaned up first? Then we’ll talk. Epona is going to need a moment before we continue. I have fresh clothes for you. There’s the river you can use to wash up, if you wish.”

She looked down at her clothing: a grey-brown shirt that was once originally white hung off her in a tattered piece and brown trousers covered in blood and grime. The rips on her shirt showed her pale skin, wan from weeks without sun. She ran her fingers through her hair; her blonde locks were knotted and frayed, and she moved to her face; her cheeks felt hollow.

Surely she looked as bad as she felt.

She nodded her head, not able to meet his gaze. “Fine.”

He grabbed the pack off Epona and handed her the travel attire she recognized. He motioned for her to follow as he showed her the river, sheltered from wandering eyes. She forced herself to look at him, trying and failing to hide the pleading in her eyes. But he had only looked at her as if she was a stranger, before walking away, leaving her alone.

She couldn’t stop the quiver in her lip as she felt the chasm between them grow to an impossible-to-cross distance. Gone was the flirty banter, no more proclamations of love. He had reverted back to knight protector and nothing more. 

Their love died in that hallway between their cells.

She squeezed her eyes shut, but it was no use. A tear escaped, followed by another, and soon the dam of her emotions burst. She covered her mouth to choke back a sob as she stripped off the dirty rags and submerged herself. Her tears mixing with the river’s waters.

She was as clean as she could be. That invisible layer of grime washed away, and her hair less knotted and slick. She dressed; the pants she wore were loose around her as her bones jutted from her hips. She had to tie the corset strings tighter, overlapping the edges, to keep it from slipping. She lifted the hood to cover her wet head.

As she emerged from the isolation, Link was standing guard, his back turned to her, that ethereal blade in his sword hand at the ready. She took a moment to really look at him. His hair tied back in his familiar style. His clothing was similar to what she had seen him in hundreds of times, the dark cape of his hood blowing in the breeze, his beige trousers and boots, and the unfaltering dark tunic beneath his guards and belts. He somehow looked enlightened, wiser as he held that sword. Or maybe the last few weeks aged him beyond logic.

His form was ridged and tense, displaying the same forbearing nature he had when they met. Perhaps he felt the same burden she now did. Did he look at her and think the same? Or was all he saw in her weakness and imperfection?

She crept up behind him, resisting the urge to snake her hands around his middle and press her face to his back. Words were at a loss as she was hesitant of what to say, choosing instead to tap him on the shoulder ever so delicately. He turned to her with careful precision, she watched as his eyes raked over her body, and when he landed on her face, something in his own cracked.

“What is it?” she asked. Her patience starting to wane.

“You are— you’re so thin.” Barely able to get the words out, he failed to hide the cracking in his voice. However, it wasn’t an insult, but rather laced with shame and remorse.

She let out a held breath, her shoulders falling distinctly. “I— I didn’t eat much of what they provided. My grief consumed and fed me. I did think you were dead.” She didn’t hide the contempt as she bore into his eyes, the blue eyes she never thought she’d gaze upon again. “How did you escape?”

He looked down to his feet, the muscle in his jaw feathered. “When that guard raised his blade to cut me down, Grante was there. The body you heard drop was the guard. Before I could even submit to what was happening, Grante knocked me out. They used the opportunity to slip me out of lock-up as a dead prisoner, bringing me to Impa at a nearby hideout. It was her plan all along. To get me out and leave you there, temporarily—” His voice wavered. “—while I retrieved the Master Sword.”

Her brows shot up as she glanced at the blade. Its holy light emitting from it against the shadows in the clearing. Ganondorf mentioned that they were all connected and that the owner of the sword would come for her. It’s the reason he kept her alive.

“You’re the Hero of Legend,” she whispered.

Link nodded.

“I knew it was you. That it could only ever be you.”

His face was tight as he gazed upon her own.

“Did you know… about me?” she asked him. She was certain he understood what she meant.

That she was— is— the most holiest of deities in all of Hyrule.

“Impa confirmed it after she rescued me. She suspected when you first came here, but she knew for sure after you were able to retrieve the first Spiritual Stone.”

“And you?”

She watched the column of his throat work. “I suspected.”

She stared at him blankly, unsure what to say. She wanted to know why he never told her, what it meant to him, what it had changed. But it didn’t matter, none of it mattered, except one.

He sent his beast to try to capture me. Except my parents—” she somehow managed to hold back the tears forming, “—they saved me, so he killed them.”

He stiffened again. Not missing that his hand flexed painfully on the sword’s hilt.

That was enough. Being in that cell for nearly three weeks had almost wrecked her body. Hearing about the murder of her parents practically destroyed her spirit, and thinking the man she loved, her soulmate, died feet away from her nearly shattered everything that was left.

But it hadn’t. She survived.

However, she wouldn’t survive this callous attitude from him in the face of everything. Every regret. Every heartache. Every scar.

Whatever you need me to be, I will be. But always as your soulmate. They would fight for this world, for all those who would be tormented, for those who had lost, for her parents, for each other. She swung her arms around his neck and lifted herself up slightly to kiss him. Her lips were chapped from the weeks in the cell, but he hadn’t cared as he returned it and moved his hands to cradle her neck.

A prayer, a promise.

They had come to a place of understanding. Their love might not have died, but something changed forever within him. Having this heavy burden placed upon him and discovering the woman he loved had been— is— the most spiritual deity, all while she was imprisoned. She understood why he might have been still quietly processing.

To be frank with herself, she truly hadn’t comprehended her own fate yet. She hadn’t quite processed everything from the past few weeks. Every moment of her imprisonment was spent in despair, then survival. Now she felt the weight of it all sitting on her chest.

Her parents died shielding her from a madman’s reach, because they loved her, but also because they knew what she was. She had shameful moments creep in since, wanting to scream at them for it, for the secret they carried to their graves. For the weight they left for her to discover alone.

But the dead don’t answer, no matter how much you beg.

They were ascending the grassy slope, nearing the Pillars of Levia by nightfall when everything had suddenly become hushed. The birds stopped squawking, the bugs stopped singing, any animal left was fleeing. Link halted Epona as Zelda held her breath. Then she heard it. A familiar sound she never actually heard before…

A whirling of machinery, metal clicking, the hiss of air compressing, shafts moving.

Link urged Epona to gallop to a nearby outcrop of trees. He grabbed her shoulder firmly, urging her to meet his gaze. She turned to him as he pressed a single finger to his lips. His blue eyes wild with fear as she saw it.

An ancient, mechanical spider-like machine was stomping in the open plain from around the corner. It was as large as a house and as quick as Epona, perhaps quicker, which was surprising given its size. Its outer body looked as if it was carved from primitive stone, similar to the shrine she had visited so long ago, except this had runes glowing pink and blue. Each foot had sharp claws, as if like knives, as it cut up the earth where it stomped. And its head spun, revealing a single eye scanning the area for threats.

She dreamed of this before. Before Hyrule, before everything.

Goosebumps littered her skin as she held her breath in hiding. Link was tense behind her, more so than before. He clearly was aware of this… monstrosity. Then she saw a faint glowing light emitting from the Master Sword within its sheath. Her eyes widened under her hood.

After a few minutes, the machine left to stalk elsewhere. She finally took a breath after the Master Sword’s glow faded. Link urged Epona to continue, hugging the mountain rock in the cover of darkness. She whispered to him, “What was that?”

She couldn’t see his face, but his voice was tight. “A guardian stalker.”

“You’ve seen them before.” It wasn’t a question.

“Yes. On my way to the castle to rescue you, I encountered one.” He stopped himself, gripping the reins tightly. “I fought it. I was lucky to defeat it. One misstep, and I would have been dead.”

She shuttered. “Why haven’t we seen them before?”

“Because Ganondorf unleashed them, pouring his malice into them. They were originally built and made to aid Hyrule… not turn against it.” His voice clipped. “They are crawling all over Hyrule Field. It’s the reason Castle Town was leveled as it was.”

When they were running from town, she was so overwhelmed by his presence that she hadn’t given any thought to how a town could be razed in that way. She was nauseated thinking about the townsfolk, praying that they escaped the carnage of that horror before it was too late.

Kakariko came into view after dusk. The narrow passage leading into the village forced Epona down to a trot, too tight for any guardian stalker to follow them in. Above them on the cliffs, Sheikah guards tracked their approach, hands resting on weapons, before waving them through.

The village yawned open from the narrow path. It was how she remembered when she was here last, except for the permanent grey sky that blanketed the world, casting shadows amongst the groups of people. There were so many more than before, some nearby the market eating around the fire, some near the front of the inn, others scattered by Impa’s house. They all looked bleary-eyed and dilapidated, with dark circles under their eyes and hunched shoulders. They were the refugees that made it here, but how many did not?

Some clocked their entrance with weariness. Fear hung in the air, and she could see them tense before realizing they were no threat and turning back towards their conversations— or whatever it was that they were doing.

Impa was descending her front steps as Link jumped off Epona first and made to help her off next. Zelda’s hood fell down as her feet hit the ground, revealing her unkempt, now dry, blonde locks. Then, everything fell silent, followed by a few gasps.

A child whispered, loudly, “It’s the Goddess.”

Zelda turned her head sharply towards Link— so fast it swam. Her throat dropped to her stomach, her face tight, and her eyes wide with anxiety. He returned a look she could not identify. Concern, fear, doubt?

A cover of stunned silence fell. The air hurtled out of the canyon village carved from rock as everyone that was previously hunched over or sitting now stood tall in a show of respect as the child’s words carried around the village. They all stared at her and Link as a Sheikah guard came to grab Epona’s reins, bowing his head to her— to them, as he led Epona away.

Before she could react and correct them, Impa was standing in front of her. She was dressed in tight, military-style clothing. A considerable dagger decorated her belt. Her grey hair was pulled back, her skin ruddy, and her red eyes looked flat. As if exhaustion had seeped all the color from her.

“Sir Link.” She greeted him first before turning to face Zelda, “Zelda.” She said her name slower, more regal, as she faintly bowed her head. “I’m glad to see you both safe.”

Zelda swallowed, feeling increasingly insecure as all the eyes lay upon her still. Everyone, and every living creature for that matter, could hear them. “Impa—” she exhaled, “these people think I’m the God—”

Impa cut her off with a shush, “Let’s speak inside.” She gestured to her home.

Zelda started towards the large staircase, it loomed, an overwhelming wave corroding her, as the crowd’s eyes followed her, heads dipping one by one as she passed. She glanced at them; some had smiles, their eyes bright and hopeful. Others stared in disbelief, mouths agape, brows raised. She heard a murmur, “The Goddess has come to save us with the hero!”

Zelda wanted to be sick. It took every ounce of her strength not to collapse. To not cry.

They must have looked straight out of the legend. The Goddess— their messiah, the promised one. And the hero with the legendary sword, created to defeat evil. Link sensed her discomfort and gently placed a hand on her back to steady her. As she climbed the stairs, she felt emptier and hollow with each step, knowing she had already doomed them all. Their faith misplaced onto her, a nobody.

She had to breathe out her mouth as the threat of weeping burned her nose.

Zelda opened the doors and entered Impa’s living room, standing in the middle, her hand clasped around her neck, as the other held herself around her middle. Her breathing was labored, the weight of what had just unfolded was crushing as Impa shut the double doors behind them. Link came to stand at her side, his arm snaked around her shoulder, squeezing gently as she tried to stifle her sob.

“Zelda.” A high-pitched voice chimed from behind her, knocking her out of the impending breakdown as she and Link simultaneously whipped their heads towards it.

“Ilya?” Zelda said, her brows high in disbelief.

She was already moving towards the petite blonde and before she knew it, embracing her. She pulled back, her hands gripping her sides. “How are you here?”

Ilya looked the same as she had before, but depleted, like everyone else. Link had come up beside her and gave her a gentle smile, the once bright and cheerful woman Zelda remembered could barely smile back at him. Something haunted now resided behind those hazel eyes.

“I and a few other survivors managed to flee the castle as the attack happened. Fledge managed to get us out.” She turned her head to the side and sure enough, there he was, quietly listening.

Link was already embracing him, when he pulled back, Fledge’s eyes landed just above Link’s right shoulder, right on the Master Sword’s hilt.

Zelda made to hug the man who had become one of her closest friends, relief flooding her as both of them were alive, but perhaps not well as Ilya continued, “Everything happened so fast. One minute I was in the stables, then the next—” she choked back on her words, her mouth tight, “monsters were everywhere, laying siege to the castle. They swarmed through town first, chasing after townsfolk, looting and burning as they went. Then they came to the stables, burning the entrance with the horses inside.” Her eyes watery, “the stable hands and I managed to get a few horses out and flee towards Mabe Village.”

As Ilya described the horror that occurred in her own sanctuary, Zelda held together her own sorrow that her friend experienced. Ilya’s once bright and hopeful hazel eyes, that were always so warm, were now fractured. Seeing the animals she had come to love and care for be mercilessly slaughtered broke something inside of her— forever.

Zelda looked at Ilya in horror as she continued, “We made it there, but a guardian found us. We tried to hide, but—.” A tear escaped her closed lids as she shook her head, “but some weren’t fast enough. The guardian blew up half the village looking for us. The few that were left, we hid until the next day. That’s when Fledge found us.”

Link looked at his squire, his loyal comrade, and asked hesitantly, “Where were you?”

Fledge, typically bumbling and nervous, had none of that. Instead, he looked cold and he spoke the same, “We were coming back from an excursion to take out a rumored Yiga Clan unit when we saw the monsters marching into the castle. We all ran in after them, trying to cut down as many as we could, but we were overrun. We tried to pull back, strategize with the position we were left in, but there was nothing we could do. It was too late…” His eyes looked down at the ground behind them.

Link tensed next to her, “Where’s Pipit? Cawlin?”

Fledge lifted his head, an effort to do so and shook it softly and turned his eyes down. Zelda gasped as she turned to face Link, pure pain flashing across his features hearing about his fellow knights.

“I managed to escape when two small children were fleeing from a moblin. I was able to kill it and get the kids out. I wanted to bring them somewhere safe, I thought Mabe Village would be secure but that’s when I discovered Ilya and a few stablehands. I am… deeply ashamed I didn’t die with my command.”

Zelda balked at his remark. Link had reached out his hand and placed it on his shoulder, a silent disclosure in condolence for the pain he felt, perhaps more for himself.

She thought of all the faces she had passed, somehow with wonder and hope in their gaze. How many of them fled as their homes burned, making impossible choices? How many tried and failed to save their loved ones and neighbors as they watched? It made everything she had gone through pale in comparison. She was blessed to help them and didn’t do anything. The guilt of it pressed against her lungs like a stone.

“I hate to interrupt, but I must speak with Zelda and Link.” Impa’s voice cutting through the tension.

Grief hung in the room as a living thing, but Impa hadn’t cared to read the room, or she did and simply did not heed their anguish.

Fledge nodded his head in acknowledgement and gave a weak smile as Ilya gave Zelda and Link a quick hug each before passing them both out the main doors. Zelda couldn’t help but huff a long breath. Despite it all, at least they were alive, even if they were broken and in pain.

Impa sat in a nearby armchair, rubbing at her face. “We need to discuss the plan for you two.”

Zelda lowered her brows, cocking her head at the Shiekah Master. She wanted to discuss plans? Now? She couldn’t even be bothered to ask how she was? Or apologize?

Impa ignored Zelda’s expression, whether it be because she didn’t care or time was so paramount they couldn’t afford it. “You two will head to the Temple of Time—”

“No.” Zelda said, her head cocking back slowly, serpentine, ready to strike.

Impa opened her mouth, “Zel—”

“No!” She yelled. She hadn’t even meant to yell it, but the visceral reaction couldn’t be contained. The last time Impa schemed without their input or knowledge had been to obtain the Spiritual Stones, which emboldened Ganondorf to launch his plan. Link had died, for all she knew, and she rotted in prison for three weeks while countless Hylian’s were slaughtered. She immediately felt weak at her outburst and backed into the closest chair and plopped down. The mere exhaustion drowned her as a wave that she was too weak to breach.

She hung her head down, palms to her forehead, as Link came up to stand beside her. Her protector rather than lover, then she became irrationally angry.

She lifted her head to meet Impa’s stare. “Why didn’t you tell me what you knew about me before?”

She knew what she meant.

Impa pursed her lips, matching her stare. “What would it have changed?”

“Everything!” she roared so loudly that Link flinched next to her. “I went in blind. I thought I was getting these stones to send me back home. As the key to unlock that door, not part of some plan for you to trap Ganondorf and use me to do it. You misled me. You misled US.” She punctuated bitterly. “You almost got Link killed because of it.”

A barely noticeable flash of regret appeared on Impa’s face before she resorted back to her stoic look as she continued to listen.

She was so sick of the quiet planning and whispers. “You have been treating me like a pawn from the beginning. You knew. You knew about me, about the Goddess from the moment you saw me.”

Impa nodded her head. “Sometimes even a pawn can kill the king.”

Rage then fury stirred in her belly. She closed her eyes, imagining all those faces of refugees again she passed on her way here. They all looked tormented and frightened of what had befallen them. Then she, just Zelda, walked by, their faces filled with hope. It hurt worse. “These people are worshipping a false god! I am not going to be able to save them; their hope is misplaced. I can’t bring back their homes or their loved ones.” She turned her face to look away from Impa’s, and she caught a glimpse of herself in the mirror.

She barely recognized herself. All the fullness in her face and her curves were gone. Her eyes were dark and swollen. Her hair was dull and lifeless. Her skin and lips pale and colorless. She looked like a walking corpse, bony and hollow. No wonder Link looked at her with pity. She felt like the sorriest Goddess anyone ever did see.

“That’s true.” Impa’s voice tore her gaze away from the mirror. “But you give them hope. Seeing the Goddess and the hero with the blade of evil’s bane at his back. That’s what keeps them going. They grew up hearing the stories of the legendary heroes and the Goddess he was sworn to protect.”

Zelda lifted her face to Link’s as he silently stood next to her, not interfering, instead letting the two women hash it out. Their eyes met, that familiar spark shot through her, the same one she felt hundreds— thousands of times prior. Remembering that vow he swore to her a year ago, before he knew who she was.

“I don’t know how—” she tore her gaze from his own, “I don’t know how to be a Goddess. I don’t have powers or any idea how to use them.”

“Perhaps you don’t need to. Perhaps you need to be present for this to work. All previous reincarnations of the Goddess had various levels of power, some manifesting with or without a catalyst.” Impa stood from her seat and walked over to her, kneeling to meet her eye level. “I am sorry for not telling you the truth. Not that this is an excuse, but I didn’t know he was hunting you. I thought playing it close to my own chest would spare you somehow. I made a choice, admittedly the wrong one.”

Zelda studied Impa’s eyes for a long time, searching them for any remaining shadows of the secret-keeper, the manipulator, the ancient Sheikah chessmaster who saw her not as a person but a piece. She expected more deflection, more calculated evasions, but instead there was only tiredness— worn thin, pooling under her eyes, slackening her jaw.

And she was so very tired herself. She wrapped her own arms around her chest to keep herself from falling apart. She recalled the stories told about her, the goddess incarnate, the beautiful and wise and strong deity of Hyrule. Did she ever feel this empty, this unsure, this ordinary?

Impa’s apology hung between them. It was not enough, but perhaps nothing would be. The only way forward is to accept that hurt and keep moving, because the world would not wait for her to heal. Ganondorf certainly wouldn’t.

She nodded her head in acceptance.

Impa stood. “Get some rest. You both can stay upstairs tonight. We’ll speak more in the morning.”

Zelda rose from the chair. Her legs were aching, her jaw was tight. Link placed a hand on the small of her back as she climbed another daunting set of stairs. The small motion was a warmth she grasped onto— the only piece to stop her from crumbling down. But as she reached the top, catching her breath, she started to well up at the thought of what they had to do.

How could she possibly save Hyrule if she couldn’t even manage a set of stairs without becoming winded? It would take weeks, months, to become healthy enough to fight or even keep up with Link as they were.

That creeping feeling of doubt flooded her. The same feeling she felt at each spring. Why her? She couldn’t save her parents, couldn’t save Link, couldn’t even save herself. She never felt more sure that the Goddess chose poorly.

She turned to Link, letting her head drop onto his chest. Just quietly breathing him in as she choked back a sob. His arms snaked around her. And he just held her, not speaking for long minutes until she slowly lifted her head to meet his gaze, giving her a weak smile.

“How am I supposed to do this?” She barely held her words together and blinked away the tears forming.

He moved his hands to her neck and cupped her face. Gently rubbing his thumb over her cheek. “I don’t know—” Her heart sunk. “—but we’ll do it together. Where you go, I go.” His eyes bore into hers, begging her to listen, to hear him, as he continued, “If you grew wings and flew into the sun, I would follow you until my own burned away. If you plummeted into the depths, I would jump after you; if you grew gills, I would swim across the sea into my arms were water themselves. There is nowhere you go that would keep me from your side again.” His thumb stilled against her cheek. “Even if it’s in death, I will follow you there. I will not fail you again.” He bowed his head to meet her forehead.

He was praying that prayer for her, not the Goddess.

Her heart fluttered. Some semblance of normalcy. She pressed her face back into the side of his neck and closed her eyes. The ash smell was still there, but underneath it, faintly, the pine. They stood like that in the middle of the room until her breathing slowed and her hands stopped shaking, and she repeated that prayer back to him in barely a whisper. “You go, I go.”

Chapter 39: Strategy

And it’s hard because these characters live with me so it’s torturous not to spend time with them. Chapter Text
He awoke so early the next morning that the darkness that hung outside pressed in around him. The faint smells of jasmine in Impa’s cozy loft settled like a comforting blanket as he thoughtfully slid his arm out of Zelda’s middle, careful not to wake her. 

He no longer cared what Impa thought about propriety.

Zelda was so thin, so frail, that he was worried he’d bruise her when he wrapped his arms around her. Every harsh line that now decorated her face and body was a reminder that he had put it there. She was out of that cell, but it hadn’t erased what she had endured— because he wasn’t there. He failed her.

He failed his friends and comrades, the same ones he’d known since they were pages together. Cawlin, the shy knight with dark violet hair who idolized Groose for some reason, Stitch, the sarcastic bug lover, and Pipit— the pain in his ass, older knight who welded mockery for others as proficiently as a sword.

They were all dead. Slayed and buried underneath the rubble in the same place they’d grown from boys to men. Fallen at the hands of the enemy, together as one. He was alive to remember them, to honor them. But he wasn’t there to fight with them.

Shame slithered within him as certain as his blood was crimson as he eyed the legendary blade he set down next to the bed. 

Unworthy.

But somehow the blade still chose him.

He eased himself out of bed one limb at a time, watching her face for any sign of stirring. He crossed to the armchair in the corner—the one with a clear sightline to the door—and lowered himself into it without taking his eyes off her. He had trained every morning of his adult life that wasn’t spent healing or in a cell, but not today. Her long flaxen hair spilled off the edge of the bed, and he tracked the slow rise and fall of her breathing until he was sure of it.

He closed his eyes and thought of yesterday. She had been in that cell longer than he had, and yet it was her voice that cut through his self-pity. A fire within her blazed, raw and infallible. She had learned of her parents’ murders and believed him dead, and still she had screamed that she loved him. And still she had not asked why he hadn’t come sooner. That question only haunted him. He had been so consumed by his own failure that it had not once occurred to him that she might not share it.

He didn’t deserve her. He wasn’t sure he ever would.

A memory popped into his mind of Urbosa in the desert. When they’d met separately from Zelda, when Urbosa read him like the yearning, longing man he hadn’t realized he already was.

She had mentioned that Zelda needed control in her life. That control was different from protection. That while he protected her against threats, she needed autonomy over her choices. While Ganondorf flat out robbed her of it, Impa hadn’t been much better. He wouldn’t be the same.

Instead, he would give her that retribution. That justice, had she wanted to take it.

She stirred awake, her green eyes flashed with rapid panic but quickly faded when they landed on his own. She visibly relaxed and gave him a lazy smile.

It devastated him all over again. Now reunited but with a chasm of pain and scars between them both. It was not the first time he had wondered how many times she had woken like this. The claws of what she endured still embedded in her pounding heart.

He wanted to bear the wounds for her, take away the suffering and pain. He already had countless scars, what was a few more? But those words chimed through him as a reckoning; he could protect her from what lies ahead, but she needed to conquer and defeat what had happened to her.
