And as she moved from the bed, with her too frail body towards him. She sat on his lap and ran her hand through the nape of his neck. Gently twinning the stray hairs that were too short to pull back. She had not spoken a word, but her expression said everything he already knew.

And goddess, did he love her. He missed her, missed this softness, missed the stillness of the world when it was just the two of them without the weight of the realm on their backs.

And he realized this may be the last time he’d see her this way. Unhurried, unguarded, in his arms in the quiet morning. So he held her close to remember her later.

They dressed and descended downstairs into the equally dark living room. Impa was already up and garbed in her military gear, and two familiar Sheikahs stood next to her, not cloaked in military dress but in their lab coats and goggles: Robbie and Purah.

They were the same as when Link last saw them, all those months ago. Intellectual and frazzled, however, like Ilya and Fledge, something lingered in their gaze, something they had knowingly witnessed on the dangerous trek to Kakariko after the siege. That vacant, obscure look in their crimson eyes.

Their heads lifted to Zelda and bent as their bodies made a show of bowing. Zelda tensed harder than she’d already carried herself, and he noted her knuckles were clenched tight and white. He instinctively reached his hand to grasp hers. Her wide eyes relaxing.

“Sir Link. Zelda.” Purah’s high-pitched voice sounded. “We must speak with you urgently.”

Impa stood nearby the entrance, her ridged posture perfect compared to that of her sister’s. She extended her hand to the sitting area for them to chat.

Link had forgotten Impa and Purah were sisters. Surely Impa had been relieved when Purah made it safely to the village they had grown up in. But now wasn’t the time to wonder as he led Zelda to the quaint sitting area off to the side of the room. They both sat simultaneously on the couch, followed by Robbie and Impa in the chairs across from them. Impa took up the free space between them.

Purah nervously looked around to their group, her eyes as wide as the rim of her glasses as she started, “We have a theory. We’ve been studying all the different possibilities since Impa told us of the suspected Goddess’ reincarnation in Zelda months ago.”

Link shot Impa a side-long look as Zelda squeezed his hand tighter. An uncomfortable reminder that the past few weeks may have been different had Impa shared her suspicions sooner.

Purah prattled on, “We’ve been scouring every textbook we have— had, in the Royal Lab and Castle Library.” Purah’s words slightly broke on the word had.

Link studied her face, assuming the Royal Lab was probably ravaged along with all the local properties surrounding the Castle. All their work, all their research gone— as if it never existed at all.

“While there are no direct stories or research on why Zelda could have ended up in Hyrule, we did find this.” She held up an ancient textbook that looked worse for wear. “This was transcribed from the days of the Hero of Time by another Sheikah researcher.” Purah opened the textbook to show a chapter, pointing at it aggressively. “The problem is, there is misleading information in this textbook. The researcher tried to memorialize the deeds of the Hero of Time. But depending on who and when they were asked, different answers are provided. We know the Hero of Time succeeded in driving back Ganondorf after pulling the Master Sword and aging seven years, but what happened afterwards?”

Different degrees of puzzled looks were exchanged by Zelda, Impa, and herself. As if they were supposed to answer the researcher’s rhetorical question.

Purah stood, unable to contain herself in her chair. “There are multiple reports. One is that the Hero of Time stayed an adult after sealing Ganondorf in the realm between worlds. Another is where he defeated Ganondorf but was sent back to his childhood. And even worse, another is where he dies without defeating Ganondorf.” She was leading her finger on the cited work. “We were able to trace clear paths with the former and latter, but the child timeline was fuzzy, so we focused on that.”

Purah continued, “To summarize what we know, the Hero of Time is sent back to relive his lost childhood. Ganondorf is alive and has not yet opened the Sacred Realm during this time. The young hero tells a young Princess Zelda what he knows and learned from his future endeavors.” Ganondorf is then apprehended and detained on these charges of treason. He is then sentenced to be executed, but that fails and leads into the Hero of Twilight era.”

Purah paused, perhaps for dramatic effect, “But, what if he escaped his fate? Instead, some time between being sentenced and executed, he traveled— to now?”

Link had furrowed his brows, trying his simple mind to grasp this concept of split realms and traveling in the rips between worlds. Zelda lifted her free hand to her mouth in quiet contemplation, her fingers nervously rubbing her lips.

Then unease skittered across his bones when he realized Zelda had been the only one to ever meet the beast of a man, actually speak to him out of all of them— and live. When he asked about her fading bruises last night, she reluctantly told him about how he threw her across the room, with little effort, as if he had swatted a fly from his space. The boiling fury Link felt knowing he hurt her had slowly eddied from him when he realized how underprepared they were to face him. He’d never been afraid to die, especially for Zelda, but if he failed because he wanted revenge, Zelda’s life would be forfeit anyway.

He shook away that brewing storm in his chest as Robbie stood abruptly, as if all the nervous energy he usually exuded hadn’t been able to be contained to a seat as he continued on Purah’s original thought.

“We believe he caused a split in the timeline, again. A fourth path— to here, now. If we follow this new theory, we need to revisit the legend to learn the why to understand the how. We’ve been combing through all the history of Hyrule and all the related legends. Each legend depicts the villain, the hero, and the Goddess reincarnated. Respectively, Ganondorf and you two. We know this Ganondorf is from the past. You, Link, are the hero and the Goddess reincarnated in Zelda but in a Zelda from the future—” he gestured to all of Zelda’s person, “—or a different realm, we still don’t fully know if it’s either, perhaps it was always mea—”

“Robbie.” Impa snapped, abruptly cutting off his tangent with a curt look.

“Right. Right.” He corrected himself as he flailed his arms. “It doesn’t matter.” Robbie continued to pace as he snatched the book from Purah’s hands and opened it. The seam of the book was worn and opened to the exact page he wanted it to. Uncoincidentally, it was a opened to the exact location from the last few months.

“We have translated text from back then. It supports our theory given everything he’s done. Why he was holding you in that cell, rather than outright killing you. It is written: ‘The resting place of the sacred triangle, the Sacred Realm, is a mirror that reflects what is in the heart. The heart of one who enters it, if an evil heart, the Realm will become full of evil; if pure, the Realm will become a paradise. The Triforce, the sacred triangles, it is a paradise that weighs the three forces: Power, Wisdom, and Courage.  If the heart of the one who holds the sacred triangles has all three forces in balance, that one will gain the True Force to govern all.  But if that one's heart is not in balance, the Triforce will separate into three parts: Power, Wisdom, and Courage.  Only one part will remain for the one who touched the Triforce, the part representing the force that one most believes in.  If that one seeks the True Force, that one must acquire the two lost parts.  Those two parts will be held within others chosen by destiny, who will bear the Triforce mark on the backs of their hands.’” Robbie recited every word. 

Link looked to his right hand, flexing his fingers. As if he’d suddenly seen something.

“We know that he used the stones to open the sacred realm and place his hand on the Triforce.” Purah continued where Robbie left off, “It’s how he had the power and strength to infiltrate the castle and overthrow the military. It’s why we believe he’s from the child timeline. Had he known the Triforce would split when he opened the sacred realm, he would have captured you both first before opening that door. That was his plan before, and he was not able to see it fulfilled as the child version of the Hero of Time had him apprehended. So instead, he was imbued with the Triforce of Power right then, thus why he held Zelda hostage, waiting for the Triforce of Courage holder to show himself.” Now she pointed at Link. “Once he had you two, the two missing pieces of the Triforce, he would head back to the Temple of Time, complete the Triforce, and make his wish— once and for all.”

Link glanced at Zelda. She had slung her hair to one side as she sat, hunched down, staring at her lap. She was spinning her ring around her finger, not meeting anyone’s stare. He had noticed that ring so many times before, but he never understood the significance of it until now. Perhaps she hadn’t either.

“And… what is his wish? His motivation for all this…chaos?” Zelda said with a conviction she already knew the answer to.

Impa’s eyes blazed. “To plunge us all into a world of darkness and evil. And of course, kill anyone who would oppose him.”

Purah set the book down. Robbie had stopped pacing.

“So… we fell right into his plan. By obtaining the Spiritual Stones in the first place?” Zelda said flatly.

“Yes. It would appear that is correct to assume.” Purah said quietly.

Link quickly chanced a look at Impa, her face made of stone. He wouldn’t blame her for that. No one could have predicted him. He would blame her for not sharing her suspicions earlier, though.

“But how did he know Zelda was the Goddess? He tried to pull her here three years ago and failed.” Link asked.

Purah’s lips twisted in what could be assumed was a sympathetic shrug. “Princess Zelda has been praying at those Springs for years. She had never materialized a Spiritual Stone. And we think Ganondorf has been here at least that long. It explains the growing force of monsters and the Yiga Clan. When he realized the Goddess wasn’t here, he went searching to speed the process, as only the Goddess can obtain the Stones.”

Link’s heart sunk, but he didn’t glance at Zelda.

Robbie chimed in, his excitement dulled to the tone of the room. “You are all connected in some twisted way. When Zelda experienced the pull from him, we started to investigate that possibility. We— you— had not realized your connection because you had no reason to suspect it. He knew how to recognize and pull those threads because he was leagues ahead of us. And when the Goddess reincarnated into Zelda then, that is most likely when you, Link, became the Triforce of Courage holder. But he only focused on the Goddess, knowing the Hero would emerge if she was in peril. Except he never suspected you since you had not yet possessed the Master Sword.”

Scattered bits of memories flashed before Link. Where had he been three years ago? He searched the cobwebs of his mind for something glaring to indicate that his destiny had been predetermined all that time ago but fell short. He had been too busy swinging swords and climbing the ranks to put any thought into meaningful signs.

“So how do we defeat him?” Zelda asked, her voice strong despite her appearance.

The corset she wore was loose; the gap between the cups and her shirt was obvious, even if every string had been pulled as tight as it could. He hadn’t failed to notice that her sleeve had fallen down three times since they sat as she silently brought it back into place on her shoulders. To anyone in the room, she may have looked weak. But he knew she wasn’t broken; she was the strongest person he’d ever known.

Impa chimed in, “Robbie and Purah have pointed out that the adult Hero of Time was successful because he drove the Master Sword into Ganondorf as the Goddess— then Princess Zelda— weakened him with holy light. If we adopt that same strategy, you need to go to the Temple of Time to face off against him.” Impa’s eyes landed on Zelda. “You are the Goddess; you are the only one who can do it.”

And then Zelda said what everyone had been thinking. “But what if my power doesn’t awaken? What if… everyone is mistaken?” Zelda’s eyes never left Impa’s, daring her to say it.

“Then we lose.”

Zelda huffed a breath, “I don’t know how—.” She closed her eyes, tightening her jaw, “— I don’t know how to do this.”

Purah thoughtfully pivoted, “Let’s expand upon that. If your powers don’t awaken, if you are at the Temple of Time and can open the Sacred Realm, in theory, if Link can defeat Ganondorf and take his piece of the Triforce from him— then either of you can wish to seal Ganondorf away. Then we’d assume all the monsters and guardians he’s controlling would cease to exist as well.”

Purah probably meant that sincerely, but even her tone was laced with a hint of doubt. Link was one of the best swordsmen in Hyrule, and even with the blade of evil’s bane on his back, could he defeat the blessed Triforce of Power holder in single combat?

Link and Zelda turned their heads to each other; he gripped her hand tighter.

“But in theory— he could do the same to us.” Zelda said, unapologetically.

“Yes.”

He expected Zelda to be trembling or scared about hearing about her certain death, but she lifted her head higher, the shadows dancing in the hollow of her eyes. “So, how do we lure him there?”

Link watched the corners of Impa’s mouth lift upwards by a hair. “My scouts have reported that as of this morning, he is still in the castle. He has realized you are no longer his prisoner and that the Master Sword welder is now in play. He doesn’t yet know that you both are here, but he will send enemies to search soon enough. As you saw on your entry into the village, we do not have to fret about guardians, but the Yiga and monsters can surely trap us in the canyon. And we don’t have a strong military presence stationed here, only the women, children, and elderly refugees—”

“We’ll leave before that can happen.” Zelda abruptly cut Impa off.

Link nodded his head in assured agreement as the images of a decimated Castle Town came flooding back.

Impa nodded back. “Then I have made arrangements for you to head to Fort Hateno. That is where the majority of our military is left. You arrive there and march to the Temple of Time with our full force at your backs. That will certainly get Ganondorf’s attention.”

“You aren’t coming with us?”

“I will stay here temporarily, perhaps only a day or two behind you. I want to fortify the village before I depart, and there are allies we have yet to hear from. Once I know their fate, I will rendezvous with you there.”

“What’s to stop him from sending his force to Fort Hateno to overrun what’s left of us?” Link had asked.

“Time.” Impa said as if a riddle. “We have time as our only advantage. If he catches onto our plan quickly enough… there will be no stopping him from capturing you both. Thus, why you two should depart today. And quietly.”

Zelda lifted her chin, her face was unavailing, but there was that spark in her that refused to be buried, as if she would carry on through sheer force of will if need be. “So, to summarize. Link and I will travel to Fort Hateno immediately under the guise of the land. Impa and the remaining forces will meet us there a day or two later and escort us to the Temple of Time so we can open the Sacred Realm, and either Link will defeat him in combat, ripping his piece of the Triforce from him, or my imaginary power will suddenly unlock for me to weaken him. But before any of that, we are somehow supposed to slip through his fingers— a man who has taken the castle, slaughtered the military, and commands every monster in this kingdom— and arrive at the Temple of Time with our lives still attached to our bodies?”

The room stayed silent for seconds, or perhaps minutes, as everyone absorbed the insanity of the feat ahead. Robbie and Purah had matching bunched faces. Impa, unsurprisingly, was neutral as she simply said, “Yes.”

“No pressure.” Zelda said just as flatly.

“Don’t fail.” Impa added.

Zelda surprised him by giving Impa a ‘no shit’ look. That time in the cell didn’t crush her spirit. He couldn’t hide the small bloom of love that grew in his chest.

Then Zelda loosed a slow breath through her nose, her eyes falling shut. A few seconds passed. When she opened them and turned to him, the corners of her mouth lifted— but above it her eyes were glassy and still, the way a lake looks beautiful and flat right before a storm. “You go, I go?”

He returned the smile, reaching his hand to cup her face, not caring the other three were staring at them with baited breath. “You go, I go.” He whispered to her.

It was settled.

Link was preparing Epona and Storm. Both well rested and saddled, at the bottom of Impa’s steps. He was packing just enough food for their journey, but nothing more besides the clothes and weapons at their backs. He hadn’t bothered to bring a tent, sleeping supplies, or anything more. The less to weigh them down, the better, in case they needed a quick escape.

All the village refugees seemed to be busying themselves as well. No crowds or huddles of curious people trying to catch a glimpse of the goddess and the hero. Impa had surely put a stop to that.

He was adjusting Epona’s saddle, barely able to focus for more than a few seconds as his gaze was torn away to land on Zelda.

She was still standing on Impa’s porch, overlooking the village. Both her hands gripped the railing, and a far-off, hallowed look pained her face.

He remembered recalling more than once that she looked like daylight made human. Now, she looked like the pale fog blanketing the mountains during the early morning. A wraith. Haunting and so at odds with who she was in her soul. But still beautiful all the same.

He loved her no matter how she looked, but a part of him wanted her to get that golden light back— the spark she came to find within herself while in Hyrule, while traveling with him. Ganondorf stole that from her with the revelations he laid at her feet.

But it would take some time for her to process it. To learn to accept it, long after their unlikely victory.

He knew because he had to do it when he learned of his father’s death. When he first heard the news, he didn’t cry or scream. He only picked up his sword, mounted Epona, and headed for the village. He slaughtered every monster in his path. Brutally. Inhumanely. And after every monster was dead, only their blood as evidence of their existence remained on his tunic. He thought he’d feel better, but he didn’t.

And that’s when he learned that revenge was sweet in theory, but when it comes to reconciling that with learning to live with grief. That was two very different experiences.

His gaze found her again. Impa now stood next to her, interrupting her intense stare with a delicate hand to her shoulder and leading her down towards Link. Zelda instinctively lifted her hood to cover herself.

The three of them converged. Impa addressed them both, “You two should get going. My reports have stated there are road blocks and traps. It’s going to take you a bit longer. I suggest taking one horse. It would be easier to defend with one. But the choice is yours.”

Zelda looked to Storm, the wild stud that let no other rider tame him except her. It was as if the horse was waiting for her all along, only to ever be loyal to her. Zelda bowed her forehead to him, embracing his snout tenderly with both hands. “Thank you, Storm, for leading me along the paths of this world safely and comfortably. Thank you for carrying me on this journey. You’re the only other male that has a piece of my heart.” She glared sidelong at Link, and he offered a small smile in return. Storm nickered his acceptance and reluctance as she pulled away.

She exhaled the horse’s shared breath and turned towards Impa. “By the way, where is Princess Zelda? Isn’t she the last surviving member of the royal family? Isn’t she now the Queen?”

The realization blew through all of them simultaneously as a cold wind. It was strange— for his focus as a knight in service to the royal family to be on this mission rather than their missing new Queen.

“She is safe. She and Sir Groose are hiding in the forbidden temple. There are still barriers in place to protect them deep within. And when you succeed and the dust has cleared, Hyrule will have a new ruler.”

He couldn’t help but try to picture what an interesting change of circumstance lay ahead for them. Because he refused to fail again. Princess Zelda as the Queen. And hopefully Zelda and him living a quiet life in Hateno.

“And what of the other leaders— Revali, Daruk, Mipha, Urbosa?” Link caught the hesitation when Zelda asked about Urbosa. Clearly, she was her favorite of the region leaders.

The closest thing to a frown he’d seen from Impa appeared, “We hadn’t heard direct reports yet. The roads to each region have been swarmed with monsters and guardians— it’s been a challenge to get information in and out.”

Zelda nodded, sadly.

“Good luck to you both.” Impa surprised him by pulling Zelda into an embrace as close to resembling true affection as Impa could muster. She whispered against the shell of Zelda’s ear, “I shouldn’t have to state the obvious, but I believe in you.”

The obvious being that if they failed, everyone they knew would be doomed. Impa pulled away from Zelda and faced Link, “I believe in both of you.”

He didn’t react with his surprise at the fierce woman’s disarming sentiment. Instead, his mouth was a flat line, and he nodded.

He helped Zelda onto Epona’s back first, then swung up with as much grace as he could to settle himself behind her, careful not to squish her in the saddle as he lightly cracked the reins for Epona to move.

And as Epona trotted out of town, there was no one to see them off or say goodbye besides Impa. Ilya and Fledge were helping the refugees find places to sleep, and Link hadn’t been able to muster it. He hadn’t wanted to say the final goodbye. The same one Zelda gave Storm.

Despite the words, her tone said it all. The same tone he’d heard in the voices of men on the eve of battle who had already made their peace. She wasn’t saying goodbye for now.

They reached Kakariko Bridge before dusk. The road had been empty the whole way— no monsters, no travelers, nothing. The silence sat wrong.

Until they crossed the bridge, and Zelda gasped at the horror in front of them.

Even from the distance, he could see the stable completely engulfed in flames. Flames so high that the embers were floating past the top of the Dueling Peaks. Fire so hot that it was cobalt.

Had the horses, the stable owner, and the guests all made it out? He shuddered at the thought. This part of the region was supposed to be untouched by Ganondorf. Zelda shook in front of him. Her shaking back reverberated into his chest. They both dared not say one word. Even Epona was quiet as he yanked on her reins to halt.

The war had found them.

The path directly to Fort Hateno was too open, too risky. He saw monsters running; bokoblins, moblins, and surely hidden others all stalking the plain to pick off easy prey. He turned towards the stable; no beings were in that path. But he knew, despite the nearby presence of monsters, they could not have set a blaze as roaring.

Guardians were nearby. Their lasers were the only thing that could create that type of destruction.

He had a choice. Hightail to Fort Hateno directly, knowing for sure that the monsters would be on their trail immediately. Epona could run fast, but with the weight of two on her back, she would be slowed. One wrong move, and they would be facing dozens upon dozens of monsters. Or…

He turned towards the stable; the smoke from the flames would mask their presence. They could sneak into Bubinga Forest, under the shroud of the trees, then approach Fort Hateno from the East, limiting their monster interactions to practically none.

But— something hung in the air down that path. And not the raging fire, nor the smoke, or the ghostly air of the evening approaching.

“Where are we going?” Zelda’s soft voice murmured.

And he made the choice that changed everything.

They both dismounted Epona. Even with her mild temperament, the closer they drew to the blaze, the more she shied and sidestepped beneath them. The smoke alone would choke her.

After Zelda was safely on the ground, he turned towards Epona, to say the same goodbye Zelda said to her steed. He placed his forehead against Epona— the horse that had been through it all with him. The gift Ilya gave him. He didn’t say a word as the horse seemed to freeze, knowing what he was trying to silently convey. He lifted his head and met her large black eye with a sad smile.

He turned to Zelda, her lips quivering, nostrils flaring, eyes full of water. She sniffed away the sorrow, reaching her hand to pet Epona’s snout.

Link unhooked her saddle and reins, dropping them at her feet and gave her a soft slap to run— to run back towards Kakariko, out of danger.

At least he could do that for his trustworthy companion.

He pulled his hood up over his matted hair and fanned the cape across his shoulder to obscure the hilt at his back. It had been days since he’d bathed. It didn’t matter; what mattered was that none of Ganondorf’s minions could recognize the two of them out here alone and sending word back.

He grabbed Zelda’s hand as they hugged the canyon walls, approaching the stable cautiously, carefully. The air was full of smoke, floating embers, and ash; it helped their disguise, but something in the air felt charged, as a snake ready to strike in the tall grass. As he gripped her hand, leading her along as fast as he could go without being noticeable, he tried not to focus on how cold her hand was. It was Din’s Summer still; the temperature was balmy and warm, especially in the Necluda Region.

Then he realized it was Din’s Summer. It had been a year since they met. In his single-minded task to obtain the Master Sword and rescue her, they had met exactly a year ago. 

And even worse, her name day— or birthday, as she called it— had passed while she was imprisoned. His heart sunk even further.

She said she never enjoyed celebrating it; it was too painful to be reminded of her parents’ death anniversary. ‘It hadn’t felt right to be so happy one day and sad the next’, she had said to him.

He stopped near the small basin of the waterfall. The rain water that collected off the Dueling Peaks flowing into its own pool. He could feel the heat from the blaze of the stable seeping through his clothes, burning his skin from the distance. Before making the decision to wade through the shallows. He turned to look at her.

Her face was still hollow; the shadows from her hood darkened her eyes. Her loose, golden hair hidden beneath. She was unrecognizable. Which was probably a good thing. She furrowed her brow at him, confused by his delay.

He reached his hand to her cheek, cold to the touch even with the heat of the blaze on them. She nuzzled into him, and her gaze softened. Her big, beautiful eyes gleamed. He leaned in and kissed her. Softly, carefully. Her lips opened for him as she stepped herself into his chest, gripping his collar tightly. Her breath was warm and sweet— tart like the apple she had eaten only an hour ago.

He wanted to memorialize this moment. This quiet, slow moment that was just them. Just here. Just now. Because he knew everything was about to change.

As her tongue rolled over his own. Teeth clanging. He would celebrate her name day—birthday— when this was over. Just as they celebrated his own in their house in Hateno a month ago. She made him a cake, that tasted terrible, and he knew that he would have to cook for them, forever. And he hadn’t cared, not as she smeared the overly sweet frosting on his face. As he furrowed his nose at the mess she made, she offered to clean him up, gliding her tongue across his cheek as she licked it off. Then somehow, frosting was everywhere, on their clothes, in their hair— soon enough, they were naked and washing it off in the too-small bathtub. Her, riding him in the basin, as his arms lay flat on her back, holding her close, water splashing all over the wooden floors until the water was good and cold.

It was the best birthday he ever had.

As he slowed the kiss, she pulled away. A sympathetic look sketched her features. As if she read all the thoughts swirling in his head, telling him mind-to-mind, soul-to-soul, that it didn’t matter. She didn’t like her birthday anyway. She just wanted him. For them to survive this impossible destiny. Together. 

He kissed her forehead, acknowledging that unsaid truth and stepped into the water.

The rain had started before they exited the water. The small drops rippling along the water’s surface then grew larger, more frequent. They pressed their sleeves to their mouths to block the paralyzing smoke. Above the fabric, blue eyes and green eyes moved through the haze.

He held her hand as they drew further from the stable. His shoulders sagged with relief, knowing that he hadn’t seen any bodies of horses or people. A small mercy. But the silence beneath the noise was what unsettled him most.

No birds or insects singing or chirping. Nothing alive and small enough to flee had stayed. Only the fire filled the absence—the deep, structural groan of a beam giving way, the sharp crash of something collapsing inward, and carrying from the flat plains, the low guttural roars of moblins. The rain hissed where it met the outer edges of the blaze. He could feel Zelda’s grip tighten each time a beam collapsed. And beneath all of it, the rhythmic squelch of their waterlogged boots, announcing them to anyone listening. He slowed his pace, trying to spread his weight across each step, willing the sound to disappear.

They crept along the open area in the plains, to the opening of the pass, and he froze, his blood going cold in the thick of summer. Zelda following suit.

A guardian stationed in the direct center of the pass. Camped to permanently halt any who tried to escape the region.

His mind went fast.

Their boots were wet. Weighing them down.

But it was getting dark, and the sounds of fire muffled them.

Maybe.

Its eye wasn’t on them yet. Yet.

So he started to run, sprinting towards Bubinga Forest. Tugging on Zelda’s hand to hurry, not able to glance at her face. Not chancing even a split-second delay. Only her cold hand in his told him she was with him.

Then his blade awoke. The glowing, ethereal light radiated from its sheath. Zinging. Begging to be released beneath the cape of his hood.

And the eye found them.

Chapter 40: Explode
Chapter Text
They had made it to the dense covering of the forest, but the guardian was still raging behind them.

A red dot danced between the trees, the guardian’s pinpoint laser closing in. Its mechanical legs churned through the mud, inhumanly fast. He didn’t need to see it to know the outcome: a direct hit would blast them to nothing, and even a near miss would raze the ground and leave them injured.

So all he could do was run for any cover. Pulling Zelda with him. And quite literally, he had to drag her behind him.

They were weaving through the trees. The canopy of leaves did little to stop the thick drops of rain pelting on them. Their boots were already heavy and waterlogged, now their clothing was drenched, making them— him, slower.

He was ducking under low-hanging branches, pulling Zelda’s hand when a blast exploded next to them, merely a few paces away. That familiar heat erupted, so hot he swore his clothes dried a little. Dirt, mud, pieces of bark flew in the air, higher than the tree canopy. He managed to stop and pull Zelda into his chest behind a large tree.

He almost got her— themselves— killed.

He gripped her so tight that it had to be painful. He eased, shoving her back to take in her face. The horror was plain in her eyes, wide and wild. Her breathing was ragged, from fear or from running all that distance, or both. Her eyes were looking everywhere but at his own.

“We have to keep going—” He grabbed her face, urging her to look at him, “—it will keep blowing apart every tree near us until there is none left.”

Until there was nothing for them to hide behind.

She closed her eyes, she wasn’t registering his winded command. Her head was shaking. Her breaths were shallow.

Then, true terror gripped him. All the commotion from the guardian stalker attracted another towards them, from Blatchery Plain. Its possessed eye scanning the trees, finding its target. The laser counting down.

He had a split second. The river was a trap if they were cut off. The open plain was suicide. That left one path: east, through the forest, toward the slim hope of Fort Hateno.

He looked to Zelda; her eyes were desolate, not here.

He had to pull her, get her out of this.

So he did.

He yanked her hand along the trees and the high grass. Avoiding roots, rocks, and shrubs. He turned over his shoulder, both stalkers still targeting them. He only caught a glimpse of Zelda's face. Any remaining color she may have had left was now zapped from her. She was a pale shadow, trying not to be snuffed out. She may have gone into shock, her legs only moving because he was tugging her.

He was moving with all his stamina. They somehow managed to put a distance between them, but it wouldn’t last. If they kept going, they might make it—

Then the weight in his hand ceased.

He turned; Zelda was lying in the mud. Felled to her knees, her hands barely propping her up.

His heart cracked as he rushed back to her. She was on her knees, helpless in the mud. He'd been pulling her too hard, too fast. Her breathing was a raw, ragged sound, each gasp a struggle for air. The weeks in that cell had hollowed out her strength. He knelt in the mud beside her, lifting her palms to see them scraped raw, blood and dirt swirling into a grisly paste before the rain washed it clean. She lifted her head, her face tense, eyes gleaming with a feverish light.

She was breaking, from the shock of it. He knew of this horrid machine, had already fought it. She only ever saw it from the distance, never seeing its true potential for death and destruction. He recognized that look. The way her mind was still trying to make sense of what her eyes had already told her.

She was muttering something, her lips shaking as she lowered her forehead to his chest.

“What?” He asked as softly as he could in the shell of her ear, but he couldn’t help his panicked tone. He’d never seen her this way. Not after weeks in a cell, not after he pushed her away. This would be what muddied her mind. “Zelda, please, talk to me.”

“My dreams—” she muttered at his chest.

He shook his own head. “What dreams?”

Her voice was like that of a child’s, a child that had known fear. “I dreamt this, before Hyrule, before everything.” She choked back a sob. “Link, my dreams always ended—”

He grabbed her face, hard. Harder than he meant to. His mouth a straight line, his jaw tense. His eyes pleading to look into his own. He didn’t want her to finish that sentence. He couldn’t bear it.

He pressed his mouth to hers, not gently, tasting rain and dirt, because he needed her to feel that he was still there, that they were both still there. It was the most inappropriate time, but he couldn’t think of anything else to do. The kiss was empty, but she stilled against him as he pulled away to take in her face. “Zelda.” He said, willing her to look at him as he whispered the next prayer, keeping his own voice from cracking. “Stay with me.”

She closed her eyes, her brows crumpled in defeat, and she nodded sadly.

The guardians they put distance between made progress and now gained on them, and there were two more that joined the hunt. Zelda stood on shaky legs, her knees cut open. He could taste the tang of her blood in the air.

Then a wave of chilling familiarity washed over him. The nightmare from a year ago. It wasn’t just a dream. The mud, the rain, her desperate face... he was living it. It had been her all along, the woman he pulled and carried. The Master Sword humming on his back. Their fate, already written.

He shoved the revelation down. There was no time to contemplate destiny when it was hunting them with laser precision.

His head jerked back into reality. She couldn’t make it at the pace they were going; she was too tired. He could carry her, but that left him unable to use his blade against the horde of monsters between them and Fort Hateno. They could hide from the guardians for only so long before more descended upon them, obliterating the forest to dust. If they decided to run or briskly walk and were too slow— 

He swallowed the pain of that thought.

So he lifted Zelda into his arms and took off running towards Fort Hateno.

He waited until he was at the edge of the forest before he made his move.

He held Zelda’s waterlogged body against his own. Her black pants, white shirt, and corset might have appeared brown due to the mud and dirt that had accumulated on her. Her cape covered her face, but had it mattered? The guardians didn’t care who they were. While his sights were scanning every which direction for the least amount of threat, her eyes were vacant on his chest. As if all the light had gone out.

She was light but heavy in his grip. Light enough that he wouldn’t get tired, but heavy enough that he would be slow. He had to time it perfectly.

The fortified wall of Hateno was in his sights. He was catching his breath, scanning the horizon. Three guardians were in the tangle of the forest, still searching for them. Two others were closing in from Blatchery Plains. He had to wait until their gaze shifted and then he’d run.

And as they did, so did he.

He took off in a mad dash to Fort Hateno. The fortified iron gate was shut. Not ideal. But he eyed guards on top of the wall, scanning the carnage of the plain. They would see him running towards them and hopefully raise it so they did not have to put themselves in a vulnerable position for long.

The rain pelted his face like a cold lance. Each drop sending chills through his fibers, down to his soul. There was no warmth from Zelda in his arms as he cradled her against him, trying and failing not to jostle her more than necessary.

He ran, dodging rocks and small craters in the earth. His boots were squishing, indenting the earth as he went.

Run. Run faster. Don’t stop moving.

It was close. A guard stationed on the wall turned to them and waved to another guard. They saw them, they were going to let them through. Only a few more strides and they would make it.

The warning from Zelda’s lips was lost as the world detonated around them. A blinding, brilliant flash of a color he’d never seen, then the earth collapsed and simply ceased to exist beneath his boots. The concussion was so strong his ears popped and he was certain something inside his head had cracked. All he could hear was a shrill, metallic screech, as though claws dug inside his skull.

His body was airborne, hurtling through the air along with the debris and Zelda until the impact slammed into his back. And for a split second the world was entirely white, then dark as he blinked mud and blood from his face.

He’d let his focus drift for a second too long. A guardian had found them. The laser blast had thrown him forward, ripping Zelda from his arms. 

The ringing was getting louder.

The Master Sword. It was begging— pleading— to be unsheathed.

He lay on the ground, propping himself up, his gloves full of silt. Zelda lay ahead of him. He had to get up, get her to safety.

He lifted her back into his arms. Her face was splattered with dirt and small cuts. Before he could have a thought on it, a red, precision dot was glowing against her shoulder. The two guardians on the plain found them.

He clocked a boulder large enough to shield them briefly to his left, and ran behind it. He sat Zelda down with as much gentleness as he could onto the cold, wet ground. Then he tore his wet gloves off, throwing them to the side. Zelda said nothing, her eyes wide as he then promptly unsheathed the blade that was singing on his back.

The blade’s holy light illuminated the space between them. He looked to her, her green eyes entranced on the blade, the light carving half her face into brightness and leaving the rest in grey. He said with as much authority as he could muster, “Zelda!”

She snapped out of her haze.

“Run to the fort on my signal. They will raise the gate to let you in. I’ll give you enough time to make it.”

She grabbed a fist of his tunic. Eyes wild. She rasped, “No.”

His eyes burned, “Zelda, you have to make it. You have to live. Not only because you are the godd—”

“Don’t fucking say it.” She hissed, tears and rain streaming down her face as she interrupted him.

He ignored her, “—not only because you are the goddess. But because I love you. Let me do this. You deserve to have a better life than this.”

Than this carnage. This war she was thrust into. Because the goddess chose her out of all the available options.

She scowled at him, her voice breaking, “You are my life.”

He didn’t have time to convince her, to beg her to run. The guardians were closing in fast. He knew what he had to do. He’d done it before, found the exact words that would make her flinch, make her pull back, make her leave. He hated himself for knowing how. He hated himself more for needing to use it again.

“You need to survive, otherwise every innocent man, woman, and child will die. You are the only one who can truly stop him.” The words were thick on his tongue, tasting of lead. The horrible truth.

She would die with him, willingly, because she loved him. But he needed her to live, not only to save the innocents but for his own weary soul to find peace soon after, when he inevitably met his own end.

She spit on the ground and seethed, “How. Dare. You. I know what you're doing. We need to do this together. It’s both of us or none.” She was shaking her head frantically, certainly not in shock anymore as her anger was palpable between them. “Just last night you promised me. You go. I go.” Her eyes were full of fire and malice, challenging him to argue with her.

He huffed, wanting to scrap with her. This was not what he meant when he told her that prayer. He needed to convince her to go, but the guardians were here. He clenched his mouth, unable and unwilling to say another word to her, and jumped out behind the boulder. Blade in hand. 

The guardian was a tree length away. Another was running impossibly fast on its spidery legs behind it. He made his move to charge directly at the closer of the two.

The mechanical creature grew taller as he approached, feinting its own defense. That possessed eye located him, the pulsing light trailing a red beam onto him. He had about twenty seconds. He ran straight at it, both hands wrenching the blade high above his head, and brought it down hard into the joint of its nearest leg.

The blade sliced through enchanted metal as if it were flesh. He didn’t understand the magic, only that it worked. He wasn’t a hero, not in his own mind. He was just a man with one desperate goal:

Zelda to live.

As each leg was cut, the guardian stalled, trying and failing to regain its composure. Its laser stunned, as if the creature needed a moment to register what was happening to it.

The second guardian was approaching fast. He maneuvered himself to put the first in front of him, blocking its view. He was testing the theory that it would not target its own kind. Which was correct.

He sprung up, with every ounce of power in his legs to deliver a fatal stab to the guardian's eye. Just as the first time he killed one, it powered down, never to be woken again.

He only had a second to catch his breath as he moved to the next, now upon him. 

He used the same tactics on the first. Disabling its legs, then its eye, then it stopped.

But all the commotion attracted more. Three were abhorrently sprinting towards him. He turned to where he placed Zelda. Seeing her face behind the small boulder, watching him. She was pale, her lips parted, her eyes fixed on him with an expression he had no name for but felt like a hand closing around his throat. He could see her heart thundering behind the boulder. He only mouthed one word to her, “Run.”

But she didn’t budge.

He breathed in a deep breath. Breathed in the charged air. The feeling of battle— of adrenaline— washed over him. He tasted that cool tang of metal. Of magic. He exhaled, and got to work conducting his own ballad.

All three approached. He maneuvered himself further from where Zelda hid, enough distance between where he was and Fort Hateno. If on the off chance she did decide to run.

But she wouldn’t. He knew her. He wouldn’t leave her, why would she leave him? She would die here before she left him. So there was nothing left to do but kill everything between them.

He cut, slashed, shredded. The only weapon he had was the Master Sword and it was gloriously violent. It had been starving for this, to sing the song of destruction and he was happy to conduct it. He let himself fall into the focus of battle, all his years of training, every scar, every hurt, every pain was building to this.

One managed to cut his leg with its razor-sharp claw. But he did not buckle, he fought through it, wincing, then leaning into the pain. He managed to take down all three.

Then the pain pushed to the surface from the gash in his leg, and the sticky warmth of wet blood glued his pant leg to his calf.

His hands shook, not from fear, but from the throb of exertion vibrating up his arms with each twitch of the sword. The ground beneath him trembled faintly, as if the force of violence had not yet finished echoing.

But before he could stop the bleeding, the bokoblins and moblins roared in the distance, finally noticing him. In the middle of the plain, with a blade lit with holy light. He stuck out as a beacon, screaming to be challenged.

More guardians closed in. The ones from the forest, now realizing their prey was out in the open.

He didn’t have time to look to Zelda; he knew she was still put where he left her as two more guardians closed in. He was becoming tired, slow, and exhausted.

Would she finally realize it? When he was dead, would she try to run then? What could he possibly do to make her go?

Not loving her. Her not loving him. A knight cannot serve two masters. Impa was right. It defied all logic, all sense. Their fatal mistake.

He quickly spun to Zelda; her mouth was tense, her eyes heavy-lidded. He couldn’t open his mouth to tell her to go, to please run. Telepathically begging her to leave him. To go.

Then a feral cry sounded from him; he made the mistake to look at her, and the guardian closest to him cut his chest. The blade passed through like he wasn't there. His tunic ripped and shredded. Zelda screamed behind him.

Red, hot blood leaked out of his steaming skin. He stifled his yell and continued. The blade in his hands crooned for him to go on. It wasn’t finished yet.

Another slash of his blade, another cut on his leg. Another cut on its legs, another laceration on his arm. He was slowing. He could sense his body— a body supposedly trained for war, beginning to fail. Each movement came slower than the last, every vibration of the Master Sword in his hand sending a new message of agony through his nerves. Three more guardians approached; the moblins and bokoblins grew closer.

The closer of the guardian’s legs was nearly sheared, but not before it managed a last, desperate swipe at his thigh. He felt the line of fire rip through him but not before he was spinning, his face meeting the ground with a crunch.

He smelled blood in the air. No, tasted it in his mouth. Mixed with grit and dirt in his teeth. As if he rinsed with sandy water, he spit the hot mixture that was pooling. Somehow he was lucky enough to miss the guardian’s laser. Or perhaps it was unlucky because the pain was hot, stinging, burning. Unbearable.

A sharp stab to his side had him roaring. He flipped to his back, a bokoblin closed in first and had stabbed him with its crude bone dagger. Its demented smile flashed at him. He grabbed his blade and stuck it in its heart. The thump of its body was enough to pull him back to reality.

He drove the Master Sword into the earth and hauled himself to one knee, the wound in his thigh screaming at the weight. He managed to lift his head. He had just enough time to register the shadow of the moblin’s bat before it connected, and then he was airborne.

Forget what he knew about pain before. That wasn’t pain, not even close. This was endless agony. Pain so deep, it settled into his joints like something that had always lived there and intended to stay. He could feel his pulse in places he’d never felt it before— his teeth, his fingernails, the soft skin behind his knees. Each breath moved through him like broken glass.

In a sick twist of fate, a guardian had been targeting him before the moblin’s hit, and the moblin now ceased its existence, only a fiery crater in the ground left. For a split, horrible second, he wished he was still there as this pain was an unimaginable suffering. Wishing to be taken away like ashes on the wind.

He laid flat on his stomach, lifting his head, inadvertently lolling it. It was too heavy. The Master Sword lay inches from his grip. He tried to move his fingers but even a twitch caused splintering pain.

The blade’s light blinking weakly in front of him, as if his own life force was tied to it. The vigor, the desire. It was dying.

“Link!”

A voice called to him. Beckoning him.

“Link! Get up!”

A temptress called for him. Leading him home. He was almost there.

He dragged his head up, one eye caked with blood and grit, and saw her: Zelda.

She was here. She was coming for him. Somehow, he managed to smile at her, or at least bare his teeth.

There is something desperate about her momentum, a force of nature more than a person. She is screaming his name, but the sound is lost in the roar of the guardians’ approach and the madness of the battlefield behind him.

He sees her lips form his name again, the sound this time cutting through the chaos. “Link!” Her voice is wild and crisp, and in that instant, every battered part of his body remembered what it was to be alive. He locked onto her, tried to forget the wounds, the pain, the hot blur of the world. She is all that matters.

He tried to rise, to meet her, but his body refused. Everything from his shoulders down is a throb of agony, threaded with heat and cold and a roaring ache.

This is the punishment for yearning for her.

This is the punishment for having her. Getting to taste her. Kiss her. Love her.

He fisted the earth in front of him. Gripping it with the last of his strength. Willing his arms to pull him towards her. Master Sword in hand. Dirt in his fingernails as he grabbed the earth to inch closer.

Crawling. He was crawling to her.

He hadn’t cared if he looked pathetic or weak. In his dying moments, he would reach her. To save her from a second of pain. She is all he ever wanted to save.

She leaned down, her eyes wild and wide. Horror shown at his broken body. Delicate hands gripped his shoulders, “Get up!” She was yanking on what was left of his tunic. It was shredded and burned.

He had to try. He would not let her die here. He pressed his palms into the wet grass and pushed. His arms held for one trembling second before they buckled, and his face met the ground again. The grass was cold against his cheek and felt so at odds with the fire within him.

She tugged at him to get up, grabbing his blade, “Please.” Her broken plea to anyone that would listen.

He tried again, all he saw was a guardian approaching, its laser targeting him. And at least a dozen more behind it.

At least it was him, not her.

He found a serene calm in these final moments. He looked to her devastated face, the last image he would ever see. But even so, death could not hold him back from her, even if— and when— his body gave out and every bone broke, he would continue to crawl to her. If he no longer had his physical form, he would wrap his spirit around her. As long as she lived, the goddess couldn’t keep him from her.

The sound of the laser’s aim pulsed louder, faster. It was about to fire. His head was heavy, he saw the red mark on his chest, over his heart. He thought of his name day, how happy they’d been. He closed his eyes.

“NO!” Zelda screamed, as he chased that golden, holy light to his end.

He collapsed, and the world dissolved into light as the laser must have landed its mark.

Link.

Link.

Wake up.

The room flipped. He was floating, dreaming unconsciously. A mix of scenes queued in his head. So vivid and real.

Zelda, standing in their kitchen, the sunlight from the window beaming on her as she smiled at something outside the window. How beautiful she was. How lucky that she chose him to live in this home with.

But then shadows rolled in like smoke under the door of the memory. The door violently swung open. Numerous foes garbed in red leather with colorless masks. They charged in, overrunning him. Grabbing Zelda. Dragging them from their home.

But a blade shone in the shadows, its holy light cutting through the darkness. It gravitated to him. Sure in his grip. He became everything he had always desired to be. But he was missing one crucial piece.

An eruption of gold. A dome of holy fire raining down amongst their enemies. A rebirth, an awakening.

Zelda.

He opened his eyes. The warmth on his skin mirrored the room he was in. The candlelight flickered against the dark-stained oak logs, casting silhouettes across the small room. A cabin.

He was no longer wet and cold. He looked at his arms, his guards were gone. He was dressed in only a loose shirt. The wounds he sustained were bandaged.

Was this… death?

He couldn't hear anything. Just his own breathing, slow and even, in a bed that was somehow softer than any he'd slept in before.

But he still ached. Perhaps it was his punishment for failing. To spend eternity with a dull ache in his side.

He lifted his head slightly, someone else was here in the room. A commanding presence. Radiating the small space.

They stood on the far side of the small room, near the only door. With a table and chairs between them. Their back was to him, draped in white linens. A matching shawl covering their head.

His voice was raw but firm, “Who are you?” He demanded to know.

The person tensed, then relaxed and turned to face him, pulling the shawl down. His stomach dropped and lifted at the same time. It was the most beautiful woman he’d ever laid eyes on. Her emerald green eyes shone on his own.

Zelda.

She watched him process everything, tilting her head in feline amusement. Standing far from him. She was Zelda, but not.

His mouth hung open, but he managed to choke out behind his dry mouth, “Am I dead?”

Zelda, but not Zelda, smirked at him. A familiar expression he hadn’t seen since they were last at their house in Hateno.

“That’s my line.” She said playfully. Her voice was different, the same tone but otherworldly. Somehow wise and young. His confused expression faded as he remembered their first meeting; she had asked the same question.

The only thing circling in his head was, “Where am I?”

She huffed a chuckle. Music in his ears. “That’s mine too. I suppose nearly dying gives you the right to recycle my questions.”

But how she appeared before him was impossible…

She strode closer, and he got a good look at her against the warm glow of the candlelight. She was whole, golden, the picture of health. Not the pale wraith she had just been. The cheeks that were hollow and carved were now lifted and full. The sun-kissed color of her skin had returned, and her blond hair was cascading on her side, shining and silken, as if real gold strands were woven into it. She was in the prayer dress, her shoulders upright and proud, not caved in and hunched.

How long had he been asleep? How was he not dead? Where the hell were they?

He breathed, “How?”

She sat on the edge of the small bed. As if she read all the thoughts that were transparent on his face, she offered him a soft smile, “I’ll show you.” She cupped his cheek; her skin was warm— comforting sparks glittered into his soul at the touch. Her scent drifted to his senses. That familiar one that was gone after her imprisonment. Now magically back.

Before he could lean into her touch. She leaned down and kissed his lips, softly, confidently.

It was Zelda.

He was propelling through his closed vision. Backtracking but too fast to hold onto anything. Then it stopped.

And the scene unfolded as a painting and settled. It was as if he was seeing it for the first time. The rain on his skin felt different—colder, sharper. A bone-deep exhaustion radiated through his limbs, a weariness so profound it felt foreign. He felt his arms tremble, his legs ache with the desperate need to run and the utter inability to do so.

This wasn't his fatigue. This wasn't his body. He was on Blatchery Plains again, but now he was looking out from behind her eyes, watching his own broken form in the mud.

Chapter 41: Explode p. II
Notes:
Long chapter drop and a long chapter note— very fitting.

First, this chapter is a monster, probably the largest one yet, but I couldn’t split it into two. To be frank, the next few chapters are all thick. And with that, we’re nearing the end. There will be five more after this to wrap up this story.

And second, I want to reiterate something, especially as we head into the climax. This story is very clearly non-canon and while there is heavy canon influence throughout; the powers and abilities are my own reimagining.

The canon version of the following events is fairly abstract and, in my opinion, was never really explored, so I wanted to take a swing at it. I hope you enjoy it.

Chapter Text
There was a blade in her lungs. A pinch on her side. A squeezing pressure in her hand, bones crushing. Rain, cold enough to steal the breath she had left.

The water in her eyes blurred her vision. They were running. Dodging branches and roots faster than her eyes could register them.

Then she fell, her knees bursting on impact.

The wet ground seeped into the cloth of her pants, mixing with the blood. Numbness replaced the pain.

Heat roasted her skin through her clothes. Burning.

The searing heat, the crushing grip, a phantom memory flickered. Not a dream, but a rehearsal. A warning she had failed to understand. Her destiny.

Link looked to her with pity and sadness and longing in his eyes. Because she was fragile and weak and pathetic.

“Stay with me.”

She couldn’t run anymore. Link pulled her into his arms.

She was going to get them killed.

They made it halfway to the Fort Hateno. And then her head went quiet.

A guardian had almost blown them to smithereens. A horrid ringing grew inside her skull as she came to. She’d landed on her back; a sharp rock jabbed beneath her, a deep, screaming pain that felt like it had ruptured something vital. She could feel the sick warmth of blood pooling inside her.

She rolled over clutching her side, curling up within herself. Then she heard it.

Beseeching. A plea.

Link?

She managed to lift her head, wincing as the ringing pounded through her.

No, Link was meters from her, on his stomach, mid-push up to run. He had not begged. He had not pleaded.

A glow from his back, the sheathed sword. A million voices spoke as one. Ancient, unearthly, somehow both distant and whispering directly into her.

She was hallucinating.

But it made her uncurl from herself. The ringing falling away.

Before she could investigate, Link had swept her in his arms. And before she could pause and think, a red, angry light flashed onto her ripped shirt. Link ducked behind a boulder, just barely large enough to shield them.

Then she heard it again, a song. A melody, pulsing and breathing into her heart. A primordial voice. It was kindred. Family. She looked past Link, his horrid, dark tunic soaked with mud and rain. That glow…

He lifted his right hand to release the holy blade from its sheath. It gleamed with a brilliance she had never seen before. A light that was not of this world. She was enthralled; the ringing in her head seemed to cease as she gazed upon the blade. That primordial voice was telling her its secret. Her secret. But it was at the end of a tunnel; it echoed into her, but she couldn’t make out the words—

“Zelda!”

Her eyes met his. The blue of them caught the light of the blade, brilliant and electric. But underneath it, something rawer—adrenaline and… fear.

“Run to the fort on my signal; they will raise the gate to let you in. I’ll give you enough time to make it.”

She sneered at him. She sneered at him, grabbing a fist of his tunic, practically ringing the water from it. “No.”

“Zelda, you have to make it. You have to live. Not only because you are the godd—”

She pushed at him, but he hadn’t moved. She hated him a year ago, when he put up walls to shut her out. And she hated him now for what he was doing. “Don’t fucking say it.” She choked out, tears and rain streaming down her face as she interrupted him.

He ignored her, “—not only because you are the goddess. But because I love you. Let me do this. You need to have a better life than this.”

Such a martyr. Such a hero. But so incredibly Link. He would always out himself first. It was just his nature.

She couldn’t hide the building sob. “You are my life.”

It was pathetic, really, but unavoidably true. It was as crucial as breathing. As essential as food. They were meant to be together for life.

He exhaled a breath as though he was blowing out nausea. “You have to survive. If you don’t, Hyrule dies with you. You’re the only one who can stop him for good.”

Her tongue had turned to ash in her mouth. She spit, probably blood and saliva onto the ground, sick with it. “How. Dare. You. I know what you're doing. We need to do this together. It’s all or none.” She was shaking her head frantically, certainly not in shock anymore as her anger was palpable between them. “Just last night you promised me. You go. I go.”

He would not break this promise to her. She would not allow it.

Before they could continue to argue their life, or rather death, pact. His tipped ears perked and the sounds of the blade were then drowned out by the whirling and clacking of machines. The guardians were close. He was already pouncing from his position to face them head-on before she could stop him.

She grasped the slippery, wet rock face, peering over it as the fight began. The man she loved running headfirst towards two guardians that were ten times his size. She hadn’t been able to focus on these wretched monsters before, but seeing them up close was worse than the lynels he faced. Worse than anything.

They moved with an unnatural speed, closing distances in a blur. Their legs were three-pointed daggers that tore at the earth, and their heads spun in a full circle, scanning, tracking. And the laser, she had already witnessed its condemning blow. Their only flaw was the countdown before firing, a few precious seconds for a target to dodge oblivion.

She shuddered. Magic and machines. Ganondorf’s malice had wormed itself into every gear and joint of these things, puppeteering them toward anything breathing, anything with a heartbeat. Toward Link. But he was magnificent. That blade fit to him and him alone. The beautiful destruction they would create together. She watched as he strategically feinted and dodged and swung that holy blade into its legs, a clean slice separating it from its body, forever in two.

Her face went blank for a moment, then crinkled into disbelief. Link had always been extraordinary. The skills and techniques she was witnessing were not something he was given or gifted when he pulled that magnificent blade. He earned it, over years of training, blood, sweat, and injuries. If anything, or anyone, in this realm was fit to be the hero of legend, it was him.

The thought barely left her as he stabbed one guardian in the eye. Then he turned to the second. She watched him jump, dodge, roll, and slice— each movement bleeding into the next, relentlessly, until the blade found its eye. The guardian’s rotor slowed. Its legs buckled one by one, folding beneath it like a closing hand. The malice drained out of it, and it was still.

But she barely had time to nurture that bloom of hope in her chest as three more caught their attention from the distance. Amongst the gray backdrop, the rain had ceased, and he turned his sodden head to her. The blue in his eyes were gone as she tasted the adrenaline in the air between them. The charged energy of a gauge maxed out. He looked animalistic as he yelled at her to “Run!”

Run to Fort Hateno. Run to safety. Run and leave him behind.

But physically she couldn’t move, and her heart would not either.

He hadn’t had a chance to check if she obeyed before the three were upon him.

He ran further away from her, from safety. He was angling himself to give her a chance to live.

But she couldn’t. She wouldn’t go. It was the most selfish thing she could do.

He was battling all three guardians at once this time. She held her breath as she watched him face off against these wicked abominations. For a moment it all stopped. He stood proud, in his dirty tunic, that gleaming blade in his hand, he flicked his wrist in challenge, as the rain started to pick up again. Splashes of blue, purple, and red— the guardian's lights against the gray dusk, burned into her memory. An epic, terrible painting taking shape. War drums that did not exist beat in her chest, a rhythm for the slaughter.

Then he was cut, a razor-sharp blade to his leg. But he did not buckle. He did not falter. He continued until all three were defeated.

Then the roar of moblIns and bokoblins.

Then two more guardians approached.

Why wasn’t anyone helping him? She turned to the fort to glare at the soldiers posted. Why weren’t they sending infantry to help him?

The answer washed over her like drowning in an icy river.

Because they hadn’t wanted to send more men to their graves.

She covered her mouth to stop the sob that threatened to break from her. No one would help. And she was too weak. Too broken. Each wound he took was her fault. If she hadn’t wasted away in that cell, if he hadn’t been forced to carry her dead weight, they could have made it—

He looked back at her for one fleeting moment, then she watched as his face twisted in pain as a cut landed on his chest.

His tunic ripped and red started growing. He caved into himself. The flesh was angry and puckered. She screamed. As if the scream would save him.

That split second cost him. She was being selfish, and now she was the reason he would die.

A cut to his arm. A cut to his leg. This was the slow motion before the crash. The inevitability of it. More guardians in the distance, as if they spawned anew each time he defeated one, and the hog-like monsters were closing in from the other side. He was trapped with only her to his back—

Then he flew, his body cracking against the ground in the worst sound she’d ever heard. A guardian’s laser just missed him, but the earth’s ground propelled him outwards. How he managed to hold onto the sword, she’d never know. Before he could even think to rise, a bokoblin stabbed him in his ribs.

Tears were streaming down her face, mixed with rain. Salt and fresh water seeping into her lips.

He stabbed it in the heart, but immediately after a moblin’s bat cracked at his other side, and he went flying into a boulder.

Perhaps it was lucky, she never thought she could feel that way about anything that caused him pain, but the next second the guardian’s laser found the moblin instead of Link, and it ceased to exist.

She waited long seconds for him to stand, but no movement came from his bleak form. If he wasn’t already—

She choked at the thought.

Every Spiritual Stone she plucked from the water, every ounce of misgiving she felt. Every sense screaming she didn’t belong. That she was a mistake. And now she cowered behind a rock, watching him lay his life down. Every swing costing him something he could not get back.

And she knew she should stay hidden, for him, for Hyrule. She knew that she had nothing to offer, no magic, no blade, no strength. Going to him would only give him one more distraction, one more reason to hesitate, one more way to get him killed.

So she stayed, clutching the rock face, her nails breaking against the unmovable stone.

She stayed.

She—

She ran to the other part of her soul.

She used the last of her energy, adrenaline she borrowed that lived in the space between them.

Each step towards him was a memory.

Waking up in a foreign bed. Her head hurt. Greeted by eyes so blue— a lagoon to dive into, floating forever underneath the surface. Her favorite color.

Another step.

Darkness pressing into her, the weight of her tether pulling her out into the field, his blade coated in blood. The terror and anger blending.

Another step.

A humble smile shared across a campfire. A blooming friendship taking root.

Another step.

A lizalfo erased, the next dropped in the sand. The heat of the desert was no match to what she felt embracing him. Safe in his arms.

Another step.

The glow of the dark sky against Farosh’s lightening as it danced around them in tune to the charged lust between them.

Another step.

Her senses frayed in a pond, kissing him— his calloused hands tracing her curves, every motion erupting fire.

Another step.

The green gown twirling and glittering as it slowed in his arms, dipping her low and the moment she let herself fall.

Another step.

The spark that was him between her legs, undulating and thrusting in her. Their sweat mixed together and dried on his forehead.

Another step.

The declaration he laid bare to her in the warm confines of their home. ‘I love you.’

Another step.

‘And when I am a forgotten knight with my bones buried deep, or my ashes to the wind, you will be the legend I want my name sung next to and remembered for.’

Another step.

‘You go. I go.’

Another step.

She kept going to him. Mud splattering as her waterlogged boots kept pounding the ground. The battlefield. The carnage around them blurring as the tunnel of her vision focused on him.

She was close now. Close enough to see him crawling to her. His knuckles white around the hilt of the sword that was fading. Close enough to witness the fear— the grit, in his eyes as he used the last of his strength to claw at the raw earth, fisting it and pulling himself to her. Smiling at her.

It broke everything that was left in her as she reached him. She tugged at his ruined tunic, her voice breaking. “Get up.”

He tried, using the flickering master sword as leverage. He was barely conscious.

Guardians and monsters behind him. Ready to bulldoze over them both.

“Pl— lease,” she sobbed, her attempts to lift him were futile. There was nowhere to hide, nowhere to run as the closest guardian’s beam landed on Link’s chest. 

They had mere seconds before it erupted. And even if she was able to somehow hide them both, dozens more guardians were closing in fast and more monsters not far off.

They never promised each other forever. Only that whisper of a prayer; you go, I go. Into the unknown. Four words that meant nothing to most, meant everything to her.

He angled himself in front of her. This time she was going to watch him die. No cell door to block her view. No one to save him. He would not escape from this.

But she would honor that prayer to him.

She wasn’t born strong. Or gifted. Or clever. But the goddess blessed her with spirit. And all she had been through, she was adaptable, and she would adapt in death. The goddess gave Link steel in his hands, she had it in her blood.

She would block that final blow with her own body. Flesh against fire as she pushed him behind her.

And the world was reborn as she screamed that defiance out into the listening universe.

First, she felt warm. Like the first sun’s rays of the morning warming her skin.

Then, a hot, scorching, burning, boiling her blood. Cooking her from the inside.

But comfortable. Tranquil.

An ancient call screaming to be released. It lived dormant in the floor of her. In the walls of her soul.

Her eyes fluttered open; everything was so bright— like she had woken up on a beach at midday with not a cloud in the sky. That white, golden filter blinding her, coming from her. She felt her own history and future collide. Faces she did not recognize, bodies that were too tall, shades of hair opposite of her own. She was not wholly herself but the sum of hundreds of lives. A nuclear reactor exploded from her soul, pouring magical, limitless energy through her veins. 

So this was power.

She wasn’t in complete control. She wasn’t operating the machine that was her body. Something, someone, took the reins. God-like.

Goddess-like.

She had not heard the whining, the screaming, the failure around them. She had not heard the ceasing of life.

She felt serene, at peace. All the fear and furor left her on a floating wind. As she exhaled and the light faded.

Her hand was raised outwards, extended towards the guardian, a golden triangle illuminated from under her skin. Matching the ring just above it. As if a tattoo that had been inked there since the dawn of time but had been dormant. 

Every guardian and monster in sight was—

Not dead.

Obliterated.

That was the nicer word for what she had done.

And the world was quiet. The grass, the air, the trees stilled. Shocked at the power they witnessed. Only the sounds of her shallow breaths. Until metal clashed against rock. A thump followed.

She lowered her hand, not yet ready to fully comprehend what had happened, and turned.

Link.

He had collapsed. The Master Sword lay next to him.

“Link!”

Blood was pouring out of him. From everywhere. He’d been hit so many times that she couldn’t count how many wounds he had. But the worst was a small one on his bicep. She knew a main artery had been cut by the way the blood gushed out. She raised her hand to stifle it while cradling his head in the other.

She had always imagined grave wounds to gush thick blood, but it wasn’t thick. It was flowing thin like a raging river. Not a chance to dam it before the destruction.

No. She awoke the power too late.

If she hadn’t been cowering behind that rock—

“He can still be saved.”

The voice made every hair on her body stand on edge. That warmth that had flooded her moments ago vanished at the sound of the age-old voice. It was robotic, struggling, emotionless— but not evil.

She dared ask the invisible voice, “How?”

A pause, the Master Sword blinking in answer, “A fairy. It hides; you must find it.”

The Master Sword spoke to her. But it was fading, with its master. Its holy luster was an indicator, tied directly to his own heart.

“Where?”

“Closeeee.”

She ripped at her shirt, producing a cloth large enough to tie around his arm. The second she finished tying it off, the mud-white linen turned rich red. If by some miracle he didn’t lose all his blood, he was certainly going to need antibiotics or some sort of cleanse to stop an infection. 

“I don’t know what a fairy is or looks like. How am I supposed to—”

A flash of her form appeared as an image bloomed in her mind: small, glowing creatures with iridescent wings. An ancient instinct, long buried, now surfaced. She didn’t just know what a fairy was; she could feel one. It was close, a subtle pull like a string tied to her heart.

She gently laid Link’s head down; he was unconscious. Probably for the best given how painful his wounds would have been. But she shook away the thought about his blood loss and quickly turned left towards a small pool with lily pads and reeds.

She stepped over the legs of a lifeless guardian. The red light in its eye had gone dark, as if it had never been a color to begin with.

She stood at the edge of the pond, closing her eyes to focus, and she heard glittering movements. Her eyes sharpened like a predator, zeroing in on a small crevice. She knelt in the water to become eye level with it, and sure enough, a strong twinkle flashed. She quickly reached her hand in to grab the creature, pulling it out.

It was furious, a tiny, buzzing sun of pure indignation. It rattled in the cage of her hands, throwing itself against the walls of her palms. She whispered to the creature, “I’m sorry. But I need you to save the man I love.”

She ran back over to Link, careful not to trip on a guardian, a rock, or any other landmine. She sat down next to him, and he had become deathly pale. She wasn’t sure he was still alive as she held her breath until the Master Sword throbbed softly.

“Now what?” She asked the sword.

Its voice sounded far away as it said, “Let go.”

She wanted to protest, but she reluctantly obeyed, opening her hands, and the fairy darted out. She braced herself to watch it fly away and give her a rude gesture in return, but it hesitated, gently fluttering its wings above Link’s chest.

Then it dove straight into his chest where his heart lay, as if his flesh, muscles, and bones were not even there. And just as quickly, it exited back the way it came, cradling him, leaving glittering dust in its wake.

Then the color returned to his face. The Master Sword regained its luster, pulsing weakly still but stronger than it had been. But he still lay unconscious. Still bleeding. No sign that he was miraculously healed. That fairy’s magic was just enough to keep him from death’s door.

“Did it work?” She dared ask. 

Silence answered her.

She laid her head on his chest, the drum of his heart beat was so faint that she let a tear fall.

She felt strong. Fully charged. As if she had been sleeping for weeks, and all that rest had culminated into power. Or maybe she likened it to a battery, her normal charge being somewhere around ninety percent on a good day. Now she pushed it well past a thousand.

If she could only give him that charge.

“Please.”

In answer, someone screamed from a distance. “Zelda!” “Sir Link!”

She jerked her head up so fast that it took a moment to focus. Two men ran from the direction of Fort Hateno. Even at this distance, she saw the details with impossible clarity: the muted colors and bold red of Sheikah uniforms, the glint of their eyes. She stood, readying herself to lift her hand, blast that newfound horrible power, but as they approached, the gray and red faded to recognition. The same uniform the guards were wearing in Kakariko. They were not the enemy.

However, she still held her guard.

They made it to her position as silent as falling snow. How they managed to not squeak with the sound of wet mud under their boots, she would never understand. Then, they bowed, low— “Goddess incarnate.” they murmured, their voices muffled by their face coverings.

But she was not their ruler. “Please. It’s just… Zelda.”

Yet they remained bowed.

She let out an exasperated breath, “Please, stand up.”

They did.
