“We saw everything.” They looked nervously upon her form. And as much as she wanted to ease their worries, she certainly understood; this power was primal and raw, it made her pause. But if they were going to treat her as some deity to be worshiped and obeyed, then she would put them to work.

“Carry him to the fort. Gently. Find a healer, the closest one from wherever they are currently stationed, and bring them here. He needs immediate attention to his wounds.”

They did as they were told, but their red eyes gleamed with doubt at his condition.

They raised him as gently as they could; Link’s head lolled to the side, and she wished she could rip this new, searing power from her chest and pour it into him instead. She grabbed the Master Sword. The hilt settled into her palm, not as a weapon, but as a missing part of herself, a long-lost limb returned.

She stood, covered in blood and mud— so much so that she forgot what color her clothes had been. And she turned her back to the fortified wall to gaze upon the plain, to assess for more monsters or perhaps see if Ganondorf had decided to show.

The rain had stopped, but the sky was still gray and lifeless. It could have been morning, afternoon, or evening; it was hard to tell. But it was light enough that she could see clearly what she had done.

What looked to be a hundred guardians lay in heaps like a discarded junkyard. Bokoblins and moblins lay lifeless, scattered throughout. How did she even manage to end their existence? Was it kind? Just stopping their heart? Or did it hurt—

Then she gazed back towards Link, watching the strong, brave, handsome knight she loved, lifeless and limp as he was carried away.

And she hoped that it was painful.

They brought Link to a small cabin nestled behind Fort Hateno. The two Sheikah guards laid him down in the small bed. They cut his tunic off and stripped him all but bare. She ground her teeth at the sight and breathed through a cry threatening to escape.

He had deep gashes, everywhere, to different degrees of layers cut into his body. How had he not fallen sooner or died for that matter? The wounds on his legs and arms had already begun to seal wrong, the skin drawing together in tight ridges, and the one across his chest still leaked, dark and slow, with every shallow breath he took. Luckily, a healer stationed here was already inside with him.

She gave Zelda a curt bow before turning her attention to Link. Her loud, notable gasp at his mangled body was grating to her heart. But she quickly recovered and got to work, pouring an unidentifiable liquid down his throat, lifting his head up to force the swallow. Then, she rubbed salve and ointments on his wounds before dressing them all.

It took her the better part of four hours to dress them all. Sheikah guards had entered frequently, checking on them both. They brought supplies and the bag that Epona was carrying inside. Informing her that she had made it safely behind the fortresses’ walls. Zelda almost sobbed in relief, knowing Link’s beloved mare was here with them.

Zelda stood in the corner, watching his chest rise and fall, as she thanked the goddess for each breath she was able to count. Beside the bed, the Master Sword’s light finally faded. It rested, synchronized to its master, needing time to recharge as well.

By the time the healer completed her work, it had to be close to midnight. She stood and stretched, then turned to Zelda.

“Zelda. I mean Goddess—” she flushed red at her mistake.

“It’s just Zelda.”

The healer nodded nervously, not able to meet her eye. “He’s alive— for now. How he survived half of these injuries, let alone all of them, is a miracle he’s still breathing.”

Zelda’s nose flared. “A fairy entered him. Would that have saved him?”

She looked surprised, her brows almost reaching her midnight-dark hairline. And now that she was facing Zelda, she noted the youthfulness on her face. Perhaps they had been the same age, but Zelda felt so much older looking at her creamy, blemish-free skin. “Are you sure it was a fairy?”

“Yes.”

She quirked her mouth to the side. “Fairies? They’re mostly legend. Stories say they can stave off death, but the knowledge is old and unreliable. They won’t heal wounds like these, but—”

Zelda rudely cut her off, “Will his wounds heal though?”

The healer furrowed her brows, unsure if she should sugarcoat the truth or be blunt. “It’s too soon to tell. The potions are fighting the blood loss, but I’ve never seen wounds from those machines. The magic in them resists normal healing. All we can do now is wait and see if his strength or the corruption wins out.”

How Zelda managed to quell the tears threatening to build, she didn’t know.

“We’ll just have to let the healing process run its course. His body will tell us when he’s ready.” She turned from where he lay, and Zelda watched as she scanned him. “If you permit me, you should let me examine you for injuries.”

“I’m not injured,” Zelda replied. And as the words fell out of her mouth, she instinctively lifted her palms, expecting to see the cuts and scratches from her fall. But her skin was flawless. Not just healed, but new. All the scrapes and bruises were gone, as if they had never been. Wiped away, forgotten.

Zelda was staring at her hands, looking for that ancient power to reveal itself as the healer quietly excused herself to allow her privacy. Zelda managed to thank her before she shut the cabin door behind her.

She took the opportunity to strip herself out of the ruined clothes. There was a small floor-length mirror next to the bed, and she took herself in. She was not only healed but glowing.

She pressed two fingers into her cheek and felt resistance, the caved-in lines forgotten. She ran a hand down her arm and found the soft give of muscle over bone, and she traced her midsection, feeling no jut of bone beneath her fingers. She turned her wrist over in the candlelight, the skin there was warm and opaque, faintly golden, the way it had looked in summers before.

And her hair, back to its healthy, faint waves. No more dull, lifeless strands. Soft and silken to her touch. Gold was woven into it and randomly placed, sparkling in the candlelight.

She was the picture of health. Healthier than she had been before. The goddess had not only restored her but nourished her. She fertilized her soul, blooming underneath her skin.

And she felt shimmering. Like the tops of a calm wave at sea on a sunny, cloudless day. The sun glittering the surface as she lay weightless. A quiet, calm beat thrummed in her ears as her face pointed to the sky. She was adrift, but not without direction. A new feeling of core wisdom and stability she’d never known.

She felt like a—

A goddess.

She wanted to revel in that thought, but Link lay broken next to her. Her balance, her courage, her soulmate. She climbed into the small bed and laid next to him, threading her fingers with his as each breath he took was a reassuring melody to her ears.

Two days had passed.

Sleep offered little escape. Perhaps she hadn’t needed it, the sheer amount of energy buzzing through her kept her energized. She hadn’t had a chance to turn her mind to focus on anything other than Link, who remained unconscious.

Both days were the same. She picked out the food they would bring her, and she would alternate between lying in bed next to Link or pacing around the small space. The first morning, she dressed them both before the healer came. For herself, she put on the ridiculously inappropriate prayer dress Impa had packed. Perhaps she thought it was a joke or wishful thinking on her part to spark that awakening, but she highly doubted it was the former.

And for Link, a standard-issue shirt and trousers that were stocked for soldiers stationed at the fort. And as she slid the cotton fabric gently over Link’s arms, it was not lost on her— the magic of Hyrule. How jewels and gemstones had elemental properties. How fairies, monsters, and magical creatures existed amongst the unexceptional. And of course, that magic extended to healing as well. But as everything is and could be— magic had limits.

The healer, a new one this time with fiery hair and fine lines around her mouth, had told Zelda she was astounded with the progress of his healing, but noting before bowing and leaving that he would have the scars for the remainder of his life.

She was sure Link would not care about the new geography that remapped his flesh. She knew that without question. And she would not care either. She had her own. Ones that could only be seen if one knew where to look, the ones that were jagged and crass. And others that were hidden, ones that would never heal, no matter a goddess’s blessing.

Her fingers brushed over the fresh bandage, and the memory of a night in Hateno surfaced. How they lay bare, cradling each other in a too-small bed, sweaty and panting as they stilled against the quiet echo of their breaths.

How she traced the scars that littered his skin then: the nick above his heart, from a sparing session gone awry. The ragged one on his collarbone from a moblin. A puckered circle on his thigh from an arrow that went through him, shot by a bokoblin.

A perfect razor line on the same thigh, from when he was accidentally stabbed. A crude zigzag near his— apparently a dagger from a Lizalfos. So close to it, she fixated on it when she took him in her mouth.

And the perfectly healed gash on his forearm. Mipha’s work, he’d admitted, and she scolded him for hiding the injury from her for weeks.

She choked down the lump growing in her throat as she noticed the new scars that weren’t covered. Remnants of the Yiga attack that propelled them down this path.

They were crudely healed. Angry; shades of white blending with pink and flesh. The one on his ankle was especially angry.

This man had given his body to this kingdom. Every inch of it. But what had the kingdom given him in return?

By nightfall, Impa had arrived.

She and her most trusted advisors came to Fort Hateno, upon the word that had reached them— the goddess incarnate had released her powers.

Impa knocked on the cabin door, where Zelda had possessively and protectively locked herself in to watch over Link. When she met Impa’s blood-eyed gaze, the color made Zelda bristle. In that forefront of her memory, all she saw was Link’s life force draining out of him. But Impa ignored the motion, instead bowing. Not as low as others had— but low enough for Zelda to note the uncomfortability of the notion.

“Zelda. I’m glad to see that you are unharmed.” Impa spoke in her even tone. There was no whiff of deception or flattery behind those words.

“More like, you’re glad to see I am not entirely myself? Or glad to see that I had to watch the love of my life die in order to open the door to my powers?”

The barest flicker of a flinch, the most Impa would ever allow, registered on her face.

Zelda hadn’t meant to come across as brash or rude. Her anger wasn’t directed at Impa. But that image of Link bleeding out on the plain was too fresh to wipe away. She put him there, even if it was to protect her.

“I’m glad you are both alive.” She looked to Link on the bed, loosely dressed in the unimpressive cotton shirt and pants, and Zelda noted a twitch of sorrow flash across Impa’s eyes. Perhaps before it would have been too quick, too fleeting to notice before, but now her eyesight and senses were honed. “May we speak in private?”

Zelda eased the tension in her body. “Sure.”

They walked outside, weaving through the tree line. Impa led her silently towards the garrison walls. She gestured for Zelda to climb the steps to the top, where increased patrol was stationed on the parapet.

Every soldier bowed low and did not rise until she passed them.

She would never get used to that. Something about it made her uneasy. She never liked drawing attention to herself. She would dress nicely, look put together, but she never, ever made a spectacle of herself.

Now she drifted by them in her white prayer dress that dragged behind her, floating as a wraith. Her only comfort was the matching-hooded shawl that draped around her shoulders. She pulled it tight to the top of her head to hide her face.

Then she spotted him, near the cabin, grazing on grass. Epona, next to Storm. A small, easy breath escaped her.

“We brought him with us after we heard what happened.”

The stud Zelda had come to love almost as much as she loved Link. His dark, black coat was the polar opposite of her white dress, but how striking they looked together. Light and dark. Contrasting to the eyes that would trace their path.

Impa had stopped at the edge of one of the walls and dismissed the soldier who saluted and bowed to them before rushing off. As was Impa’s authority, or was it still?

What was left of the Hyrule army? Did Link still have a captain to answer to? She knew many of his friends and comrades were dead, but how many were left? And how could she feel any one loss when they were all piled so high: the king’s death, her parents’ murder, the razing of Castle Town. Each horror was a stone added to a wall she was building inside herself. Now, seeing Link broken in that bed, she felt the entire structure threaten to collapse under the weight of it all.

Or perhaps she had become numb to it all. Nothing shocked her anymore.

Impa turned towards the plain, placing her hands on the rough, porous wall. The scenery ahead of them was unclear, covered by the dark, starless night, but the sconces that hung from the fortress illuminated her limited view. More soldiers lined the moat, some in shiny armor, others in the tight garb of the Sheikah. Tents and campfires scattered with men laughing and talking.

Impa looked straight ahead, able to see something perhaps Zelda couldn’t. “Every able-bodied person who can fight is garrisoned here. The last stand. The goddess’s last stand.”

Zelda only thinned her lips.

“The soldiers were told to garrison behind the fortresses’ walls, but they refused. They wanted to be on holy land. They thought being where you stood would bless them.”

Zelda could not contain her scoff as she shook her head, letting out a frustrated breath. “I’m just a person. I’m just Zelda.”

“But you aren’t.” Impa turned to her, gripping the sides of her shoulders as she fired back, in the no-nonsense tone she remembered and appreciated. “You are the goddess, whether you like it or not. She chose you. How you awakened your powers, when you used them, how you released them—it doesn’t fucking matter—”

Zelda balked at the swear.

“What matters is that this is where you are. This is what you’ve been dealt. You can use it for good, or you can continue to ignore it.”

Zelda opened her mouth to argue, but her tongue was heavy in her throat.

“I saw what you did.” She paused, carefully choosing her next words. “The annihilation. Judging by Link’s condition, it was an act of desperation, when all was lost?”

Zelda nodded slowly.

“And now you stand vigil at his bedside.” Impa continued, her tone unwavering. “Tell me what it is you fear?”

Zelda’s silence was a wall of its own. She could feel Impa’s sidelong gaze upon her as she faced the plain. The gaze was as sharp as the blade on her hips, and she knew what Zelda was thinking, what she was terrified of: that the power that saved them could only be summoned by the one thing she could never bear to witness again.

“I won’t let him die for it.” Zelda whispered. “I can’t.”

Impa nodded at the truth laid bare. “Zelda, you need to find that… agency inside you. The feeling of release without fear. I need you to play the part, the part you hate, be the deity you are, be the goddess. Nurture that seedling of hope that is trying to claw its way towards the sun.” She waved her hand over the wall. “These men below are laughing, for the first time in weeks. They’ve lost their friends, their comrades, their families. But they are here, smiling and laughing with hope in their hearts.”

Zelda swallowed and pushed past the pressure behind her eyes.

“I’m sorry to ask this of you, it’s not fair. You’ve been through too much, too young. But I need you to do this. Link needs you to do this for his home. Your home, perhaps.”

Zelda’s walls that she numbly built were crumbling. “But… but what if I cannot? I don’t even know how I had done it. I was struggling to even make it to him when he was crawling to me, broken and dying. I was ready to die, knowing that I would go with him. I couldn’t even begin to understand how to harness that now without putting him in that position again.”

Impa’s eyes softened, her grip felt warm. “I cannot begin to understand how this power works. But I’ll tell you from experience, your heart is the conduit for this power. Fear, hatred, love… they do not create the light, they only focus it. What you feel will determine if it is a beacon or a wildfire. Lean into that, and you will give it direction. I wish we had more time for you to train and understand it, but we don’t. All I can ask of you until Link wakes is to search and reflect upon yourself, to pray, to ask, to look for the answers. Tunnel within yourself for that reaction.”

Zelda lifted her head, even though the weight of the words pressed down her neck. She was never a good actor, but she could be this. She could try. For them. For Link. “Okay. What do we do first?”

The corners of Impa’s lips pulled upwards.

Zelda slunk to the edge of the river’s waters. The same bend where they had last been happy, the same spot they were ambushed, before their fate was sealed.

Or perhaps their fate had been sealed the moment she dropped into Hyrule.

It was dawn, the sun was rising over the silhouette of the fortress, trying to push through, but the clouds held.

Everything felt achingly familiar.

The wind, the birds, the life around her ceased. Holding their collective breaths for her to speak. Bowing to her.

Who was she even praying to at this point? Herself?

After their conversation, Impa pulled her into a small stone room within the fortress’s walls. Three armed and rough men stood around a table with a parchment map spread out. Each of their features was hard, scarred, and tired from years of battles and fighting. Yet when she entered the room, the golden hope, they eased.

One audibly swallowed, another tucked his hands behind his back, and the third looked briefly at the floor as if he’d been too shy. She noticed the wonder and awe in their eyes, in their stature. And behind that, she saw the young boys they once were.

However, this time, she did not cower or pull her hood close. This time, she lowered it. She stood straighter, letting her shoulders stand proud.

She could do at least this for them— be the symbol of hope.

They discussed strategy in terms she barely understood; pincer movements, flanking routes, lines of supply. But when one of the commanders tapped the map and looked to her, ‘You and the hero will be our spearhead. We will keep clear the surrounding area while we leave you to your work.

‘Work’ was the nicer term for what they needed her to do. But she nodded all the same, agreeing to the role. A role she never asked for.

She wasn’t tired as the glow of the orange sun hung behind the gray backdrop. Apparently, it was the first time in weeks that the sun had tried to break through. Hyrule’s weather was in tune with Ganondorf’s hatred. Yet her explosion of light reminded everyone that the sun will still rise and fall even if you cannot see it.

Impa escorted her to the river’s edge. Every horrible memory swam in her veins, chilling her blood. The sad songs of their oblivious happiness mocked her. She turned to Impa, the girl in her still afraid and sad as she voicelessly asked, “Who do I pray to?”

Impa grabbed her hands, tenderly, cupping and squeezing them, some warmth seeping into her. “Prayers don’t always need to be spoken to the goddesses. Sometimes it’s more about the truths we need to say aloud.”

She dropped her hands and left. Knowing Zelda had to do this next part alone.

And there she stood, on the edge of the river’s soft current. She didn’t have to submerge herself to lay bare the truths to herself, but the ritual had come to be a fabric of familiarity. Who would have guessed? So she lifted the hem of the dress, pushing against the heavy current as she waded closer to where she could be waist-deep.

And closed her eyes.

She imagined the wind, the trees, the earth, the sky, the water— everything that made up this land she stood on. The land she now felt vibrate and thrum with power. The sky was lifeless, but she swore the clouds parted briefly. The grass was still vibrantly green. The trees still cleaned the air they breathed. The water still rippled. The wind still carried the scents of it all.

She had sat in the water until her kneecaps had turned to mush, and her skin was wrinkled and cold. She searched every part of her body, every part of her shredded soul, to find and manifest that power that lay within.

She tried to think of strength. Of fortitude and perseverance. Of optimism.

But it was all so ridiculously loud. Because behind her closed eyes, the only scenes that replayed were of Castle Town. Of burnt homes. Broken toys. Of desolate faces in Kakariko.

Of Link bleeding out in her arms. Her father’s head bent at an impossible angle. Her mother’s soft smile before her eyes went lifeless. And she smelled that copper tang in the air. Felt the cold, dampness settle into her marrow.

Her fist balled, she threw her arms down to hit the water, to hurt it as much as she’d been hurt. But light sputtered and skipped off the water’s surface like a flat rock.

And she thought of Ganondorf’s twisted smile as he told her of the murders he delighted in. She pictured his hands, the force of them throwing her across the room, the laughter reverberating in the dark, the sick satisfaction of inflicting pain and fear. The echo of her own screams when she realized it was not a dream, and the moment she tunneled too far, never to climb the walls of herself to escape.

She gritted her teeth and drove her fists into the water again.

This time, a shock of heat spasmed out from her knuckles and the surface of the river cracked and steamed.

She gasped and jerked her hands back. The water wasn’t boiling, not exactly, but it heaved and roiled around her wrists, white darts of light flickering in the churn.

She stared at her hands, and watched the light dance along her skin, blinding her as bright as polished steel. It coursed along her fingers like a chain. A tangible rope. And she leaned into that thought and watched the chain grow thicker, until it enveloped her whole arm, then the other and soon after she was burning with the raw essence of light in the river’s water. Had anyone seen, she was a beacon, a port to sail to.

Or something far more dangerous, something—or someone—to stay away from.

She pushed that pent-up power outwards to blast into the canyon’s wall at her front. The light streaked and skittered. And as she let that power dissolve, the heat subsiding, she replayed all the memories— the love, the fear… the hate. And that power within her was a steady flame fueled by love and fear for Link. But another emotion had that furnace raging, uncontrollable and destructive.

And a cruel, satisfied smile formed as that new feeling took root.

She stood at the desk of the small cabin, her pulse loud in her ears, and waited.

Then she felt it.

The Master Sword stirred and purred to her. Pleased that she was here. That both its masters were.

She closed her eyes and smiled before a voice asked from behind her, “Who are you?”

Chapter 42: Golden
Chapter Text
His eyes jolted open.

A sharp ache in his ribs was the first thing he felt, a violent thumping in his skull the second. He ignored them both, pushing himself up. His eyes found the Master Sword first, intact and resting by his side. Then they found Zelda.

Zelda. Who was paradise. The feeling of sunshine on his skin in the early hours of the morning, those glittering rays of light made human. But she wasn’t human anymore, not really.

Apprehension tightened her features; her body was rigid, her smile strained.

Her memories flooded him, a torrent of sensation not his own. He saw his own collapse through her eyes, the terror that spurred her forward as his body failed. He tasted her agony, felt the weight of her imprisonment, and watched his own desperate crawl toward her. It was a pathetic attempt to save her, he knew, a final, failing gesture before the world dissolved into light.

The realization snapped like a whip.

Holy. Fucking. Goddess.

He swallowed, his throat as raw as Gerudo sand. When Zelda handed him a cup, he drank it down too fast, the water hitting his empty stomach like a stone. A wracking cough seized him, and he doubled over, ribs clenched in pain.

There was so much he wanted to ask her, to talk to her about. But all he could manage was, “I’m sorry.”

Her lips thinned. “You’re sorry?”

He met her eye for a brief moment and looked away. “I’m sorry I couldn’t—”

“If you say for failing, or for not protecting me, or for any related reason, I’m going to knock you out again.”

He met her eyes again at her interruption. Expecting a playful look or smile. There was none. She was unnaturally still. Anger held in her brows, a newly lit fire in her eyes. She continued, “The only thing you need to be sorry for is sacrificing yourself for me—”

“I didn’t—”

She ignored him with a lifted hand, “—let me finish. Don’t say you didn’t mean it that way. You can’t feign ignorance in hindsight.” Her glare was sharp enough to make a hardened man wither. “No more self-sacrificing bullshit. No more treating me like some hurt animal you have to protect. I can save you as much as you save me, and if there is one thing we should know by now, it is that we don’t do well keeping things from each other. Our misunderstandings and lack of willingness to be transparent nearly cost us everything.”

She looked to him for acceptance, daring him to argue. But every time he looked at her, he saw the cell, the imprisonment, the exhaustion carved into her face. He hadn’t looked at her since and seen just her, only ever what he had failed to prevent.

She grabbed his hand, “I love you. You’re my soulmate. You go, I go, that’s what you promised me. You don’t get to take that responsibility on all for yourself. That’s not how this works. When are you going to realize that we are better together? Your actions are what unlocked my power. We are equals. There is no goddess without a hero. No hero without the goddess.” She squeezed his hand harder, the warmth laced between them. “No me without you.”

He let her anger roll off onto him, because she was right. He had made the choice for her. Given her no information, no say, no chance to weigh in on her own fate. She had spent her whole life receiving news of her own fate secondhand, from her parents’ sacrifice to Impa’s veiled words. And he, of all people, should have known better.

He nodded. “You’re right. I love you. And as much as it pains me to say, if I decide to go, I know you’re coming with me.”

“I’m glad you finally get it.” she said.

He let out an exasperated breath. “You were incredible.”

She lifted her lips, the smile reached her eyes, shining so bright. Somehow greener, like true cut jewels now, “Thank you.”

It was a raw, primal force not seen in a millennium. When she showed him the memory of its unleashing, he felt the fire forged from the sun as if it were his own. The might of a goddess, the blessing she now wielded.

His eyes swept over her glowing, gilded form. “You’ve changed so much since I last saw you.”

“I think it’s the power… a blessing? It’s fixing me. The Goddess cannot have her vessel appear weak and malnourished.” She rubbed at the line of her jaw, a strange look on her face, as if exploring unfamiliar territory.

Wait.

Her lips hadn’t been moving, but his had?

His face twisted in confusion, while hers grew in feline amusement. She drilled into him, daring him to ask as he pushed an impossible thought out.

“You’re radiant. Like the sun after a long rain, and the world is happy to see you again.”

“Thank you.” Her voice rattled in his head but had not entered through his ears; her lips hadn’t moved.

His brows lifted as he said aloud, “How?”

“I’m not sure… perhaps because we are fated Triforce welders—” she held up the back of her hand, a faint glowing triangle was there, as she picked up his hand to show his own to him. “—or it’s my new powers. But either way, it’s certainly handy for what we have to do next.”

He trailed his fingers over the fabric of her prayer dress, the motion grounding him. He’d nearly died, and she had been awakened, all in the space of three days. He was still processing the shift between them when she spoke aloud, her voice pulling him from his thoughts. “I can speak to it, as well.”

She waited for his confused look to give way to recognition as she turned her head to the bedside dresser. The sacred blade was sheathed on top of it.

“It spoke to me. Because its life force mirrors your own, it told me you were dying. It told me you only had moments left to live.”

“It actually spoke?” 

“Not literally. It was mind to mind. Spirit to spirit. It feels familiar, as if I’ve known it my whole life. I suppose I have, since she created it.”

He paused. Choosing his next words carefully. “Are you still… you? Or is she here too?”

Zelda’s eyes were one second locked onto his own, then wandered down his body. He tried not to twitch, wondering who or what was looking at him at that moment. She then rose and walked over to the Master Sword. She seemed to command the space differently, her presence making her appear taller, more imposing. Yet when he focused, she was the same height, the same woman he’d met.

She placed her hand on the hilt, her voice familiar yet deeper with newfound wisdom. “I’m still me. But the Goddess… she’s here, too. A whisper in my blood.” She paused, searching for the words. “It’s as if I was colorblind, and now I see everything. Her memories are here, flickering images of past heroes, ancient events, but they’re like a library I don’t know how to navigate yet.” She lifted the sword with an unnerving familiarity and laid it on the bed. “The blade knows me. It laments. But my thoughts, my heart… they are still my own.” She offered a smile, though a hint of uncertainty lingered.

The tightness in his chest eased. He reached out to cup her cheek, and she greeted him by nuzzling into it. Her skin was as soft as velvet linens, and he tried to remember if it had always been. He pulled her to him, resting his forehead against her own. Trying that connection again. “I love you.”

She huffed and smiled, but the lines of her face were tight. “I love you.” Her voice rattled in his head as if it had always lived there. “I was so worried about you.”

“I know.”  And he did, he felt every expanse of her terror, her sorrow, her despair. “I knew you were tired, but now I know what you felt, that cell took everything from you.” His voice echoed down that mental pathway he found, sounding as if he was underwater with her.

“It’s alright.” She pulled back and lifted her gaze to stare at him, a breath away. He could see that gold by her pupil. That whisper of the goddess that was always there. “I would endure it all again, for Hyrule. For you.”

He looked at her deeply, and nodded before touching his lips to hers.

The feeling was as he remembered. She tasted like the first rays of sun in the morning. He felt serene and weightless, as an ocean breeze rolling off the surf. And they melted into each other as it deepened. Urgent and savory as his hand cradled her neck, caressing the silken strands tangling amongst his fingers, as hers found the sharp joining under his ear, caressing his pulse.

And he wanted to stay there. But then the Master Sword sang to him too.

They had work to do.

Zelda grabbed his bracer from the floor to hand to him as he sat on the edge of the bed, in an unfamiliar tunic, flexing his fingers. A stiffness had settled in his joints during his few days of recovery.

She pulled back the curtain from the lone window, the gray light entering the cabin in an unwelcome sight.

A knock at the cabin door sent him snatching the Master Sword from its scabbard before a second could land, as if Ganondorf himself would bother knocking. Zelda huffed her appreciation with a soft smile as she opened to a scrawny, younger guard. He nervously dropped to his knees, bowing to her before turning his attention to Link and the holy blade.

Link wasn’t sure which had the guard more enthralled.

He carried a bag of supplies, food, and water for them both. Zelda took it without hesitation, and it was clear this was part of her routine the past few days. The guard left with word that Impa and the captains were waiting for them at the garrison once they were ready.

They ate quickly as Zelda filled him in on the more tactical details that transpired between Impa and the remaining captains. And as she finished, she stood and smoothed the prayer dress she hated, and he wondered aloud why she was wearing it.

“It’s a symbol,” she said, “A part I need to play. Temporarily.”

Since her… unleashing, Fort Hateno had become the beating heart of the resistance. Impa's call had gone out across the land: all who could fight were to gather here. For three days, they had trickled in from every corner of Hyrule, traversing mountains and deserts to answer. And now it was time to see what remained of their army. Time to plan the attack. But not before Zelda played her role.

She moved to face him, the scabbard draped in her hand. He hooked it to his back, buckled the belts on his chest, and sheathed the holy blade, the soft scrape of the Master Sword settling into its sheath echoed between them.

Her eyes landed on his scabbard belt, and she moved to adjust it, her fingers trailing the sides of the old leather against his chest. Then her gaze lifted to the indigo hilt that poked over his right shoulder as her hand fell, finding his, intertwining their fingers.

“Are you ready?” She asked.

Zelda may have had a new confidence, but apprehension still lived between them. He’d been in battle, tasted the adrenaline on his tongue. But this was the end of something, one way or another.

“No.” He said as her eyes then found his, wide and full of trepidation.

He let go of her hand and moved both of his gloved hands to her cheek, to trail in her neck as he leaned in and kissed her softly and slowly. Savoring her lips.

Her hands instinctively wrapped around his back, her tension fell away as his tongue found hers. Letting themselves have this, just a little longer, just one more breath of each other before the world came back in.

They pulled apart, her lips slightly rosy, he gave her a half-hearted smile, “Now I’m ready.”

They shut the door of the cabin and all the air left the woods. Only the sounds of the river’s running water in their ears.

He looked north, and remembered the events that led to this. The tension in his spine was palpable because Zelda found his hand, remembering it too and silently tilted her head towards the opposite way, to move forward. He laced his fingers in hers and followed her.

The moment wasn’t lost on him. How full circle it had become. How much they’d grown separately and together since. So much had happened in just a short month.

She led him down the rough patch of road. No longer muddy from the rain that ceased, but still damp beneath his feet. A low murmur, the collective breath of hundreds of soldiers, coaxed them to follow. As the path opened, and they turned a corner, behind the old crumbling stone walls of Fort Hateno stood the remainder of Hyrule’s army.

As they moved toward the plain, he saw them. Every soldier, knight, and Sheikah master stood in a procession. They faced each other, forming an honor guard, an aisle that led from the garrison bridge out into the open plain. 

They were silent. Standing straight in lines of five deep, as stiff and still as training mandated. They were waiting for them. For her.

While it was still just them, he dropped back a step and Zelda turned quickly to him with furrowed brows. He racked his brain for that pathway between their minds, locating it and speaking down that tunnel directly to her. “Let me trail behind you. Just keep your head straight. Trust me.”

Her lifted shoulders breathed a sigh of relaxation as she gave him a slight nod of acknowledgment. He now knew what was happening, the part Impa wanted her to play.

They crossed the raised iron gate leading from behind the safety of the fortress walls. She was floating with each step, radiating preternatural grace. Her white dress was the stark reminder of what was good, holy, and pure. Her golden-spun hair smoothed to near stillness, fell in shallow waves on either side of her as the matching white hood was pulled over the crown of her head. He could not see her face, but he knew she wore determination and strength there.

And the world seemed to still as every head turned to her. The soldiers he could see had a twinkle in their eye, fighting a wondrous smile. He saw as they tried not to gape. How the air shifted, fear that had gripped the plain suddenly parted in place of hope. And before she could step across the threshold of their path, they dropped to their knees.

Bowing.

They each fell to their knees in unison on either side of them, as if they were blocks, suddenly knocked over, a wave of kneeling men lining either side of their path. Holding whatever weapon they had in their hand, as their free hand crossed over their heart. They kept deadly still, their faces vertical with the ground, chins held high, exposing their necks. Dressed in degrees of uniform and garbs, some fresh, others bloodied or dirtied from what they’d done. Hundreds, maybe thousands lined their path.

She continued down the path, unhurried and regal— as if she was born to it. Hylian soldiers and knights had faded to kneeling Zoras and Ritos, then Gorons and Gerudo warriors. They had all come from the deepest reaches of Hyrule, witnesses of unspeakable carnage, battling the twisted nightmares of Ganondorf, bleeding for friends, family, or comrades over the last few weeks. And there was no reason or logic behind it; however, they had still bowed. To gaze upon the goddess. To honor her for appearing. To ignite that spark into a flame.

He could not see her face, but her shoulders were straight, and she did not waver or shudder as she floated over the uneven, muddy terrain. Steady and tranquil. The part she had to play.

And if the goddess had to pick a mortal to embody her in physical form and spirit, she chose right.

And he was happy to devote himself to her.

They neared the end of the path. Impa, other ranking captains, and Auru were standing together facing them on a raised knoll. Auru’s metal chest plate was dented and caked with mud, as if he hadn’t had a moment to change before arriving.

And then his knees almost buckled at the figures next to them. He saw Mipha in her battle armor, which provided little more coverage than her usual attire, her infamous trident in hand, and her amber eyes dazzling. Next to her, Daruk offered a wide, toothy smile, but his eyes held a new weariness. Urbosa radiated feminine rage, her legendary shield and scimitar at her waist; blood had surely dripped from the blade on her journey here. And Revali—Link could barely suppress a grim smile. The Rito's arrogance was a palpable force, as was his envy at Zelda's ascension. Yet he was here, the Great Eagle Bow across his back. They all stood with Impa, waiting.

Zelda approached them, turning to climb the uneven landscape without stumbling. They bowed. All of them. Even Revali in all his stubbornness.

He followed behind her, but could not stop his gaze to the plain at their back and his jaw unhinged at the sight.

It was one thing to see it in the vision she showed him. There had been so much distraction, and her focus had been on his dying form. Now that he could see it in the cold light of day. All he could do was ask her mind to mind, not able to hide his stunned horror yet already knowing the answer: “You did this?”

Dozens upon dozens of guardians lay in heaps. Scraps of machine, as if never full of malice or life to begin with. They fell where they stood. Twisted limbs and cold, archaic stone. A pile of crude weapons, clearly used by monsters, were collected and placed near a heap of guardians. There were too many to count.

She did not look back as she replied. “For you.”

It was not a wonder that everyone bowed in respect. She was not royalty; they had no obligation to bow to her. But he had barely been able to destroy five guardians without losing his life. She ended their carnage with one raise of one hand.

As she reached the open spot on the dais, the highest point, above them all. She turned to face the masses. To present herself. The hope of Hyrule.

He unsheathed the Master Sword, holding it disarmed, as he was the last to bow before her, his arm draped over his knee as he lowered his head. Yet it was the only time her movements were quick—human— during this display. As she jerked her body towards him. His head suddenly chimed with her lovely voice: “You do not need to bow.”

He’d been intimate with her. Kissed her, licked her, spilled himself into her. And he would continue to bow for her, ignoring the pressing pain in his joints. He knelt as her equal, offering his sword not in submission, but in partnership. His eyes met hers, and he let a barely perceptible smirk show from under his brows. The intimacy of shared purpose. 

The woman he loved.

He did not flinch or move as he replied back to her: “I will kneel for you, for all to see and witness, but not as your servant, but your friend, your lover, your soulmate. And I will worship you until the end.”

He took her hand, extending it to his lips, and kissed. Honoring and blessed to know her— not the goddess— but Zelda. As he watched her nose flare and eyes gleam. A ghost of a nod followed before she turned back to the masses. Her posture pin-straight, her head titled up as she lifted her hand to the pale sky.

He felt her exhale and strain before him. She was ripping apart Nayru’s sky; clouds parted, the hole grew large and bright. She was pulling the sun through with her power, her magic. The overcast that gripped Hyrule for weeks was lifting. She was the deity of the three; the power of the land that grounded her, the spirit of the life to fuel her, and the wisdom of the sky to bless her. All three were triangulating as she illuminated herself, that fire within her for all to witness.

Every knight, soldier, farmer, boy, Rito, Zora, Goron, and Gerudo warrior, all with knees in the mud, looked to her. Thousands of eyes watched the magic rippling from her as that beam of white light shone down on her. Her hand and the sky converged as one, the light growing so bright he had to squint.

The energy rippled, the Master Sword on his back delighted to be in the presence of its maker again as the sun’s beams pushed through, shining on her and the army in front of her.

He heard Revali muttering under his breath. Envious, yet uneasy at the power he witnessed from one he deemed irrelevant before.

“I am not Hylian.” She called out, her voice powerful and ancient and lovely. “I was not born here. But I will fight with you, for your family, for your friends, for this land. My home.” She turned to Link, that light she harnessed in answer growing brighter, “with the hero and the sword that seals the darkness!”

Gasps and sobs broke the stunned silence. Then a collective cheer as the army of Hyrule’s creatures lifted their weapons in hope and solidarity. 

The show Zelda had to display. To prove that she was real, that the goddess had come to fight for her people, not a moment too soon.

He would have followed her to any end, but he understood why some may need the extra nudge. And it was impressive, to harness light, the ultimate symbol of holy promise to defeat evil’s darkness. Impa’s suggestion, no doubt. But as everyone’s reactions varied from stunned silence to tearful joy, he looked past the goddess and to Zelda underneath.

She was healthier, confident, stronger. But watching her tremble to unleash this power or pull it to her, fade to a steady, sure hand made him pause. He was watching it unfold before his very eyes. Heady off the power she now possessed.

He remembered the first time a blade was pressed to his palm, the weight too heavy, the metal too sharp, the reality too real that he was now the decider of fates. And the first time he slayed a monster, a lowly, bokoblin, all that fear shaped to strength he never knew he possessed. With every monster slain, his hand grew steadier, and without a sword in hand, it felt like a missing appendage. He grew bold, the adrenaline and the scent of blood became sought-after senses. To rid the realm of evil at the tip of his blade became the only mindset he maintained. Fueled by the fury that they had taken his father from him, and as a result, his mother too.

But the more he slaughtered, the less he felt.

And as he watched her pull back that light from the sky, and then push it out in a show of strength. As everyone marveled at her; Impa satisfied in her achievements, Urbosa smirking in assured victory, Daruk slack-jawed in awe, and the faces of the Hylian army looking to her with desire yet unnerved by what they witnessed. He looked to Zelda’s face, and perhaps only he could see it there hidden beneath her luminous skin, buried behind her glowing emerald eyes—

Vengeful rage.

Night had fallen, and the small cabin that had been his healing bed was now a war room, crowded and lit by lanterns that cast long shadows. Every captain and leader that stood on the grassy knoll with them earlier crowded around the lone table. His gaze went straight to the map that was rolled out, ripped and dirty from its travel.

The brightly colored figurines representing Hylians, Ritos, and the others were clustered at the rendering of Fort Hateno. But it was the large, discarded pile of pieces to the side that held his attention, a silent testament to the soldiers who would never march again.

Perhaps they had peace now.

“It’s been three days. We have to move at dawn, otherwise we leave ourselves open to attack.” Auru said in his gravely voice, thick with confidence and worry.

“Strategically, isn’t Fort Hateno the best place to stay? The open field can be used as an advantage, and if needed, we can pull back behind the fort to regroup.” Captain Krin asked apprehensively. Link had only briefly crossed paths with the yellow-haired captain in his early days as a page. His young face was the same, except for the fresh, angry new slash that lanced the side of his neck just above his tunic.

“An open field leaves us open to assault. They’ll converge from dueling peaks and override us before we know what hit us.” Auru traced his finger along the river through the twin peaks.

“Well, we have the goddess now; she can decimate the front line before that happens.”

Everyone turned to Zelda, who was lounging against the hearth. Her arms were crossed, her face tight. Link stood next to her.

“We could do that, but I’d rather be on the attack than the defensive.” Impa said. “If we sit here and wait for the next assault, that doesn’t help us solve the problem. Ganondorf will continue to generate monsters and send them towards us.” “The only way to win this is a direct strike. We must get Link and Zelda to the Temple of Time and seal the door for good.” She had moved two wooden figures, one a stained yellow and the other painted blue, down the pathway of the river, sliding them all the way to the Great Plateau, where triple the amount of wooden figurines sat all stained blood-red and in the shapes of monsters.

A silent Sheikah spy was already leaving the room after passing a note to Impa that she had quickly read and balled into her hands. “We know the bulk of the force is there, so we need to plan a unified assault.”

The many spies Impa had at her command were the other reason why no one questioned the additional groups of monster figurines spread throughout Hyrule’s regions. Mipha, Daruk, Urbosa, and Revali left minimal troops behind in their respective regions to starve off the invasion, at great cost to pull together here. This would not be a long war, but rather an epic battle.

“That’s a brilliant idea.” The nasally, sarcastic chide of Revali cut through the tension behind Daruk. “But last I checked, the Great Plateau is on, oh what’s that word called—” Revali held his wing to his chin in a show of mock thinking. “Oh, I know… a plateau.”

“Alright, Revali, we get it.” Urbosa said, her voice sharp with all the grace and swagger the Gerudo warrior could muster.

Revali ignored her. “We can fly there, of course, but I don’t suppose you plan to have us shot from the sky while your forces nap beneath us.”

“That’s enough.” Urbosa’s fury laced the room; he swore lightning danced along the ceiling. “My people may not have wings, but we can scale those cliffs and fight tenfold what your legion can do.”

“Please—” Mipha’s quiet plea as she cupped her hands. “We need to work together, not argue amongst ourselves.”

“Easy for you to say, Princess.” Revali spat. “Last I checked, your people have more wealth than all the other regions combined; it makes for some shiny, impressive weapons—”

“We don’t need your people to win this war, bird.” Urbosa fired back, cutting him off. Her gaze a dagger’s point.

“Enough.” Impa’s hands struck the table, her eyes burning into each of the regional leaders. “We don’t have to get along to be allies, but we do need to learn to work together if we are to succeed. But make no mistake, each of you has a role in what comes next.” Her eyes focused on Link and Zelda in the distance. “I already have a plan to breach the walls and get the whole army through. Now, if you are finished, can I continue?”

Revali huffed a breath in reluctant agreement, and Urbosa smiled at Impa with warning on her painted lips as Impa laid out the plan of attack.

Link listened, his focus sharpening as Impa spoke. She wasn’t just assigning troops; she was weaving their strengths together. The Gorons and their strength, the Rito and their aerial abilities, the Gerudo’s agility, the Zora’s spear mastery, and the highly disciplined and trained Hylian army. And as she turned to him and Zelda, he saw how they were not the spearhead, but the dagger she meant to slide between the ribs of the forces to the heart of the Temple.

It was… insane. Brilliant. Risky. And as Impa spoke, Zelda’s smile grew.

Hours later, as the cabin emptied, leaders dissolving into the night to brief their captains and lieutenants. And at dawn, they would move as an army of one. Link pictured the map in his mind, Impa’s finger tracing the line of the Squabble River down to the ruins of the Outpost. From there, the final push. In two days, they would be at Ganondorf’s feet.

Link and Zelda had made to move outside the cabin, to let anyone else stay comfortably in, but Impa insisted they remain. No one was going to make the goddess and her sworn hero— her lover— sleep in a common tent.

The last to leave were Urbosa and Mipha, the former warmly squeezing Zelda’s shoulders as she bent down to whisper in her ear, while the latter had embraced him and quickly thanked the Goddess that he was alive and well. As they crossed the threshold into the dark night, only Impa remained. Her jaw tight and body rigid. She clearly had something to say privately to the two of them.

“Are you two set with this plan? Everything hinges on you.” Impa’s voice was steady, but Link had been around her long enough to read the worry tightening her features. He wondered if it was for their safety, or if she, too, had noticed the unnerving shift in Zelda, the change he was beginning to fear he was the only one seeing.

“Yes. More than set.” Zelda said. Her body was lounged in the small chair by the bed. “I find it clever, the Demon King won’t know what hit him.” she said, an uneasy smile on her lips.

Impa turned to Link, her face was tight as he nodded in agreement.

Zelda rose from the chair, “But... I’m going to need something more practical if I am to fight.” She gestured down the front of her white prayer dress. “This did its part.”

She gave a curt nod and beckoned them to a small chest tucked in the corner, one he hadn’t noticed during the chaos of the meeting. Impa opened it and pulled out an ensemble that had Zelda gaping.

It was modest dark pants and leather boots, perfect for riding, the same Zelda had worn hundreds of times. But the top—it was incredibly perfect and fitting for who she now was. A royal blue sleeved tunic that could have passed as a short dress, except for the slit enabling her to move freely. Threaded in gold embroidery and a modest neckline, a white-lined cape hung behind, so featherlight it seemed to stir in the still air. She approached the garment in a trance and traced her fingers along the ribs, a scaled, hard texture shimmered—

“Dragon scales,” Impa said, as if answering his unspoken question. “Incredibly rare but functional. It won’t stop a laser blast but will block a dagger or spear.”

Zelda lifted her lips in a careful smile. “You just happened to have this?”

Impa returned the sentiment, “I never had any reservations about who you would become. And once you did become that, I had no doubt you would want to fight in the mud with the rest of them. I asked Greta to fashion it for you after she measured you for your gown, shortly before the collapse.” Zelda gently lifted her chin as Impa clasped her hand. “You may not be a Hylian by birth, but you are in spirit. The type of person who protects their home and their people. We are lucky the goddess chose you.”

Zelda twitched her head in a small nod as she cleared her throat. “Thank you, Impa.” Her voice tried not to waver.

“And for you,” she addressed him as a peer, holding up a royal blue tunic that matched his red one. “A champion’s tunic, for the legendary hero, with some improvements.”

His old tunic was beyond repair, shredded by the Guardian’s assault. Impa had not only replaced it, but improved it. He ran his hand over the new chain mail, its links tighter and lighter than his old set. With his familiar leather cuirass and bracers, it would feel like a second skin. He would be more than prepared.

Impa handed him over the tunic, and she stepped back. She looked over both of them, her eyes taking in every detail of them before turning to leave. “I’m sorry to you both.” She said, her voice low, her back to them.

His brows went up as Zelda pursed her lips, then said. “Why are you sorry?”

“For all you two had to go through, and still need to face,” Impa said, her usual confidence gone. “I knew what it meant when you landed here. I knew you were the goddess, but that you didn’t know how to unlock your power. So I placed our most skilled knight with you. I pushed you together because the prophecies gave us little time. I orchestrated it. For my part in the injuries you bear, visible and hidden, I am sorry.”

Zelda was silent for a long moment, her expression unreadable. She walked to Impa, her steps deliberate. “You used us.” It wasn’t an accusation, just a statement of fact. She looked from Impa to Link, a complicated emotion in her eyes. “But it worked. My love for him unlocked this power. His love for me let him draw the Master Sword. Perhaps destiny needed a push. We can carry the burden, because we carry it together.”

Link watched the Sheikah Master give a forced smile. “Until the morning, then.” She turned and left before they could say more.

Zelda turned to face him now, a smile blooming on her face. She seemed to be the only one with optimism about what was to come. 

“Well, we have a few hours yet.” Zelda said, extending her arms to wrap around his neck.

He let his eyes close as her scent relaxed and hardened him simultaneously. He felt that looming countdown at their back, but she started to nuzzle her nose into his neck.

“Zelda…”

She licked the column of his throat in answer.

He groaned.

There was so much he wanted to do with her here. As the cabin blanketed them from the world outside, he wanted to hold her close, kiss her until they were both swollen and chafed, have her skin marry with his own, letting her warmth in to become his, perhaps for one last time.

But they were out of it. The abyss of nerves he felt in his center did little to calm him. That feeling he felt before battle approached. He hated it. He’d much prefer an ambush— no time to doubt or fret.

He knew she could take care of herself, that she was more powerful than him, stronger than any living creature in this realm, but that didn’t stop him from wanting to capitalize on their time together. The plan was contingent on so many things going right, if one went wrong—

“Hey.” She pulled back, he’d been gone to his internal worries, leaving him unresponsive. Her eyes met his and matched it.

She squeezed her arms around him, lifting her hand to scrape the back of his neck in comfort. “We’re going to make it. We end this brute and go home to live our lives, the way we want to live it. We’re almost there.”

She was so hopeful, so optimistic. He didn’t want to patronize her that she hadn’t seen war or battle. That the commanders who spoke in rooms like this one, who moved pieces across maps and called it strategy, rarely knew the names of the men those pieces represented. Many of those beyond the walls, the ones laughing, drinking, and celebrating her this evening, would not live to see the next sunrise. The choices made in this very room were sending them to die.

He snaked his hands behind her waist and held her glowing form close as he breathed her in. “I’ll love you forever, Zelda. Whatever world comes after this one, I will find you in it. I love you now, and I will love you then, and there is nothing in this realm or the next that will change that.”

Zelda’s face twisted at the thought. “While I appreciate the profound declaration. How about just, ‘I love you, forever.’”

He leaned in and kissed her. Her hesitation matching the energy he put out. But he deepened, quickened it. Opening to tie with her tongue and teeth. Whispering her command back onto her lips, “I’ll love you, forever.”

They hadn’t been this way since their home. The memory felt like it belonged to another lifetime, before imprisonment and the brink of death had burned away everything but the fight to survive. Not that he needed it, but he missed that intimacy. That closeness he shared with her.

But she quickly broke the kiss, “Are you… healed? Enough for…?”

He certainly wasn’t whole. There was a dull ache on his ribs. A stiffness in his legs. The cuts and stabs he sustained were healed enough for mobility if not itchy from scabbing over. But even if he was blown to smithereens, he would have said, “Nothing would stop me from this.”

He snaked his hand deeper into her hair to graze against her scalp as the other gripped her backside.

The wicked smile that was completely her slowly graced her features as they continued that hurried, but slow passion. She lifted up his shirt, carefully, avoiding the scrape of every new scar he had… and they littered him in scores.

He backed her towards the bed— the small, most likely sweat and blood-soaked mattress he lay dying on for days and halted the movement.

“They’ve changed the sheets.” Zelda spoke to him in his mind.

She seemed to be much better at this mind reading, pathway connection between them as he fumbled before recognizing the sunlit beam to connect to hers, “You can read my mind now?”

“No. But I assumed since you stopped at the edge.”

She pushed him down, gently yet controlled, to sit on the side of the bed. Before his heart could tumble, she stood in front of him, reaching her hands behind herself to undo the buttons of the dress.

“It’s hard to take this off if I’m straddling you.” Her brows lifted.

“I could have done it.”

“Oh, I’m sure you could have, but perhaps you deserve a reward.” As she punctuated that last word, the dress fell to the floor with a soft sound.

He was so glad he hadn’t died.

She was as he last remembered her in this position. Her curves and edges defined and soft. The gilded color of her skin made her glow against the shadows cast from the candlelight. Her hair was long and flowing, soft waves spun from silk and swept to one side, the strands covering her breast, as the other lay heavy in the cool air. And her center—

She was already lifting her hands, and that horrible and beautiful light poured out of her as a wild scream ripped from her lungs. It was so close, he needed to cover his face with his free hand as he squinted through it. She launched everything that had built inside her, all her power and loathing, to make good on her threat.

The energy she thrust forward wasn’t just light; it was Gerudo lightning crackling around a core of Death Mountain’s fire. It hit with the crushing force of a Lanayru wave, a hurricane from the Tabantha canyons focused into a single, devastating beam. 

And as that continuous light poured out of her and met Ganondorf’s flesh, it was as if it was being harnessed within him; he was as close to the sun as a person could be. Light and fire encasing him, bubbling as primordial ooze on the surface. Zelda continued, her arms starting to quiver as she flexed her hands to steady herself, tethering to Ganondorf himself.

The light that was where Ganondorf stood rebounded, beams of light and fire crackled into the temple walls, the roof, shattering the windows; glass, lead, and shrapnel rained down upon them. Where Ganondorf stood was now a shadow of fire, and that energy had nowhere to go but out. As part of the temple wall crumbled down, the gray light of the morning reminded them where they were amongst the now crumbling ruins of the sacred temple.

And after an eternity, that light stopped coming from her. She crumpled to the ground, and Link rushed to her side while Ganondorf remained wreathed in flame. The anger had barely melted along with her, but there was a semblance of her beneath it as she looked into Link’s eyes. Her pupils, not as large as they were, but exhaustion drooped them. A lone blood trail dripped from her nose as she panted.

But it couldn’t be that easy. As they watched the wildfire crackle and die, Ganondorf stood before them, untouched by the flames that had enveloped him, but perhaps only slightly fazed by what had been done to him. And that hatred turned to fear upon her face.

The last of the fire died on his skin, leaving it unburnt and glowing with faint embers. Her rage had not incinerated him; it had tempered him as newly forged steel. Making him unbreakable. He smiled. “You mistook who is in power here. I will happily drag your lifeless bodies to the altar to create my new world.” He unsheathed his mighty blade, settling into a painfully familiar fighting stance.

The pathway between them had grown cool, albeit still warm, and she spoke to him, her tone leaking exhaustion and disgrace. “A new plan then.”

Link didn’t hesitate as he launched himself at Ganondorf, the glowing blade in his hand, as both blades met in a horrible crash.

Chapter 44: Time
Notes:
TW: Blood, gore and death

Chapter Text
The clash of Link’s blade against Ganondorf’s was a grating screech that vibrated through the stone.

She wasn’t just going to kill him.

No. She would unmake him. Scour his shadow from the world’s memory. She would beg the goddess for the power to undo the pain he’d caused, to unwrite his entire history.

The sound of both blades joining shuttered loose rubble from the damage she’d done to the strange and irreplaceable temple. She hadn’t meant to launch herself at the brute, but a seething pressure had built behind her ribs until the only release was to throw herself at the source of the pain.

He killed Link’s father. Just as he did her own. And yet Link hadn't run that holy blade through him in impulse. His stance hadn't wavered, his grip on the Master Sword steady even as the admission slipped past Ganondorf's lips. A control in him, she could only marvel at.

But she was not controlled. She never learned to master that in the short time between her awakening and now. And because of that, she’d thrust them into chaos.

Before that, everything had gone to plan. From the cliff face where Revali had left her, she saw the plan unfolding perfectly. Below, Goron bombs cleared a path for the Hylian legion, a moving stampede of steel with Link and the holy blade at its helm. To the south, she could just make out the Gerudo legion scaling the cliffs. The Rito circled high above, a storm of feathers and arrows ready to be unleashed. And behind the teeming hordes of monsters, behind the glowing Guardians, Ganondorf waited in the ruins of the Temple of Time.

And she would break their line, incinerate the mechanical guardians, and give the army its opening. And she watched Link leading them all, how gallant and majestic he looked upon Epona, Master Sword raised skyward to catch the glow she poured down from the cliffs. Fearless and completely trusting of her abilities.

This time, the power had not come from love. It was easy to lift her hand, to harness that light. Even easier to push that power out upon them. She watched as the fire erupted in a steady stream, the shriek of the machines a discordant song in her ears. A dark thrill pulsed through her at the thought of Ganondorf watching, furious. That she had become what he wanted her to be.

Something cracked deep in her marrow, a heat that was nothing like her holy light. It wasn't warmth; it was poison, flooding her veins, searing a path straight to her heart. It beat a frantic, vicious rhythm against her ribs.

Rage. Unspoiled and vicious.

Rage that had no limits. And she would use it against him. Be worse than him.

But she’d lost her cool, erupted sooner than planned. The rage had seized her heart, threatening to burn her alive from the inside. A phantom cough echoed in her mind, Link’s. A flash of his pain had told her the embers of her own fury were scorching him through their connection. She had to get it out, had to aim it at its true source, before it consumed them both.

So she readied herself again as she watched Link’s blade crash against Ganondorf’s in matched strength. Beneath the dead sky hanging over the temple she had ruined, she dug into that power.

Her mother’s eyes going cold, her father’s head slumping against his shoulder, the biting chill of the prison floor, she drew on it all.

Her power grew, and she watched the light dance upon her fists, trailing up her arms. She felt that warmth pulse in her ears. She held as Link parried and clashed and dodged Ganondorf’s blows.

But he was too close.

She positioned herself around them, running to the altar, but Ganondorf tracked her and angled himself further away. Purposely putting Link’s back to her. She couldn’t possibly launch herself at him again while not killing Link first. And he seemed to know this, as his brow lowered in malice.

Light blazed behind her eyes, her teeth grinding against a scream building in her throat. Her own power was a cage, and the bars were beginning to melt.

She ran out of the temple through the blown-out walls to find the nearest target to punish. A dark-furred lynel raised its scythed blade over a fallen Gerudo warrior. Zelda extended her hands, and an eruption of fire overtook the beast. Unlike Ganondorf, the beast was bucking and wild, clearly pained by her actions before collapsing on its horse-like body. Dead.

The Gerudo warrior stared, her eyes wild and wide, the terror on her face slowly giving way to dawning comprehension. Then, as if all the sound of battle rushed back in, she nodded to Zelda in thanks and launched back to her feet to fight.

Zelda wouldn’t stop either. She looked back towards Ganondorf and Link, locked in a fierce dual. Ganondorf was a mountain of muscle and malice, yet Link met every crushing blow without giving an inch of ground, the Master Sword a conduit for a strength that defied the limits of his body. He had gone toe to toe with each of Ganondorf’s blows, and she knew the monster wasn’t pulling any punches.

She wanted to reach out to him, caress his mind, assure him, and plan a new strategy, but she dared not distract him. One wrong move, and that wicked blade in Ganondorf’s hands would cut him in two. So she looked back across the plateau and scanned to where her aid would be best served.

From the ruined temple, she saw the Gerudo forces, a whirlwind of coppery skin and gilded blades moving in a synchronized dance. Elemental magic flashed as sapphire-hilted swords met fire-breathing lizalfos and ruby blades shattered icy ones. Under Urbosa’s command, they were a self-contained storm, holding their own. They didn’t need her.

Then she spotted a makeshift stone ladder on a preserved wall against the temple and began to climb. As she reached the top of the mostly intact roof, carefully walking along the slated tiles, she looked to the west.

The Rito were in various positions, flying and stationary in the deep snowy cliffs. Their arrows rained down as a continuous shower upon the moblins and lynels that approached. Shrapnel and fire exploded every few moments as explosive arrows landed. Yet in the hail of rapid fire and precision strikes, the monsters still gained ground. For every one blown to bits, more pushed through, and she knew that if those monsters made it to the Rito’s position, they were not proficient in hand-to-hand combat— it would be an all-out slaughter.

Even worse, the Rito who were closest to the approaching horde flew away to reposition themselves. But an organized line of lynels with bows in their hands promptly shot them down. The harvest-colored Rito fell lifeless in the snows, never to fly again.

She stood rigid, the sky feeling stripped where the Rito had just been. A cold void opened in her chest, a space behind her chest empty. She swallowed the burning in her eyes, fisting her hands in anger, the fire growing hot within her. She held her fists up, watching light trail her arms in a steady silver flame. Then she extended it outwards, toward the line of lynels with bows in hand.

She bellowed as she looked to the empty sky, and soon the monsters were ash where they stood.

Revali flying high above his legion faced her, wings flapping, unevenly, from wounds or dying stamina, she did not know, but he lifted a wing to his forehead in a gesture of thanks.

As they found temporary stability to reform their lines, she moved along the roof to the north, scanning the Zora positions and where they needed aid. Her eyes fluttered in rapid movement, trying and failing to identify one area where she could help.

Batlike creatures with one piercing eye moved in a sea of clouds above them, diving and scraping and scratching the Zora as they focused on gelatinous, octopus-like enemies that seemed to spring up from the ground to shoot projectiles before oozing back into the earth in quick succession. All while others fought hand-to-hand against shades of colored bokoblins.

While individual Zora were locked in combat, the diving bats and ground-dwelling creatures were wearing the rest down. There was not one area she could attack that would help them from this angle. If she didn't act, she wasn't just watching a battle, she was watching the end of the Zora.

Unless…

Her gaze fell to the forest’s edge, a wall of green that could become a wall of flame, an inferno that would not distinguish friend from foe. For a heartbeat, the sheer recklessness made her waver. Then a bokoblin’s spear drove into a Zora’s chest, and the choice was made.

The air charged as the fire took on a life of its own, roaring where the fighting was thickest. The ground-dwelling monsters melted in the heat while smoke choked the bats from the sky. It was working. The Zora turned as one, diving into the shallow pond as the terrified bokoblins fled from the inferno, straight onto the waiting spears of their amphibious allies.

She saw the kind and wonderful Zora Princess amongst her people, wading in the shallow waters as the fire passed on either side. And Mipha had not seen her amongst the now-burning forest and the choked air, but she imagined Mipha’s relief as sure as she had.

And now she turned to the true north, back to where the piles of guardians still lay lifeless and smoking with dying fire. The Hylians, Sheikah, and Gorons were fighting the remaining forces. And she wanted to shun her eyes away from the sight and wish it all away.

Gorons unmoving, laid sprawled out as lifeless as rocks. Smashed and beaten by monsters as large as the temple, with the same glowing crimson eye as its bat kinfolk. Daruk and the small handful of Gorons left were doing what they could against the monstrous, gluttonous giants, but they were just delaying the inevitable.

She breathed out her quiver as she built that power up, and then pushed it out into one of the giants. Knocking it clear off its feet to drop like a downed tree off the side of the cliffs. She rallied herself again, and again, and again until all the giants were gone. Swallowing the blood pooling against her teeth.

The Sheikah were harder to trace, evenly matching themselves against the Yiga Clan. The gray and crimson fabrics melding together, their fighting tactics the exact same, attacking as quickly as the wind, disappearing and snapping back into existence with blades and fury in their hands. She watched them fight, two sides of a broken mirror, and the stories Impa had told her finally clicked into place. The Yiga were once Sheikah.

While the Sheikah held their own, the Hylian army made her shoulders sag.

The ringing of steel, the wet crack of bone, each sound was a heave in her gut. She forced her eyes to stay open, swallowing the bile that rose in her throat. They needed her help, but she could not use her light to help from this angle.

She had to get down.

She peered below in the temple, minutes or hours had passed, as such was the chaos in war. Link and Ganondorf were still locked into each other in this singular battle. The beads on Ganondorf’s temple said enough, Link was not making this easy, he took his assured victory for granted. Link was clearly tired, his movements more strategic and slowed. It reminded her of the three lynels he faced upon the red mountaintop, except this time, he learned from his mistakes. He wasn’t relying on the same brute force Ganondorf employed. He was considering each action and reaction, matching it and using his strengths and sword as leverage.

She only pushed out a feeling of love, not daring to speak to him to distract. Embracing him in that pathway, pushing any strength she had left into him. As she reached the bottom, her boots crunching on the rubble of the temple ruins, she saw what she imagined renewed vigor in Link— knowing he would hold his own as she left to descend the hill and help the Hylian army.

She ran into the carnage. The battlefield was muddy and lifeless. Scenes from Link’s fall just days before scarred her vision. This was horribly familiar, yet worse than watching the man she loved almost die. Ballads never sang of this; the mud, the smell, the sheer, brutal waste of it all. There was no glory here.

Piles of armor, with husks of bodies underneath, lay around even fewer monsters. Discarded weapons, a fingertip away from stiff hands. The horror was absolute, beyond anything she could have imagined. The smell of copper was choking, the taste of agony and pain and suffering was worse. The disgust made her power easy to call, and as a moblin butchered a soldier, she launched a beam of fire at the blue beast, cindering it to nothing.

She rushed over to help the soldier, only to find it was not a man, but a boy lying there.

His armor was weak and brittle. Probably whatever was left from wherever they could scrounge amongst the ruins after the castle fell. His too-big helmet had already lain nearby, blown off after he fell. His fawn hair was the same as Fledge’s, but his eyes, the color of stained wood with speckled amber, looked at her with awe and fear.

The memory of him impressed at Link’s blade registered through the mud and grime. It was the boy from Fort Hateno, who brought food to them.

Her first instinct was to yell for help, but as she lifted her head, she shut her mouth. The havoc upon the land said enough; no one could.

“Let me help you.” She swallowed a painful sob as she spoke to the nameless boy. Her hands went to the wound that was shredded to the bone, while blood poured out like a river. And as the words came out, she knew there was no helping him in this life, only giving him mercy in the next.

She took that dagger full of mud and ichor and lifted it high above his heart. She shook as the dagger, sharp and sure in her hand, wavered above him.

But she could not plunge it into him, even if it was a mercy. And she sat and tearfully lowered the dagger. The boy looked disappointed and relieved before she watched the life leave his wide, amber-flecked eyes. And her whole body tensed as she covered her mouth to stop a wailing sob, her eyes forcing shut, allowing only one tear to drop for the nameless boy that was too young. Too innocent to be here. He should have been left back at the fort with the others.

Ganondorf may have started it, but they decided his fate. She slid her fingers over his eyelids and rose on watery legs, the boy’s discarded dagger in one hand, a fistful of fire in the other, as a sharp jab hit her in the back.

She whirled to be face-to-face with a red bokoblin. It had stabbed her, right in the scaled area of her armor. Its head tilted, its movements jerky and unnatural. Its tongue lolled, too big for its mouth, and its eyes glowed with a frozen, mindless blue as it waited for her reaction. Her eyes were fire themselves as she darted out her hand to stab the beast in the chest, where a heart would be if it had one. It shrieked as it fell, a jarring sound that made her lips curl into a grim smile. For good measure, she threw a ball of fire at it, reducing the creature to ash.

She waited for the satisfaction to rise, of sending this creature back to the depths to never recover.

But it didn’t come.

She turned her power on the field, a raw extension of her will. A moblin charging a Hylian knight became a pillar of fire. A pack of bokoblins dissolved into screaming embers. Each blast was kindling laid on the pyre of her grief she tended to. She watched them writhe, skin melting from muscle and bone as they were set aflame. Their monstrous wailing the match. For the boy unmoving at her feet, left in the mud.

But the rage left only a hollow echo. All this fire changed nothing. Only one would stop this madness.

Dagger still in hand, dripping an unnaturally colored liquid, she marched back towards the Temple of Time.

She entered through the blown-out wall. Link and Ganondorf were still locked in their duel.

Zelda pressed herself against the shattered stone, her breath catching at the sight before her. The chamber had become a ruin of their fury. The altar cracked, the Spiritual Stones scattered, the floor scorched in branching black marks where Ganondorf's dark magic had struck and missed, each one spreading outward like a dead tree's silhouette.
