The air itself seemed to war between them, hot with malice and sharp with the promise of rain from the open ceiling above.

Link's arms were shaking against the full might of Ganondorf's power, his jaw clenched to match the blade's wrath. He was keeping pace with the monster that towered over him. For every crushing blow Ganondorf brought down, Link answered with two, faster and desperate. His Master Sword singing through the air in arcs of opalescent light. She saw him duck beneath a swing that would have split a tree, roll through ash and debris, come up slashing at Ganondorf's ribs. The Gerudo king twisted away just in time, the blade's edge slicing his robes.

Ganondorf had clear marks upon his arms and chest, delicate scratches Link had landed on him dripping in red. He did bleed. But so did Link. Zelda could see the dark stain spreading across his tunic from a gash she hadn't witnessed, the way he favored his left leg, the tremor in his sword hand that he fought to hide. Neither had gone down, and neither seemed willing to.

Ganondorf laughed, a sound like grinding stone, and raised his fist. Dark energy gathered, sickening and wrong. Link didn't retreat. He planted his feet and raised his blade, the steel catching what little light remained. The power surged forth. Link met it with a cry, his sword cleaving through the shadow, dispersing it into nothing.

Neither advanced. Neither broke. They stood ten paces apart, locked in a stalemate that felt absolute. A cold certainty settled in her gut: this would only end when one of them was utterly destroyed.

She readied herself, pulling that light from within to launch at Ganondorf, and as if he sensed her presence, he slammed his fist down into the ground. Link and she flew back by the sheer force of it into the rubble.

Her head buzzed, her back throbbing, but her armor took most of the blow. She reached for Link in that mental pathway, “Are you okay?”

She held her breath as silence answered her. She refused to believe that would—

“I’m alright,” his voice replied, sluggish with an exhaustion she could feel through their connection.

Before she could ask him what happened, Ganondorf panted and then roared, “Enough!” His blade dropped at his feet, no more than ornamentation as spit flew, “I am the mighty King. I will not be bested by the likes of you two!” He lifted his hand, glowing with the Triforce of Power as it burned him beneath his skin. He went to all fours, convulsing with a racking cough.

And swirling, choking magic covered the temple, sucking out whatever light remained, cloaking them in darkness as something horrible transformed before them.

Ganondorf was already mountainous in size compared to the average man, but she watched under furrowed brows as he grew, larger than a lynel, and stopped once he was as tall as a two-story house.

He became the beast she always knew him to be. Bone-white fangs burst from a snout that had become long and boar-like. His hands lengthened into bladed claws, his feet hardened into hooves. Curved horns swirled into being, protecting his face. His eyes were depthless and dark, any soul he might have had now extinguished. Finally, two monstrous long swords materialized in his scaled, leathery hands.

Link stood in her peripheral, whipping his face with his arm and spitting out blood. And before Zelda could speak to Link, to tell him she loved him in the face of this. She charged herself, tapping that well again— this time she reached past the point where it hurt, past the point where her body told her there was nothing left. To burn hotter than fire. Bleeding herself dry.

They looked to each other, unspoken words between them. She should say it all to him in these moments. But she only managed behind burning eyes a smile. Before launching her light at the beast Ganondorf had become.

This time she held it, she had to, for Link to get close, to drive the Master Sword through him. The light poured from her palms in a torrent she could no longer control, raw sacred power forcing itself through her as though her body was a doorway too narrow for what was passing through it. She felt herself coming apart at the seams of what she was.

Her knees buckled, but she locked them, refusing to fall. She used her anger to fuel her. Using everyone Ganondorf had hurt to stoke it. Her mother, her father, Pipit, Cawlin, The King of Hyrule. For all the unknown Gerudo, Rito, Zora, and Gorons lying wounded or still fighting around them. For the nameless brown-haired boy with cheap armor.

The heat was overwhelming now, a furnace consuming her core, and she could feel something tearing inside her chest, something vital giving way. Warm liquid traced paths down her face, gathering at her jaw, her chin, dripping onto her chest. She tasted salt and copper on her lips. Sweat and blood, she realized dimly, were pouring out of her.

She was dying.

She heard her name. It felt like a calling from home.

And she knew she would die here, in this temple, at this moment. The sealing magic demanded a vessel, and she had offered herself freely.

This was a pain beyond fire, beyond tearing. It was a silent excision, the goddess’ blessing was devouring her from the inside until nothing was left. Her vision swam, red-tinged at the edges, but she could still see Link through the haze of light and blood. See him fighting, see him moving toward Ganondorf with that terrible, beautiful focus he wore in battle. Almost there. Just a little longer.

For him, she would burn.

“Zelda— you're dying— enough.” Someone was speaking to her through labored pants.

But she searched— clawing at the scraps in her soul, any piece of fury and rage to fuel it, just a bit longer. She would wipe Ganondorf off this land, wipe his name from memory.

“Zelda. Stop.”

Where was Link? She could not see past the blinding light.

Ganondorf was roaring in satisfaction, pain—

“Zelda!”

And she was propelled outside the temple with a force of a battering ram, as if she’d known what it felt like. Her head snapped back into the dirt as a silent yell choked out. Her eyes opened to darkness, blurred color slowly coming into focus. Blue was the first color she noticed.

Not sky blue, not dark blue. A blue like a lagoon.

Link was on top of her, bloody, sweaty, dirty, his eyes blazing wild with worry as he gripped her firm and steady. He tackled her from her spot, avoiding the fire. She was ready to yell at him, accuse him, ask him why, as she sat up and noticed a massive, crushing boulder where she had just stood.

“We have to move. He’s bringing down the Temple.” Link yelled as she winced through his words.

He grabbed her hand and yanked her hard and away as another piece of the ancient building crashed down where they stood. Ganondorf was not winning his duel, so he used the next best thing to try to crush them to death.

Link weaved them through the rubble and debris. Master Sword in one hand, hers in the other. She felt the blood oozing out of her pores, pooling in her mouth, but she ran with him behind a lone pillar, out of the danger of the caving roof. He ducked and took her face in his palms, scanning and searching her for injury.

“I’m okay,” she said, her voice a raw scrape against her throat. “Are you?”

He nodded, his jaw tight. There was a new angry gash on his arm, his tunic dark with what she prayed was mud, his eye swollen shut.

She spit the blood that pooled in her mouth and managed to say, “We’re losing.”

Link only lowered his eyes as the ground shook. Ganondorf was searching for them, stomping on his hooved legs.

She choked back on every bit of hurt in her throat. “You’re not going to tell me to stop?”

“Not this time.”

A weak noise escaped her tightly closed lips as she lowered her forehead to his shoulder and shook. “I’m sorry I can’t weaken him. I’m sorry I’m not enough.”

He lifted up her face and shook his own.

She sniffed back the blood that continued to drip from her nose and used her free hand to whip it away. “Why are you so calm? Why are you not angry at Ganondorf for this—” she flung her hand outwards towards the army around them. “—or what he said about your father.”

“I am angry,” he said, his eyes scanning the ruins for Ganondorf. “But revenge won’t make me whole. I will not remember my father for falling. I will remember how he used to clean his blade every night, the pride he took in it. I remember him dancing with my mother in the kitchen to the songs of the chimes outside the window on a breezy evening. I remember him teaching me how to care for my sword, but also for those around me.”

Hot tears cut paths through the grime on her cheeks, each sob a ragged spasm that stole her breath. She could feel loose strands of hair clinging to the sticky mask of blood and snot, a ruin she couldn’t hide from him. She wanted to close her eyes and retreat back to Hateno, in their home, to serenity. But not all stories end with a happy ending.

“To the end then.”

“And past it,” he whispered against her lips, and kissed her once more, like a promise he had no business making. And she wanted it to be perfect, their last kiss, but it was anything but, before he pulled away and launched himself back towards the beast.

She had said goodbye to the love of her life, as she watched him run towards death. And she closed her eyes— but instead of channeling that fire, she looked for the person who gifted her this cursed destiny. She needed answers before she perished too. And she silently begged that part of herself she knew she shared with her for a reception. Just a moment of her time, she deserved that much before she greeted death in understanding, as brilliant light eclipsed her, sending her into the unknown.

She was weightless. 

All the noise— the screaming, the metal clashing— was sucked out in a vacuum, almost painfully. She could not see the temple ruins, or the overcast sky. She couldn’t see Link.

Her ears felt covered, a pulsing rhythm allowing sound to come rushing back in. The minerals that she tasted and smelled were nonexistent. And she was no longer boiling alive.

This was where the goddess spent her eternity, and Zelda tried to keep a check on her anger. The goddess sitting here in her pearlescent garden, untouched, unchanging, while all her people bled and died. While she and Link had bent and broken to fit in the casket of this burden.

And she was going to tell her that, as a figure approached, bathed in light. And Zelda squinted her eyes to see the goddess in her true form as she got closer. But her throat dropped, knees buckled.

“Mo—mom?” she breathed, the word catching in her throat.

Her mother stood before her, glowing in an ethereal form. Her smile brighter than any light she could have mustered, but she was as she remembered her. A royal blue sundress, flowing just above her ankles. Her chin-length flaxen hair fell in perfect waves. Her matching emerald eyes sparkling with small crinkles in the corner. The golden triangle ring they both wore and her favorite woven sandals, the ones she had worn down to the soles.

Her legs gave out, and she collapsed, a folded tangle of limbs upon the stone. Blubbering, sobbing, and shaking as her palms met the floor to try to ground herself to a reality she did not know.

Yet her mother looked down at her with reverence.

“Ho—how are you here?” She managed to say. Her voice small and childlike in the presence of her mother. Whether it was real or she was already dead, she didn’t care.

Her mother spoke, her voice gentler than she remembered, “You called for me, my sweet girl. This power you carry… it was your inheritance. I’m so sorry it has brought you such pain.”

“Where am I?”

“Think of this place as a quiet breath between worlds. You’ve paused your own story for a moment to be here with me, but you cannot linger. Your world is waiting for you to exhale.”

“Are you alive?” she questioned in a fragile wish of breath.

“No, honey, you are merely speaking with my spirit.”

Zelda strangled a sob as she lowered her face to the ground. Her mother approached, as she had done so many times when Zelda was little. Fingers of pure light lifted her chin, a touch that was not corporeal, but a warmth bloomed deep at the contact.

Behind the cloudy vision, looking so carefully at her beautiful mother, who death had stolen from her, “I never wanted you to die for me.”

“Oh— sweet Zelda. That was never an option. I would do it all over again for you to have a life. I’m just sorry you’ve been put through so much, too much.”

Insecurity crept through her in a familiar stream. “Why didn’t you tell me?” she demanded, “You could have prepared me for this, for him. And now you’ve died for me just to fail at this moment.”

Her mother’s lips pulled tight, as she let out a breath, she swore she felt it on her face. “We made a choice, we never knew if it was the right one. We just wanted to spare you from that pressure. The burden of this is more than most can handle. I know what it feels like to have a boot on your chest. To suffer—” She watched her mother tense at the implication before continuing, “But while you’ve been put through it, you have joy in your life, wonder at the new world, a love greater than legends.”

“But I can’t do this, he’s too strong. I tried. My light can’t penetrate him to weaken him. I didn’t have time to learn about this ability.”

Her mother smiled, but her eyes distant, “You already have the power to diminish him. You’ve always had it. But you’re letting the anger be the guiding light, while the truth stays in shadow.”

“How can I not be angry when he’s killed and hurt everyone I love?” she cried, surging to her feet. “He almost killed Link, he shattered me beyond the physical. He’s a poison, a blight on the air we breathe. For generations, every living thing will feel his shadow, will be haunted by it for the rest of their lives!”

“If that’s what you want to remember about us, about them, about your home. Then you will not defeat him.”

Zelda’s eyes were narrowed, her mouth opened to protest, to argue, but promptly shut.

“You already have the answer, channel that feeling, and you will defeat him.”

The air shifted, and the garden’s gilded gates began to bleed like a fresh painting left in the rain. The scent of her mother’s roses faded, and the comforting breeze on her skin turned warm again. The vision was letting her go.

“You must go back.” Her mother said, lifting her chin to face her, “I love you, Zelda. I hope that one day you will understand why I kept certain truths locked away, where they couldn't hurt you. I wanted you to have a life first, and some doors should stay closed until we are ready to open them. Please know, I am here, always.” She finished with her glowing hand over her heart.

Zelda could not quell the tears falling as she closed her eyes and smiled. “I love you, Mom.” And with those words, the vision dissolved, plunging her back into the rising chorus of war.

She opened her eyes to the dull ground beneath her feet, the broken sky above her, vacant eyes of the lifeless bodies scattered around them. The temple that stood for millennia still lay in ruin. Link was charging towards Ganondorf’s beast form.

She had been given a gift, a moment outside the storm to find her center. She knew what she had to do.

She let the tears that she had hoarded drop and lifted her hands in front of her, dried blood coating her fingers and exhaled, lifting them to the sky. She shook with a force unknown to all as she ripped open the clouds, a fissure cracking the sky, letting the sun out of its cage to harness upon it. And she felt a warmth kiss her cheek in that pocket of rays. In greeting, in comfort, “I am here. I am with you.”

And she was a seed, buried in the dark earth of her grief, clawing her way to the surface towards the light.

And she broke free, and climbed.

Memories of her home, filled with sunlight and warmth and color. Memories of her new home, filled with Link’s mother’s painting, smelling of lavender and pine, the promise of possibilities. Of Link kissing her breathless, their connection forging an unbreakable chain. Of her dress, sparkling and flowing. Of riding atop Storm, free and wild in the fields of Hyrule.

All that was good and pure flooded her, not as memory, but as a presence. She was the queen of her own destiny, her consciousness expanding to become the sea, the sky. She was every blade of grass, rooted in the land she was carved from. She was the joining, the split, the Triforce embodied. Everything in balance.

And as the Master Sword rose and clanged against the dark beast’s weapons. As Link held his position, his arms trembling with the strain of each deflected blow. She bundled the energy she possessed and extended it out. Knowing he wouldn’t burn.

And that surge of power hit Ganondorf in a steady blast of light, the beast writhed and screamed in fiendish sounds as she held it. Link’s good eye widened as he stared at her, and she met his gaze with a smile. The beast seized, bound and helpless against the chain of light snaking around his monstrous form.

Their eyes met across the chaos, a single, unwavering point of stillness. He held the sword, she held the light, and between them, the world fell away. She reached across that silent bridge between their minds, “Link, now!”

And he did not hesitate.

Chapter 45: Embrace
Notes:
(See the end of the chapter for notes.)

Chapter Text
The Master Sword went through flesh, muscle, and bone. Cutting through centuries of compacted malice, as the tip met the dark heart that beat inside.

Link braced his feet, both hands wrapped around the grip, and pushed. The blade advanced further, and something black and viscous sprayed from the wound, sizzling against the marble where it landed.

Ganondorf screamed.

Not a roar of pain, but something reminiscent of surprise. The beast’s massive body bucked, hooves scraping deep grooves in the temple floor, and the sword wrenched from Link’s grasp.

“Zelda,” Link sent into her mind, his voice barely recognizable.

She was there at a distance. Her hands raised, and the light that poured from them was different— not the uncontrollable fire— but something steadier and softer, a brilliant gold that held Ganondorf as surely as chains. There was no tremor in her arms, her eyes were clear, fixed on the beast as the world bent to her will.

The beast’s head swung wildly. The black, depthless pits for eyes found her. But for the first time, the thrashing wasn’t pure rage. It was the wild, mindless flailing of a trapped animal trying to escape.

And as Zelda approached, that light grew brighter, breaking the shell of the monster on the surface, leaving behind the dying form of the man Ganondorf once was. The Master Sword sticking out of his chest.

“You cannot kill me,” he snarled, his voice a wet rasp from the blood pooling in his chest. “We are destined to be together for all eternity.”

Zelda came closer, the sounds of broken glass crunching under her boots with each step. The light around her hands intensified, brightening from gold to a white so pure it was every color, as she raised her chin.

“I’m glad I can fulfill my promise,” she said, her voice level. “To send you to the dimension between realms, where you can never hurt anyone again.”

Behind them, the ruined altar of the temple and the Door of Time stood open and ready, mystically untouched within the ruins.

Zelda flexed her fingers and Ganondorf’s howl rose to what was left of the roof. He thrashed against the sword stuck in his chest, but he couldn’t touch the blade even if he wanted to, the magic of the sword barred him from using it against them.

“Do you mind?” she said to Link, tilting her head. Her voice dripping with a smugness as if Ganondorf wasn’t in the room.

“With pleasure.” He shuffled himself over to Ganondorf, grabbing the hilt of the sacred blade and yanked upwards violently, as an inky river flowed from his chest over the pure marble.

Zelda extended her fingers in a force, concentrating what energy she had left to move Ganondorf’s unwilling form towards the Door of Time, that chain wrapping around him to lead him to his tomb for eternity.

Stone cracked beneath Ganondorf’s writhing kicks. His hands were still bent into claws that scraped the floor with a horrible screech. And as he approached ever closer to his fate, Zelda buckled, fighting against any ounce of power the Triforce still gifted him.

She held, her body shaking with the strain. He was only a mere breath away from the depthless unknown of what lay behind the door, when his face twisted, eyes full of threat towards Zelda and a voice filled with malice to match, “You may banish me for now, but I promise you, Zelda, you will never know peace. Just as the one before you had destroyed and split her soul to escape me.”

Zelda flashed her teeth as he thrashed still, nearly breaking her hold before contorting his head to Link, “And you, benevolent hero, you will always be bound to a duty you will resent. That sword will break your spirit, again and again.”

Zelda’s teeth were chattering as she forced him to move, but he continued, “Neither of you will ever know peace. I am but a dream compared to the nightmares I will rain upon you. We are locked in this fate forever.” And he managed to lift his hand, to remind them of the Triforce of Power that still was etched upon him.

And a scream ripped from Zelda’s shaken form, the last of her strength expelled as she thrust him back into the depths of the unknown, slamming the stone door shut behind him.

The sound that followed was heavy and final. A boom that shook dust from the ceiling and left his ears humming.

Silence poured into the temple, as he only heard the blood moving in his own veins and the strained pull of his breath.

The Master Sword dimmed in his hand. The blue of the blade duller now, exhausted. He stared at it, then at the closed doors, then at Zelda.

Her hands were still raised, though the light had faded from them. Her braids had come loose, as golden, tangled hair blew outwards from her mouth. There was a smear of blood across one cheekbone dusted with mud, and her battle leathers were torn. The memory of her spewing fire was still scorched behind his eyes, but the woman standing there now seemed hollowed out by it, the fury replaced by a quiet.

Their eyes met across the ruined temple.

He took a step toward her, but his legs gave out, and his knees hit the marble with a crack that echoed against what little walls remained. Pain flared through his bad leg, but it was muffled as Zelda crossed the distance between them.

She sunk down in front of him. Her hands found his face, cool palms against his hot skin. He gritted through it to focus on her moving lips. “Are you okay?”

He nodded. He was in one piece. “You?”

She smiled, a small, forced motion, nothing like the fierce grin she wore on the battlefield, “I’m alive.”

Around them, the temple was in ruins. The altar cracked, the Spiritual Stones scattered across the floor like thrown antiques. Daylight streamed through the hole in the roof, pale and thin, illuminating the devastation in merciless detail. Broken stone, shattered glass, and the black scorch marks of Ganondorf’s magic branched across the floor like rotted veins.

And beyond the temple walls, the sounds of battle changed. The screaming had stopped, replaced by a stunned murmur.

They had done it.

He let out a breath that felt like it had been trapped in his lungs for years. Zelda’s steady hand slid from his face down to his hand, covering his knuckles where it still gripped the Master Sword’s hilt.

“We won.”

For a long time, they simply sat amidst the ruin, the silence filled by their own tattered breaths. He watched dust motes dance in the slivers of daylight, feeling the deep thrum of exhaustion in his bones, until Zelda shifted beside him.

She helped him to his feet. His ankle that had not fully healed before this battle threatened to fold him under with every step, but Zelda’s arm wrapped around his waist, her shoulder under his, holding him upright as they treaded their way through the rubble of the temple’s blown-out wall. The Master Sword now sheathed at his back, the weight a comfort at its purpose fulfilled.

The battlefield opened before them, and the silence of the temple was replaced by a sudden, overwhelming wall of sound. The moans of the wounded, the distant shouts, the range of smells. It all hit him at once.

A Hylian soldier lay face-down in the mud, one arm outstretched toward a snapped bowstring just beyond his curled fingers. His hair, the color of wet sand, was matted flat against his skull by mud and filth. The back of his tunic was torn open, revealing a wound too clean and deep to have been made by anyone other than a Yiga Clan assassin.

Three moblins were heaped together near a smoking guardian, their blue skin gone gray in death, crude weapons still clutched in stiffening hands. The smell hit him then, thick and copper-sweet, and he turned his face away, breathing through his mouth.

They walked. Each step sent a jolt up his leg, causing him to sink further into the churned mud, which was studded with arrow shafts and discarded blades. Smoke drifted in thin gray ribbons, carrying the acrid scent of burned magic.

Zelda’s grip on his waist tightened. He could feel a fine tremor in her fingers brush against him.

The sloping hills at the foot of the temple opened ahead of them, and Impa was there. Her Sheikah garb was spattered with mud and darkness, one sleeve torn to the elbow, revealing a forearm crosshatched with shallow cuts. She stood straight-backed despite it, chin lifted, watching their approach.

Beside her was Urbosa, her shield dented and gems missing from sockets, her scimitar notched along the edge, and a crust of dried blood at her hairline where something swung at her and barely missed. Deep lines of fatigue were carved around her eyes, but her chin was high, her gaze burning with a fire that hadn’t yet gone out.

Daruk’s massive form was slumped, one hand braced against his knee, holding himself upright, as the other hand rubbed his neck. His rocky hide was scored with deep gouges, but he didn’t seem to pay mind.

Mipha leaned on her silver spear, planted in the earth beside her. She was the least marked of them, her scales gleaming in the thin sunlight, but her eyes were hollow. He knew her healing magic had its limits, but seeing the proof of it in her eyes was a fresh kind of affection he hadn’t known he possessed for her.

Revali was perched on a chunk of fallen masonry, one wing cradled awkwardly against his chest. His feathers matted with blood and ash. The usual haughty tilt of his beak was gone; instead, his shoulders were slumped, his gaze fixed on the sky with an unnerving stillness.

They descended the hillock in silence. Each step its own small agony.

The leaders just watched them. No one moved to help, no one spoke.

And they stood amongst the group, looking as sorry as the rest. Impa looked from Link to Zelda and back again, taking in the blood, the dirt. “How did you finally do it?” she asked.

He looked at Zelda. She stared at the ground, the thin line of dried blood from the corner of her mouth to her cheek still evident.

She looked up, not meeting anyone’s gaze directly. “I realized I was angry—” her voice hoarse, as she cleared her throat, “I was so angry. And it felt good. He’d taken so much, from so many, and I wanted him to burn for it. I inadvertently channeled light into fire.”

Link felt that lick of heat, recalling the sight.

“He’s made of hatred,” she continued. Her fingers curled, then relaxed. “And I saw it in his eyes, the same look that I felt in my own heart. I was becoming the very thing I was trying to destroy. I was never going to weaken him enough for Link to get the final blow in.”

A phantom pain lanced through him. He could still see it: the shared bridge between them crumbling, blood weeping from her eyes and nose as she gave herself over to the power. He’d screamed for her to stop, seconds before the boulder careened toward her.

“So I let it go. I stopped fixating on my hatred of him. I stopped thinking about what he’d taken and started remembering the good. The memories of sunlight, goodness, and love.”

Urbosa relaxed her posture. Her eyes softened on Zelda’s face with an intensity that bordered on protective.

Revali shifted on his perch. His injured wing twitched. “So all that power,” he said, his voice uncharacteristically quiet, stripped of its usual edge. “All that light. It was... happiness?”

Zelda shrugged, “Ganondorf has never known joy or love; it's something he couldn’t see, and that channeled light barreled right into him. He didn’t know how to defend against it.”

They all stood in silence for a moment. The simplicity of it was stupid, and she turned to him. Her eyes found his, and she stepped closer, her hand brushing against his own to curl around his fingers, a touch so light he barely felt it.

“I’m just sorry that it took me so long to get there.” Zelda stared at their feet, her voice soft and broken, “That so many had to die before I realized that.”

“No.” Urbosa said, slowly shaking her head, “You never apologize.”

Zelda looked to her, to them. They all agreed, nodding their heads, forcing smiles against the fatigue, or looking at her with new appreciation. Not a moment after, Urbosa turned to bark orders at a Gerudo scout who had appeared at the base of the hillock. Daruk heaved himself upright with a groan that sounded like settling stone. Mipha already glided down the slope toward where the wounded were being gathered. The battle was over, but the work was not.

For this one moment, standing in the thin sunlight on a hillock strewn with wreckage, he focused on the light pressure of Zelda’s hand in his. The warmth seeped through, a small anchor in the devastation.

Something worth the cost.

They sat on the cool masonry of what was the altar— now ruined, as the sun started to dip behind Mount Hylia. The warm sorbet of colors bled into evening as beams cut through the fluffy clouds. It was a sight she never imagined she’d see again.

That light caught the three fist-sized Spiritual Stones where they lay in the rubble, sparkling despite the dust-hazed air. She looked at them and felt nothing, just three unnaturally large gems in a pile of rubble. And she stared, spent and drained, as a cool breeze kicked up the air, swirling the debris, before caressing her face as if in thanks.

The sounds of the battlefield became a low, constant mumble; voices calling orders, the creak of wagons being brought forward for the wounded, the occasional sharp cry of pain.

She felt the dried sweat upon her brow, as her hand moved to scrub it away. She closed her eyes, her hand hovering over her brow. The intention behind the movement dissolved, leaving only the weight of her own arm in the air.

Her head was a muddled mess of whatever was left. Maybe she had boiled pieces of herself away, or this was simply what pure exhaustion felt like. And her stomach growled in answer.

A half-eaten apple was handed to her immediately after.

It took every effort to turn her head towards Link, as she took the fruit with a half-smile.

She looked at him, her first instinct to glance away from the damage, but she forced her gaze to remain, to take it all in.

His right eye was already muddled with disturbing shades of brown, swollen and shut. The gash in his arm was deep, but thankfully not as deep as others she’d seen on him. His blue tunic was clawed and shredded, a muddy crimson blooming from his abdomen, his guards missing, cut off in the heat of battle, only his cuirass remained. And his sandy hair was stuck together with bits of ichor.

It had been hours since she had sealed Ganondorf behind the mysterious doors of the fallen temple, and they watched as the remaining monsters and Yiga Clan bolted in retreat. Realizing that their leader had fallen— their protection ceased— they ran to hide or regroup or do whatever monsters do. Those who were still vertical picked off any that remained.

She closed her eyes, and the last few hours played out behind them. Finding strength she hadn’t known she possessed, she and Link had gone to help where they could. They’d found survivors, helped form a queue for the healers arriving from below. They’d refused potions, giving them to others who needed them more. 

It was only after dragging herself through mud and wreckage that she’d stopped beside the body of a young Sheikah, no older than her. His ruby eyes were open, fixed on the sky. He was one of dozens, hundreds, their faces becoming a blur of the same-shaped eyes, noses, and mouths. She wondered if anyone would know his name, or if he would become just another number in a historian’s record.

And she bit into the tart apple, the burst of sweetness quelled the burning in her eyes as she tried to think of anything else.

“I saw my mother,” she blurted out, eyes pinned to her feet.

“When?”

She gripped the apple hard enough to bruise it. “Right after you kissed me goodbye, I begged the goddess for an audience. To yell at her, curse her, to ask for help, but instead I was brought to my mother. I’m not even sure it was real—” Her voice cracked.

“What did she say?” His brows moved, one lifting higher than the swollen one. The motion was clearly painful.

Zelda let loose an exasperated breath, “That she loved me. That I possessed the sealing power all along. And that— that she was sorry.” His face narrowed at her as much as it could. “She was sorry for this burden, sorry that she never told me. And that there were more truths to discover, but there was no time.”

The tenderness in Link’s voice didn’t help, “What do you think she meant?”

“Perhaps I imagined it all— maybe a figment of my imagination after I lost so much blood, my body finding something to grasp onto, to keep going.” She took a bite of the apple, chewing slowly. “Or, it was real. And she spoke on shared experience.”

“You think your mother was the goddess?”

“No… right?” She looked at him reproachfully. “She couldn’t have been. I was with her my whole life, there was never a threat, never any sign of that kind of power.”

And Impa now approached them upon their small slice of calm amongst the rubble. Her footsteps were not quiet as the limp in her gait was evident. Zelda stopped her thoughts from becoming words— she wasn’t ready to reveal something that intimate with Impa, despite it all.

“The hero and the goddess.” Impa said, and had it been anyone else, it may have sounded like mockery.

Zelda sighed. “I could go my whole life without hearing that name again.”

Link huffed a delirious laugh next to her.

“Fair enough.” She sat upon a slab of temple wall, or roof, in front of them. Her dagger in her belt, but missing its sheath. “Either way, thank you both, for all you’ve done.”

“We couldn’t have done it alone.” Zelda paused, her face tight and nose warm, “We at least have our lives. That’s thanks enough.”

Link found her hand. Caked in dirt and drying blood, their fingers interlaced until it was hard to tell where one of them ended and the other began.

Impa’s lips tightened. “You’re right, the kingdom has dues that cannot be paid. All we can do is remember them.”

They fell into a shared silence, which Impa broke by tossing a healing elixir to each of them. And before Zelda could open her mouth—

“Everyone who could be helped has received care. Now it is your turn.” Her gaze settled on Link’s swollen face. “That eye needs it before it gets worse,” she said, her voice stern but laced with an undeniable concern.

They drank deeply, and that healing potion flourished within her, healing what it could, ignoring what couldn’t.

Zelda set the small flask down with a clink as Link did the same. And watched as almost immediately his eye started to open. Still mottled and horrible stains of yellow but much better.

Perhaps she was still delirious from blood loss, or battle, or witnessing things that would never clear from the corners of her mind, but she asked any of them that may have had the answer, “Do you think Ganondorf was always this way? Was he born like the rest of us, and his environment made him evil? Or was he inherently wicked?”

Philosophers and scholars have been arguing about it in her world since the dawn of it. Surely theirs had as well.

But maybe there was more Impa hadn’t shared with her, and she had to know.

Impa sighed, “The histories only tell of his ambition. Whether the Triforce of Power corrupted him, or simply gave him the means to act on what was already there… I don’t know.”

“Or maybe it was the power itself. The feeling that you’re indebted to it. I felt it, it’s a frightening thing.” Zelda rubbed her knuckles, unable to meet Impa’s eye. “Unrestrained, I would have burned along with the revenge I wanted.”

“But you didn’t” Impa’s voice was soft, “Zelda, what you accomplished, I don’t believe anyone else could have done. You had only days between the awakening and now to try to tame it, and you figured out quickly that your emotions channeled it— but you also had the immense wisdom to pivot in the heat of battle. You realized something most go their whole lives without ever learning.”

Zelda hung her head before Link’s hand slid to her lap, to rub his fingers along her knuckles.

“Do you think Ganondorf meant what he said? When I sealed him?”

“What did he say?”

Zelda bristled, remembering the threat that felt like a blood oath she hadn’t agreed to. “That I will never know peace, just as the one before had shredded her soul. And that Link would be bound to duty, which would break him. That he’ll be back, because we’re destined to this entanglement for eternity.”

Link had inadvertently stopped rubbing his thumb along her hand.

“I think… a mad man who is about to be sealed for all eternity would say anything to stop it.”

“Maybe.” Zelda stared at Impa, “Perhaps you’re right… there is no escaping that fate?”

She was sure she had shut the door, that her sealing powers had done something no brute force or other could. But could another open it?

“He’s sealed for good,” Impa read it over her face, “That is beyond a doubt.”

Zelda nodded, forcing herself to believe that truth.

“However, on to another matter. And this may be somewhat misguided, but it should be mentioned—” Impa said, “the stones are here.” She gestured toward the three gems on the floor. “I would imagine you are able to use them to portal yourself home. If that’s what you want.”

The words landed between them like something dropped from the roof of the temple itself. Zelda felt Link stiffen beside her.

Everything that had started it.

She looked at the stones. They glowed with a soft, internal magic, of what embodies the sky, the land, and the life, and for a moment she allowed herself to imagine it.

Leaving Hyrule. The disorientation of her return. The faces of Linda and Maren, which had started to muddle and blend in the forgetful haze of time. To a life that continued without her.

And she missed them. She imagined the door to her old life closing, and a jarring hurt squeezed her.

“I don’t know how. Ganondorf pulled me here.”

“He may have pulled you here, but you can learn to walk the realms as sure as he learned his magic.”

Never seeing them again. Never going back to her hometown to walk along the graves where her parents lay. But something within her fundamentally changed. And just as she remembered to foster the joy that created her light. She would brand them into her heart.

“You do not need to answer right away, think about it—”

She picked up the closest stone to her, the emerald. It was warm, thrumming with a power that could never be explained in this life. As surely as the weight in her palm settled, she thought of Maren’s unsolicited visits, always intended with care. Linda’s confidence, her fire— the same fire she welded. She imagining telling her everything that she had done in Hyrule, and how she would believe her without a second thought.

A whole life waited for her.

But a life she no longer knew how to live. She closed her hand around the stone, she looked up at Impa, her eyes clear, holding it out to her. “I am home.”

The words came out quieter than she intended, but easily. True.

Impa’s lips pressed into a thin line, but the corners of her eyes softened. Exhausted and red-rimmed, her gaze held Zelda’s. For a fleeting moment, she wasn’t the Sheikah master, but a woman looking at the woman she had mentored, fought for, and nearly lost. A flicker of pride, of sorrow, of profound respect passed between them before Impa took the stone from her hand.

“Then go,” Impa said, her voice rough. “You’ve seen and done enough. Go home.” She turned, already moving away, already becoming the Sheikah master again, shoulders squaring beneath the weight of what came next.

“Wait.” Link’s voice so raw, scraping. He pushed himself upright, wincing. “We can’t just—”

“There’s an army of able bodies,” Impa said, not turning back, and when she spoke again her voice softened, with only just a slight edge. “You’ve given enough, hero. Both of you. Go home and heal. It’s not the last you’ll see of me. I’ll call upon you in a few days.”

And she was gone before Link could protest further, her footsteps fading into the general murmur behind the temple ruins. Link stood where she left him, swaying slightly, his eyes darting outside the broken wall.

Zelda approached him. Her body much less stiff and hardened as she stepped in front of Link, placing her hands in a tender caress on his shoulders and sliding them back to curl in his hair. His eyes fluttered shut, a low sound escaped his throat as he leaned into her touch.

“Darling,” the word felt strange, something from her life before, but as she saw a small crinkle in his eyes, she smiled. “Won’t you take me home?”

“Yes,” he said, looking at her as if he already was there.

They rode all night. At their second stop to water the horses, it took all her remaining strength just to pull herself back onto Storm’s saddle, her muscles stretched too tight in revolt.

And they did not speak as the landscape unfolded around them in shades of blue and black. She took in every inch as if it were the first time. They passed the twin peaks, their massive silhouettes blotting out the sky. They cut across Blatchery Plain, quiet and still, a different landscape from the carnage it had taken before.

A breeze blew through them and wisps of hair fell in her face, the rest in ratty tangles, and she didn’t have the energy to push it back. She barely had the energy to hold onto the reins.

Dawn came, painting the clouds in peach as Hateno emerged from the morning mist. The stars faded one by one, and the night unraveled around them. The windmills turned lazily. Smoke rose from chimneys.

They rode through the village gate. No one awake to see them pass. It was so unbearably, mundanely normal that she felt her throat close. These people had slept through the night. They would wake and milk their cows and till the ground, completely ignorant of the ravages of the war.

Their horses instinctively turned towards their house off the path. It looked exactly as they left it.

She dismounted, and her legs nearly buckled. A sharp pain lanced through her ribs with every breath, a counterpoint to the dull throb in her muscles. A sudden chill traced its way down her spine, a cold that had nothing to do with the morning air. A small expense to be a goddess, a give and a take. A cost and a price.

Storm stood patient, blowing warm air against her neck, and Zelda leaned into him, if for a moment to not collapse, but when she straightened something caught her eye. On the back of the house, where the stable lay, past the garden path.

She blinked, wondering if she had truly lost her mind.

It was small— perhaps the size of a bathroom— built to match the stone of the house and topped with a cedar roof. A carved wooden door was set into one wall with an intricate handle of polished metal.

She turned to Link, both his eyes mostly clear despite their unrest. His gaze fixed on her, his brows drawn together, watching her reaction with a quiet intensity.

“You built this?” The question was only the first of a dozen that suddenly flooded her mind.

How long had it been? Six weeks? More? She’d been a prisoner. He’d been hunting for the sword. When could he have found the time to come back here?

“Not with my hands, but I had it commissioned before we left. It was… a gift, for you, upon our return, before…”

She already knew before, as she was already moving towards the small addition, any ache wiped away by the wonder of what was behind the door. Link followed her a safe distance behind.

She stood in front of the expertly carved door; it was new, fresh wood—burned glyphs and patterns swirling in a beautiful scene she didn’t understand.

“Go on,” he said. His voice was rough with exhaustion but steady beneath it.

She pushed the door, feeling the wood grain beneath her fingertips.

For the first time since she’d arrived in Hyrule, since learning she was a deity’s heir, she allowed herself to be surprised.

“A shower?” she whispered.

“I tried to design it based on how you described it.” She felt him squeeze behind her in the small space. 

Rich, stained cedar planked the walls, filling the enclosure with a clean, warm scent. Her eyes followed a copper pipe up the stone exterior to a nozzle overhead, its lever gleaming. Beneath it hung a bundle of eucalyptus and lavender. She observed a small bench, a stack of fresh towels, and a single bar of soap. Each detail a quiet testament to his consideration. It was perfect.

“When?” She asked him on the verge of an emotion she hadn’t been able to hold down.

“I spoke with the builders before we left. It was meant to be a surprise for our return.” He gestured toward the pipework. “A water wheel brings water from the stream that runs along the back of the house, and rubies heat it beneath the floor before it enters the pipe.” His voice dropped, “I hope it… resembles what you’re used to.”

She could only hear her heart in her ears as she took in every inch of the beautiful craftsmanship. Every detail considered, every comfort provided. Her hand reached to the lever and pulled as water sprayed in a steady stream, its patter on the floor like summer rain as fog began to build toward the ceiling.

“Is it…?” he asked, his voice catching.

The sheer care of it rooted her to the spot, a warmth spreading from her chest to her limbs. She could feel his stillness behind her, the weight of his unspoken hope pressing in on the small space between them.

So she turned to face him and kissed him.

His lips were tender, and she poured every ounce of her gratitude into the press of their mouths.

The scents and the haze brought a renewed sense of vigor that rippled through her as she savored his kiss. As she let herself enjoy it for purely what it was, without having to remember what it would feel like or if she would have to go without it.

The tension in his shoulders eased under her touch, and his kiss deepened in response.

The world outside fell away, muted by the earthy-scented steam. Here, there was only the sound of their breathing and the solid warmth of his body. Home.

She pulled the tie from his hair, letting her fingers comb through the freed strands. The only time she ever saw it down was when they were undone. Then she pulled back and started to untie his sword belt, settling it down in the corner to watch over them, as his eyes tracked her every move.

Her fingers shook as she managed the intricate fastenings of his leather cuirass. And her eyes met his, an unspoken understanding, as she lifted his tunic over his shoulders, careful to avoid the tenderness in his joints. And she moved to the chain mail underneath as it swiftly thudded to the floor.

His chest was bare and bruised, but his hands were steady as he moved to her armor. She felt the weight of the war lift from her shoulders as he pushed it back to fall behind her. He worked slowly, not with urgency, but with a quiet reverence. His touch, the careful work of stripping away the death, the destruction, and the pain until all that was left was skin.

They stood before each other, naked in the rising steam. She stepped into the spray, knocking her head back as she shut her eyes, letting the water hug and caress her, and every fiber of her being seemed to uncoil at once.

It was perfectly warm as it trailed the column of her neck, down her front. She lifted her hands to smooth her hair, and she felt the grime begin to loosen. It ran in rivulets down the threads of her body, pulling every bit of grime down with it. A hushed sound caressed her ears, whispering that she hadn’t needed to do a thing; it was the water’s turn now to take care of her.

She opened her eyes. Link stood patiently away, his eyes coveting the water that dripped from her as he gave her the space to indulge. And she pulled him in, wanting him to experience the rebirth of the water and watch the trails of it upon his skin.

Her hands slithered to his shoulders and spun him into the waters’ way as she kissed him. This time it was passionate, and she pushed into his body to be flush with him. And the minerals of Hateno’s spring waters lingered in every opening and tongue-curling motion.

As the water sluiced away the grime and the scent of home filled her lungs, a fierce, undeniable pulse beat through her— a need to feel, to live. She quickened, tightening her embrace around him.

She rested her forehead against him, a single, shuddering breath passing between them. The scent of cedar, the heat of his skin, it was real. It was home.

And she loved him so much it hurt. Her equal, her savior.

Her hands roamed over him, feeling every thread and ridge of his body, dedicated to training and the sword. And his hands explored her, with the same unhurried attention.

Until she snagged a puckered edge on his torso and he flinched. Her eyes flew open to find the wound and apologize, but her gaze fell to the floor.

She watched the red water pool at their feet, and slowly give to pink then clear before swirling down the drain. 

All she saw were eyes the color of stained wood with amber flecks. A boy’s face, looking up with awe and fear. The slick hilt of a dagger gripped in her hand. His blood, pooling dark beneath him. The images slammed into her, and the air left her lungs in a gasp she couldn’t stifle.

She could not stop it more than she could stop the sun from rising or the earth from spinning, as more images flooded her. For the Zora lying face down near the water they loved. For the Gorons who would never roll home to Death Mountain. For all the discarded weapons near lifeless hands. For all that had died for the life of others.

Arms encircled her, holding her tight. There were no words, only the gentle scrape of his calloused hands on her back, the cradle of his palm against her head. The solidness of him was the only thing giving her permission to fall apart.

She couldn’t contain the great, heaving sobs as her tears blended in the water’s spray, as she trembled in Link’s embrace.

She wept for the nameless who would never return home. Her mother’s laugh, her father’s quiet wisdom. She grieved for Link's body, for the new, permanent artwork that lay upon his skin. And last, she sobbed for herself, for the new scars now scabbing her heart for what she endured.

She wept, and he simply held her.

She didn’t know how long the water rained around them, only that their skin was pruned and swollen. He held her still, his solid weight the only anchor keeping her from joining the water down the drain. But with each breath, the sobs started to lessen, and she watched the water carry the rest of the war down the drain.

Notes:
Wanted to check in with you all before the final chapter..

When I started writing this over two years ago, I had first envisioned some heartfelt moments and smutty scenes. However, a real plot formed and as I progressed the story, an emotional depth I hadn’t realized came to pour out of me.

While I would debate that the violence and themes of loss are canon to the fandom— i.e. hidden behind vibrant colors and lack of gore in the games, Shadow Temple, Beneath the Well, Majora’s Mask— for a modern Zelda character, this would not be typical for her. Witnessing such violence would be traumatic and I did not want to rose color her point of view on that.

I do, however, want to apologize for lack of transparency to you all from the beginning. I would have been more forthcoming when I started publishing that this may deviate in tone from typical fanfics of this nature… but I do hope you enjoy it all the same.

Alright, long winded talk over. One chapter left. I have buckets of feelings about this and more to preview for you.. but we’ll talk in the next.

Chapter 46: Ring
Notes:
The last chapter.

There are so many things I want to say. Two and a half years of thoughts and feelings somehow have to fit into a few paragraphs.

First, a little about where this story goes from here. Then, at the end of the chapter, I’ll leave my personal thanks and acknowledgments.

This story was born during a run in March of 2024. The warm spring air, the smell of blooming flowers, and the endless green trails where I live stirred something in me. It became my love letter to a game that shaped my childhood. From the very beginning, this was meant to be a standalone story.

…Until it wasn’t.

A few months ago, another idea found me. Then another. Then another. Books two, three, four, and five arrived in rapid succession. And when I say arrived, I mean they crashed into me like a tidal wave. Once I came up for air, the path ahead was impossibly clear. These characters weren’t finished telling their story. This world wasn’t ready to let them go.

So while this book comes to an end, their journey does not.

The next story will begin right where this one leaves off. I’m going to spend some time nurturing Book Two before I begin publishing it, so I don’t have a release timeline just yet. When I’m ready, I’ll also post an epilogue to bridge the two stories. For now, though, I’m marking this work as complete. After all, it seemed cruel to leave you all staring over the edge of a cliff for an unknown amount of time.

If this story meant something to you, I hope you’ll subscribe so you don’t miss what’s next. If subscriptions aren’t your thing, check back toward the end of the year.

Now… enjoy the final chapter. I’ll meet you again at the end.

(See the end of the chapter for more notes.)

Chapter Text
Every step was a fresh torture in her thighs.

She planted her boot on another sharp incline of rock, her breath pluming. Ahead, Link moved with an infuriating ease, his silhouette dark against the deepening twilight.

How he found joy in this in his free time was beyond her.

However, the sky was so beautiful as it started to reset. From this height, it felt as though she could lift her hand and brush the vibrant twilight blue that rivaled the hue of Link’s eyes. Each star contrasted a brilliant glow that winked down at them as a kindred cousin to her light.

While she may be heir to the sun, the stars burned too.

It had only been six weeks since the battle of the plateau. Six weeks since ‘The Battle for the Sacred Realm’, or ‘The Fall of the Demon King’. Just two of the names some had already tried to immortalize, which neither seemed to land upon her ears in a remarkable way. Perhaps one day someone would find the right string of words to capture what had happened that day. But she hadn’t cared to be written into it.

Six weeks since she broke down in the beautiful shower Link had built for her.

Six weeks since he held her through it. How he let her cry into him in a sobbing, wracking mess, until the rubies’ magic faded.

Now, as she finally made it to the flat expanse of the mountain, ready to collapse, that same chill in the warm air brushed against the sweat on her neck, bringing the bite of that memory back. How he toweled her off, cradling her in his arms as he took each stair to the bedroom with care. How he laid her down with such tenderness before climbing behind her to cuddle her, stroking his finger against her arm in comforting circles. How they both slept in that too-small bed for two days.

On the third day, she pulled only a semblance of herself out of bed, forcing herself to be vertical before falling back to be swallowed by the sheets. Link had already been to town and back to stock their supplies. But she couldn’t manage it. A brick lay upon her chest, crushing her as she stared at the ceiling, wondering if she had imagined it all. If the powers she possessed weren’t just figments and seeing her mother had just been a moment of non-lucidity.

The fourth day brought that intimate rage. She stomped through the house, the yard, finding their battle clothes in the foot of the shower. She threw them in the fire pit at the edge of the property and raised her hand. Burning them with that horrible power she thought she’d never use again. Her leathers, Link’s tunic— all just shredded cloth soaked in sweat and blood. It was beyond salvaging.

The leather blackened and curled, the stench of it thick and familiar in her nose. Flames licked at the bloodstains, turning them to smoke. Heat bloomed on her cheeks, and for a second, it wasn’t the fire pit but the searing ruin of the temple, his laughter echoing in the ash-choked air. A scream built in her chest, she couldn’t release. She had bound him, but she couldn’t bear the sound of his name.

The fifth day, she left their property. She hadn’t gone far, only to the lab. She went alone and stared over the sea as the sun rose and the crystallization of the opening colors faded to blue. And she had begged to see her again. If her mother had appeared to her at that moment of need, she could again.

What she wouldn’t give to ask her what she meant, where she was, where her father was… she would give back every bit of this blessing to have another moment.

The sixth day brought a crippling hurt.

She spent it collapsed in the grass, letting the autumn sun bake into her skin, chasing a warmth that couldn't touch the emptiness inside. No matter how many leaves she watched fall and how the autumn breeze rustled them against the house, it stirred nothing inside her.

On the seventh, as the sun rose, that seed within her broke through. She was alive. He was alive. And that would have to be enough.

And it would be, eventually. The hauntings of what they endured and witnessed clung to her, cobwebs in the corners of her soul she might never reach. But when Link’s hand found hers in the dark, she held and sunlight poured in. This life was not an accident and he was not a coincidence. It was a wave she was learning to make peace with, cresting with the joy and diving through the pain. She would learn, in time.

And on that night, Link and she discovered each other again. In the dark, small surviving space between what they had been and what they were becoming.

Then, on the eighth day, as if the wind had overheard her acceptance, duty and life had found them again.

Impa arrived that morning, sat in their homely kitchen, the scents of squash and cider followed her as she explained the aftermath that unfolded after the battle.

After they had cleared the area, the temple lay in ruin, but they had confirmed the Door of Time held. For good measure, they placed round-the-clock guards there.

Before the war, Princess Zelda had entered the dilapidated Forgotten Temple with Groose; but it was Queen Zelda who emerged. She was now the ruler of Hyrule, her coronation would take place in the coming months. She wanted to rebuild and reset, but first she wanted to greet the saviors of Hyrule. Anointing them both before the court of who was left.

Zelda hadn’t cared to return to the castle, where her trauma was cut into and poorly stitched up deep within the belly of the castle walls, but Link deserved to be given that honor, even if he said he hadn’t cared otherwise.

They agreed to return if the ceremony would be brief, only for their eyes, the Queen, Impa, and whatever high-ranking military was left. No pomp and circumstance. With a nodded agreement, they traveled back to where it began on the ninth day with Impa.

They arrived back at Castle Town, where the embers from the smoking cinders of the once lively town had ceased. The carrion had vacated as had the crows, and all that was left was pieces of foundations. As she passed through, her eyes locked onto the few spots of color left in the charred town before watching the Hylians pick through the skeletons of their homes. It wasn’t about finding what they’d lost, but what was left. Perhaps, like her, they were discovering how little they truly needed.

The castle was stacked with military, a presence thicker than before as they lined the road towards the sanctum. Ganondorf’s dark magic had left scorch marks upon the doors like jagged scars, and some tapestries still hung in tatters, ugly reminders of a tenure no amount of quick cleaning could fully erase.

As they walked into the grand room atop the highest tower in the castle. It was brighter than before. The sun had opened the room, chasing the shadows from the vaulted ceilings and grand staircases. The black and crimson that Ganondorf preferred was replaced with royal blue and maroon tapestries, golden-threaded trim with the Triforce upon it.

She lifted her face high, but the hall's new brightness couldn't erase the gloom that crawled upon the walls in her memory. His laughter seemed to echo off the grand arches, and a phantom pain flared in her arm. She flinched. As if he’d felt it too, Link stepped into her space, his gaze catching hers. The Queen, the court—they all faded. There was only the solid warmth of him, a silent promise that pushed the ghost from the room and replaced it with the memory of the ball. Where he had held her and waltzed into her heart to stay.

Her heart slowed and found a shard of peace as she lifted her gaze to the second story. It was not Ganondorf sitting upon the throne, but the young Queen.

She was a breathtaking marvel of a Queen.

She rose and floated down to greet them, in a high-necked royal blue tunic, a fine laced corset, and a flowing dress to match, all in harmony with gold thread spun from precious metal. Her posture was resolute, her gait like a prized horse in procession. Her hair was straighter, silkier, just as her skin was flawless and smooth like a newly burgeoned flower— untouched from years shrinking from the ages of the sun. She was the version of Zelda that wasn’t tossed around with the grit of sand and salt.

Shame clawed into her throat, hitting the back of her teeth. Queen Zelda was a perfect, unbroken reflection of who she may have been. She even held herself with regal poise in the same room her father was murdered in, the same room that had taken him away, made her a queen.

All she could do was smile at her, and the mirror smiled back.

“Thank you, Goddess blessed, for saving my kingdom,” the Queen said, her voice the texture of gossamer. However regal she was, she let a twitch slip in that smile.

Zelda bowed her head and gave a curt curtsy, “You’re welcome, my Queen.”

And the Queen turned to Link, and her eyes scanned him from boot to head. Assessing, perhaps wondering what life would have been like had he been assigned to her as her personal knight instead of Zelda. And her eyes finished at the hilt of the Master Sword as she cleared her throat in the politest of manners.

“Sir Link of Hateno, thank you for saving my kingdom.”

“You’re welcome, my Queen.” And he bowed low. But something in the way he bent and scraped made Zelda’s jaw tighten.

But before she would allow herself to linger in that feeling, Queen Zelda took the ceremonial blade from Auru’s hands and motioned for them to both kneel low.

Link knelt.

But she froze.

Her knuckles were turning pale and painful, as her back instinctively tightened, shoulders pushed in. Bracing for someone to violently push down on her as she felt that rising burn—

But Link grabbed her hand, and she found his eyes, grounding herself in them. The blue within them was that wave, she would dive to avoid drowning in that abyss of gloom. Swimming towards that memory, imagining how he held her nights before. And she crested that wave to tread and kneeled. Letting go of her knight's hand as she went.

Queen’s gaze swept over them, her perfectly shaped lips tightening for a fraction of a second. All Zelda could feel was the anchor of Link’s gesture. A private smile touched her lips as she lowered her neck, accepting the cold kiss of the blade upon her shoulders. When it was his turn, Link was the perfect knight, and as they rose, she felt a quiet shift. She was goddess-blessed, now Lady Zelda. And Link, finally, an official royal knight of Hyrule.

“How may I repay you for all that you’ve done?” The Queen asked.

A dozen selfish demands sparked in her mind. Mainly, a lifetime free of duty so she could spend their life free and wild. But she pushed it down. This wasn’t about her. It was about Link, and whatever he wanted was the barest fraction of what the kingdom owed him. Zelda looked to him, conceding to him with a look.

Your choice.

“I ask if I can stay in service to Hyrule, but stationed outside of the castle, preferably near Hateno. I could lead monster control crews in the area, or provide guard duties nearby.”

The Queen looked as though she was trying hard not to swallow a sour sweet, “You would sacrifice your career at the castle to stand on guard duty?”

“Yes. I want to be in service to Hyrule, but I also choose to be close to Zelda. I’m sure she would be delighted to join me, when she is able.”

A warmth spread through her chest, fierce and protective. He had every right to ask for a title, a keep, a life of comfort— but he only asked for a life with her.

The Queen lifted a questioning brow toward her, and Zelda buried a smirk. “It would be my honor, Sir Link,” Zelda said.

The Queen opened her mouth—

“—However, before you decide, if I can request a… stay of duties? If only for a few weeks.” She gave a peek smile to the Queen for the abrupt response.

The Queen only clasped her hands together to hang down, waiting for another interruption that hadn’t come. “Granted. Anything for the Hero and the Goddess.”

“The region leaders arrive in the morning for a council,” Link murmured as they ascended the torch-lit stairs. “Impa asked if we could stay for it.”

“A council for what?” Zelda asked.

“To discuss aid and resources needed for after the war. Everyone is a bit stretched, considering.”

“I understand,” Zelda sighed. “Then we can leave?” She glanced at him, and he squeezed her hand while throwing her a nod.

Link and she had decided to return to their apartments. According to Impa, they were fairly untouched by the siege. As they opened the door to Link’s room first, his hand upon the Master Sword’s hilt, the rooms were heartrendingly familiar. Dusty but left as they had before the trek to Mount Lanayru. 

As Link cleared her room, he left her to gather what she wanted as he did the same.

She ran a hand over the gilded furniture, the smooth, cool surfaces feeling alien under her hardened fingers. A life contained within these castle walls, perfect and regal, belonged to the Queen. But the memory of sun on her face and the hum of power under her skin was a truer home. She looked out the window, past the battlements to the distant mountains. She could no more be caged in this room than the sun itself.

She opened her chest of clothes, tracing the now strange, foreign fabric of the modern white dress she'd arrived in. A chill chased her muscles, the realization of how a different woman entirely had worn this dress a little over a year ago. While she knew it would physically still fit, it would chafe against her newfound self. Unpleasantly.

She lifted the white dress to pick through the rest, her emerald ball gown lay beneath. She looked at the gems, each one shining in an array of prisms against her blurred sight. While she was so thankful that this dress survived the sacking, remembering the heavenly memories, that swell within her rose—

“It’s okay to feel sad for those who have lost things. You did not inflict that upon them. You’ve lost just as much too.”

She turned her whole body to him, still clutching that unearthly fabric close, and met a pensive look on his face. She should have known he would see right through her.

“I know, and while both of us have lost so much, I can’t help the guilt at how much we still have. We have our home— uncorrupted, and we have each other.” She dipped her chin, “It’s so stupid to be thankful for a dress while some lost everything… and everyone.”

He lifted her chin to meet him. A warmth she didn't know she continued to need blazed in his eyes. “Do not let yourself be swallowed by guilt that you don’t deserve to feel.”

She managed a thin smile, though it didn’t reach her eyes.

They slept in Link’s room that night. For the last time, she listened to the muffled sounds of the castle, the distant clang of armor, and the whisper of wind through the battlements. She cuddled closer to him, his embrace shielding her from the ghosts of this place as she waited for the chasing sun to naturally drive them away.

And as that dawn arrived, so had the leaders.

With handshakes, pats on the back, fond embraces, and a slight nod of a head— they had all greeted each other in one of the hastily restored council chambers. A private room on the west side of the castle, near Impa and the other captains’ personal chambers. The room had been decorated like all others before; tapestries with the Hyrule crest, arched ceilings, upholstered chairs that had never been sat in. A large, long table was situated in the middle, with rows of chairs facing each other and nothing decorating the surface.

Mipha sat opposite Link, with Urbosa between Zelda and the head seat, and Impa opposite from there. Daruk stood awkwardly, knowing the chair would not hold him, while Revali sat furthest from the head of the table. Auru, Krin, and the remaining captains filled the seats that were left.

And last, the Queen emerged, looking regal and polished as they all stood awaiting her to take her seat at the head.

Hours blurred into a tide of worries. Zelda caught fragments—‘…dwindling stores before the first snows…’ from Auru, his voice a low rumble. ‘…farmland still scorched…’ Krin’s clipped report.

She traced the wood grain of the table, the smooth lines a stark contrast to the frayed nerves in the room. Neither of them were seasoned with politics. She was the spirit and he the sword— invited surely, out of a formality. But he sat beside her, a perfect, stoic knight, his tension palpable in the stillness of his shoulders. Until his stomach rumbled, and a blush crept across his cheeks. As if on cue, servants appeared with platters of food, and the debate resumed over the clink of flatware.

Each region’s unresolved issues bled into each other. Urbosa spoke of her concern in the Gerudo Region, the Highlands in the north seemed to house the remaining Yiga Clan. She wanted to extract them, root and stem. Impa’s tighter jaw seemed to agree. Goron Village was untouched, but within the canyon, moblins and lynels regrouped, causing supply chain issues for traveling merchants to and from.

Mipha’s described a tightening cordon of lizalfos and elemental monsters camped all around the Domain, pushing towards Akkala. If they didn’t start driving them back, they may never be able to safely leave. While Revali noted more trolls and bokoblins swarms between Tabantha and the ridge would hinder all travelers but him and those with wings.

As the food became cold, and voices leveled, a plan was proposed. Monster control crews would be dispatched, teams of all races to first tackle the Lanayru region, then the plain, and work their way across Hyrule from there. Link had volunteered to lead the first, and as much as everyone denied him, it was useless. He was who he was.

And while she was still blessed by the goddess, her power had dimmed. She felt it lurking under her skin, a forge unlit— perhaps only needing a spark to activate it, but she would not rush to try. She would go with him to help, learning how to fight with traditional weapons. As she packed the scimitar Urbosa had gifted her, it would be a perfect start.

However, not before their few weeks of rest first, as Zelda requested.

As they said their goodbyes, Urbosa hugged her, and she allowed herself to linger in her embrace for longer than the others, before pulling her back to say, “Enjoy your well-deserved time with your knight.” She winked, and Zelda fought a blush. “See you in a month.”

The words tethered them all together as Zelda nodded to Urbosa, agreeing to both her and her new duties. The newly formed council consisting of those in the room had all agreed to return on the 7th of each month, to track progress of the monster control plans, manage trade discussions, and to address whatever aid was needed.

And as the sun was low, not yet meeting the horizon, Link and she exited the gates of the castle, together. This time they had a wagon hooked to Epona’s saddle, full of their things, as they had planned so long ago.

The two weeks that followed were full of tranquility and recovery.

They spent most of their time in Hateno, unpacking and planning— and showering together.

Each day that passed, Link’s scars melted further into his skin. Only truly noticeable when he’d come from outside without his shirt on, and the sun had baked him bronze, and the small white reminders stood stark against it. 

She was working on her own too, the hidden ones that tarnished her. How she’d close her eyes on a particularly foggy day or if she’d see deep boot prints along in the mud after a hard rain. How a momentary trance at a triggering sight would cause the clashing of steel to play in her ears or the cries of men to echo in her ribcage. But a warm hand would weave through her fingers, a solid presence reminding her they were on the other side.

Fledge and Ilya visited. He was no longer a squire but a knight, and Ilya, who had tended to the wounded horses on the plateau, tended to Fledge in the immediate aftermath. Zelda watched them, the way Fledge’s eyes lingered on Ilya’s with a desire she recognized in how Link looked upon her, or how Ilya’s ears tipped pink when she was near him— actions no longer casual. How the war had forged something new between them, a quiet treasure found within each other, built on a foundation of old friendship.

They had asked to be stationed near Hateno as well, together.

Then, about a month after the battle, they had all traveled to the castle to honor their fallen comrades.

Every person slain was accounted for and documented. While it was decreed that each year after on the anniversary of the battle, all regions would unite in a Day of Remembrance for those fallen. Each had their names carved upon a wall that still stood in Castle Town. She watched Link as he read, saw the flicker of recognition in his eyes as he passed the names of Pipit, Cawlin, and Strich, the hilt of the Master Sword ever present behind him.

After the ceremony, Zelda checked the records. She searched by ages 14-18, those with fawn hair color, and last with wood-stained, amber-flecked eyes. Looking for one name. And found it.

Talo of Goponga Village.

She traced her fingers over the grooves, the stone warm from the afternoon sun but not nearly payment enough for how short his life had been. She could only offer him her apologies and hope one day he heard them, and it mattered.

And when they returned to Hateno, Impa had left them alone, as promised. The quiet that settled over her seemed only to stir Link. There was only so much yard work or housework he could do.

That became more than clear as Zelda sat outside with an exceptionally steamy book she found from Link’s mother’s collection, or at least she assumed— about a young hero and a princess cloaked in dusk and how they were an unlikely duo tasked to save Hyrule. As Zelda flipped a page to a scene where the princess and hero have to share a bed at the inn, a motion pulled her from the page.

Zelda tried not to peer over the folds of her book, but she couldn’t ignore his incessant pacing. He’d chopped enough wood for a small village and was now fumbling with planks for a bed he didn’t know how to build. Then his gaze snagged on the Master Sword, sheathed by the front door. It was a look she knew well, a longing so profound it seemed to pull at him physically. His hands, made for that hilt, were adrift.

So, in the final week of their downtime, she suggested they travel, like old times. The smile that bloomed upon his face made him look youthful in ways she’d rarely seen upon him.

Link brought her to Lurelin Village, a two-day ride from Hateno through the southern mountains. As they descended into the fishing settlement nearby the cape, a quiet gratitude settled in her. Here, families smiled with their whole bodies. Children knew steel only as eating utensils, and the air was thick with the smell of campfire smoke and fresh fish, not blood and ruin.

This was what they had fought for.

They walked the beach to the tip of the cape. Finding the island in the distance, they promised each other to explore one day, to satiate their shared curiosity. And Zelda let herself be small and solitary as the afternoon sun warmed her back, and she let herself mix with the breeze. The sea thickened and tangled the strands of her hair as the wind blew it around her.

Seashells tumbled in the surf, rolled from the water’s churn only to be dragged back again. An endless, violent cycle. Yet, she saw how the salt and sand had polished them from discarded husks into the earth’s organic trinkets. She dipped her toes into that joining, letting the gritty sand scour her skin.

Let it polish me, too, she thought.

The next morning, Link suggested a hike.

Which was very, very loose to what he actually meant.

It was a climb.

Muscles that hadn’t existed were stretched and pulled, a reminder that while the Goddess blessed her with divine health, her body still had limits. Link, of course, breathlessly strolled up the mountain without breaking a sweat. It threw her back to the beginning of their journey— when he was quiet and reflective, a perfect, infuriating machine.

When she’d gasped for a rest, he’d just shaken his head, jaw tight. “Have to make the campsite.” That single-mindedness, a virtue on the battlefield, felt like pure cruelty now. She let herself imagine tripping him.

And here they sat upon the mountain’s ridge, six weeks since the battle. Ready to rest for the night.

The sun had left an extraordinary array of colors that had her only slightly forgiving Link for the intense workout, as the shadow of the mountain cast them into darkness only a few moments later, and the stars started to blink into their existence.

“As much as I want to throttle you off this mountain for rushing us up here, why don’t we just scale to the top tonight? Wouldn’t it be a nicer view at the peak?” she asked him as she set down her bag.

Link huffed a laugh as he pounded a stake into the ground, setting up their tent for the night. “The sun rises on the other side. I figured this way we won’t be baking in our tent first thing in the morning.”
